title: Capital Without Usury
subtitle: Jewish, Christian, and Islamic Finance from Scripture to Non-Extractive Capital

paragraphs: Somewhere in the world today — at a kitchen table, in a bank's glass office, on a phone screen held in one hand on a bus — a person is agreeing to pay for money. The paper in front of her, or the scroll of it, runs to dozens of pages, and she has been taught by her whole civilization to look for one thing in it above all: the rate. If the number is low, the deal is good; if it is high, the deal is bad; if it is very high, someone may eventually use the word predatory, which is very nearly the last moral word modern finance keeps in stock for a loan. Every other question the document could raise — what happens to her in a bad year, who decided that her need should carry a price, why the lender's money is entitled to grow while her wages are not — has no box on the form. She signs where the flag says sign. So do we all.

It was not always like this, and that is the first thing this book has to say. For the greater part of recorded time, in most of the civilizations that kept records, the deal she just signed would have been examined before it was priced, and examined by professionals. Three great religious traditions, Judaism, Christianity, and Islam, built entire departments of law around transactions like hers: courts that could order the increase given back, scholars who classified such contracts clause by clause, preachers who thundered about them by name, and institutions, some still running, designed to make them unnecessary. The machinery was not ornamental. Confessors' manuals carried chapters on lending the way tax codes carry schedules; charitable pawn banks were chartered because sermons demanded them; partnership deeds were drafted, in more than one legal language, so that the money's conduct could be audited against scripture. Two further traditions, in India and across the Buddhist world, built their own distinct machinery beside the Abrahamic three. The subject of all that law had a name. In English it is usury, and if the word now sounds antique, like a disease no one catches anymore, that is not because the thing it named went away. The thing it named became normal. What went away was the surrounding architecture of questions — a moral architecture of finance, drawn with a jurist's precision and maintained for millennia, which the modern world dismantled without ever quite refuting. This book is about that architecture: what it was, why five traditions thought it worth building, how it was lost, and what it would mean — concretely, contractually, arithmetically — to build it again.

sections.title: The Wrong Starting Point
paragraphs: Begin with the word itself, because the modern meaning is a trap. Ask almost anyone today what usury is and you will hear something like: charging too much interest. The definition feels self-evident, and it silently decides everything downstream of it. If usury is an excessive rate, then the moral question about lending is a pricing question (where to draw the line), and the answer will always be a number, argued about the way speed limits are argued about, set by statute, revised by lobbying, different in every jurisdiction and every decade. Some rate is fair; some rate is too much; the argument is over which. Modern consumer law has become expert at this, and within its limits the expertise is real: disclosure rules can force a lender to compress his whole product into one comparable number, and comparison is a genuine protection. It is also, on the older view, the smallest of the protections — a civilization checking the price tag on a transaction whose nature it has stopped examining.

The traditions this book reads did not start with the price. Their question was not how much a loan may charge but what kind of thing a loan is, and behind that a question so basic it tends to embarrass the people who ask it: what is money for? A rate, after all, is just a price, and a price is the answer to a question you have already finished asking — price of what, for whose use, surrendered by whom, under what constraint. The old law of usury lived entirely in those prior questions. It asked what was really being sold when a lender charged for a loan: the money's use, the time, the risk, the borrower's lack of alternatives. And it was prepared to rule, and for a very long time did rule, that some of those things must not be sold at any price, because they were never the seller's to begin with.

That is why the interest rate is the wrong place to start, and why this book will spend so little time on the question that dominates modern discussion of credit. A rate measures the size of a claim; it says nothing about the claim's nature. Two loans at the same twelve percent can be different moral objects entirely — one a priced service between parties who could each have walked away, the other a slow transfer of a family's future to the one party who could afford to wait. The number on the page is identical; everything that matters is elsewhere. It is in who carries the loss if the venture fails, in what the lender truly put at hazard, in what the borrower could and could not refuse, in what the money was doing to the two of them across the time it was owed. The traditions kept their eyes on the elsewhere. Usury, as they used the word, named a relationship before it named a number — a particular way one person's money can come to sit on another person's life — and a relationship cannot be audited with a percentage.

The borrower is the reason the stakes are what they are, and it is worth being plain about her early, because she will be present on nearly every page. Across most of the written record, lending's typical object was survival — grain until harvest, rent until wages, medicine until strength — sought by someone whose alternatives had already run out. A contract signed on those terms is voluntary only in the thinnest sense of the word. The traditions understood this without embarrassment, wrote their lending law as if the desperate borrower were the normal case, and treated the moment of her need as something close to sacred ground: the one moment when another person's money should arrive as help or not at all. Whatever else separates Torah, Gospel, and Qur'an — and plenty does — they agree with one voice here. Need is not a market.

sections.title: One Suspicion, Three Languages
paragraphs: The traditions arrive at lending from different histories, in different languages, with different pictures of God. Yet each of them, independently, developed a version of the same suspicion: that there is something wrong — not imprudent, wrong — with money that multiplies simply because it is owed. The Hebrew Bible forbids the Israelite to take increase from a poor brother's loan and builds release and restoration into the calendar itself. The Christian scriptures push mercy past the boundaries of kin and prudence, toward lending that expects nothing back, and the Church that read them spent well over a millennium refining a law of just exchange whose center held that a loan, as such, earns nothing. The Qur'an declares trade lawful and riba forbidden, warning those who persist of war from God — language the scripture does not use lightly — and fourteen centuries of jurisprudence have been spent drawing the boundary that verse announced. Three bodies of scripture, three legal civilizations, one conviction reached three times: money lent must come back the same sum it went out; gain must be earned by something real. It must come from somewhere.

Each tradition then built law, and the law is where this book lives, because law is where conviction is forced to become specific. It is one thing to preach against exploiting the poor; every civilization has managed that. It is another to decide whether the lender may keep a grateful borrower's small present, or lodge in the borrower's guesthouse, or buy his wheat at a price fixed before the harvest is in; whether a partnership whose money can lose nothing is a partnership at all, or something else in a partnership's paperwork; whether rent, which everyone permitted, differs in principle from interest, which almost no one did — and if so, where the difference bites. The rabbis of the Talmud, the canonists and scholastic theologians of Latin Christendom, and the jurists of the fiqh schools each spent centuries on precisely such cases, and their three case-literatures, enormous, technical, and for centuries mutually unread, kept arriving at one another's answers. Reading them together, mechanism by mechanism, you watch three legal systems that could not consult each other converge on the same handful of distinctions, the way three bridge-builders on three rivers converge on the arch. The recurring shape is telling you something about the load.

That convergence is the deepest reason Judaism, Christianity, and Islam must be read together rather than in three polite, separate volumes. Read alone, each tradition's usury law looks like an idiosyncrasy — a covenantal quirk, a scholastic obsession, a scriptural severity — and reading alone is how the old polemics got their footing, each tradition free to imagine that its neighbor's practice was the real scandal. Read together, the three look like independent witnesses to one hazard, and their testimony can be cross-examined the way witnesses' testimony always should be. Their agreements identify what the hazard is. Their disagreements, just as instructive, mark the places where a genuine design choice exists and honest law can go more than one way. And the reader gains a second sight no single tradition can supply: whatever blind spot each system carried, the other two tend to see it, name it, and solve it, which will matter enormously in this book's final chapters, when the three toolkits are laid out on one bench.

Two other traditions join the book at its turning points, as guests rather than exhibits, because each answers the same question from ground the Abrahamic three do not occupy. Hindu Dharmaśāstra never prohibited interest; it regulated increase: rates scaled to the venture's peril, ceilings past which no debt may grow. It stands, therefore, as the great structural alternative: the measure, where the others built a wall. Buddhism enters from the opposite side, beginning not with commerce but with renunciation, and its monastic history poses the question every financial institution in this book must eventually face: what becomes of an ideal once it acquires a treasury? Neither guest is decoration. Each holds a piece of the design problem that the Abrahamic traditions handle differently or not at all, and the book pauses twice, once for each, to learn it.

sections.title: The Braid, Not the Survey
paragraphs: A book about three traditions usually means three books stapled together: the Jewish material, then the Christian, then the Islamic, each in its own chronology, meeting only in a comparative afterword. That design was rejected here on the day this book was conceived, for a simple reason: it keeps the traditions in the very silos this subject needs them out of. The questions that matter — what makes a loan a loan, who may profit from danger, when a partnership is honest, what may be charged for lateness — cut across all three literatures, and any one tradition's answer sharpens the moment it is set beside the other two. So this book is organized by financial mechanism, not by religion. Each chapter takes up an instrument, and the traditions meet inside it. When the subject is the naked loan, you will read the rabbis on ribbit, the scholastics on the mutuum, and the jurists on qard in the same sitting; when the subject is partnership, the iska, the societas, and the mudarabah share one chapter because they are, structurally, one idea answering to three names. The braid is the book.

The braid imposes a discipline that a survey never has to face, and the reader is entitled to hear it stated as a promise. Each tradition is presented from within — as its own authorities frame it, in its own categories, with its living disputes marked as disputes — before it is compared with anything. No tradition is the trunk from which the others branch; no tradition plays the foil; no tradition is here to serve as the cautionary tale in someone else's sermon. Halakha and fiqh are functioning legal systems with contemporary practitioners — there are rabbinic courts ruling on investment contracts and shariah boards reviewing them this week — and they are written about here in the present tense they deserve. Where a tradition quarrels with itself, and all of them do, vigorously and on the record, the quarrel is reported rather than adjudicated. A reader determined to discover which of these traditions the book privately considers correct should prepare for disappointment.

Read this way, the traditions disclose something that reading them as mere prohibition always hides: they were protecting something, and they knew what it was. A prohibition, examined closely, is a drawing in negative space; trace its edges and you find the outline of what it was built around. The lending law of all three traditions traces the same shape. A person, embedded in a community, moving through time, who must be able to survive a bad year without becoming someone's revenue. An exchange whose terms both sides can actually see. A venture whose gains and losses land on the people who truly shared it. Wealth that moves toward need without being owed anything back. The prohibitions were the fence; that fourfold figure — the person, the visible bargain, the shared fate, the unpriced mercy — was the garden. From prohibition to design is this book's whole trajectory in a phrase: its first movements recover, from the fence-building, what the traditions were protecting; its last movements take the protected thing seriously as a specification and ask what financial architecture would protect it now.

sections.title: Old Doctrine, Modern Money
paragraphs: It may seem a long way from Deuteronomy to a venture term sheet, and one ambition of this book is to convince you that it is a shorter walk than it looks. The instruments answer to new names (liquidation preference, cumulative dividend, guaranteed return, first-loss tranche), but the moves are old, and the traditions' lawyers, who spent centuries auditing contracts for increase traveling under an assumed name, would find today's documents strenuous but not strange. A preferred share that must be paid its fixed percentage before any partner sees a coin; a certificate that promises repayment at face value no matter what befalls the asset behind it; a penalty schedule that out-earns the loan it claims to discipline: the medieval casuists had files on all of these. They simply filed them under the older, franker headings. Much of this book's second half consists of walking modern financial furniture past three old legal systems and writing down what they notice. Nor is the exercise a museum tour, because nearly everyone alive is inside at least one of these contracts — a mortgage, a pension, a policy, a loan — and usually on the borrowing side of the paper.

Their most unsettling notice concerns not any single instrument but the direction of drift. Every tradition in this book has watched its own safeguards bend back toward the thing they forbade — this is one of the book's central findings, and it is as much confession as accusation: the permitted workaround that becomes the product, the exception that grows until it is the rule, the old words kept on as labels for instruments that rebuild, payment by payment, what the words once forbade. The book gives the modern chapters of that story their full weight — the long quiet that settled over the usury question in Christian Europe, the workaround become industry standard in more than one tradition, the new secular moralities of finance that inherit the old ambitions and not the old tests. It tells those stories from inside each tradition, in the voices of each tradition's own critics, who are invariably the sharpest available. And the point of the drift story is not that the traditions failed. It is that they kept noticing — that each maintained, sometimes for centuries at a stretch, an internal audit honest enough to tell its ideals from its instruments. That capacity for self-suspicion turns out to be as valuable an inheritance as any doctrine.

Beneath all of it, waiting for the mathematics that could finally state it, lies the question this book regards as the traditions' deepest and least understood — the missing mathematical question of finance. Who survives the path over time? Modern finance is built, to a degree that surprises people meeting the fact for the first time, on averages: the expected return, the mean outcome, the performance of the portfolio as a whole. But nobody lives in an average. A family, a founder, a fund, a village moves through its years in order, each loss resetting the next year's starting point, and somewhere below them all there is a floor — call it ruin — where the story simply stops. An arrangement can be attractive on average and lethal along the path; some of the most respectable structures in finance are exactly that, and the obligation that falls due regardless of the harvest is the oldest of them. The traditions could not write the equations. But look at what they built — the release valves, the ceilings, the harvest-sharing, the pools — and you keep finding machinery whose effect is to stop one bad year from becoming an ending. Where the modern mind optimized the average, the traditions guarded the path. A late chapter will do the arithmetic properly and show that this is not a metaphor: solidarity has a mathematics, the mathematics comes down on the traditions' side, and a young science — ergodicity economics — has lately begun writing proofs underneath their oldest instincts. Usury law, read at this depth, was survival engineering, built long before the tools existed to check its work.

sections.title: How This Book Moves
paragraphs: The book moves in six long strides — Scripture, law, institutions, evasion, mathematics, design. It may help to walk the route once before setting out.

It opens by clearing the ground. Part I frames the question the whole tradition asks — what is money allowed to do? — locates lending where the traditions located it, between neighbors rather than between abstractions, and assembles the small cast of contract forms, from loan to gift to pool, whose boundaries the rest of the book will patrol. Part II goes to the sources of the fire: the Hebrew Bible's covenant economy, the New Testament's radicalization of mercy, the Qur'an's war against riba, each read on its own terms and in its own order, for what it actually says. Part III turns scripture into legal grammar: what makes a loan a loan, why the traditions chased hidden benefit into the smallest corners of social life, how price fraud and overreaching were policed, and what danger genuinely licenses. There the first guest interrupts, and Dharmaśāstra's regulated increase asks whether a wall was ever necessary at all.

Parts IV and V are the constructive heart of the old world. Partnership — societas, iska, mudarabah, the merchant's commenda — was the traditions' great escape from usury, the form in which capital could earn by honestly sharing a venture's fate, and the book lingers there on questions that will sound startlingly contemporary: how capital and labor divide a venture's gains, who absorbs its losses, why profit may come only from profit. Then come the mercy institutions — the gemach, the qard hasan, the Monti di Pietà, the great engines of alms — which together answer a question modern finance has stopped asking: what credit becomes when it is designed for the borrower's survival rather than the lender's return. The second guest arrives at that part's close, and Buddhist renunciation puts its unsettling question to every institution in the book.

Part VI descends into the engine room: the centuries-long technical debates — actual loss, forgone profit, illiquidity, penalty — in which some of the finest legal minds of Christendom argued over which compensations a lender may take without selling what was never his, while their Jewish and Muslim counterparts ran the same inquiries in their own idioms; the part closes with deception, uncertainty, and the anatomy of consent. If you want to know where this book's analytical machinery was forged, it was there. Part VII tours the instruments those debates produced and constrained — sale-based finance, leases, certificates, insurance and its mutual-aid ancestors, endowments and asset locks — and pauses, toward its close, for the chapter on ergodicity and the mathematics of mutual aid, where the book's quantitative thread is finally tied. Part VIII is the tragedy, told without nostalgia: interest secularized, the question unlearned, and each tradition's modern reckoning — the heter iska at industrial scale, Islamic finance's benchmark problem, Catholic social teaching's uneasy silence, and the market's replacement moralities of ESG and impact.

Then the book stops looking backward. Part IX rebuilds the tradition as arithmetic: a ledger that makes every euro of return say what it is for, risk priced without being worshiped, waterfalls and preferences read as the geometry they are, invisible labor made visible, true surplus told apart from the merely available, and the whole assembled into a non-extractive return formula — the traditions' tests restated as something a spreadsheet can check. Part X builds with it: a fund, a contract library, an analyzer, an accounting, and, because every tradition in this book testifies that sincerity alone keeps no institution honest, a closing chapter on the temptations of religious finance and the governance that guards against drift. A conclusion gathers what the traditions teach. Six appendices (glossary, timeline, contract typology, metrics, worked waterfalls, and a reading guide) turn the book from an argument into a reference.

Different readers will want different doors. The practitioner impatient for the design work can go straight to the last two parts and follow the citations backward; the reader who came for history can settle into the first eight and treat the arithmetic as a promised destination; the skeptic who suspects that religious finance is a contradiction in terms is asked only to stay through the partnership and mercy chapters before deciding. The book was built, though, to be walked in order. Its later chapters lean on its earlier distinctions the way upper floors lean on the ones below, and the reader who arrives at the modern material with the old grammar in hand will hear things in a term sheet that cannot otherwise be heard.

A word, finally, on how it is written. This is a work of history and analysis, not of devotion, and it assumes no faith in the reader — only a willingness to entertain the possibility that five civilizations, over spans measured in millennia, kept concluding there was something here worth a jurist's whole career. The technical terms of four legal languages appear because precision requires them; each is explained on arrival and cataloged in the glossary at the back. Scripture and law are quoted sparingly, in named standard renderings, and the book prefers wherever possible to show how a text was read and used by the people whose law it became. And one rule of respect holds throughout: every tradition speaks here through its own authorities, including its own critics, and never through its rivals' caricatures.

Why, then, does usury still matter? Not because the word deserves reviving for its own sake, and not because the old world was gentle — it was not, and nothing here will pretend it was. Usury still matters because the thing the traditions built their law around has not changed. Need still borrows; money still multiplies while it is owed; and between those two facts, now as ever, ordinary lives are won and lost. Every contract that moves capital settles the old questions somewhere in its clauses — puts a price on someone's need or declines to, hands the bad year to somebody, lets the money share the venture's weather or exempts it — whether or not anyone involved can hear it happening. The traditions heard. They asked their questions out loud, for millennia, in public, with penalties, and they left behind not a nostalgia but a toolkit: definitions, tests, instruments, institutions, and a standard of proof for every coin that claims to have been earned. The wager of this book is that the toolkit still works — that money's longest conversation is not an heirloom but an unfinished project, waiting for builders. The person on the bus, signing where the flag says sign, is owed more questions than the rate. What follows is the long history of the people who asked them, and the beginning of asking them again.

chapters.title: Sterile Gain and Living Exchange
chapters.label: Chapter 1

paragraphs: In the year we call 594 BC, an Athenian merchant and poet named Solon was made sole archon, with extraordinary powers, by a city sliding toward civil war. The trouble was debt. Attica's small farmers had borrowed from their richer neighbors against the only security they had, which was themselves. Stone markers called horoi stood planted in fields all over the countryside, each one announcing that the land under it was encumbered, and the men who worked those fields — the hektemoroi, "sixth-parters," whose name says they owed a sixth of their harvest, though scholars still argue over the arithmetic — had discovered what every indebted farmer in history discovers eventually: a bad year does not cancel a fixed obligation. It compounds it. When the crop failed, the farmer borrowed against next year. When next year failed too, the creditor took what the law allowed, and the law allowed the man. Athenians were being seized for debt, sold as slaves, some of them abroad. This was not an invading army doing it; it was neighbors, holding paper — or rather holding stones — against neighbors.

Solon's remedy, enacted in his single extraordinary year, was called the seisachtheia, the "shaking-off of burdens." He canceled the debts, pulled up the stones, banned all future lending on the security of the person, and set about recovering Athenians who had been sold overseas. We know all this partly because the constitutional history that circulated under Aristotle's name — the Athenaion Politeia, written by Aristotle or his school — quotes the poem Solon wrote afterward in his own defense, and it is one of the most remarkable documents in the history of finance: a politician's memoir, in verse, about a debt jubilee. Let the black Earth be my witness, he says — the mighty mother of the Olympian gods, from whom I pulled up the horoi planted everywhere; she was enslaved before, and now she is free. He brought home men who had been sold abroad, "one justly, another not," men who had wandered so long they no longer spoke Attic Greek; and those enslaved on their own soil, trembling before their masters, he set free.

Here is the detail worth holding onto. There were no coins in this story. The first true coins had been struck only a generation or so earlier and a sea away, in Lydia — bean-shaped lumps of electrum, a natural gold-silver alloy washed down the river Pactolus at Sardis; Herodotus says the Lydians were the first people we know of to strike gold and silver coin — and Athens would not mint its own until around 560 BC, decades after Solon laid down his office. The debts that nearly wrecked Athens were counted in grain, oil, and weighed silver. Interest-bearing loans, for their part, had been running in Mesopotamia for the better part of two thousand years before anyone owned a drachma; the loan is older than the coin. Money's most dangerous power — the power to bind a future person to a past promise, and to grow while it waits — needed no mint, only a harvest, a ledger, and a bad year.

So the oldest debt crisis on record in the Western tradition arrives before money, in our narrow metallic sense, even exists, and the first great financial reformer answers it not with a rate cap but with a boundary: there are things a loan will no longer be allowed to reach. Solon did not regulate the price of credit; he redefined its jurisdiction. That move — asking not how much money may charge but what money is allowed to do — is the founding question of this book, and it is the question Judaism, Christianity, and Islam would each, in their own vocabulary and for their own reasons, spend the better part of three thousand years answering.

sections.title: The Fourth Function
paragraphs: Every economics textbook, more or less since textbooks began, tells you that money does three jobs. It is a measure — a common yardstick that lets you compare a goat, a haircut, and an hour of legal advice on a single scale. It is a medium — the thing you accept not because you want it but because everyone else will accept it in turn, sparing the shoemaker the chore of finding a hungry farmer who happens to need shoes. And it is a store — a way of parking today's surplus for tomorrow's need, wealth in a form that does not rot, rust, or need feeding.

The analysis is ancient, and its most influential early statement belongs to Aristotle. In the fifth book of the Nicomachean Ethics he works out how a city of specialists — builder, shoemaker, doctor — manages to trade unlike things fairly, and his answer is that money makes them commensurable: everything can be measured against one thing, and that one thing, he notes, exists by agreement rather than by nature. The Greek word for currency, nomisma, comes from nomos, law or convention, and Aristotle leans on the pun with evident satisfaction: money is called what it is called because it is not natural but conventional, ours to alter or demonetize as we please. A page later he adds the store-of-value point — money is a kind of pledge for the future, a guarantee that if we do not need a thing now, we can have it when we do. Measure, medium, store: the whole textbook triad, in place before Euclid.

But the textbook list has a fourth item, usually left off because it makes the others look less innocent. Money is also a claim. Every unit of it is a kind of standing invitation the rest of society has not yet honored: hold a coin and you hold everyone else's obligation, diffuse and anonymous, to hand over real goods on demand. In that diffuse form the claim is harmless enough — nobody in particular owes you the loaf your coin will buy. The moral temperature changes when the claim acquires a name and an address. Lend the coin, and the abstraction condenses into a relationship: now a particular person owes you, and the ledger that records it is no longer a note about things but a note about him. Measure, medium, and store are jobs money does with the world. Claim is the job money does with people, and it is the one function of the four that can wear a face.

The ancients, who lived closer to their creditors than most of us do, saw this with painful clarity. The book of Proverbs — here and throughout, biblical quotations follow the New Revised Standard Version — needs eight words for the sociology of the whole thing: "the borrower is the slave of the lender." In Solon's Attica that was no figure of speech, and the horoi in the fields were its paperwork. A measure measures whether you love it or not, a medium circulates indifferently, a store simply sits; but a claim ranks two people, one above the other, for as long as it stands. Of the four, the claim is the only function with a politics.

Notice, too, an oddity in the store-of-value function that the ancients found genuinely strange and we have stopped noticing. Real wealth decays. Grain must be eaten within a few years, cloth wears, a herd must be tended and fed through every winter it survives, and even a house demands its endless small tribute of repair. To hold wealth in the world is to fight rot, and mostly lose slowly. Money alone is exempt. The silver in the strongbox neither eats nor sickens, and — once lent — it does something no barn full of anything has ever done: it grows by itself, on schedule, in the dark. A shepherd's flock might double in three years of good luck and hard labor. A moneylender's silver at the customary rates would double in five with neither. Every farmer who ever mortgaged a field understood the asymmetry in his bones: he had borrowed something immortal and was repaying it with the sweat of something mortal. Interest is the only harvest that ripens in every weather.

That asymmetry is where the unease begins — the feeling, older than any of the three traditions this book braids together, that when money starts behaving like livestock, something in the order of things has quietly gone wrong.

sections.title: The Offspring of Metal
paragraphs: You can read the unease in the words themselves, because the ancient world, with a candor later ages abandoned, named interest after baby animals.

In Sumer, where the earliest interest-bearing loans on record were written into clay some four and a half thousand years ago, the word for interest was mash — the same word that means "goat kid." In Greek it was tokos, "offspring," the ordinary word for what is brought forth at a birth. In Latin it was fenus, which carries the fe- root of fecundity and fetus, the syllable of breeding. The economic historian Michael Hudson, who traced this barnyard vocabulary across three millennia in a study aptly subtitled "Máš, tokos and fænus as metaphors for interest accruals," points out what the metaphor originally made plain: a herd genuinely does throw off kids and calves in season, and a lender's claim was imagined to breed the same way — a newborn increment arriving with each new moon. The image was not chosen by critics of lending. It was the lenders' own accounting language, cheerful as a stock ledger. Only later did philosophers turn the metaphor around and ask the obvious question sleeping inside it: a she-goat is alive; in what sense, exactly, does a shekel give birth?

The practice the words described was already old, regular, and legally domesticated long before anyone thought to philosophize about it. In Old Babylonia the customary rates held steady for centuries — one-fifth a year on silver, one-third on barley — and the Laws of Hammurabi, around 1750 BC, simply wrote the custom into stone as a ceiling. Mesopotamian kings coped with the wreckage the same way Solon later would, by periodic clean-slate decrees that canceled consumer debts and sent the pledged family members home. The pattern repeats so regularly across the ancient Near East that it amounts to a rhythm: credit expands, the countryside sinks, the ruler wipes the slate, and the cycle breathes in again. Nobody in Babylon argued that interest was unnatural. It was as natural as the flood, and you managed it the same way, by occasionally opening the gates.

The Greeks were the first to move the question from management to metaphysics, and the man who fixed its terms for the next two thousand years was a doctor's son from the north, born at Stagira in 384 BC, who spent twenty years in Plato's Academy, tutored the boy who became Alexander the Great, and settled at last in Athens to run his own school, the Lyceum, from about 335 BC. Aristotle came to money the way he came to everything — constitutions, tragedies, the parts of animals — by asking what it is for, and his answer sits in the first book of the Politics, in a stretch of argument (1256b to 1258b, in the scholars' numbering) that may be the most consequential few pages ever written about finance.

Aristotle distinguishes two arts that look alike and are not. The first he treats as part of oikonomia — household management, the ancestor of our word "economics" — and its business is provisioning: getting the goods a household or a city actually needs to live well. Acquisition of this kind has a built-in limit, because needs have a limit; the pantry can only hold so much, and a family can only eat so much. The second art he calls chrematistike — wealth-getting as an occupation in itself — and in its suspect form its business is not provisioning but accumulation: buying in order to sell, holding in order to gain, treating the household's tool as the household's purpose. This second art, he observes, has no natural stopping point at all. There is a quantity of grain that means "enough grain." There is no quantity of money that means "enough money," because money, being merely the measure of everything else, sets no measure for itself. A man provisioning a household knows when he is done. A man accumulating money is never done, and Aristotle's diagnosis is that such a man has mistaken the instrument of living for living itself — has turned all his arts, medicine and soldiering and estate management alike, into ways of making coin, as though that were the end and everything else existed for its sake.

Then, near the stretch's close (1258b), comes the verdict that echoed for millennia. Trade for gain already sits low in Aristotle's ranking, an exchange in which men profit from one another rather than from nature. But one practice sits at the very bottom. Usury — the petty weighing-out of small coin at interest — is hated most reasonably of all, he says, because here the gain comes from money itself rather than from the thing money was invented to serve. Money came into being for exchange; interest makes the coin itself the parent of more coin. And here he reaches for the old barnyard word and turns it into an argument: this is why interest is called tokos, offspring, for the young resemble their parents, and interest is money born of money. Of all the ways of getting wealth, he concludes, this one is the most contrary to nature. The pun had been sitting in the language for centuries, as innocent as a farmer's ledger. Aristotle picked it up and made it a charge sheet: the lender is running a stud farm for an animal that is not alive.

It is worth being precise about what the argument does and does not claim, because the whole coming tradition depends on the distinction. Aristotle is not saying that surplus is wicked. The farmer's field yields more than was sown; the potter's clay leaves the wheel worth more than it arrived; even the merchant, moving grain from where it is cheap to where it is dear, can be doing the city a service. All of that is increase with a source: nature grows, labor transforms, exchange serves need. His objection lands on one precise spot — increase without a source, gain that purports to spring from the sterile instrument itself, from bare time and bare possession. The distinction between the household's economy and the money-getter's art is really a distinction between wealth that feeds life and wealth that merely feeds. And though Aristotle wrote as a pagan philosopher with no covenant, no revelation, and no particular tenderness for the poor, he had built the exact conceptual shelf on which three revealed religions would later find their own convictions already waiting, labeled in Greek.

His Roman readers kept the shelf stocked. Cato the Elder, that flint of republican rectitude, opens his farming manual by noting that the ancestors' laws condemned the thief to repay double, and the usurer fourfold — from which, he adds dryly, you may judge how much worse a citizen they thought the moneylender. Cicero preserves the same Cato in conversation, being asked what was the most profitable part of estate management and answering, with the patience of a man ranking the obvious, good grazing; then adequate grazing; then poor grazing; then plowing. And when the questioner, working down the list, finally asked "What about money-lending?", Cato answered: "What about murder?" The quip is less about lending than about category — the suggestion that somewhere between the pasture and the loan book, a man stops farming and starts feeding on his neighbors.

sections.title: Not a Matter of Percentages
paragraphs: To modern ears, "usury" means charging too much — an interest rate with the decency dial turned past ten. That meaning is real, but it is a late arrival, and if you carry it backward into the old texts you will misread every one of them. For roughly two thousand years, in the Latin West and its Greek and Semitic neighborhoods alike, usury did not name an amount. It named an act.

The Latin tells you plainly. Usura is just "use" with a suffix: a payment taken for the use of money. The canon lawyers who systematized the Church's teaching — Gratian's great twelfth-century compilation is the landmark — defined the sin with arithmetic bluntness: to lend and to expect back anything beyond the principal, anything at all, is usury. Not anything excessive; anything. One denarius over, on a loan of a hundred, fell under the same name as fifty. The rabbis drew the line at the same place for loans inside the covenant community, and the Qur'an, in the verse this book will circle back to many times, tells believers who repent of riba that they are entitled to their principal — no more. Three legal cultures, one geometry: the loan repays its own amount exactly, and the first coin past that boundary changes the transaction's species.

Modern usage inverted this. When the English Parliament, in 1545, passed "An Acte agaynst Usurye" that in fact legalized interest up to ten percent, the word began its long slide toward meaning only the forbidden remainder — the excess above whatever a legislature currently blesses. That slide matters to this book because it silently replaced a question of kind with a question of degree. Under the old definition, the moralist asks: what sort of transaction is this, and may it yield gain at all? Under the new one, the regulator asks: is the price fair? Both are real questions. But they are different questions, and the traditions this book reads were asking the first one. When a medieval rabbi, a scholastic theologian, and a Basra jurist condemned usury, none of them was running a price check. They were running a classification: this gain has a source, that gain has none; this contract shares the world's risk, that contract has arranged to be immune to it.

Which brings us to the pair of terms in this chapter's title. Sterile gain is the increase Aristotle diagnosed: a return that claims to grow out of money's bare existence — out of possession plus a calendar — while the lender contributes no labor, adds no thing, and stands exposed to none of the venture's weather. Living exchange is everything on the other side of the line: the sale that moves a real good to the person who needs it, the hire that pays for a tool's genuine use, the partnership whose return is carved from a harvest that actually came in, the gift that asks nothing back. The traditions never doubted that money could lawfully pass through all of those and come home larger. The farmer sells at profit; the shipowner charges freight; the partner shares gain; scripture and canon and fiqh bless every one of them, in terms we will spend chapters unpacking. What they refused to bless was the increment with no parent but the coin itself — the gain that would have accrued identically whether the borrower's venture flowered or drowned, because it fed not on the venture but on the obligation.

Put that way, the old doctrine stops looking like squeamishness about numbers and starts looking like an audit rule. Ask of any increment: where was this born? If the answer runs through soil, sweat, skill, cargo, or shared hazard, the traditions could find a home for it. If the answer is "the loan itself" — if the money claims to have bred — every one of them reached, independently, for the same verdict Aristotle reached, and several of them reached it without ever having read him. Sterility, in this vocabulary, is not an insult to money but a job description. A measure is supposed to be barren, the way a yardstick is supposed to stay thirty-six inches long; a ruler that grew while you measured with it would not be a marvel but a fraud. The scandal of usury, for every tradition in this book, was precisely that it asked the yardstick to calve.

sections.title: Tool, Master, and the Space Between
paragraphs: Beneath the classification runs the first moral distinction of the whole subject, and it can be said in a sentence: money is a tool, and the trouble begins when the tool starts giving the orders. Aristotle's word for the disorder was chrematistics — the condition of a man, or a city, in which the means of exchange has quietly promoted itself to the purpose of existence, so that fields are farmed, ships sailed, and skills practiced no longer for what they yield in life but for what they yield in coin. The tool is not wicked; a hammer is not wicked. The question is who is holding whom. And the reason the usurer became the emblem of the inversion — rather than the miser, who merely hoards, or the glutton, who merely spends — is that lending at interest is the one arrangement in which the tool appears to work by itself. Every other way of turning money into more money at least routes the increase through the world: a cargo, a workshop, a field. The interest-bearing loan routes it through a person, which makes the borrower the plant and the machinery of the lender's increase.

Watch what the different motions of money do to the space between two people, because everything the traditions later built assumes you can see it. A sale, honestly struck, is the most self-liquidating of human transactions: goods pass one way, price passes the other, and the parties walk off free of each other, equals at the start and equals at the end. A gift binds — anthropologists have filled libraries with the webs of obligation and return that gifts spin — but it binds laterally, in a fabric of reciprocity where this year's giver expects to be some year's receiver. The loan is the odd one. It stretches a transaction across time, which no sale does, and for the whole of that stretch it holds the two parties in ranked positions, which no honest sale does either: one waits, the other owes. Proverbs' eight words sit at the bottom of this like a survey stake. Add interest, and the rank acquires a motor — the longer the inferior position lasts, the more it costs, so that time itself, which falls on both parties alike as rain does, becomes revenue for one of them and erosion for the other.

Whether that arrangement is tolerable depends almost entirely on who is borrowing, and why — and here the register must be plain, because for most of recorded history the typical borrower was not a merchant financing cargo but a family financing survival. A subsistence loan is negotiated between a man who can wait and a man who cannot, and every term in it prices that difference. Dependency, in such lending, is the collateral. The farmer who pledges the field eats this winter by mortgaging every winter after, and when the debt finally takes the field, or the daughter, the ledger records a voluntary contract, freely signed. The ancient world knew exactly what these contracts were worth as descriptions of freedom. That is why its oldest financial documents are shadowed by its oldest financial institutions — the Mesopotamian clean slate, the Solonic shaking-off — and why the Hebrew word for interest is not a number but an injury.

Neshekh, the Torah's primary term, means "bite." Its companion terms tarbit and marbit mean "increase," and the rabbis' later word ribbit — cousin, across the Semitic languages, of the Arabic riba, "increase" — keeps the same root. The vocabulary is the doctrine in miniature: what the lender calls growth, the borrower wears as a wound. And it matters to the shape of this whole book that Israel's law was asking the relational question centuries before Aristotle asked the philosophical one. "If you lend money to my people, to the poor among you," says Exodus, "you shall not deal with them as a creditor; you shall not exact interest from them." What the verse forbids is not a rate but a stance — the creditor's stance toward a brother — and Leviticus gives the positive command in five words: "let them live with you." Lending inside the covenant is a form of upholding a neighbor whose ruin would be the community's own. Chapter 4 will walk this legislation properly. The point here is its axis: the Torah never asks what money is — it asks what the loan is doing to the two Israelites at either end of it.

Christianity inherited that axis and pushed it past the boundary of kin. In Luke's Gospel the instruction is to "lend, expecting nothing in return" — a sentence that treats the loan not as commerce to be regulated but as mercy to be perfected, with the enemy included in its reach. The early Church legislated accordingly where it could; the first ecumenical council, at Nicaea in 325, used its seventeenth canon to strip lending at interest from the clergy. For a thousand years the Christian case against usury ran on Scripture and the Fathers. Then, around 1260, the Flemish Dominican William of Moerbeke produced the first Latin translation of Aristotle's Politics — a book the Latin West had known only by rumor — and the theologians discovered, with the delight of people finding their family portrait in a stranger's attic, that the pagan had reasoned his way to their conclusion. Thomas Aquinas welded the two arguments together within a generation: usury is unjust, he argued in the Summa (II-II, q.78, a.1), because money is consumed in its use like wine, so that charging separately for the money and for its use is selling the same thing twice — selling, in his phrase, what does not exist. Aristotle's sterile coin had become a premise in a theology of justice. But the graft took because the stock was already living; the Church did not learn its unease from the Greek; it learned Greek for its unease.

Islam ran the same convergence in reverse, which is what makes the comparison so instructive. The Politics, almost alone among Aristotle's major works, was never translated into Arabic — the Muslim philosophers who handed Latin Europe so much of its Aristotle simply never had this text — so the Qur'an's war on riba, and the whole edifice of fiqh built on it, owes the philosopher precisely nothing. Yet the Qur'an's own framing turns on the same two categories this chapter has been drawing. Those who devour riba, it warns, will claim that trade and usury are alike; the verse — 2:275, here and throughout in M. A. S. Abdel Haleem's rendering — replies that "God has allowed trade and forbidden usury." In a single breath of scripture, living exchange is blessed and sterile gain refused. And when Muslim thinkers later supplied the philosophical commentary, they supplied it from their own resources: al-Ghazali, writing around the year 1100 in his Ihya Ulum al-Din, argued that the dinar and dirham were created as means and measures — stones with no use in themselves, made so that everything else could circulate and be valued — and that riba is precisely the perversion by which the measure is made an object of trade in its own right, deflected from the purpose for which God fashioned it. It is very nearly Aristotle's argument, arrived at without Aristotle, and it rests on the premise that money's purpose was assigned not by convention but by its Creator.

Three traditions, then, met one question in three vocabularies. The Torah asks it as covenant — whether my brother is still standing upright beside me when the contract closes, or has quietly acquired a master. The Gospel asks it as mercy, auditing what the loan gives against what it takes; the Qur'an, as justice in exchange, sorting the increase that is trade from the increase that devours. None of the three needed the Lyceum to reach its answer, and none of the three treats the question as economic in our narrow sense. What is being audited, in every case, is a relationship — the space between two people with money moving across it — and the shared conviction, older than all three scriptures in its Mesopotamian bones, is that certain motions of money poison that space no matter how politely the paperwork reads.

sections.title: The Birth of Moral Geometry
paragraphs: Once you ask the question that way, a program follows, and the traditions — being legal civilizations, with courts to run and contracts to enforce — followed it. If some motions of money are life-giving and others predatory, and if the interest-bearing loan cannot be told from the honest sale by the size of the numbers on it, then the moral work has to be done by form: by sorting every transfer of wealth into its species and giving each species its own law. What may a loan do that a sale may not? And why may a house earn rent, and a partner take a share, when a lender's hundred florins may earn nothing at all? The answers cannot be found by staring at percentages. They can only be found by drawing the figures precisely and testing what each one does to the people inside it — a discipline it is fair to call moral geometry.

Eight figures will do most of the work of this book. The loan, where wealth crosses with an obligation to return it. The sale, where goods and price cross once and the parties part. The rent, where a thing's use is let while the thing itself comes home. The partnership, where money and effort marry and share one fate. The gift, where wealth crosses and nothing legal comes back. The tribute, where wealth moves because power demands it. The tax, where it moves because a community requires it of its members. And the pool, where many pay in so that whoever among them is struck may draw out — the figure, as later chapters will argue, in which the traditions' deepest answer to ruin was hiding all along. Every financial instrument ever devised, from a Babylonian barley advance to the capital stack of a venture fund, is one of these figures or a splice of several; and nearly every evasion in the long history of usury is a splice dressed as a single figure, which is why the traditions' lawyers became the world's great connoisseurs of disguise.

Drawing those eight figures carefully — definitions, boundaries, and the tests that tell one from another — is the business of chapter 3, and the chapters after it will spend the rest of the book watching the three traditions build, police, and repair them. But the founding insight of the whole geometry belongs here, at the door, and it is Solon's insight before it is anyone's theology. The Athenians did not solve their debt crisis by finding the right interest rate, and the traditions of Jerusalem, Rome, and Mecca did not frame their law of money by asking what capital could bear. All of them began from the other end, with the person standing inside the contract, and ruled on what must never be done to him — and then, having planted that boundary stone, set about designing every form of exchange, hire, partnership, gift, and common pool that could flourish on the lawful side of it. The prohibition was never the whole of the architecture. It was the surveyor's mark from which a civilization of permitted forms was measured out, and the rest of this book is a walk through the buildings.

chapters.part: Part I — The First Question: What Is Money Allowed to Do?

chapters.title: The Poor, the Brother, the Neighbor, and the Stranger
chapters.label: Chapter 2

paragraphs: Long before money was coined, it was lent. The clay tablets of ancient Mesopotamia — surviving by the tens of thousands, baked hard and still legible after four millennia — include contracts by the basketful, and a great many of them are loans: a farmer takes seed barley in the spring and owes barley back at harvest, with its increase; a household takes silver and owes silver the same way. The rates were as settled as anything in that world. Hammurabi's laws, in the eighteenth century BC, simply took them for granted — a third again for barley, a fifth for silver — and even the vocabulary had the calm of long habit. The Sumerian word for interest, mash, is the word for a goat kid: increase named for the way a flock increases, a full millennium and more before the Greeks made the same move with tokos, "offspring," the pun Aristotle turned against the whole business in the argument chapter 1 has already visited. Interest, in short, is among the oldest institutions in recorded civilization, older than the alphabet, older than coined money by well over a thousand years, and for most of that history nobody blushed about it.

But there is a second genre of document in those same archives, and it tells you what the first one cost. When the barley failed, the loan did not. The debtor pledged what he had — first the field, then the house, then, without embarrassment anywhere in the record, the persons of his household — and a bad year could turn a farmer into a tenant and his children into someone else's servants. So, from time to time, a Babylonian king would proclaim what the Akkadian texts call misharum, "justice" or "equity": debts wiped, pledged persons sent home, the slate cleaned. The best preserved of these edicts, from King Ammisaduqa of Babylon, survives nearly whole; Assur had its own word for the release, andurarum, and scholars hear that word again behind the Hebrew deror, the liberty that Leviticus 25 proclaims in the Jubilee. The Greeks knew both the crisis and the remedy: Solon's seisachtheia, the "shaking off of burdens," canceled Athens's debts in 594 BC, freed the citizens enslaved for debt, and banned the practice thereafter. Rome, by the traditional date 326 BC, abolished its own institution of debt bondage, the nexum, through the lex Poetelia Papiria — after, so Livy tells it, the mistreatment of a bonded young debtor scandalized the city. Everywhere the ancient record shows the same pairing: interest as routine tool, and debt as a slow machine for converting a neighbor's bad season into his servitude — a machine so reliable that whole legal orders had to be interrupted by royal decree just to keep societies from consuming their own members.

The three traditions of this book grew up in the long shadow of that world, and each of them refused a piece of it. None of them refused lending; each, in fact, commands it, with an insistence that surprises modern readers. What they refused was the machine. And the manner of the refusal is the important thing. A royal clean slate treats the debt crisis as weather — it gathers, the king intervenes, it gathers again, and between edicts the machine runs freely. The traditions set out to change the climate instead: to build the restraint into standing law, daily habit, and the community's picture of itself, so that no king's mood was required. Their opening question about a loan was accordingly not the modern one of what money may earn but the older one of what this borrower is to the lender. A brother, said the Torah. A neighbor, said the Gospel, and then redefined the word. A brother in faith and a soul in hardship, said the Qur'an. Everything the coming chapters will build — the contract taxonomies, the partnership law, the charitable engineering — rests on those answers. This chapter is about the answers themselves: where lending sat on the moral map before anyone drew up the rules.

sections.title: The Borrower at the Door
paragraphs: Picture the borrower these laws have in view, because he is not the borrower of a modern textbook. He is a smallholder in a village of perhaps a hundred souls. His wheat came up thin, or the tax collector came through, or a child fell sick in the wrong month. He does not walk into an institution and fill out an application; there is no institution. He walks to the house of a man he has known all his life — a kinsman, or a neighbor with two good harvests stored — and he asks. Everyone in the village will know by evening that he asked. The man he asks will sit beside him at the gate for the next forty years. Whatever passes between them is not a bargain between strangers, priced by a market; it is a change in the standing of two households that must go on living side by side. In societies of this kind — and ancient Israel, the Galilee of Jesus, and seventh-century Arabia were all societies of this kind — a loan is an event inside a web of kinship, and everyone concerned can feel the web tighten.

That is why the ancient moral literature of debt reads as kinship literature. The Hebrew Bible's lending laws barely mention the market; they say brother. Where English translations write "kin" or "community member" or "another Israelite," the Hebrew underneath is usually one small word, achikha, your brother — the vocabulary of family, not of commerce. And the laws are addressed in the second person singular, to a lender who can see the borrower's face: if you lend to him, if you take his cloak, if your eye is mean toward him. Nothing in that idiom is accidental. Debt in a village is a new relation laid over an old one, and what the law cares about is what the new relation does to the old.

The stakes ran in one direction only. The borrower in view borrows to eat, to sow, to pay the tax — not to expand. If the loan fails, the sequence was as fixed in Israel's memory as in Babylon's archives: the pledge is taken, the field passes, the household follows. The book of Kings preserves the cry of a prophet's widow to Elisha: "Your servant my husband is dead; and you know that your servant feared the LORD, but a creditor has come to take my two children as slaves" (2 Kings 4:1). Centuries later, in the middle of the fifth century BC, Nehemiah heard the same cry at scale from the families of Judah — some mortgaging fields, vineyards, and houses to buy grain in a famine, some borrowing against their land for the king's tax, some already handing sons and daughters into servitude — and the creditors were not foreign conquerors but their own kin. Nehemiah's anger, and the public restitution he extracted, fields and orchards and houses and the interest itself given back, treated the crisis as exactly what this chapter's traditions always understood it to be: a family devouring itself.

Modern categories mislead here in a second way, and it is worth disposing of the confusion early. The ancient world did have commercial credit; Mesopotamian merchant houses ran long-distance trade on it, and Part IV of this book will watch all three traditions build superb instruments for exactly that purpose. The scriptural fire against interest was never primarily about that world. It was about this one: the neighbor whose need has delivered him into your hands. Keep the trader seeking capital and the family seeking bread distinct, because every tradition in this book eventually learned to keep them distinct, and most of the worst readings of the usury laws come from mixing them back together. The texts we are about to read legislate for the second case, the borrower at the door. A rate is a number; a brother is a claim.

sections.title: The Poor of Your City
paragraphs: The Torah's great interest texts all locate lending the same way before they regulate it. The earliest, in the Covenant Code of Exodus, deserves to be heard exactly, in the New Revised Standard Version's rendering: "If you lend money to my people, to the poor among you, you shall not deal with them as a creditor; you shall not exact interest from them" (Exodus 22:25). Notice what is and is not forbidden. Lending is assumed — commanded, elsewhere. What is forbidden is a posture, dealing with the poor "as a creditor," and a practice, the exacting of interest, for which biblical Hebrew's sharpest word is neshekh, the bite. The law then descends immediately into a poor man's evening: if his cloak is taken in pawn, "you shall restore it before the sun goes down; for it may be your neighbor's only clothing to use as cover; in what else shall that person sleep?" (22:26–27). The lender's claim is real, and the law does not cancel it; the law makes it bend, every single sunset, before the body of the borrower. And the reason given has nothing to do with economics: if that borrower cries out, "I will listen, for I am compassionate." The creditor is not the senior party in the room. God has taken sides in advance.

Leviticus widens the frame from a night to a life: "If any of your kin fall into difficulty and become dependent on you, you shall support them; they shall live with you as though resident aliens. Do not take interest in advance or otherwise make a profit from them, but fear your God; let them live with you" (Leviticus 25:35–36) — the Hebrew pairs neshekh, the bite, with tarbit, the increase, and bans both. Here the interest ban sits inside a command to support. The falling brother is to be caught, held upright, kept beside you, and the refusal of increase is simply what catching him means; you cannot brace a man with one hand and bill him for the bracing with the other. Deuteronomy adds the rhythm of time — the seventh-year release, the warning against the hardened heart and the closed hand as the release year approaches — and everywhere the same address: your brother. Chapter 4 will walk this legal architecture properly, pledges and millstones and Jubilee and all. What matters here is the location. Lending to the poor is not filed under commerce in the Torah. It is filed under rescue, in the same drawer as the gleanings left standing in the field and the tithe set aside for the widow, and the tradition's name for that drawer became tzedakah — a noun built on the root for justice. Care for the poor brother is not generosity beyond the law's requirement; it is the requirement.

The rabbis inherited that location and deepened it. Their term of art for forbidden increase is ribbit, and the tractate that governs it, Bava Metzia, keeps breaking out of case law into moral astonishment. Rabbi Yosei, in a baraita preserved at folio 71a, marvels at the blindness of lenders at interest: a man called wicked to his face will fight the insult all his days — yet these bring witnesses and a scribe, pen and ink, and solemnly sign a document attesting, in the baraita's own words, that so-and-so has denied the God of Israel. On that page, charging a brother for his need is not sharp practice; it is apostasy with paperwork. A few lines on, Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar reads Psalm 15 — the psalm that lists refusing interest among the marks of the person fit to dwell on God's holy hill — as a working prediction: the fortunes of such lenders collapse and do not rise. And when the sages asked who should be lent to first, they answered with a map of nearness drawn from the wording of Exodus itself (the verse they cite as 22:24; English Bibles number it 22:25): "my people" before others, the poor before the rich, your own poor before the poor of your city, the poor of your city before the poor of another town. Obligation, in this tradition, has an address. Mercy is not a mist hanging evenly over humanity; it runs through channels — household, street, town — so that every poor family is some particular community's first responsibility, rather than everyone's-in-general and therefore no one's.

sections.title: The Neighbor Who Proved Neighbor
paragraphs: Jesus taught inside this Torah world, in an occupied agrarian province where the borrower at the door was an everyday figure, and his teaching on lending begins from Israel's premises and then leans on them, hard. The Torah had commanded the open hand toward the poor brother and forbidden profit from his need. Jesus, in the Sermon on the Plain, removes the last vestige of return: "If you lend to those from whom you hope to receive, what credit is that to you? Even sinners lend to sinners, to receive as much again. But love your enemies, do good, and lend, expecting nothing in return. Your reward will be great, and you will be children of the Most High; for he is kind to the ungrateful and the wicked" (Luke 6:34–35). Matthew's version of the saying is blunter still: "Give to everyone who begs from you, and do not refuse anyone who wants to borrow from you" (Matthew 5:42). There is no regulation in any of this — no rate cap, no pledge law — only a family resemblance held up as the standard: lend the way your Father gives, to the ungrateful and the wicked, without a meter running, because that is what the children of this particular Father do. The Torah had disciplined the loan to protect the brother. Jesus turns the loan into an imitation of God.

Then there is the question of who counts, and Luke stages it as a legal debate, which is what it was. A lawyer, quoting Leviticus — love your neighbor as yourself — asks the natural lawyer's question about the statute's scope: "And who is my neighbor?" (Luke 10:29). It was a fair question, and an old one. Leviticus 19:18 sits in a chapter addressed to Israel about Israel, and its own thirty-fourth verse had already stretched the command outward — "you shall love the alien as yourself" — so the argument about the boundary was Israel's own argument, running long before the lawyer stood up. Jesus answers with the story every reader knows and none quite domesticates: a man beaten half-dead on the Jericho road; a priest and a Levite passing by on the other side; rescue arriving in the person of a Samaritan, for Luke's audience the sectarian enemy from over the hill. Then the question comes back reversed: "Which of these three, do you think, was a neighbor to the man who fell into the hands of the robbers?" The lawyer's category has been turned inside out. Neighbor has stopped being a status the wounded man must qualify for and become a practice the passerby either performs or refuses. "The one who showed him mercy," the lawyer answers, and hears: "Go and do likewise" (10:36–37).

The church took the reversal literally, and taking it literally changed the economics. If neighbor has no outer edge, the Torah's brother-rule acquires no outer edge either: every borrower is the brother, and what Israel had guaranteed inside the covenant — need met without a meter — Christian teaching would in time claim for anyone in need at all. That is the seed of a remarkable and demanding doctrine. The church's usury ban, when it came, would bind toward every human being, and the Fathers who built it reached for precisely these verses. Chapter 5 will weigh the whole New Testament witness, including the harder texts, and later chapters will watch councils and canonists turn the posture into law — and watch what it cost to mean it, because the cost is the honest part of the story. A boundaryless mercy is a glorious wager. Everything depends on whether the mercy can be sustained everywhere once it is owed everywhere, and a good deal of the history ahead of us, from the Fathers' sermons to the Monti di Pietà, is Christendom straining to make good on the Samaritan.

sections.title: Devouring the Wealth of Others
paragraphs: Seventh-century Mecca had no king and no bureaucracy; it had clans, a sanctuary, customary honor, and trade. A merchant town in a subsistence landscape is a place of hard asymmetries — caravan fortunes on one street, families a single bad season from destitution on the next — and between them stood no institution but kin solidarity and the lender. The practice the Qur'an confronted there had a name, riba, from a root meaning to swell or increase, and the commentators describe its signature move: when a debt fell due and the debtor could not pay, he was offered the choice of paying now or watching the sum grow. Deferral meant doubling. A season's shortfall could compound into permanent clientage — the old machine of Babylon and Athens, running on desert time. The Qur'an's earliest word on the subject, from the Meccan years, already sets two economies against each other; here it is in M. A. S. Abdel Haleem's rendering: "Whatever you lend out in usury to gain value through other people's wealth will not increase in God's eyes, but whatever you give in charity, in your desire for God's approval, will earn multiple rewards" (30:39). In Medina the register sharpens to command — "You who believe, do not consume usurious interest, doubled and redoubled" (3:130), the old practice named to its face — and finally to the fiercest sentence any of the three scriptures aims at this subject: those who persist in riba after the warning are to expect "war from God and His Messenger" (2:279). The long passage that carries the threat (2:275–279) also carries the argument. The taker of usury will rise "like someone tormented by Satan's touch"; to the protest that "Trade and usury are the same," the answer comes back flat: "God has allowed trade and forbidden usury."

Hold on to the Qur'an's characteristic verb, because it is doing this chapter's work. Wrongful gain, in the Qur'an's idiom, is eaten. "Do not consume your property wrongfully," runs the verse on corrupt dealing, "intending sinfully and knowingly to consume parts of other people's property" (2:188); and a passage addressing an earlier covenant community — one that assumes the Torah's own ban — condemns "taking usury when they had been forbidden to do so" and "wrongfully devouring other people's property" (4:161). The verb is akala, to eat, to devour. Gain from a neighbor's need is not pictured as a fee, a price, or even a theft of objects; it is pictured as a mouth closing on another person's substance. The image belongs to the same moral universe as Nehemiah's assembly: the strong consuming the weak through claims rather than swords. And, exactly as in the Torah, the alternative on offer is not a world without lending but lending relocated. The believer's wealth, the Qur'an insists, already carries the poor inside it — a recognized right, a haqq, belonging to the beggar and the destitute (70:24–25) — discharged through zakat, the purifying share, through sadaqah, the voluntary gift, and through the loan the tradition calls beautiful, the qard hasan, whose story belongs to chapter 16. As for the debtor already caught, the instruction is direct: "If the debtor is in difficulty, then delay things until matters become easier for him; still, if you were to write it off as an act of charity, that would be better for you, if only you knew" (2:280). Even the unwinding of old usury is drawn with a draftsman's balance: "You shall have your capital… without suffering loss or causing others to suffer loss" (2:279) — the closing Arabic is a matched pair the tradition treats as a maxim, wrong not and be not wronged. The principal is honest. The increase was the predation.

The community that received these verses heard them as family law, because a family is what the new community was. "The believers are brothers" (49:10): the ummah was kinship rebuilt on faith, wide enough to hold the Meccan migrant and the Medinan farmer in one household, and the riba ban stood among its founding solidarities — inside this brotherhood, need shall not be farmed. Chapter 6 will read the whole Qur'anic case and the machinery that grew from it. For now, mark the location, because it is the same location: like the Torah's, the Qur'an's lending ethic lives where kinship, worship, and survival meet, and it arrived, like Israel's, as the charter of a community surrounded by the older machine and determined not to reproduce it.

sections.title: The Boundary and the Shield
paragraphs: Every ethic of brotherhood must eventually answer for the man who is not my brother. The three traditions answered differently, and the differences — each with its own cost and its own genius — frame much of the history this book has still to tell.

Deuteronomy answers with a boundary, and the verse must be read exactly, because few verses in Scripture have been read worse: "You shall not charge interest on loans to another Israelite, interest on money, interest on provisions, interest on anything that is lent. On loans to a foreigner you may charge interest, but on loans to another Israelite you may not charge interest, so that the LORD your God may bless you in all your undertakings in the land that you are about to enter and possess" (Deuteronomy 23:19–20; the Hebrew, which numbers these verses 20 and 21, says throughout simply your brother). Within the covenant the ban is total — money, food, anything lent. Toward the nokhri, the foreigner, ordinary commercial terms are permitted. Read from within the tradition, this is not a license issued against outsiders; it is the visible edge of a family's internal welfare law. The interest ban belongs to the same cluster as the gleanings, the tithe, and the release year — solidarities a kinship community guarantees its members — and the nokhri of this verse is the outside party to whom those solidarities were never owed in either direction: the trader passing through, who lends at interest himself and expects to borrow the same way. The vulnerable outsider was another case entirely. The ger, the resident alien, is not the nokhri: him the same Torah orders Israel to love — "you shall love the alien as yourself, for you were aliens in the land of Egypt" (Leviticus 19:34) — and him Leviticus 25:35 folds into the very support command we read above, "as though resident aliens… let them live with you." The boundary marked where the family's guarantees ended, not a wall against the weak.

The rabbis, custodians of the verse, handled the outward permission with visible unease. The Talmud's discussion at Bava Metzia 70b–71a turns the clause over like a suspicious coin — what exactly does la-nokhri tashikh permit? — and then hedges whatever it permits: lending at interest to the outsider should be limited to what one needs for a livelihood, the sages ruled, lest the lender learn from his ways; and the precedence rules cut against the profit in any case, for faced with a gentile borrower at interest and a Jewish borrower for free, the free loan to the brother comes first. Whatever Deuteronomy's boundary allowed, the tradition declined to let it become a vocation. Nor was the boundary ever a boundary of mercy: the same Talmud rules that the poor of the nations are sustained together with the poor of Israel, their sick visited and their dead buried, for the sake of the ways of peace (Gittin 61a). One dark sentence must be entered here and then left for its proper place: centuries later, Christian polemic would seize on Deuteronomy's two clauses — a ban Christendom applied to itself, a permission whose exercise it pressed upon Jews and then despised them for — and build from them the slander of the "Jewish usurer," an afterlife that belongs to its makers and that this book confronts in chapter 17 and Part VIII. The verse in its own house is covenant economics: unlimited duty inward, honest commerce outward.

Islam met the same boundary question and removed the boundary in the other direction: the riba ban follows the act, not the relationship. In the law as the great majority of jurists settled it, a Muslim may not take riba from anyone — believer or unbeliever, neighbor or stranger — because the prohibition attaches to the transaction itself rather than to the borrower's membership. The schools did argue an edge case, as legal schools do.
