This is the same Cassius whom chapter 11 met naming the lion's partnership, the societas leonina, void because one party had arranged to take gain without exposure. The two rulings sit in adjacent sentences of the same fragment, and together they draw the line with Roman economy: a man who risks nothing and takes profit is a lion; a man who risks his season, his industry, his one irreplaceable voyage — that man has stake enough, and may be spared the money-loss because he is already standing under a loss of his own. The laborer was never the lion. The laborer was the other animal, the one who actually hunted.

What counts as labor's stake, once you start itemizing it honestly, turns out to be a longer list than a timesheet. There is skill — the industria of Ulpian's clause, the difference between a man who can sell flax in Sicily and a man who can lose money in any port in the Mediterranean. There is time, though the traditions handled time with tongs: waiting, by itself, earns nothing — the rabbis' agar natar, the reward for waiting, is chapter 7's forbidden core, and none of the three systems ever paid the clock as such. What they paid was time filled: months of attention spent inside the venture, which is not waiting but working. The distinction sounds thin until you watch it operate. Two men each part with a hundred coins for a year. The first spends the year at home while his coins sit in a stranger's shop, and the year, as a year, entitles him to nothing — that was the whole scandal of Part III. The second spends the year walking beside his coins, buying and haggling and keeping the books by lamplight, and the traditions will pay him for every month of it — not because the calendar turned but because he filled it. The coins and the calendar are identical; what differs is a person's presence inside the venture, and presence is what the instruments of chapter 11 were engineered to price. There is reputation, and it is astonishing how much of the old commercial law is really a law of names: chapter 11 noted that the mudarib's true collateral was his standing in a world of repeat engagements, and the Geniza merchants ran ventures from Egypt to the pepper coast on little else. A man who lends his good name to a venture has put something real and ruinable into it — names, unlike coins, cannot be re-minted. And there is the contribution the modern economist reaches for first and the traditions touched last and most gingerly: opportunity foregone, the profit the working partner might have made elsewhere with the same months. The scholastics would eventually build an entire disputed doctrine — lucrum cessans — on that thought, and this book quarantines it where it belongs, in chapter 20, among the technical debates. For now it is enough to mark the asymmetry: the traditions were quick to see labor spent and slow to credit labor hypothetically redirected, and the caution was deliberate. Spent months can be witnessed. Imaginary alternative months can be claimed by anyone, about anything, in whatever amount flatters the claimant.

So the schedule of honest contributions stands at something like this: money ventured; work performed; skill applied; standing staked; and, under heavy guard, alternatives genuinely surrendered. Every instrument in chapter 11 is a machine for pairing the first item with the middle three. The question that separates the traditions from the term sheets of our own day is what happens to the items that are hard to count.

sections.title: The Wage for Trouble
paragraphs: The rabbis' answer runs through the shopkeeper we have already met. What the Mishnah demands for him, and what the Talmud at Bava Metzia 68b proceeds to size, is a wage: the investor who sets a man trading on half profits must pay him for the toil he spends on the investor's half. The Talmud's measure is a small masterpiece of practical psychology — pay him "as an idle laborer," which the tradition unpacked as roughly what a man of his trade would accept to down his own tools and mind someone else's. Not a full market salary for the work, notice; the shopkeeper is, after all, also working his own half and keeping its whole profit. The wage prices the marginal imposition — the trouble — and the halakhists' shorthand for the category became sechar tircha, the wage for trouble, the payment that keeps the working partner's sweat from silently subsidizing his financier.

Two refinements show how carefully the principle was held. First, the wage's size collapsed over the centuries into a formality: later authorities let the parties stipulate a token — the codified rule in the Shulchan Arukh's laws of interest, at siman 177, is that even a single dinar suffices. That looks at first like the rule decaying, and is nearly the opposite. The dinar is doing declaratory work: it forces the contract to say that the manager's labor is a compensable contribution and not a courtesy, and once said, the rest of his compensation can ride honestly in a tilted profit split — the iska's other standard device, met in chapter 11, giving the working partner a fatter share of gains than of losses precisely because his work is worth something. What the halakha would not tolerate was zero: the pretense that management of another man's money is free. Second, the codifiers' gloss draws the boundary from the other side: where both parties put in capital and one happens to manage, the wage requirement relaxes — a true two-sided partnership is not a creditor-debtor pair in disguise, and the manager's own capital, working under his own hands, already pays him. The rule was never a labor tax on partnership as such. It was targeted, with the rabbis' usual marksmanship, at exactly the configuration where unpaid labor could function as interest: one man's money, another man's sweat, and a loan half sitting in the middle of the relationship. Price the sweat, even at a dinar, and the categories come clean: what the worker does for the deposit half is service, sold; what he does for his own loan half is his own business; and nothing is left traveling, unnamed and unpaid, alongside a loan.

It is worth pausing to admire what the rabbis have done here, because it is the mirror image of everything Part III condemned. Part III's villain was the charge without a contribution — the lender billing for risk he had shifted away, for time he did not own, for need he did not create. The sechar tircha rule attacks the opposite fraud: the contribution without a charge. Both rules serve one ledger-keeping instinct: every real input priced, no phantom input paid. A tradition that spent chapter 8 hunting benefits that flow to the lender unpriced was never going to miss the benefit that flows from the worker unpriced — the same crime with the arrow reversed. Chapter 8 watched the rabbis count a borrower's unaccustomed greeting as interest; a season of unaccustomed shopkeeping stood no chance of slipping past them.

sections.title: The Mudarib's Portion
paragraphs: Islamic law reached the same destination by the boldest route of the three: it made the profit share itself the wage.

Recall the mudarabah's severe geometry from chapter 11. The rabb al-mal brings capital and only capital; the mudarib brings effort and only effort; profit divides by a pre-agreed ratio; monetary loss falls on the capital alone, the working partner losing his months and his hoped-for share. Inside that geometry, the ratio is not an incentive bonus sitting on top of the mudarib's compensation; it is his compensation, entire. His labor has no other price: no salary, no retainer, no management fee accruing quietly whatever the venture does. The classical jurists were explicit about the exclusion, and their reasoning cuts to the structure's heart: a fixed draw for the mudarib would be a claim against the venture that pays regardless of outcome — and a payment regardless of outcome is precisely the payoff shape the whole contract exists to banish. Pay the worker like a creditor and you have smuggled the creditor back in through the servants' entrance; worse, in a losing year his fixed wage would eat into the rabb al-mal's capital, making the laborer a lien on the very coins whose loss is supposed to be the capitalist's own clean burden. So the rule held: the mudarib eats from the profit or he does not eat from the venture at all. Modern codifications state it with regulatory bluntness — Malaysia's central-bank standard on the contract, to take one living example, provides that the mudarib "is only entitled to profit" for the works integral to the venture "and shall not earn any additional fee for such works" — while preserving the classical safety valves: the venture's own direct expenses, the mudarib's road and lodging among them, come out of the mudarabah's purse rather than the worker's, and the financier remains free to hire the same man, by a separate contract at a separate fee, for work genuinely outside the venture's scope. The line the jurists are holding in all of this is the line between reimbursing a venture's costs and guaranteeing a worker's gain.

The tradition liked to teach the contract's texture through a story its compilations preserve about Abbas ibn Abd al-Muttalib, the Prophet's uncle, a man who would hand over mudarabah capital only on conditions: do not carry my money by sea, do not take it down a valley, do not buy livestock with it — and if you do, you stand guarantor for the loss. The report has the stipulations reaching the Prophet, who allowed them; modern codifications still cite it as the contract's pedigree. Whatever the chain's strength — the compilers transmit it at report level — the jurists drew from it the design point that matters here: the rabb al-mal may fence the mandate, by route, commodity, or season, because the money is his to fence; what he may not fence is the outcome, because the outcome was never anyone's to sell.

The severity, though, ran both ways — and this is the part modern summaries most often miss. If the mudarib's ratio is his wage, then the mudarib's labor is never, under any failure of the arrangement, simply forfeit. Let the capitalist promise funds and never deliver them after the agent has begun the work: the jurists' remedy — echoed in the same modern standard — is that the rabb al-mal must cover the expenditures incurred and pay the man "fair and reasonable wages," what the classical books call the wage of his like, ujrat al-mithl. The same remedy backstops a mudarabah that turns out to be void for a defect in its terms: the invalid contract converts, retroactively, into an employment at a fair wage, because whatever the paperwork's failings, the labor actually happened. Sit with that for a moment. The tradition's default is that work performed creates a claim that survives the death of the very contract that priced it — the ratio while the partnership stands, the fair wage when it falls, and at no point zero. A legal system reveals its priorities in its wreckage rules, and when a mudarabah collapses, the fiqh's first question is the one this whole chapter has been circling: has the man who worked been paid?

One more feature completes the picture. The profit ratio, being labor's price, was genuinely negotiable — a half, a third, two-fifths, whatever the parties' judgment of the work's worth and the market for agents would bear, with the schools' usual disputes at the edges. What it could never be was a number pinned to the capital: the classical rule, again preserved in the modern codifications, voids a "share" expressed as a guaranteed sum or as a percentage of the capital amount, because either device unhooks the worker's pay from the venture's truth. The ratio prices the pairing of one man's money with another man's months, and it must bite on the profit that pairing actually produced. Chapter 14 will make that principle — returns defined only on real outcomes — the spine of its argument; here it is enough to see whose interests the rule was written in. A ratio on actual profit is the only wage that cannot be faked in either direction: the capitalist cannot promise it and then starve it, and the worker cannot collect it out of a venture that produced nothing.

sections.title: Payment for Real Work
paragraphs: Latin Christendom's version of the principle arrives from an unexpected quarter: not from its partnership law, which it largely took over from Rome with the Digest's staircase intact, but from its agonized defense of the merchant himself.

The schoolmen inherited from the ancient world, and from a strand of patristic suspicion, the sense that commerce as such — buying to sell dearer — hovered near sin. Aquinas's rehabilitation of the trader, in the question of the Summa immediately before his question on usury, turns on a single move: he looks at the merchant's margin and asks what it is for. Gain sought as an end in itself is the appetite that "knows no limit," and it earns from Thomas the coldest of acquittals — not sinful in itself, merely base when it serves nothing. But gain directed to keeping a household, to relieving the needy, to stocking one's country with what it lacks — that gain, he writes, is sought "not as an end, but as the wage of his labor": non quasi finem, sed quasi stipendium laboris. The margin, morally read, is a paycheck. Trade is work — the sourcing, hauling, storing, risking, judging that chapter 9 watched the just-price doctrine struggle to see inside the price — and the man who does that work may eat from it, in measure, like any other worker. The phrase became a load-bearing category of the whole scholastic economics: stipendium laboris, payment for real work, the title under which human effort collects inside transactions that superficially look like money moving against money.

Set the phrase beside the partnership doctrine and the Christian schema snaps into the same two-column shape the other traditions drew. Capital's title is ownership-at-risk: the investing partner earns tamquam de re sua, because his money stands exposed inside the venture. Labor's title is the stipendium: the working partner, the merchant, the agent earns because his effort is a real cost and a real contribution. Two titles, two different justifications, and the entire scholastic case against usury can be restated as the insistence that these are the only two — that every florin of return must trace to ventured property or expended work, and that the lender of a mutuum, having transferred ownership and performed no service, holds neither. The loss-side doors — the damages and foregone gains of the extrinsic titles, Part VI's subject — open off the same corridor, but those are compensations for what lending cost the lender, never payments for what he contributed; the schema does not confuse making a lender whole with making him a wage-earner. When Benedict XIV's Vix pervenit reaffirmed the old doctrine in 1745, chapter 7 noted, it carefully left the door open to titles arising outside the loan itself; the wage of labor had walked through that door centuries earlier and no serious voice ever tried to shut it on honest work. Even the institutions this book will meet in Part V ran on the principle: when the Monti di Pietà charged the poor a small fee on pledge loans, the defense that carried the day — chapter 17 tells the story — was precisely that clerks must be paid and buildings kept, cost and labor recovered, profit never taken. The tradition that would not let money earn as money insisted, with the same breath, that people must earn as people. Its horror of the one was the exact shadow of its respect for the other: usury takes without contributing, and there is no surer sign of the taking than that somewhere nearby, someone's work is going unpaid.

sections.title: The Invisible Partner
paragraphs: Now walk the three doctrines forward eight centuries and stand them in front of a startup's capitalization table.

The founder of the modern venture is the most heavily contributing partner any of this chapter's lawyers ever imagined. She brings the skill and the industria; she brings the months — commonly years — of labor; she stakes her professional name on the venture's fate as thoroughly as any Geniza agent staked his on a cargo; she has usually surrendered, concretely and provably, a salary elsewhere, the very lucrum cessans the scholastics fenced with conditions, here made verifiable by the job offer she declined. There is a small historical irony buried in that fact: the scholastics fenced lucrum cessans with conditions precisely because foregone profit was easy to claim and hard to witness, and the modern founder is the rare claimant who can document her foregone alternative to the dollar — she is also the claimant for whom the modern instruments make no line at all. Frequently she also lends the venture money in the most honest of forms: the below-market salary, the payroll she skips in a bad quarter — capital contributions in every substantive sense, extracted in sweat rather than wired in. The folk term for all of this is "sweat equity," and the folk term is a confession: everyone can see the equity is bought with sweat; the books just have no line for the purchase.

Because here is what the capitalization table records: money. It records it beautifully — to the cent, by date, with the price per share carried to four decimals. Capital contributions enter the venture's permanent memory the moment they arrive. Labor's contributions arrive differently: they trickle in nightly, they never pass through a bank account, and the accounting system books them not as contribution but as cost — a salary expense, kept artfully low — or does not book them at all. The founder's stake, the common stock, is what the arithmetic leaves over after every priced claim is served, and chapter 10 already toured the devices that push it to the queue's end: preferences, seniorities, guarantees, each one shifting risk onto exactly the participants whose contribution the ledger never learned to see. What the ledger cannot see, the ledger will not pay. The result is a structure the traditions had a name for. Recall what the societas leonina actually was: not, in practice, a contract announcing that one party takes all the gain — no one signs that — but any arrangement whose payoff, once every clause has operated, leaves one party's contribution compensated and the other's absorbed. A venture in which capital's input is priced to four decimals and labor's input is priced at whatever residue the waterfall happens to leave has not escaped the lion so much as modernized his bookkeeping. The difference from the fable is that no clause announces the division; it emerges, politely, from the arithmetic.

And the founder, note, is the lucky one: she at least appears on the capitalization table, however junior her stock. Below her stands a stratum the documents see even less. Employees who took thin salaries against options; contractors paid late through a tight quarter; the spouse whose second income floated the household while the venture consumed the first — co-investors all, by any substantive test this chapter's lawyers would recognize, and none of them anywhere in the arithmetic. Chapter 38 gives them their own accounting, under worker claims and invisible contribution; chapter 10 already exposed the mechanism that makes their seat the worst in the house: shifted risk rolls downhill toward the participants least able to spread it, and unpriced contribution rolls with it.

The traditions' three answers, set side by side, read like a single design brief written in three languages. From the rabbis: no venture may treat the working partner's labor as free, and the pricing must be explicit — a stated wage, even a token, so that the contract itself confesses labor's claim, with the working partner's tilted share doing the substantive paying. From the fiqh: the worker's share is a first-class claim defined on real outcomes, immune to being fixed away, and it survives even the contract's own death — the venture that consumed a man's months owes him the wage of his like though every other clause should fail. From the schoolmen: work is a title to return as fundamental as ownership itself, and any structure whose returns cannot all be traced to ventured property or expended labor is collecting for a phantom. Put affirmatively, as the design brief this book will hand to Part IX: a venture's surplus belongs to its contributions, and the schedule of contributions is longer than the wire transfers. Money ventured, yes — first out of the arithmetic, as every tradition agreed, standing at its own risk. But also months spent, skill applied, names staked, salaries foregone, risk absorbed by the people least able to spread it. Ulpian's three-word list — pecuniae, operae, cuiuscumque alterius rei — is a contribution schedule; the traditions' whole labor doctrine is the insistence that the schedule be filled in honestly and paid in the order mercy and truth require. What that means in the vocabulary of modern instruments — how a term sheet would actually price founder labor, worker claims, the contributions no wire ever carried — is the assignment of chapter 38, which revisits this chapter's three terms by name, and of the surplus arithmetic of chapters 39 and 40. The old lawyers, who priced a shopkeeper's trouble at a declaratory dinar and made a dead partnership pay a living wage, would not have found the assignment strange. They would have found it overdue — eight centuries of compound arrears on the one debt their ledgers never let go invisible.

chapters.part: Part IV — Partnership as the Great Escape from Usury

chapters.title: Loss Allocation and the Truth of the Contract
chapters.label: Chapter 13

paragraphs: Return to the portico by the Genoese harbor, and let the year turn. In chapter 11 two men stood before the notary Giovanni Scriba and signed a commenda: one man's money, the other man's voyage, the profit to be divided on the standard split. Now it is the following spring, say, and the traveler has come back up from the quay with his sea chest, his account book, and nothing else. The venture is gone. Prices broke in Alexandria; the cargo sold for less than it cost to load it; what the pirates and the port fees left, the homeward freight consumed. Before witnesses, as the contract requires, he renders his accounting — every purchase, every sale, every charge — and the investor, who is out three years of savings, asks his questions and hears the answers. And then the two men do the thing this whole Part has been building toward, the thing that made the instrument worth a chapter of anybody's book. They part.

No debt follows the traveler up the hill. No lien settles on his house, no claim passes to his heirs, no ledger anywhere records that he owes the investor so much as a bent denarius. The money is simply gone, the way a harvest is gone after hail, and the two of them walk away from the wreck unequally bruised but equally free. One street over, that same spring, some shopkeeper who financed his stock with a plain loan is learning the other arithmetic: his venture failed too, and his creditor is owed one hundred twenty, today, out of whatever he still owns. The venture's death did not touch the debt. Chapter 10 watched that claim ride out every storm that killed the things it paid for; a loan, whatever else may be said of it, does not know how to lose.

Who loses, then, if the venture fails? The partnership instruments answer with a map — this loss to this man, that loss to that one, drawn before the venture begins — and the map is the subject of this chapter. Prosperity flatters every contract; failure cross-examines it. When the returns are good, loan and partnership look like cousins: money went out, more money came back, everyone is smiling. The difference between them is written entirely in the bad year, in who eats what when there is less at the end than there was at the beginning. The traditions understood this, which is why their partnership law spends so little ink on dividing gains and so much on allocating losses: the gain side takes care of itself, and the loss side is where the contract either tells the truth or is caught lying. Three questions organize everything they built. Where does honest loss fall — loss that arrived by weather, war, or the ordinary treachery of markets? When does blame move it — what must a manager have done before his partner's loss becomes his debt? And what happens to the whole structure when someone tries to draft his way out of his seat? The answers, across three legal civilizations, agree so closely that by the chapter's end we will be entitled to call the agreement what it is: a geometry.

sections.title: The Ledger of Failure
paragraphs: Chapter 12 itemized what each partner brings to a venture — money, months, skill, standing. Failure reads the same schedule backward. When a venture dies an honest death, every real contributor loses the very thing he contributed, in its own coin and nobody else's.

Capital loses money, and only money. That limit deserves more admiration than it usually gets. The investor's downside in every instrument chapter 11 walked — societas, iska, mudarabah, commenda — is bounded at the sum he ventured: the venture can consume his stake entirely, and then it must stop, because nothing in the contract converts his loss into anyone's debt or reaches past the ventured purse into the rest of his estate. The fiqh states the boundary as cleanly as anyone: monetary loss falls on the capital, up to the capital, and the rabb al-mal has no complaint beyond it. His hundred could become zero; it cannot become minus twenty.

Labor loses the months. The traveler's season, the mudarib's year of roads and warehouses, the working partner's daylight — spent in full, recoverable never. The books of the fiqh put it with a plainness that has worn well: when a mudarabah loses, the financier loses his money and the agent's labor has gone in vain. That loss is as real as the contribution was, and the traditions' refusal to pretend otherwise is half the moral architecture of this Part. The Roman lawyers, chapter 12 found, built the other half of the same thought into the Digest's partnership title: a partner may be spared any share of the money-loss where his labor is worth as much as the loss — si tanti sit opera, quanti damnum est — because, the jurists reasoned, a man's industry is itself a stake, and often a greater one than coins. Read from the failure side, the ruling says something exact: the laboring partner was never exempt from loss at all. His loss was simply denominated in a different currency, and he pays it first, automatically, the moment the venture fails — before the investor has even opened the account book. And there is a third loss the ledgers never captured, which chapter 11 met as collateral: the manager's name. A venture that dies under a man's hands leaves a residue of doubt on him, deserved or not, in exactly the world of repeat engagements where his name was his fortune.

Notice what the traditions did not do with these losses: they did not try to equalize them. No rule anywhere requires the investor to reimburse the traveler's wasted season; no rule bills the traveler for a tenth of the sunken capital. The two losses are incommensurable — coins against months — and the instruments let each fall where it grew. What looks at first like rough justice is, on a second look, the only honest accounting available. Each partner ventured what he ventured; failure takes precisely that. The alternative designs all smuggle in a guarantee somewhere — of the investor's money by the worker, or of the worker's wage by the investor — and the traditions rejected both directions by name, the first as the very definition of disguised lending, the second, more interestingly, with a precision the fiqh spelled out and chapter 12 already met. When a mudarabah collapses for a defect in its terms, or a financier promises capital and never delivers it after the work has begun, the law pays the worker — expenses, plus the wage of his like, ujrat al-mithl — because the arrangement itself failed, and the failure of an arrangement is somebody's doing. But when the arrangement holds and the market simply answers no — the goods bought soundly and sold at a loss, the season honestly bad — the worker's remedy is nothing, because a ratio of a profit that never existed is nothing. The line could not be drawn finer: the law compensates labor for a broken contract, never for an unlucky one, because a venture's ordinary death is nobody's doing.

Nobody's doing: that is the premise the whole allocation rests on, and it is also the premise that wrongdoing destroys. The rest of this chapter is about what happens at that boundary — and each tradition, it turns out, patrolled it with the same three-part grammar: honest loss lies where the map says; caused loss moves to the causer; and the map itself may never be redrawn by guarantee. We take the traditions in turn, starting with the one whose instrument confesses its own hybrid nature right in its name.

sections.title: Two Purses in One Coat
paragraphs: The iska, the rabbis' investment contract, is half loan and half deposit — palga milveh, palga pikadon, in the Nehardean formula chapter 11 unpacked from Bava Metzia 104b — which means it is also two loss regimes stitched into one coat, and the stitching is where its honesty lives.

The loan half loses like a loan. Those fifty coins became the manager's property on the day the iska was signed, and property perishes to its owner: if the stock they bought burns, sinks, or sells at half price, the loss is the manager's alone, and he owes the investor fifty at settlement in every possible world. On this half he stands where chapter 7 put every borrower — at the top of the Mishnah's ladder of keepers, liable even for sheer accident, because what he holds is his and what he owes is arithmetic. The Mishnah's ladder, met at Bava Metzia 7:8, grades the four keepers of other people's property by the benefit they draw: the unpaid guardian, who swears about what happened and goes home; the paid guardian and the renter, who answer for theft and loss but not for catastrophe; and the borrower, all benefit and all liability, who pays for everything up to and including the wolf that could not have been foreseen. The iska's loan half simply is that fourth rung, and the rabbis never pretended otherwise.

The deposit half loses like a deposit. Those fifty remain the investor's property, trading in the manager's hands at the investor's peril, and when the market takes them the loss is his — that peril being, as chapter 10 established, the entire license for his share of the gain. The Mishneh Torah, codifying the instrument in its partnership laws, states the two regimes with a bluntness that settles every boundary question: the administrator is responsible for the loan half "even if it is destroyed by forces beyond his control," while the other half "is considered an entrusted object" at the investor's risk — "if the half that is considered an entrusted article is stolen or lost, the administrator is not liable to pay," which is exactly why that half's profit belongs to the investor (Sheluchin veShutafin 6:2, in Eliyahu Touger's rendering). Notice how far the owner's peril runs: theft and loss on the entrusted half stay on the investor's account, not the manager's. The manager is a keeper of that half, never its underwriter — and what no keeper escapes, on any rung of the Mishnah's ladder, is negligence. What negligence means for money, the Talmud made concrete enough to touch. Money, rules Shmuel at Bava Metzia 42a, has only one proper safekeeping: burial. The same page tries the case of a man who deposited coins with a fellow who tucked them into a willow hut, where they were promptly stolen — a keeping Rav Yosef dissected with a lawyer's relish: against thieves, he ruled, the hut was effective safeguarding; against fire it was negligence; and a keeping that begins in negligence stays liable however the blow happens to land — the rule the Gemara, after recording a dissenting version, fixed as the law. On the same folio, a bailee who tells the owner he cannot remember where he put the money collects Rava's shortest ruling in the tractate: every "I do not know" is itself negligence — go pay. And when professional treasure-diggers grew common enough that buried coins stopped being safe, the law moved the standard — money now wanted hiding in the roof beams; then, when dismantlers learned to search beams, between the bricks of a wall; then, when tappers learned to sound walls, in the handbreadth by the floor or the ceiling, where tapping tells nothing — because negligence is measured against the current state of the burglar's art, not against the customs of one's grandfather. The Shulchan Arukh's laws of interest, chapter 12 found at siman 177, keep the whole machinery in working order.

One more rule from the same chapter of the code completes the loss map, and it shows how honestly the machinery was built. Where no separate wage is paid and the parties stipulate nothing, Maimonides rules, the default division is asymmetric: the manager takes two thirds of any profit and bears only one third of any loss, the gap between the fractions being his wage for handling the entrusted half (6:3). Read that against chapter 10's baraita and the design leaps out. Near to profit and far from loss — the posture the tradition brands wicked in an investor — is the law's own default for the working partner, and it is not a lapse but a payment. The asymmetry that would be usury when capital buys it with drafting is justice when labor earns it with months; loss allocation, the rabbis are saying, follows contribution, and the manager's months are a contribution the settlement cannot give back.

Stand back from the details and look at what the instrument is doing. One venture, one purse, one man walking the market — and two complete, opposite answers to the question who loses, running side by side in the same coat. Market ruin on the loan half: the manager. Market ruin on the deposit half: the investor. Negligent ruin anywhere: the negligent. The iska never resolves the tension between loan and partnership; it declares it, half and half, and dares either party to claim confusion. A modern instrument that behaved this way would state on its face which fifty of your dollars were guaranteed and which fifty were genuinely at sea — and it is exactly the absence of such candor, chapters 37 and 38 will argue, that lets modern capital collect a partner's premium on a creditor's terms. The rabbis' contract could not lie about its downside, because its downside was its definition.

sections.title: The Trustee's Hands
paragraphs: The fiqh sorted every holder of another person's property into one of two postures, and the pair does more work in Islamic commercial law than any other distinction in this chapter. Property can sit in a yad al-daman, a guarantor's hand — the borrower's hand, the usurper's — where the holder owes the thing back whatever befalls it. Or it can sit in a yad al-amana, a trust-hand: the depositary's, the agent's, the partner's, the mudarib's — where the holder answers for his conduct but not for the world's, and the thing, if it perishes innocently, perishes to its owner.

Everything the tradition says about loss in the mudarabah unfolds from filing the mudarib under the second hand. He is an amin, a trustee. The capital in his saddlebags is not his and never becomes his; its market fortunes belong to the rabb al-mal as completely as its profits would have; and no clause may move him to the other hand — the classical rule, still printed in the modern standards chapter 10 cited, that the mudarib shall not guarantee the capital, and that a mudarabah stipulating such a guarantee has stopped being a mudarabah. The maxim the books attribute to the caliph Ali carried the loss half of the doctrine across the schools without dissent: loss follows the capital, whatever the profit agreement says. The severity runs both ways, as this book keeps finding. The financier who wants his money warranted has an instrument for that — it is called a loan, and it earns nothing; the financier who wants earnings has the mudarabah, and it warrants nothing. What he cannot have, in any school of the law, is the hybrid: the trustee's yield from a guarantor's hand.

But the trust-hand is a posture of conduct, and conduct can forfeit it. The jurists' liability switch has three settings, and the modern codifications state them in a formula so compact it reads like a fuse rating: the mudarib bears no loss absent his ta'addi, his taqsir, or his breach of the specified terms — transgression, negligence, or violation of the mandate. Transgression is doing what the contract never authorized; negligence is failing the care the undertaking demands; breach is crossing a fence the financier drew. Chapter 12 met the fences in the story of Abbas ibn Abd al-Muttalib, who released capital only on conditions — no sea carriage, no valleys, no livestock — and the fiqh's rule for the far side of the fence completes that story: step outside the mandate, and everything that happens out there happens to you. Inside the fence, outcomes belong to God and the market and therefore to the capital; outside it, or beneath the standard of care, or past the edge of honesty, they belong to the man who put them there. When the switch flips, the trustee becomes a debtor — not because he guaranteed anything, but because the loss stopped being weather and became conduct. The modern standards run the same current, in words worth quoting because a chapter about drafting should show the drafting: a manager of investment capital "is a guarantor of the capital, at its nominal value, in case of his negligent acts or omissions or his non-compliance with the investor's conditions" — whether he manages as mudarib, partner, or agent (AAOIFI's 2008 sukuk resolution, restating its standards).

Here is the fiqh's version of the line every tradition in this chapter draws, and it is worth stating at its full width because it answers one of the ToC's plainest questions — what separates ordinary business failure from culpable loss. Ordinary failure is the contract operating. The mudarabah prices uncertainty by seating the parties inside it; a season that answers no is the instrument telling the truth, and the loss it delivers is as lawful as the profit it might have delivered. Culpable loss is the contract violated: the venture's outcome manufactured by a party rather than found by the world. The first kind of loss stays on the map; the second moves, always, to its maker. And past negligence stands fraud, for which the tradition reached not for a partnership rule but for scripture. "You who believe, do not wrongfully consume each other's wealth but trade by mutual consent," runs the Qur'an's commercial cornerstone (4:29, in M. A. S. Abdel Haleem's rendering, as throughout this book) — a verse chapter 9 set at the foundation of the fraud rules, and chapter 23 will meet again at consent's edge. A manager who reports a loss that never happened, or hides a profit that did, has passed beyond mismanagement into consuming his partner's wealth by falsehood, and the whole apparatus of unlawful devouring — the Qur'an's own word for it — closes over the act.

One evidentiary note completes the portrait, and it says something about the tradition's temperament. The trustee's hand carries a presumption: the mudarib's account of an innocent loss stands unless the financier can prove the switch flipped — fault must be alleged and proved rather than presumed from an empty purse. A legal system that wanted to flatter capital would have run the presumption the other way, and made every failed agent a defendant. The fiqh trusted first, structurally, and spent its vigilance where chapter 11 located it: in the world of repeat engagements and carried names, where a suspicious loss cost an agent his livelihood more surely than any court could. How the traditions policed loss claims when documents replaced reputation — the oaths, the witnesses, the settlement formulas — belongs to the next chapter, where the heter iska's machinery gets its own accounting.

sections.title: Weather and Wrongdoing
paragraphs: Rome, as usual, had laid the grammar out first, and Latin Christendom, as usual, inherited the grammar and supplied it a conscience.

The societas allocated loss by agreement against a default of equality: partners share as they stipulate, the Digest's partnership title says at 17.2.29, and absent stipulation they share equally — with the one absolute boundary chapter 11 made famous, that no partner may be seated where he cannot lose at all, on pain of the arrangement being a lion's partnership and void. Within the map, the Roman question was the same one the fiqh asked: when does a partner's loss become his partner's fault? The answer sits farther down the same title, at 17.2.72, in the tri-grade grammar Roman lawyers applied to almost everything. For dolus — fraud, the designed injury — a partner answers always. For mere accident, casus, he answers never; accident lies where ownership put it. The middle grade is the interesting one. A partner answers his partner for culpa, for negligence — but the Digest declines to hold him to the meticulousness of the ideal custodian, the exactissima diligentia the law demanded elsewhere. The standard is diligentia quam in suis: a partner owes the common venture the care he habitually gives his own affairs, no more — and the fragment appends the tartest sentence in this chapter's sources by way of justification. Whoever takes on a careless partner, it observes, has only himself to blame — de se queri debet. You chose him; his ordinary sloppiness was part of what you chose; the law will protect you from his betrayals but not from his character.

It is a strange little standard at first meeting — liability graded to the defendant's own habits, so that the naturally careless man is judged by a gentler yardstick than the naturally careful one — and then its wisdom opens. Partnership is not a service purchased from a stranger; it is a joining of fates, entered with eyes open, and the law declines to let one partner demand, after the fact, a partner different from the one he shook hands with. What the standard preserves is precisely the weather. A man trading with his customary competence who guesses wrong about the price of pepper has not wronged his partner; he has been the partner he always was, in a world that answers to no one. Culpa begins where a man falls below his own norm — where the loss traces not to the world's uncertainty, nor to his settled nature, but to a lapse: care withheld from the common purse that he would have spent on his own. The Roman line and the fiqh's line land within a hair of each other, drawn from opposite ends: ta'addi and taqsir measure the agent against the undertaking's objective demands, diligentia quam in suis measures him against his own demonstrated self, and both are patrolling the same border between the loss that happens to a venture and the loss that is done to it.

The schoolmen took over the whole chassis — Aquinas's acquittal of the investing partner, chapter 11 found, turns on the money trading at the owner's risk, its gain licit tamquam de re sua — and what Christian moral theology added was less a new rule than a new insistence on why the rule mattered. Gain is honest, in the scholastic account, exactly where loss was possible and genuinely shareable: the merchant's profit is the stipendium of his labor and the fruit of his ventured property, and his losses are part of the same calling — the misjudgments of an honest trader are his own to eat, covered by no one, exactly as his skill is his own to sell. What the schoolmen would not allow was the sorting of loss by anything other than truth. A partner's fraud, in the confessors' analysis, belongs to theft and restitution rather than to usury — the sin reclassified by causation, because a man who manufactures his partner's loss has taken property, whatever instrument the two of them signed. And a financier who arranges immunity from loss while collecting a partner's gain commits the opposite falsehood: his contract asserts an exposure that does not exist. Naviganti, chapter 10's decretal, condemned the sea lender on precisely that reading — his premium was fixed, his exposure partial, his claim alive through every ordinary failure of the venture — and the same pontificate that blessed the commenda cursed him. Rome's civil lawyers, the rabbis of Babylonia, the jurists of Baghdad and Cordoba, and the canonists of Bologna disagreed about nearly everything else in this book. On the proposition that loss must lie where the contract's truth puts it — on ownership for weather, on the wrongdoer for wrong — they speak, without having conferred, in unison.

sections.title: The Geometry of Downside
paragraphs: Which brings us to the guarantee, the one device every tradition in this chapter prohibited by name, and the reason this chapter carries the title it does.

A guarantee, chapter 10 taught, destroys no risk; it readdresses the parcel. Within a partnership, that readdressing has a specific and fatal meaning. The instruments of Part IV all run on one engine — gain licensed by exposure — and a clause that removes a partner's exposure while preserving his gain does not merely tilt the deal; it stops the engine and leaves the body rolling on momentum and paperwork. The traditions' verdicts are interchangeable to a degree that still startles. Guarantee the iska's deposit half home whole, and the deposit dissolves into loan and the investor's yield into ribbit — the boundary chapter 11 marked as the structure's one unforgivable clause. Extract a guarantee of capital from the mudarib, and the mudarabah is void, the "profit share" riba in a partner's costume — the rule the standard-setters still print. The rabbis' character sketch at Bava Metzia 70a, which chapter 10 read, gives the arrangement its lasting portrait: the man seated near the gains and far from the losses is the baraita's wicked man, whatever his documents say. And when Latin Christendom's financiers finally engineered the thing in its perfected form — the contractus trinus, three separately licit contracts stacked into one guaranteed return, partnership plus capital insurance plus the sale of uncertain profit for a certain one — the papacy answered on October 25, 1586, with a bull whose first word is "detestable." Sixtus V's Detestabilis avaritia condemned every partnership pact providing that "the very principal, or capital be always safe" in the managing partner's hands, or that a fixed sum be paid "yearly, or monthly" as gain; declared such conventions "illicit and usurious," raising no obligation civil or natural; and then, in the same breath, restated this chapter's whole doctrine as the honest alternative — partnerships of money and labor formed "honestly, sincerely and with good faith," the contractors to cast up "the fruits, costs and losses, and let them share and divide them fairly and justly." That the fight did not end there — that Lessius and the century after him would defend the triple contract until the doctrine itself gave ground — is Part VIII's story, and chapter 11 already posted its signpost. What matters here is the shape of the objection, which never changed and which aimed past the greed at the falsehood: the triple contract labeled as partnership a position from which loss had been drafted away.

Why is the guarantee corrupting, rather than merely generous? Because the loss it removes from one seat does not leave the theater. Show me where the losses may not go, and I will tell you what the contract is. Route the venture's downside away from capital and it must land on the working partner — the arrangement every tradition condemned first and most fiercely, the worker underwriting the financier — or on some stranger to the venture, or on the truth itself: the loss unreported, renamed, rolled forward, buried in an account nobody may audit, which is the corruption chapter 14 will find waiting inside the heter iska's settlement clauses and chapter 32 inside instruments that replicate a bond in a partnership's clothing. The modern standard-setters patrol that corner with drafting of their own, and their texts repay reading. The guarantees standard forbids stipulating any guarantee in a fiduciary contract — for partnership managers it is "not permitted... to guarantee the capital, or to promise a guaranteed profit," nor may such contracts be "marketed or operated as a guaranteed investment" (AAOIFI Shari'ah Standard 5, art. 2/2/1) — because, the same standard explains, a guarantee from the man managing the investment "turns the transaction into an interest-based loan." What survives is exactly the residue the old lawyers would have watched: a guarantee volunteered outside the contract's walls, by a third party or even by the manager himself acting, the standard says, "in a different capacity" (art. 2/2/2), and the disclosed reserve account — built from the venture's own earnings against its own bad seasons, which is no guarantee at all but the pool of chapter 3 wearing modern dress. The seam strains where it always strained: a promise that may not be sold inside the contract stands just beside it. Chapter 26 meets the arrangement doing heavy lifting under modern sukuk, and the tradition's own critics, chapter 32 will show, have said the sharpest things about it. The diagnostic, in every century, is the one this chapter has been assembling: find the seats the drafting has made incapable of loss, and you have found the parties who are no longer partners, whatever the cover page announces.

That diagnostic deserves its full name, because Parts IX and X of this book intend to use it as an engineer uses a level. Call it the moral geometry of downside. Every venture, chapter 10's conservation law says, carries a fixed load of possible loss, and every contract distributes that load across the people in the room — visibly or invisibly, honestly or not. The upside arrangements tell you what the parties hoped; the downside map tells you what they are. Read a modern financing the way the rabbis read the baraita's postures — by where each party sits when the venture fails — and the familiar instruments confess with remarkable speed: the liquidation waterfall is nothing but a loss map with the losses at the bottom, drafted distance from ruin, priced and sold by the tier; chapter 37 runs that arithmetic in the traditions' terms. The seats nearest the loss, chapter 38 will show, are held disproportionately by the people who never saw the map — workers, founders, the small and the late — and chapter 10's sober accounting of shifted risk is really this chapter's doctrine read at industrial scale. And beneath the whole geometry sits the fact the traditions grasped in their bones and the mathematics of chapter 28 will state exactly: a loss allocated to a seat is lived there as a sequence rather than an average, and some seats can be ruined — which is why the seating of the downside deserves to be read as a deal's substance and not its fine print.

The old lawyers would want one more thing said, because everything in this chapter can sound like a machinery of blame, and it was built as a machinery of peace. An honest venture, honestly failed, ends. That is the gift the instruments of chapter 11 gave the people who used them: the investor's loss stopped at his stake, the traveler's at his season, and nobody left the accounting owing anybody a life of installments. The traditions built contracts that knew how to die — cleanly, all losses suffered, all losses final — because they had seen the alternative, the claim that failure cannot kill, walking through every farm and workshop of the ancient world with a ledger in its hand. Loss allocation is the truth of the contract, and the truth had a mercy in it. But an ended venture leaves one question standing, and it is the last one Part IV must answer. The losses have found their seats; the survivors are looking at what remains in the till; and before anyone touches it, somebody must say what part of it is actually profit — what the venture must first pay its costs, its people, its reserves, and its future before anyone may call the remainder his. That is chapter 14's question — why profit must come from profit — and the traditions' answers to it turn out to guard the same wall this chapter has been walking, from the inside.

chapters.part: Part IV — Partnership as the Great Escape from Usury

chapters.title: Profit Must Come from Profit
chapters.label: Chapter 14

paragraphs: The caravan is home. Say it came up from the Yemen coast with the winter convoy, and that the mudarib who took it out three years ago is sitting tonight in a Fustat courtyard with his investor, a lamp, a scale, and the sacks and bales of everything the venture now is: pepper sold and silver taken, flax traded for indigo, a bad debt in Aden written on a scrap of paper, a donkey nobody has valued yet. Tomorrow, before witnesses, the accounting. And at the center of the accounting sits a question this Part has been circling for three chapters and must now answer head-on, because every rule the traditions built comes to a point exactly here, at the table where the money is divided. The investor's capital comes off the top first — that much every school agreed. The ratio bites what remains. But what remains? Which of these coins are the venture given back, and which are the venture's increase? Until that question is answered, the ratio has nothing to bite; and how a legal system answers it — what it lets the parties call profit, and when — turns out to be the deepest test of whether its partnerships are honest.

Chapter 12 priced the labor. Chapter 13 seated the losses. This chapter completes the arch: it asks what may honestly be called profit, and it defends the answer the three traditions gave in unison — profit is what a venture actually produced, counted after everything the venture owes, and nothing else may wear the name. The negative form of the rule sounds almost too simple: no one may claim profit before real profit exists. Yet each tradition spent centuries fortifying that simplicity against a single, endlessly renewed assault — the attempt to write the profit down in advance, as a number, in the contract itself. So the chapter starts with the assault.

sections.title: The Number Written in Advance
paragraphs: Recall what makes a partnership lawful in every legal system this book reads: the investor's return rides the outcome. Now watch what a fixed return does to that architecture — not a tilted ratio, which chapter 12 defended, but a stipulated number: pay me a hundred and twelve next Michaelmas; pay me two dirhams a month per hundred; guarantee me, as the bull Detestabilis avaritia condemned in 1586, "yearly, or monthly... a certain sum" for the life of the company.

The corruption is not that the number is greedy. It may be modest — modesty was never the point, and when Benedict XIV's Vix pervenit met the argument that a moderate charge on a loan should pass, it rejected the adjective outright: the doctrine was never about the size of the gain but about its source. The corruption is that the number is written. A stipulated return is knowable before the venture does anything, which means it is not a share of what the venture does; it is a claim that merely uses the venture as its address. The moment the investor holds it, three things die quietly inside the partnership. His exposure dies, because a fixed claim is precisely what chapter 13 watched the guarantee create — a seat from which loss has been drafted away, the near-to-profit-far-from-loss posture the baraita calls wicked. His interest in the venture's truth dies, because a man owed a hundred and twelve in every state of the world has no further question to ask about the world; the books may say anything. And the working partner's claim dies last and worst, because a fixed charge, unlike a ratio, does not shrink when the harvest does — it eats out of the venture's substance in the bad year, out of wages and stock and seed corn, exactly the way chapter 10 watched the sea lender's premium survive every ordinary failure of the voyage. Rome's lawyers had refused the naked version — the lion who takes gain without loss — and the traditions refused the actuarial version dressed as a partner's share. The stipulated number is the loan's payoff smuggled into the partnership's clothing, and all three systems, meeting it, said the same word: void.

Run the two payoffs through one bad year and the incidence shows plainly. A venture of a hundred comes home worth ninety-eight. Under a ratio, the investor's share of profit is a share of nothing: the two-coin loss falls where chapter 13 seated it, and the books close. Under a stipulated twelve, the venture owes a hundred and twelve out of ninety-eight, and the twelve is paid — if it is paid — out of capital, out of wages withheld, out of stock sold at the wrong moment; out of the venture's body, since its increase does not exist. The fixed number does not merely misdescribe the bad year. It bills it, and a charge that collects out of substance in precisely the seasons there is no increase is this book's oldest acquaintance in its newest coat.

Their alternative is the instrument this Part has been assembling piece by piece: the ratio. A half, a third, two-fifths of profit — the commenda's three-quarters to the stans, the Talmud's tilted splits, the mudarabah's freely bargained fractions. It is worth pausing on what an odd object a ratio is, because familiarity has made it invisible. A ratio is a number that cannot be computed. Signed on the dock, it says nothing at all about what the investor will receive; it is an algebra with one variable missing, and the missing variable is the future. Only when the venture comes home — when the pepper is sold, the debts are collected or mourned, the costs are paid — does the ratio acquire a value, and the value it acquires is manufactured out of the venture's actual story and nothing else. A ratio asks the world what happened; a rate tells the calendar what is owed. That single design difference carries the whole moral load. The rate-holder is a creditor whatever he is called, because his claim matures by the mere passage of dates — the agar natar, the wage of waiting, that chapter 7 found at the forbidden core. The ratio-holder cannot collect a coin until there is truth on the table: an accounting, a valuation, a real remainder. The traditions did not merely prefer the ratio; they built their entire licensing of investment on the fact that a ratio is, structurally, a question — and a question, unlike a demand, keeps everyone honest who must answer it.

sections.title: The Ratio's Discipline
paragraphs: The fiqh states the prohibition with the most doctrinal machinery, and its machinery repays a close look because every gear exists to protect the same thing: the connection between the word "profit" and an actual remainder.

Begin with the rule chapter 11 met at the contract's founding: the mudarabah's profit clause must be a fraction of profit — of profit, not of anything else. Stipulate the rabb al-mal a fixed sum and the contract is void; stipulate him a percentage of the capital — ten on every hundred, however the venture fares — and it is equally void, because a percentage of capital is just a fixed sum wearing arithmetic. The modern codifications keep both bans in force: no guaranteed profit, no pre-determined amount to either party, the working partner's ratio his only compensation. The schools quarreled, as chapter 11 noted, over how far profit shares could stray from capital shares in the musharakah — the Shafi'i and Maliki masters required profit to track capital exactly, invest two-fifths and take two-fifths, any contrary clause voiding the contract, while the Hanafi and Hanbali schools let agreed ratios diverge from capital shares, since one partner's work, skill, or standing may be worth paying for; chapter 12's whole argument lives inside that second position. But notice what even the strict schools were policing: proportion between partners — fairness in the division of a real remainder. About the form of the claim there was no quarrel anywhere: profit shares bite realized profit; loss follows capital, pro rata, in every school; and nothing upstream of realization may be promised, priced, or paid as if it were profit.

Then the discipline that gives the rule teeth: you may not call it realized until the capital is whole. The jurists' working principle — there is no profit until the capital is made good — runs through the classical books as consensus, and it does an enormous amount of quiet work. Interim gains are not yet anyone's; a good first year followed by a bad second has produced, in the law's eyes, whatever the whole story produced, and early distributions are advances against a truth not yet known. The modern standards preserve the principle with accountants' precision, and the drafting is worth quoting because it shows a medieval doctrine alive inside modern paragraph numbering. The mudarib's entitlement to his share arises when profit appears, says the AAOIFI mudarabah standard, but "this entitlement is not absolute, as it is subject to the retention of interim profits for the protection of the capital"; it hardens into a right only at distribution, "when actual or constructive valuations take place" — the final division made on what the assets actually sold for, or, where the venture continues, on a sober fair-value reckoning. And the same article reaches the subtlest corner of the counting-room with a rule the scholastics would have stood and applauded: receivables — the venture's uncollected promises — enter the reckoning at their cash-equivalent value, "after the deduction of a provision for doubtful debts," and in valuing them "neither time value (interest rate) nor discount... shall be taken into consideration." Sit with that for a moment. Inside the arithmetic that decides what may be called profit, the tradition polices its own founding prohibition: even here, especially here, time is not money. A paper claim on next year is worth its honest collectibility, not a penny more for the waiting, because the moment waiting acquires a price inside the profit computation, the whole quarantine has failed from within.

The standards even domesticated the impatience. Profits may be distributed early, "on account" — the phrase is the drafters' own — provided the distribution is revised when the real valuation arrives: early money is provisional money, an advance against a truth not yet known, callable back if the truth disappoints. What may never be arranged is the reverse. The 2008 resolution forbids a manager to undertake to cover shortfalls with loans in the same breath that it permits the disclosed reserve chapter 13 met — because smoothing paid out of the venture's own retained truth is honest, and smoothing paid out of borrowed pretense is the old sin with better cash management.

The halakha ran the same discipline through its own instrument. The iska's settlement, chapter 13 showed from the Rambam's codification, unwinds the halves in order — the loan half restored in every world, the deposit half restored from what the venture holds, and only then a division of increase, computed on what actually happened, with the manager's asymmetric fractions doing their labor-pricing work. And Rome, with characteristic economy, had put the whole principle in the design of the societas itself: the partnership's gain was whatever the common venture held above its contributions when the accounts were struck — Cassius's condition, chapter 12 found, priced even a partner's labor against the loss, which is to say the Roman lawyers were netting contributions and outcomes against each other from the very beginning. Three legal languages again, and one grammar: profit is a conclusion. It sits at the end of an audited story — capital restored, costs paid, claims proven — and every attempt to move it forward in time, toward the signing table and away from the truth, is the same attempt this book has been tracking since the wall went up: to be paid as an owner of outcomes while standing somewhere outcomes cannot reach.

sections.title: The Oath and the Fee
paragraphs: And yet the most instructive document in this chapter is the one where the discipline bends — because watching exactly where and how a tradition lets its own machinery flex shows what the machinery was for.

Chapter 11 introduced the shtar iska's descendant, the heter iska, and chapter 31 will follow its enormous modern career, in which the instrument stands behind the interest-bearing operations of banks serving observant communities. Here is the joint on which everything turns. An iska investor's return, we have seen, is licensed by the deposit half's genuine exposure, and chapter 13 left the verification question standing: the venture's truth lives with the manager, so how does the investor ever collect without simply taking the manager's word? The classical documents answered with evidence law. The condition the tradition attributes to the Maharam of Lublin, and which the later standard forms adopted, runs in two halves: a claim of loss is believed only on the testimony of acceptable witnesses; a claim of low profit — less than the figure the parties named — is believed only under a biblical oath. Both halves are exquisitely calibrated to the theology of testimony: losses are public events, the kind witnesses can know; profits are ledger events, the kind only an oath can reach. And the documents added a third clause, the one that made the instrument's fortune: the manager may decline the oath and pay the named figure instead — the specified return, which the modern forms allow to be a fixed sum, a percentage, even a number keyed to prevailing interest rates — and upon paying it he owes no verification at all.

Run the machine forward and watch what it produces. An observant merchant takes financing under a heter iska. The venture does what ventures do. At term, he can open his books to witnesses, swear a biblical oath about his profits — an act the tradition regards with a seriousness modern readers must work to recover; the documents could even stipulate the oath be taken publicly, in the synagogue — or he can pay the named figure and be done. Almost everyone pays. The oath is heavy, the books are private, the figure was set with exactly this outcome in mind; paying-in-lieu is not an abuse of the instrument but, as the halakhic literature itself says plainly, a basic premise of how it functions. The result, visible from any distance: a stream of fixed periodic payments, sized like interest, timed like interest, keyed — in the modern forms — to the same benchmarks as interest, flowing under a document whose every clause is partnership.

Scale then finished what convenience began. The modern instrument's furthest form is the heter iska klali — the general iska, one master document executed by an institution and covering, prospectively, every depositor and borrower who ever walks in. The compendia record the halakhists' own unease in nearly comic register: some proposed hanging the document on the wall of the establishment, others objected that a sign nobody reads binds nobody; the banks of Israel fold the heter iska into their standard terms, and the posekim reason, with impeccable contemporary realism, that a customer is bound by an institution's known conditions whether or not he has read them. The debate is its own portrait of the instrument's late career: a partnership form so successful at wearing a loan's face that the last live question is whether anyone on either side of the counter remembers the partnership is there.

The tradition knows. That is what makes this section instructive rather than scandalous, and the internal debate is precise about where the live nerve sits. May a manager who knows there was no profit pay the fee anyway, buying his way past an oath about a fact he could truthfully swear to? A minority of authorities balks exactly there — at the point where the payment stops summarizing an uncertain truth and starts replacing a known one. The majority answers with the instrument's own logic: the fee was bargained as the price of not verifying, the investor genuinely cannot know the books, the manager is buying peace and privacy, and both parties walked in with open eyes. Meanwhile the same literature patrols the boundary that would turn candor into farce: a document naming as valid witnesses only men in a far city who cannot possibly know the venture is invalid — verification that cannot occur is not verification; an iska written over investments that are inherently unverifiable, hidden holdings no witness could ever attest, cannot carry a witnesses-clause at all. The line the poskim are holding, through every refinement, is the line this whole chapter defends: the structure must keep a real, live channel to the venture's actual outcome. Narrow the channel, price the passage, let commerce buy its convenience — but the moment the channel is drawn on paper in a way that can never carry truth at all, the instrument stops being an iska with a toll and becomes a loan with a costume. Whether the modern instrument, at scale, still keeps the channel open — whether anyone, anywhere in a heter iska banking system, is really being asked about outcomes — is the hard question of chapter 31, and the tradition's own posekim are its sharpest interrogators. What Part IV takes from the document is its unembarrassed honesty about the tension: the heter iska is a machine for living beside the profit rule under commercial pressure, and its drafters left the seams showing — the witnesses, the oath, the fee — precisely because a seam you can see is a seam a court can police.

sections.title: Proportion and the Actual
paragraphs: Latin Christendom's contribution to this chapter is a pair of measuring instruments: one for the share, one for the substance.

The share first. Scholastic partnership doctrine inherited Rome's rule that shares follow agreement against a default of equality, valid wherever a partner "contributed something more — of money, of labor, or of any other thing" — and moralized it into a doctrine of proportion: gain is honest when it answers to contribution, each partner's fraction a judgment about what each brought. Chapter 12 walked the components — ventured capital earning tamquam de re sua, work earning its stipendium laboris — and the just-price machinery of chapter 9 supplied the background conviction that exchanges answer to something real. What the schoolmen added at this chapter's doorstep is the other instrument: a test for whether there is anything real to share. Their word for it was actual. Gain had to trace to an actual venture, actual labor, actual cost, actual peril — and the most quotable statement of the principle came, fittingly, from the same council session that approved the era's great experiment in non-profit lending. In 1515, blessing the Monti di Pietà — whose small charge was allowed as "a moderate sum for their expenses and by way of compensation," intended "exclusively to defray the expenses of those employed," and "provided that no profit is made therefrom," a story chapter 17 tells whole — the Fifth Lateran Council paused to define the enemy, and its definition is the entire chapter in one sentence: "For, that is the real meaning of usury: when, from its use, a thing which produces nothing is applied to the acquiring of gain and profit without any work, any expense or any risk."

Read the definition backward and it becomes a construction manual. Honest gain requires a thing that produces — a venture, a field, a workshop, something with actual fruit in it — and it requires the claimant's presence inside the producing: his work, his expense, his risk, in some real combination. Usury is the null case on both axes at once: barren source, absent claimant. That is why the tradition could bless the Monti's charge in the same breath — costs actually incurred, recovered without a grain of profit, fail both halves of the definition's accusation — and it is why the scholastics' term lucrum cessans, profit merely hoped for elsewhere, spent centuries under suspicion the moment claimants tried to collect it as if hope were harvest; Part VI re-opens that file.

The same instinct for the actual disciplined the doctrine's own exceptions. When Vix pervenit restated the tradition in 1745, chapter 7 noted, it left carefully standing the titles that can arise alongside a loan — but every title on that list is a claim about something actual: a loss suffered and shown, a gain concretely interrupted, a default that in fact occurred. The door the encyclical held open was a door for facts, never for numbers written in advance. And where contribution itself needed pricing, the tradition let real markets do the measuring. The commenda's standard splits — three-quarters against a quarter in the one-sided form, half against half where the traveler also ventured a third of the coin — are chapter 11's textbook figures, and they are proportionality quoted at the going rate: the Mediterranean's own long-run judgment of what a season of a man's life was worth beside a season of a man's money. The Catholic instruments and the fiqh's converge from opposite workshops onto the same specification: the one polices the claim's proportion to real contribution, the other polices the profit's derivation from real remainder, and both refuse the word "profit" to any number that was written before the world answered.

sections.title: The Till, Truly Counted
paragraphs: Which leaves the counting itself — and here the old doctrine turns its face directly toward the modern reader, because the assault on the profit rule did not end when stipulated returns went out of fashion. It moved inside the books.

Consider what must be true before the pile on the table contains any profit at all. The capital must be back — both traditions' first rule, Rome's netting, the standards' retention-for-protection. The costs must be paid: the venture's own keep, the road and the warehouse, the mudarib's lodging that chapter 12 saw charged to the venture's purse rather than the worker's hide. The wages must be paid — not as a courtesy after the split but as a claim before it, the entire lesson of sechar tircha and the idle laborer's wage: labor is a cost of producing the surplus, and a "surplus" computed by leaving labor unpaid is not a surplus but a confiscation with good bookkeeping. The venture's known wounds must be provided for — the doubtful debt in Aden written down at what it is honestly worth, the standards' provision "for doubtful debts" doing in modern dress what the sworn accounting did on the quay. And something must be held against tomorrow — the reserve that chapter 13 watched the modern standards bless as the licit alternative to guarantee, the venture's future standing as a quiet claimant at its own settlement table. Only after that procession — capital, costs, wages, provisions, reserves — does a remainder appear that the traditions were willing to call by the name. Profit is a remainder, and a remainder cannot be promised. It can only be found, at the end, by counting honestly; which is why chapter 11's formula — a partner's return is discovered, never written — was always an accounting doctrine wearing a moral one, or the reverse; the traditions would not have recognized the distinction.

Honest counting, notice, is not free. Every device in this chapter costs somebody something — the sworn accounting on the quay, the witnesses, the valuations actual and constructive, the provisions argued line by line — and chapter 11 named the temptation that expense whispers into every investor's ear: wouldn't you rather just be owed the number? The written return is, among its other characters, a refusal to pay the audit's toll. The traditions kept paying it, century after century, because the toll purchases the one thing the fixed claim can never deliver — a payout that is true. Modern practice has even learned to skip the counting altogether: a distribution financed by fresh borrowing declares a surplus no operation ever produced, profit conjured out of an enlarged claim on the future, the stipulated return's logic run backward through the till.

Now name the modern inversion, because the ToC does: profit before wages, reserves, and mission. A venture that declares distributable surplus while its workers are underpaid against any honest measure of their contribution has moved labor's claim below capital's in the very computation chapter 12 spent itself ordering the other way. A venture that distributes while running its reserves to the bone has spent its own future as if the future were income — handed tomorrow's anti-ruin cushion, chapter 10's vocabulary, to today's claimants. And the mission — the purpose the enterprise exists to serve, the care of the town, the craft, the customers, the commons — can be liquidated into "surplus" a quarter at a time without any single act of theft, merely by counting it as nothing; the charters Part X studies exist, in large part, to make that particular zero impossible to book. Each of these produces a number that looks like profit, audits like profit, and distributes like profit, and each is the stipulated return's quieter descendant: a claim paid out of the venture's substance rather than its increase, extraction booking itself as fruitfulness. The old lawyers had a whole taxonomy for gain that traced to no real remainder, and Part IX — where founder labor, worker claims, true surplus, and the non-extractive return formula get their modern accounting, chapters 38 through 40 — is in large part the exercise of running their taxonomy through a contemporary income statement. Chapter 39 will even take this chapter's question for its title: what, truly counted, is surplus?

The traditions' answer, assembled across this whole Part, fits in a breath. Surplus is fruitfulness — the tokos question of chapter 1 finally answered in the affirmative register. Aristotle called interest the unnatural offspring of a barren parent; the partnership doctrines are the traditions' portrait of the natural kind: real increase, born of a fruitful venture and present human effort, counted after every honest claim, shared in proportion to contribution, by people who stood inside the story. Where those conditions hold, all three traditions not only permit the gain — they praise it, defend it, and build their commercial civilizations on it. Where any fails, the gain is extraction wearing increase's face, whatever instrument delivers it: a stipulated sum, a guaranteed partnership, a fee that replaces a known truth, a distribution carved out of wages or reserves or mission. So Part IV closes by adding its third stone to the rule of the gate. Chapter 12: every real contribution priced. Chapter 13: every loss in its true seat. And now: no profit claim before real profit exists — the payout waits for the world, counts everything the venture owes, and takes only what is genuinely left.
