The loss must be actual — arisen, nameable, not the standing condition of being without one's money, which is simply what lending is; a lender who calls the bare absence of his coin an injury is pricing time again, and the tradition sent that claim to a different file, where chapter 21 will find it. It must be caused — by the borrower's failure or by the transaction's own external burden, not by the lender's imprudence or the ordinary weather of markets; a borrower answers for the losses his conduct made, not for his creditor's whole commercial life. It must be shown — narrated, dated, totaled; a wound that cannot answer questions is a story. It must be proportioned — repair runs to the injury's edge and stops, and whatever crosses that edge has left the title and needs another name. And it may be counted once: a delay already avenged under a penalty clause may not bleed again as damages — one wound, two names — though the penalty's side of that seam belongs to chapter 22's file. None of these fences is decorative. Remove any one and the title turns, quietly and lawfully, into the very thing it was built against.

What happened next is the part of the story modern finance would recognize as its own biography. Commerce thickened; money stopped sitting still; chains of obligation ran through the fairs so that one missed repayment could topple a row of promises, each fall a documentable cost. The title standardized — the safest claim in the confessors' manuals — and its scope grew with the commercial world's genuine capacity to be wounded. The theologians of Salamanca spent their best casuistry on it: Domingo de Soto holding the cautious line, insisting the word "damage" never float free of proof; Luis de Molina integrating the title with the civil lawyers' machinery, so that a sum agreed in advance against breach is honest exactly insofar as it estimates probable, provable, real loss, and a disguised rate exactly insofar as it does not; Leonardus Lessius, whom the merchants of Antwerp consulted and who is remembered for carrying his questions onto the exchange itself, mapping how loss, foregone gain, and risk overlap in a working merchant's affairs. Then Juan de Lugo, in Rome, gathered the family into a synthesis — his great treatise on justice appeared in 1642 — reading foregone profit and imperiled principal as varieties of one broad category of compensable detriment. It was the most powerful statement the doctrine ever received, and the most dangerous, for a reason the reader can finish before the sentence does: the broader "loss" grows, the less it excludes, and a category that once repaired burned barns becomes available to anything a clever claimant can describe as a wound. When Benedict XIV's Vix pervenit restated the center in 1745 — from the loan itself, never; from genuine titles outside it, possibly — the restatement was necessary, chapter 7 saw, precisely because the century's best minds had built this title an empire. The door that document holds open is the door this chapter walked through; the audit's remaining work is making sure of what comes through with it.

sections.title: A Loss Must Testify
paragraphs: The halakha ran the same audit inside a different courtroom, because its actual-loss problem lived inside its own investment contract. Chapter 13 drew the iska's loss map: half the capital a loan, the manager's property and the manager's peril; half a deposit, trading at the investor's risk, that risk being the entire license for the investor's gain; negligence anywhere moving the loss to the negligent. On that map, the rule that the investor bears the deposit half's honest losses is the load-bearing wall — and it creates an exquisite problem of knowledge. The venture's truth lives with the manager. He kept the books, walked the markets, watched the cargo sell or fail to sell. If his bare word could seat a loss on the investor's capital, what would the investor's exposure be worth? Every mediocre year could be reported as a wounded one, and the very openness to loss that makes the investor's gain lawful would make him his manager's insurance.

So the tradition priced the claim in the currency courts respect: evidence. The machinery, which chapter 14 walked clause by clause through the heter iska's documents, runs on a division its drafters took from the theology of testimony itself — a claimed loss is believed only on the word of acceptable witnesses, because losses are public events, the kind the world sees; a claimed shortfall of profit is believed only under oath, because profits are ledger events, known finally to the man who kept the ledger. What matters to this chapter is not the machinery but the principle under it. Loss-language is cheap, and the halakha made it testify. A loss that wants to cross from the manager's mouth to the investor's account must arrive with its papers in order — which is, note, the same demand the scholastics were writing into the confessional in the same centuries, aimed the other way. The Latin doctrine polices the lender who claims a wound against his borrower; the halakha polices the manager who claims one against his financier's capital. Opposite claimants, and one shared instinct: whoever brings the claim, an actual loss is a fact with witnesses, or it is a story.

The Talmud had set the tone long before the standard documents. Rava rules on the manager of an iska who suffered a genuine loss, then labored until later gains replaced it, and told the investor nothing (Bava Metzia 105a): at settlement he may not reopen the ledger and say, bear the old loss with me. The Gemara answers him out of his own motives: for this you toiled and made it good — so that men would not call you a loser of ventures. The ruling is small and its edges are sharp. An actual loss is an event in an account, not an anecdote available at settlement; a wound the venture's own later gains have healed has ceased to exist, whatever it cost the manager's pride to heal it; and a loss claim is presented fresh or not at all. Buried in the ruling is an accounting principle this chapter will shortly meet again wearing Arabic: recovery precedes division. Gains fill the hole before anyone may call them gain.

And the halakha's own lender — the creditor this chapter opened with, damaged by his borrower's failure? Here the rabbis were stingier than the schoolmen, and the stinginess was policy. The wage of waiting is forbidden outright — chapter 7's agar natar — and how the law disciplines a delaying debtor without ever selling him time, along with which of a creditor's losses from delay it deliberately declined to price, is chapter 22's file. But one paragraph of the codes shows the tradition drawing exactly this chapter's line in its own hand. A litigant who wins his case collects, as a rule, nothing for the cost of the litigating: the codified rule is blunt that the loser is not obliged to make good his opponent's expenses, though the suit dragged the winner to a court in another city (Shulchan Arukh, Choshen Mishpat 14:5). Going to law is the price of living under law; process is nobody's wound. But let the defendant refuse the court — ignore the summons, force the plaintiff to spend money compelling his appearance — and the same paragraph reverses: now he pays all the expenses his defiance caused. Read the two halves together and they are causation doctrine in miniature. The ordinary costs of pursuing a right lie where they fall; the costs manufactured by a man's wrongful conduct follow the conduct home. A defendant defying the court's summons and a borrower defaulting in Molina's Castile were answerable, on this point, to one idea — expense caused by fault is a compensable wound, and expense caused by life is not.

sections.title: Furnishing the Reason
paragraphs: Islam's actual-loss doctrine begins where its usury law begins, in the settlement terms of the war verse. When the Qur'an commanded believers to abandon their outstanding increase or know themselves at war, it stated the repentant lender's entitlement in a clause chapter 6 read whole: "You shall have your capital if you repent, and without suffering loss or causing others to suffer loss" (2:279, in M. A. S. Abdel Haleem's rendering, as throughout this book). La tazlimuna wa-la tuzlamun, runs the Arabic close: you do not wrong, and you are not wronged. The clause is this entire chapter in one sentence. The lender is restored to his capital, all of it — the settlement does not fine him for repenting — and he is stopped at his capital: above it he wrongs, below it he is wronged. Restoration full, enrichment none — the boundary the schoolmen spent their casuistry fencing is drawn here in the founding text, as a condition of peace.

Inside the fiqh's own investment contract the doctrine turns technical, and the technical word is the right one: impairment. Chapter 13 filed the mudarib among the trustees — the capital in his saddlebags never his, its market losses falling on the rabb al-mal as completely as its profits would, his liability switching on only at fault. The modern standards state the file with an accountant's flatness the classical jurists would have recognized as their own. "A loss is depletion from the value of capital," states Malaysia's central-bank standard on the contract — loss defined as a fact about the capital rather than a feeling about the year — and the trustee is not answerable "for any impairment of asset" unless the loss traces to his "misconduct," his "negligence," or his "breach of specified terms" — ta'addi, taqsir, mukhalafah al-shurut, the fault grammar chapter 13 anatomized, now wearing its Arabic labels: weather to the owner, fault to its author. But the clause this chapter exists to notice is the quieter one beside those: in the case of loss, the standard directs, the mudarib shall "furnish the reason for the occurrence of loss." There is the witnesses-rule again, in regulatory prose. A loss is not a number the trustee reports; it is an event he must narrate — what happened, when, from what cause — because the presumption run in the honest trustee's favor is a presumption about honest men, not a dispensation from bookkeeping. The fiqh and the halakha, sharing so much anatomy in these contracts, share this too: the capital's owner bears the true wounds, and truth is established, never merely asserted.

Then the standards do the arithmetic of healing, and it is Rava's arithmetic. The classical rule — the schools state it as consensus, and the industry's standard-setters print it still — is that a running mudarabah has no profit until the capital stands whole: losses are made good from the venture's own gains before any gain exists to divide, and what the working partner draws mid-venture he draws provisionally, on account, his unsettled share described in the standards' own idiom as held back as a protection for the capital until the final reckoning, when the venture is wound up in fact or valued as though it were and the account finally speaks. Set that beside the manager of Bava Metzia 105a, who filled the hole and could not afterward dig it up again, and the two traditions are keeping one ledger discipline in two languages. Recovery precedes distribution. A venture's wounds heal out of the venture's own flesh first; "profit" is the name of what remains once the capital has been made whole; and impairment is measured on the whole story — netted, cumulative, final only at the end — never cherry-picked transaction by transaction toward whichever reading flatters the claimant. Chapter 14 built its argument on the profit half of that sentence. This chapter adds the loss half, and notes the symmetry: a tradition that would not let profit be declared before it existed was never going to let loss be charged before it emerged.

One more piece completes the strand. When the modern industry met the lender-side problem squarely — the financed customer in default, the institution genuinely out of pocket — it reached for this chapter's title and split repair from punishment with a cleanness the schoolmen would have envied: compensation capped at the institution's actual, shown loss, and everything punitive routed away to charity — machinery that belongs to chapter 22's file and gets its full hearing there, critics included. What the Islamic strand contributes to this file, distinctively, is the refusal at its foundation. At no point, in any of its instruments, is "loss" allowed to become an asset of the lender's. It is a fact about capital, borne by capital's owner, moved only by fault, escorted always by an account of itself, and bounded on both sides by the war verse's terms of peace — no wronging, and no being wronged.

sections.title: The Average and the Event
paragraphs: Modern credit does something with loss that no scholastic imagined, and the difference is the sharpest analytical edge this chapter can hand a present-day reader. A modern lender prices loss before it happens. Chapter 10 stood in front of that machinery at full strength — expected loss, the chance of default multiplied by its cost, priced into every loan on the book so that the many who repay fund the losses of the few who cannot — and reported what the arrangement does to the people who must live it one path at a time. What belongs to this chapter is the categorical point underneath: an expected loss and an actual loss are not the same kind of object, and the whole title hangs on the difference. An expected loss is a price; an actual loss has an address. The expected loss lives in the lender's models — a property of a portfolio, smooth, attached in advance to everyone, caused by no one, suffered by no one in particular. The actual loss lives in the world: it happened on a date, to a person, from a cause, in an amount. Damnum emergens compensates the second and only the second — after the event, from its author, in its measure. The discipline is not squeamishness about mathematics. A charge collected in advance, from every borrower, whether or not the wound ever occurs, is not repair; what it sells is the possibility of loss, and the possibility of loss is simply lending itself, the one thing the wall forbids the lender to sell at all.

None of this outlaws prudence. An institution may hold reserves; one that did not would be gambling with money the community trusted to it, and the funded reserve is among this book's honored instruments. But a reserve is the pool's tool — built from named contributions against the book's bad years, at home in chapter 27's architecture — and the discipline is naming. Book reserve-building as "damages" and a communal buffer has been converted into a per-borrower fine for a wound no borrower caused. The moral ledger begins at the label, and the label must say what the money is for.

The same sorting settles the question this chapter's brief calls administrative loss, because "administration" names two different things a lending institution spends. The first is the ordinary running of the counter — the appraiser, the clerk, the vault, the ledger. That is not a wound at all; it is work and expense, and the tradition titled it honestly as such: the stipendium laboris of chapter 12, the recovery the Fifth Lateran Council licensed for the Monti in the settlement chapter 17 told — "a moderate sum for their expenses and by way of compensation," "intended exclusively to defray the expenses of those employed," and, the clause bearing all the weight, "provided that no profit is made therefrom." The mercy institutions of Part V run the same discipline at their own chosen severities: the gemach ideal of chapter 15, where donations carry the overhead and the loan comes home clean; the qard hasan rule chapter 16 reported, actual servicing cost per transaction and nothing indirect — salaries, rent, the building itself expressly unbillable to the borrower, because the alternative loads mercy's overhead onto the people least able to carry it. Across all of them the shape is identical: sustainability licensed, priced off an auditable cost ledger, pointed downward by design; profit from the need to borrow, never. The second thing "administration" names is different in kind — the workout, the collection file, the second appraisal, the lawyer: administration that a particular default made necessary. That is damnum proper, caused expense chargeable to its causer, on proof, at cost, after the sorting of cannot-pay from will-not-pay that every tradition demands before any remedy fires. Two files, one counter. An institution that keeps them separate can sustain itself without extracting; an institution that merges them has found the oldest door out of the wall — bill the running of the shop to the borrowers as "losses," and the shop will profit by the poor exactly as if no wall stood.

sections.title: When Repair Becomes Revenue
paragraphs: Every fence this chapter has walked was built because someone had been caught climbing it, and the climbs have not changed in five centuries; only the drafting has improved. The classic moves are four. The wound can be invented — a loss asserted that never occurred, a fee that answers to no event. It can be inflated — real damage priced past itself, the hundred-florin injury healed at three hundred. It can be pre-priced — written into the contract as a standing sum payable however the world turns, at which point it has stopped describing anything and become the price of time under a nobler name. And it can be double-billed — one delay collected as penalty, again as damages, again as fee, four clauses nursing one wound, each collection past repair being precisely a surplus with no title under it. Behind all four stands the oldest test the tradition owns, older than any of the drafting: watch the direction of the lender's hope. Chapter 8 met it in Consuluit — the mere hope of gain from a loan is enough to convict — and it reads a damages clause as easily as it read a friendly gift. A lender who dreads his borrowers' wounds holds a compensation clause; a lender who can budget for his wounds has begun to sell them.

Now read a present-day facility agreement with the file open. The default apparatus — the rate step-up, acceleration, cross-default — chapter 22 audits entire; around it stands the quieter loss-recovery furniture, and it sorts with surprising speed. Costs-and-expenses clauses, under which a defaulting borrower pays the documented outside costs of enforcement, are the defiant defendant's rule and Molina's integration in modern boilerplate: honest damnum, so long as the invoices are real, itemized, and not run through a collections operation that turns a margin on them. Break-costs clauses — the charge when a borrower repays early or fails to draw, computed as what the lender actually loses unwinding the funding arranged for him — are the doctrine's most exact modern artifact and its neatest boundary marker: computed from the actual cost of the funds, the clause repairs a caused wound; computed from the profit the lender had hoped to earn across the loan's remaining life, the same clause steps, mid-formula, out of this chapter's title and into the next one's — from the loss that emerged to the gain that ceased. Increased-costs clauses, which pass to the borrower the expense of new regulation landing on the lender, stretch the causal fence to its creaking point: the loss is real and documentable, but the borrower did not cause it, and a claim whose causation runs "you were nearby when my world got expensive" has quietly become mutual insurance billed as damages — an arrangement with an honest name and an honest home, neither of which is this file. The reader now owns the method, and it travels: name the event, trace the cause, demand the papers, measure the repair, count once, and watch the hope.

For the builders — and Parts IX and X of this book intend to build — the file compresses to a working grammar. Trigger on events, never on the calendar alone: no damage without a happening. Document as an institutional habit, not a courtesy to auditors: the invoice is the modern witness. Cap and proportion: repair ends at the wound's edge. Net honestly: recovery already achieved — the mitigation that worked, the resale that covered, the hole the venture's own gains refilled — comes off the claim first, as Rava ruled and the standards still rule. Book loss-recovery in its own line at zero margin, so the ledger itself can testify that the line is repair; and watch the budget for appetite — chapter 22 built that audit for penalty income, and it reads identically here, since a lender whose year balances on projected borrower failures has inverted his purpose whatever each clause recites. Route anything above shown cost away from the house; chapter 22 found that conduit built, at industrial scale. And keep the mercy sort upstream of everything, because a wound-claim pressed home against the destitute repairs nothing and ruins someone, and every tradition in this book wrote that boundary before it wrote this title. Chapter 40 will hold the grammar to arithmetic — its return formula carries actual cost recovery and actual loss recovery as named, separate, bounded lines — and chapter 44 will give the ledger its audit. What they inherit from this chapter is a title already disciplined: backward-looking, event-born, proven, proportioned, counted once.

The audit's first hearing can close with its finding, and the finding vindicates the wall rather than breaching it. The traditions never required the lender to bleed for his obedience; they required him to prove. Damage, expense, default, impairment — each may be repaired, to the coin, from its cause, and such repair is the one payment above principal that leaves the wall standing, because it looks only backward, at what is already true. The next claim on the docket refuses that direction. It is the merchant's claim, and it is not a lie: had I kept my money, I would have earned with it. Aquinas heard it and answered in a single clause — "he must not sell that which he has not yet" — and the tradition spent the following centuries discovering how much commercial truth was pressing against that fence from the other side. That hearing is chapter 20, "Lucrum Cessans: The Profit That Was Not Made," and it opens where this chapter closes: at the property line between what a lender lost and what he merely failed to gain.

chapters.part: Part VI — The Great Technical Debates

chapters.title: Lucrum Cessans: The Profit That Was Not Made
chapters.label: Chapter 20

paragraphs: Two men in the same lane lend the same sum on the same day. The first is a wool merchant with his capital already committed: the fleeces bought, the cart hired, the buyer at the autumn fairs half promised, the whole small machine of a season assembled and pointed down the road. His neighbor comes to the door in genuine need, and the merchant — because the man is his neighbor, and the traditions this book reads had spent centuries telling him so — unloads the cart, sells the fleeces back for what he paid, and lends the money interest-free until winter. The second lender lives across the lane with the same hundred in a strongbox, where it has sat since Easter doing what coins do in boxes. He lends it on the same terms, to the same sort of neighbor, with the same open hand.
At winter both are repaid in full, to the coin. And both, standing in the lane, say the same sentence: I am the poorer for it. I could have earned more elsewhere.

One of them is telling the truth about a loss. The other is telling a truth about money — which is a different thing, and the difference is this chapter. The merchant can name his elsewhere: that buyer, those fairs, this wool, a margin his trade earned last year and the year before. The strongbox has no elsewhere; it has every elsewhere, which amounts to none — an infinite address book with no house in it. Out of the space between those two sentences the scholastics built the most contested instrument in their whole toolkit: lucrum cessans, the gain that ceases, the profit that was not made — the claim that a lender may sometimes be compensated not for what the loan took from him but for what it prevented him from getting.

Chapter 10 shelved the four extrinsic titles and called the risk title the most treacherous, because an uncapped charge for danger prices a permanent condition of lending. This title earns a different superlative: the most dangerous. Not the most abused — every title was abused — but the only one whose corrupted form eventually stopped needing an advocate. Generalize the merchant's claim to the strongbox, let every coin bill the world for its imaginary career, and you do not merely breach the usury wall; you replace the civilization that built it with one in which the wall looks insane. That civilization is ours. The claim this chapter examines is no longer an exception argued by lenders; it is the axiom taught to every first-year finance student under the name opportunity cost. Chapter 7 promised that the lucrum cessans debates would ask whether forgone time-bound opportunities can be real losses. They can. Whether that answer can be kept from devouring everything else these traditions concluded — that is the file, reopened.

sections.title: The Claim from a World That Did Not Happen
paragraphs: Begin with what makes the claim strange, because its strangeness is load-bearing. Every other compensation the traditions weighed points at something in this world. Actual loss — the file of chapter 19 — has a wound to show: a bill paid, a barn burned, a cost incurred because repayment failed. The penalty of chapter 22 has a broken date. Even the risk title of chapter 10 points at a position actually held. Lucrum cessans points at nothing here at all. It asks a court, or a confessor, to compare the world as it stands with a second world that never happened — the one where the loan was refused and the wool went to the fairs — and to bill the borrower for the difference. The lender's purse is exactly as full as his contract promised. His grievance lives entirely in the subjunctive.

That is why the title is elastic in a way no honest wound can be. A loss already suffered has edges; witnesses can walk around it. A profit that was prevented has whatever size the claimant's imagination allows — the merchant would have cleared ten, or say twenty; the deal would surely have closed. Chapter 12, pricing labor's contributions, met this exact asymmetry and quarantined it here: the traditions paid readily for months actually spent inside a venture and balked at months hypothetically redirected, because a spent season leaves witnesses and a redirected one leaves only the claimant's word. The quarantine was wise. This is the one title where the evidence for the claim is, by construction, a story about a world nobody inhabits.

And yet the claim would not die, because sometimes it is true. The medieval lawyers met it long before anyone had a term for it. William of Auxerre had ruled the calendar off the market — the usurer sells time, which is the common possession of all creatures, the argument chapter 7 walked — and that ruling holds here in a way worth noticing: what the merchant lost was not time, which belonged to him no more than to his neighbor, but a use he had built inside it. The canon law's first accommodations came, tellingly, not in loans but in sales. The same decretal chapter 10 read for the risk title, Naviganti, cleared in its quieter clauses the man who pays now for grain deliverable next season, and the seller who charges above today's price for payment at a term, wherever the future value was genuinely in doubt — verisimiliter dubitatur, as the Latin verified there has it; and the decretal's cast — grain, wine, oil, a man on the road to the fairs — kept the question commercial rather than speculative. Future value had entered the moral arithmetic of price. If a thing could be worth more now because of what it was concretely about to become, then a man deprived of that becoming had perhaps lost something real.

The first canonist to let the reasoning touch the loan itself was Hostiensis — Henry of Susa, cardinal-bishop of Ostia, remembered as the most brilliant canonist of his century, whose rhymed count of thirteen lawful exceptions the schools memorized. Among the thirteen stood the gain that ceases, and the shape of his opening mattered more than the fact of it. The claim was not for everyone. It belonged to the lender who was not in the business of lending — the merchant whose money was ordered toward trade and who lent it away from that order, at cost to himself. The restriction carries the whole logic. A professional lender who pleads lost profit is pleading that this loan cost him the chance to make another loan at interest: the title would justify usury by pointing at usury, a circle the canonists refused to walk. The alternative gain had to be licit, which meant it had to be something other than the thing under judgment. From its first appearance, lucrum cessans was admitted only as the exception of a man whose real vocation lay elsewhere — and everything dangerous in its later history is the story of that restriction wearing away.

One more thing belongs in the file before the theologians take it up, and it is a date. The phrase every modern reader reaches for — opportunity cost — entered economics in 1894, as the title of an article in the Quarterly Journal of Economics, a few years after Friedrich von Wieser had systematized the doctrine under the name alternative cost. The concept the phrase names is treated today as timeless common sense, the first axiom of choice. It is worth insisting that the axiom is younger than the bicycle, while the question of whether a forgone gain can be a real loss had by then been argued for six and a half centuries. The medievals did not lack the concept. They had it, examined it, and put conditions on it that the modern form quietly dropped. What follows is what the conditions were.

sections.title: The Slow Yes of the Schoolmen
paragraphs: Aquinas answered first, and his answer — a no with a door in it — governed the debate for as long as the debate stayed honest. The text is a few lines in the usury question, and this book has touched its edges twice; here it must be read whole. A lender, he allows, may without sin agree with the borrower on compensation "for the loss he incurs of something he ought to have, for this is not to sell the use of money but to avoid a loss" — the clean restorative title that chapter 19 files, quoted here as throughout in the English Dominicans' rendering. But compensation for the profit he would have made with the money is another matter: the lender "must not sell that which he has not yet and may be prevented in many ways from having" (ST II-II, q.78, a.2, ad 1).

Sit with the reason, because it is better than a rule; it is an observation about the future. The merchant's ten of profit, so vivid in the lane at winter, was never his. It depended on the road staying open, the buyer staying solvent, the price staying up, the wool staying dry — a season's worth of contingencies, any one of which could have eaten it. To charge the borrower for that ten as though it were a possession is to sell a certainty the seller never owned: the borrower pays in hard coin for a profit that existed only in the weather of one possible year. Worse, the compensated lender ends up better off than the merchant he claims to be — he collects the venture's imagined fruit without its labor, its costs, or its risk, a harvest with the farming subtracted. Aquinas saw where the logic led: every lender would discover, upon lending, that he had been on the verge of something lucrative. The no was a fence around exactly that meadow.

But Aquinas built the door himself, sixteen questions earlier, and the later tradition walked through it carrying his own words. In the treatise on restitution he asks what is owed when one man injures another not by taking what he has but by "preventing him from obtaining what he was on the way to obtain" — blocking a wage, an inheritance, a sale already approaching. Something is owed, he answers, and then comes the sentence on which the whole later doctrine of foregone profit balances: not the full amount, "because to have a thing virtually is less than to have it actually." His example is the one this book has been waiting for since chapter 14 asked whether hope could ever be collected as if it were harvest: the sower. A man who has sown his field does not yet have his harvest — nondum habet messem in actu, sed solum in virtute — he holds it "not actually but only virtually," as seed holds wheat; and one who wrongfully destroys the sown field owes for the crop accordingly, at a discount the size of the world's uncertainty, "according to the condition of persons and things" (ST II-II, q.62, a.4). Read the two texts together and the apparent contradiction becomes an architecture. In the loan contract, profit not made may not be sold — that is q.78, guarding the mutuum. In the court of restitution, a future good wrongfully prevented may be compensated — that is q.62 — but only as what it was: a probability, priced as a probability. Hope is compensable at hope's price, never at harvest's. The whole conservative discipline this chapter ends with is already in that sentence, and it is Aquinas's, not ours.

What pushed the tradition through the door was not theory but Provence. Peter John Olivi — born near the coast at Sérignan around 1247, handed to the Franciscans at Béziers at about twelve, censured at Paris in 1283, cleared at Montpellier, dead at Narbonne in March 1298, his tomb demolished twenty years later — spent his last years in a town full of merchants, and did them the unusual honor of watching what their money actually was. In the Tractatus de contractibus, the treatise on contracts he wrote there in the mid-1290s, he observed that money firmly committed by its owner's settled purpose to a probable profit is no longer mere coin: it carries "a certain seminal character of profit, which we commonly call capital" — quod communiter capitale vocamus, the merchants' own word, taken up by a theologian for the first time. His books were confiscated in his lifetime and condemned after it; Bernardino of Siena kept a manuscript of the treatise all the same, and a century and a half later carried whole passages of it, word for word and without the dangerous name, into the sermons that made him famous — the doctrine traveling under a saint's voice because it could not travel under its own. Olivi's point was narrow, and its narrowness was its power. He did not say money breeds; the mutuum stayed barren. He said that not all money is situated alike: coin inside a working commercial process — his word seminal, seed again — differs in economic kind from coin in a box, and interrupting the process can cost its owner something as real as trampled grain. The claim of the wool merchant in our lane is Olivian, and the claim of the strongbox is not, and the distinction between them — a productive alternative actually in train, against the general fertility of money — is the hinge on which every later formulation turns.

The fifteenth century said the careful yes. In the commercial cities the case kept arriving in the confessional, and the great pastoral theologians — Antonino, the pastoral theologian of merchant Florence; Bernardino of Siena (1380–1444), Franciscan preacher to the same world — admitted that a lender genuinely torn from a concrete trade could be compensated for it, while spending most of their ink on the abuses: the lost profit invented after the fact, the habitual lender in a merchant's costume, the gain valued at fantasy prices, the borrower's need quietly doing the pricing. Cajetan, the great Dominican commentator on Aquinas, supplied the Thomist reconciliation: a future gain sufficiently determinate — a transaction arranged, a practice standing, a market waiting — could be treated as virtually possessed, so that its loss fell under q.62's restitution rather than q.78's ban; everything then hung, as it still does, on how much work the word virtually is allowed to do. Conrad Summenhart at Tübingen, whose seven-part treatise on contracts was printed at Hagenau in 1500, folded the title into a general anatomy of exchange, asking of every payment what it actually paid for. And Salamanca inherited the settled question and disciplined it. Domingo de Soto, the school's Dominican conscience, pressed the universalization danger — admit the title to everyone and the prohibition dies in its sleep. Luis de Molina wrote the conditions into their mature form: a real alternative use; an intention actual or at least virtual, standing in the lender's ordinary practice rather than invented for the occasion; a gain foreseeable with reasonable probability; a causal chain from this loan to that loss; a valuation kept sober. Leonardus Lessius, pressing the logic of money markets to the edge where the bare deprivation of liquidity itself becomes a burden, opened the neighboring file this book keeps closed until chapter 21. And Juan de Lugo, gathering the whole tradition, fixed the three conditions that became the common teaching — the sententia communis of the manuals. The loan must truly cause the profit to cease. Nothing may be demanded beyond the value of the profit that ceased. And the compensation must not be taken upfront — because a lost future gain, deducted at signing, has become a guaranteed present one, and a guaranteed present return on a loan is the thing itself. When Benedict XIV restated the usury doctrine in 1745, chapter 7 noted, Vix pervenit left standing the titles that arise from reasons "not at all intrinsic to the contract"; the gain that ceases had by then carried its conditions for two centuries, a lawful claim exactly as wide as its proof.

Notice what the slow yes never conceded. At no point in four centuries of development did the tradition hold that money as such earns, that time as such is billable, or that the market's going rate is anyone's entitlement. The title that emerged is a tort dressed as a title: a specific injury, done by this loan to that venture, proven by the claimant, discounted for the world's uncertainty, capped at the injury's size, collected after the fact. Everything else — every claim in the family of the strongbox — the schoolmen went on calling by the old name.

sections.title: A Grievance, Not a Debt
paragraphs: The halakha heard the same claim and gave an answer of a wholly different shape: it looked the loss in the eye, named it, and declined to make it a debt.

The text is short enough to hold in the hand. One who idles his fellow's purse, rules Rebbi Isaac in the Jerusalem Talmud — takes money entrusted for trade, say, and lets it lie — has against him "nothing but a grievance," a tar'omet: a grievance the court acknowledges and declines to price. And the same passage draws the line that shows exactly where the wall stands: idle a man's field and you owe him, for a field bears fruit by nature; the fallow season is a harvest that was really coming, and its destroyer pays. The purse is different in kind. Coins bear nothing by nature — that has been the traditions' finding since chapter 7 — and so the law, asked to compensate the purse's imaginary year, refuses to presume a counterfactual it spent its whole jurisprudence declining to presume. Chapter 22 met this ruling among the costs of delay; read from this chapter's angle it is something more pointed: the halakha's direct verdict on lucrum cessans. The claim is not dismissed as false — the grievance is real enough to be named in law, which is its own kind of honesty. It is dismissed as unpayable, because the only meter that could price it is agar natar, payment for waiting, the forbidden core itself in chapter 7's gloss. A tradition that would not let a lender charge for the days was not going to let him charge for what he dreamed the days contained.

The refusal was not innumeracy about commerce, and the proof is what the same law pays without blinking. The working partner's months are compensated scrupulously — the idle-laborer wage of chapter 12, sized at what a man would take to down his own tools — because months spent inside a venture are witnessed fact, not counterfactual. Labor's forgone alternatives get a real price; money's forgone alternatives get a sympathetic shrug. The asymmetry is deliberate and evidentiary: it is the same line Molina would draw with intention and causality, drawn instead with the court's oldest instrument, the question of what can be proved.

And then the tradition built its lawful channel, whose logic is the most elegant answer to lucrum cessans any of the three traditions produced. The problem: a man with genuinely productive uses for his money — the Olivian lender, the man with real elsewheres — cannot be paid for forgoing them, because on a loan that payment is ribbit. The halakha's solution, met in chapter 11 and priced in chapter 14, was not to relax the rule but to dissolve its premise. Recharacterize the financing as an iska, half loan and half deposit, and the money's productive career no longer stops at the borrower's door: the deposit half remains the investor's own capital, trading in the borrower's hands at the investor's peril, and what the investor collects is not compensation for a profit forgone elsewhere but his share of a profit sought here, in the venture his money actually entered. The forgone gain is never paid because it is never forgone. Where the schoolmen disciplined the counterfactual, the rabbis abolished it — by making the lender a participant in the factual instead. The heter iska's settlement machinery — the named figure, the heavy oath, the fee that buys the oath's silence, sized in the modern forms even to prevailing rates — is chapter 14's file and chapter 31's reckoning, and this chapter borrows only its skeleton: the named figure is, in substance, a conservative model of expected gain, agreed in advance, collectable only because the capital that earns it genuinely stands in the wind. Whether the modern instrument keeps that condition true at banking scale is precisely the question chapter 31 holds open. The logic, though, is complete already: the halakha's answer to "I could have earned more elsewhere" is: then go earn it — and if you would rather lend, we will write you into the earning, at your own risk. It is the one answer in this chapter that makes the lament structurally impossible to utter.

sections.title: Time in the Price, Never in the Loan
paragraphs: The fiqh drew its boundary with a draftsman's economy, and the boundary runs straight through the middle of this chapter's subject: time may take a share of a price; time may take nothing of a loan.

The second half is the older and harder rule, and it is absolute. Money in a qard has no rental rate; increase stipulated for the term — at signing or, in the original abomination, at maturity: the jahiliyya creditor's pay-or-increase, which chapter 22 found standing at the doctrine's birthplace — is riba without further analysis. No version of "I could have earned more elsewhere" survives contact with this rule, because the rule is a refusal to let money's time be priced at all, and a lost hypothetical return is nothing but money's time wearing a costume. The strongbox lender of our lane has no case in the fiqh, and neither, on a loan, does the merchant.

The first half is the seam, and the jurists never pretended otherwise. A sale may carry a deferred price above the cash price — the murabaha's installment markup, the credit sale the Prophet himself used — and the manuals say why with unembarrassed clarity: the deferment takes a share of the price, as the jurists' own formulation has it. Chapter 24 walked the seam at full instrument length — the ownership interval, the disclosed cost, the price that never grows once set — and watched each tradition patrol its own version of the line: the Mishnah's rent-and-sale pair, the canonists' doubt clause, Aquinas's flat ruling that the naked deferral premium "has the character of a loan." The point this chapter needs from the seam is narrow: the fiqh's acknowledgment that time has value is real, and it is quarantined inside contracts about things, where the premium can answer to ownership, risk, and service. What may never happen is the migration of that value out of the sale and into the debt as such. The entire modern architecture of Islamic finance lives on one side or the other of that line.

Which makes the tradition's modern encounter with lucrum cessans the most clarifying in this chapter, because it happened in committee, in writing, within living memory. In 2000 the Islamic Fiqh Academy at Riyadh took up the penalty clause — the contractor who delivers late, the supplier who defaults — and resolved the question with two sentences that map the whole terrain. A penalty clause is permissible "in all financial contracts except when the original commitment is a debt," where it is "usurious in the strict sense." And the loss it may compensate "includes the actual financial loss suffered by the partner, any other material loss and the certainly realisable gain that he misses due to his partner's default or delay" — though never "moral prejudice" (Resolution 109 (3/12)). Read the second sentence twice, because there it is: the "certainly realisable gain that he misses" — lucrum cessans, admitted by name in everything but Latin, under the strictest formulation of the probability condition anywhere in this chapter: not probable gain, "certainly realisable" gain. The first sentence holds the boundary: everywhere except the debt. A builder's default may cost you a harvest, and the harvest may be billed; a borrower's default may not, because on the debt the only thing "lost" is money's time, and money's time is not a compensable good. The tradition's own standard-setters then split, as living traditions do, over how far actuality can stretch: Malaysia's regime lets an Islamic bank keep ta'widh — compensation capped at its actual, demonstrated loss — while routing every further gharamah to charity; the AAOIFI standards refuse the bank's income even that, allowing only the charity-routed donation clause of chapter 22, with critics on each side of the gap. It is a genuine ikhtilaf, argued in the tradition's own categories, and this book reports rather than referees it. But notice what nobody in the dispute defends: compensating a financier's forgone market return on a debt. On that, the committee room of 2000 and the schools of the classical centuries hold one line.

And yet the industry those jurists supervise runs, in bulk, on a number that comes from exactly the place the doctrine forbids. The markup on the murabaha that carries, by the industry's own much-quoted estimate, up to four-fifths of Islamic finance was priced for decades against LIBOR — the interbank interest rate itself — and, since the benchmark's demise in 2023, against its successors. Chapter 24 gave the defense its full hearing: Usmani's ruling that "merely using the interest rate as a benchmark" does not corrupt a sale that is genuinely a sale, and his own caveat in the next breath, that the institutions "should get rid of this practice as soon as possible." What this chapter adds is the name of the danger. A benchmark is a generic market return; a generic market return is the strongbox's claim, the exact object four centuries of conditions were built to exclude; and an industry built to honor the prohibition, pricing its permitted seam off the forbidden meter, has imported through the back office the one number its doctrine exists to refuse. Whether that is prudence, contradiction, or an honest transition still under way is the quarrel of chapter 32, and it is the tradition's own quarrel, conducted by its own scholars in its own vocabulary. Here it stands as the chapter's sharpest modern exhibit: the benchmark problem is lucrum cessans generalized — the market's elsewhere, priced into every contract, unexamined — arriving inside the very legal system best armed to recognize it.

sections.title: The Horse and the Gate
paragraphs: Everything the three traditions concluded can now be said in two sentences. A productive alternative — particular, licit, intended, interrupted — can ground a real claim, cautiously priced. A generic market return can ground nothing, because it is not a fact about the lender; it is a fact about the market, and the market lost nothing. The whole moral geometry lies between those sentences, and the modern mind, trained on the second sentence's logic as if it were the first's, has mostly lost the ability to feel the difference. So state it operationally. The market return is what anyone could have earned, which is why it is proof that no one in particular lost it. A claim of foregone profit is exactly as strong as its particularity: the moment it can be made by any holder of money about any loan, it has stopped describing an injury and started describing a wish.

This is why "I could have earned more elsewhere" — our second lender's sentence, and every term sheet's — is not enough, and the traditions' conditions, laid side by side, are simply five questions the sentence cannot answer. Earned it where — in a named venture, or in the whole weather of the market? Earned it how — was the alternative licit, or is the claimant billing his neighbor for a forgone extraction, the circularity Hostiensis closed in the thirteenth century? Was it intended — standing in the claimant's actual practice before the loan, or discovered afterward, when grievance went looking for arithmetic? Did this loan cause its loss — or would the gain have arrived anyway, or failed anyway? And what was it worth — the brochure's number, or the sober figure that survives Aquinas's discount, net of the costs, the labor, and the risk the real venture would have charged for it? A claim that passes all five is the wool merchant's, and every tradition in this book would hear it. A claim that fails them is the strongbox's, and the sentence that carries it is not evidence of a loss; it is a description of money, spoken in the tone of an invoice. The last question belongs to the borrower, and it is the oldest in this book: who is being asked to pay? Where the answer is a person in need, the traditions' verdict does not soften with the rate — the lender's imagined world is being billed to the one party in the room who never lived in it.

Now watch the horse come through the gate, because the image is exact. A Trojan horse is not a battering ram; it enters as a gift, welcomed, because it looks like something the city already honors. Lucrum cessans entered the usury doctrine as compensation — restitution's cousin, justice for wool merchants, a tort with conditions. And inside it, folded small, sat the entire future logic of capital: if a forgone gain can be a loss, then money has a normal yield it is always forgoing; if money has a normal yield, every loan deserves it; if every loan deserves it, the yield is not a claim to be proven but a baseline to be assumed — and whoever asks capital to serve without it is imposing a cost, which must be measured, priced, and recovered. Run that chain to its end and the burden of proof has silently changed hands. The schoolmen made the lender prove his elsewhere; the modern order makes the borrower — the enterprise, the mission, the patient project — prove why capital should ever accept less than its elsewhere. Böhm-Bawerk built interest's modern foundation on the premium of present over future goods, answering William of Auxerre rather than refuting him, as chapter 7 showed; Wieser and the marginalists generalized the alternative into the very definition of cost; and by the time the phrase opportunity cost had a journal article to its name, in 1894, the exception had finished becoming the axiom. Nothing in the machinery is arithmetically wrong. The discount rate, the hurdle rate, the cost of capital — each is the strongbox's sentence, compounded and institutionalized: true as mathematics, and morally identical to the claim the traditions spent six centuries refusing, that the world owes money its imaginary career. The Fifth Lateran definition chapter 14 quoted named usury as gain sought "without any work, any expense or any risk"; the generalized opportunity-cost claim is precisely such gain, sought not by argument but by definition — the wall not breached but declared, from inside the new axioms, never to have made sense at all.

The traditions' reply is not to burn the horse. It is the reply they gave at every gate in this book: open it, and price what is actually inside. Forgone gain is sometimes real; therefore model it — conservatively, which this chapter's sources specify with surprising completeness. Compensate after the fact, on proof, never as an upfront deduction — Lugo's third condition, because a lost future paid at signing is a guaranteed present, which is interest. Compensate the particular, never the index: a named alternative, in the claimant's real practice, causally severed by this financing — Molina's conditions, Hostiensis's restriction, the Yerushalmi's evidentiary instinct. Price hope as hope: discount the claimed gain for every contingency the real venture would have faced — the sower holds his harvest only in virtue, and the compensation runs "according to the condition of persons and things," net of costs, labor, and risk, never gross. Cap it at the loss: the title restores; it must never out-earn the venture it mourns. Demand a licit elsewhere: a forgone extraction is not a compensable injury. Refuse the double count: the same deprivation may not be billed once as lost profit, again as delay, again as liquidity — the files of chapters 19, 21, and 22 name distinct wounds or they name nothing. And refuse the universal: a clause that appears in every contract has stopped compensating anybody for anything. A claim built to those rules is rare, small, late, and provable — which is to say, it looks nothing like a return on capital, and everything like what the tradition said it was: damages. Chapter 12 noted the irony that the one modern claimant who can meet this standard to the dollar — the founder with the declined offer letter in her files — is the one for whom the instruments make no line; the arithmetic of honoring her, and of refusing the strongbox politely, belongs to Part IX, where chapter 35 turns these conditions into working models and chapter 40 builds the return formula that keeps them honest.

So the answer promised in chapter 7 can be given whole. Can a forgone, time-bound opportunity be a real loss? Yes — when it was a particular man's particular venture, lawful in itself, already in train, killed by the loan, and mourned at its honest, discounted, after-the-fact price. That loss the traditions saw, named, and — each in its own grammar — paid: the schoolmen by a tort with conditions, the rabbis by writing the lender into the venture, the jurists of Islam by admitting the "certainly realisable" harvest everywhere except the one contract where money pretends to be a field. What none of them would pay is the other claim — the elsewhere of anyone, owed by everyone, forever — and their refusal is the finding this chapter has met at every turn: the profit that was not made is not a possession, and billing the world for it does not become justice by being called compensation. The deprivation of liquidity — the burden of simply being without one's money, the subtlest of the family's claims — is the file of chapter 21; the boundary between honest uncertainty and manufactured blindness closes Part VI in chapter 23.

chapters.part: Part VI — The Great Technical Debates

chapters.title: Carentia Pecuniae: The Deprivation of Liquidity
chapters.label: Chapter 21

paragraphs: For twenty chapters, "without money" has meant the borrower. It was the borrower's empty hand the covenant codes shielded, the borrower's cloak that had to go home by sunset (chapter 4 carried it there), the borrower who stands in the proverb chapter 1 set at the front door of this whole subject: "the borrower is the slave of the lender" (Proverbs 22:7, NRSV). In the moral grammar the scriptures built, the lack of money is a condition to be relieved; it is the reason lending exists.

This chapter is about the moment the lack of money changed sides. Late in the long Catholic argument over usury, in the generation when moral theology kept office hours within walking distance of the great exchanges, a Latin phrase began doing new work: carentia pecuniae — the lack, absence, or deprivation of money. Not the borrower's lack. The lender's. For the term of a loan, the argument ran, the lender is himself a man without his money. He cannot spend it, place it, or answer an opportunity with it; he endures, for a season, the peculiar poverty of the fully solvent; and that deprivation — not any loss he can document, not any venture he can name, just the bare state of being without — is a real burden, and a real burden is worth a price.

Part VI has been reading the lender's honest claims one file at a time: actual loss is chapter 19's file, the profit that was not made is chapter 20's. This is the third file, and the strangest, because its claim is the thinnest and the widest at once. Thin, because it asserts no event — nothing burned, nothing missed, nothing broken. Wide, because if it is good once it is good always: every loan, by definition, leaves the lender without his money for a term. A title that rides on the definition of lending is no exception to the usury prohibition but its photographic negative, and the question of this chapter is whether the tradition could admit the claim without unsaying everything it had said since the Psalms. The question was fought out by name, in print, by some of the most commercially literate minds Christian theology ever produced, and this chapter will watch the fight.

One thing should be said plainly before the lawyers take over. Across the table from every lender who was ever "without his money" sits a person without money in the older sense — that is why he came. A doctrine of compensated deprivation would pay the solvent man for his temporary lack out of the pocket of the man whose lack is the emergency. The traditions never forgot which of those two deprivations their scriptures were about, and neither will this chapter.

sections.title: Ready Money
paragraphs: Begin with what the claim gets right, because it gets something right. Money in hand is more than the goods it could buy; it is the power to act before anyone knows what acting will require. The merchant with cash meets the fire, the bargain, the tax collector, and the funeral with the same instrument, and meets each on the day it arrives. The merchant whose capital is out on loan meets them with apologies. The old classroom examples of wine and wheat never quite capture this, because a cask drunk is simply gone, while money lent is only elsewhere — still yours in law, owed back whole, and useless to you at exactly the moments when money matters most. Sixteenth-century commerce knew this in its bones. On the exchange at Antwerp and at the fairs of Castile, readiness had a market of its own: the man who could pay today was in a different business from the man who could pay at Easter, and the difference between them was priced daily in the terms of bills and deposits. Modern finance has names for what those merchants saw — liquidity preference, the liquidity premium, the term premium — and a yield curve to draw them with; chapter 7 met the theory's respectable ancestor in Böhm-Bawerk's agio, the premium present goods command over future goods of like kind. None of this is fantasy. To be without one's money for a term is a real constraint, and the longer the term, the realer it gets.

The question is what kind of reality it is, and the neighboring files of this Part supply the measuring sticks. A lender who, because his money was out, had to borrow at cost to meet an obligation of his own can show a wound: that is actual loss, chapter 19's business, compensable because demonstrated. A lender whose money was already committed to a particular venture, and who let the venture go in order to lend, can show an interruption: that is chapter 20's business, and the tradition hedged it with demands for concreteness and causation precisely because it reaches into the future. Carentia pecuniae claims neither. It names no cost incurred and no venture interrupted; it says only, I was without my money, and being without money is as such a disadvantage. Strip away the Latin and the three claims sit in plain view: this loan cost me something; this loan cost me that; this loan was a loan.

And hold the mirror steady while the distinction settles. The borrower's side of the table knows everything the merchant knows about readiness, without the vocabulary. A household one repair away from ruin is living the economics of liquidity, not reading about them; chapter 15 drew the line between the temporary liquidity shock and the permanent ruin it becomes when no one will lend. The very fact that makes ready money precious to its owner — that life's demands arrive unscheduled — is the fact that brought the borrower to the door. Any doctrine of compensated deprivation must answer for that symmetry. The lender's carentia ends at the due date; the borrower's lasted until the loan.

So the question Part VI must put to this title is exact: is the deprivation of liquidity a burden standing outside the loan, which justice may weigh the way it weighs loss and risk — or is it the loan itself, wearing its own definition as a grievance? The tradition did not duck. It put the title on trial.

sections.title: The Trial of a Title
paragraphs: The shelf of honest claims was already crowded. The classic extrinsic titles had earned their places by pointing at something genuinely outside the mutuum: a documented loss; a concrete forgone gain; the genuinely imperiled principal that chapter 10 called periculum sortis; the penalty for culpable delay that chapter 22 will put on trial next. Around them stood the working claims institutions live by — stipendium laboris, the wage of real administrative labor, and the recovered expenses that chapter 17 watched the Monti defend all the way to the Fifth Lateran Council. Carentia pecuniae was proposed as one more shelf-mate, and the proposal did not come from nowhere. It came up from the exchanges, where the lack of money visibly had a price among merchants long before it had a theology.

The first great commercial moralist to rule on it said no. Luis de Molina (1535–1600), the Jesuit whose De iustitia et iure brought scholastic doctrine as close to working markets as it had ever stood, rejected the title on grounds that cut to the bone of the contract: the obligation of not reclaiming one's money for the term is not a separable service the lender renders on top of the loan; it is inherent in the mutuum itself. Granting time is what lending is. To charge for the granting is to charge for the loan — and beyond the analysis Molina saw the arithmetic, warning (as the historian Fabio Monsalve summarizes him) that the concession would be "extremely dangerous in opening the doors to usury." A claim available to every lender on every loan amounts to a general repeal, however modest each invocation looks.

Then came Leonardus Lessius (1554–1623), the Jesuit of Louvain whom the merchants of Antwerp consulted on the morality of their dealings, and who went to the exchange himself to question the most experienced of them. In the usury chapter of his De iustitia et iure (1605), Lessius did what no scholastic of his rank had done: he formulated the title and accepted it. When a lender binds himself for a term not to call his money home, that self-binding, he argued, is a real obligation distinct from the loan — in Monsalve's rendering, "an obligation that can be separated from the loan contract itself and is worth a price or compensation." And the price was not to be invented by theologians; it was already there, in the common estimation of the merchants, who paid daily to have money ready and charged daily to go without it. "Regarding interest as the market price for money," writes Wim Decock, the episode's modern historian, "Lessius took the first step to integrate the doctrine of interest-taking and money-lending within the doctrine of just pricing." The scholarship's own name for the episode is the title of Toon Van Houdt's study of it — "Lack of money" — and its verdict on the stakes has been steady since John T. Noonan's Scholastic Analysis of Usury (1957): Lessius is credited, in Decock's words, with formulating and accepting the title "in an unprecedented way... thereby undermining traditional scholastic teaching on interest and usury."

Be fair to the man, because he was no smuggler. Lessius was describing an economy that existed. Antwerp's money market was real; the burden of parting with liquidity was real; and merchants who would never dream of gouging a poor neighbor were pricing one another's patience on the exchange every morning. He also saw the difficulty in his own position, and said so: on a bourse as busy and as international as Antwerp's, it had become impossible to know any given lender's situation and motives — and the whole diagnostic method of the older doctrine ran through exactly that knowledge. Every earlier title was tested lender by lender, burden by burden: show the loss, name the venture, prove the peril. A title tested only against the market's going rate cannot be examined case by case; it can only be blessed wholesale. Lessius answered that the just price of money's lack, like the just price of wheat, could be left to common estimation. His critics answered that wheat is not the thing the usury prohibition exists to protect.

The greatest of those critics arrived a generation later, and he cannot be accused of rigorism. Juan de Lugo (1583–1660), the Madrid-born Jesuit who taught at the Roman College and whose De iustitia et iure (1642) so impressed Urban VIII that its author was made a cardinal the following year, was the most permissive systematizer the doctrine of the titles ever had. It was Lugo who gathered the lender's honest claims into a single architecture: "There are three chief titles, which can cleanse a mutuum from the stain of usury: emergent loss, risk, and cessant gain; and these three can be comprehended under one; emergent loss" — so runs Monsalve's translation. Read the roster twice and notice what is missing. The theologian willing to comprehend forgone profit and imperiled principal as losses of a sort refused to read the bare lack of money as one of them. Admit carentia pecuniae broadly, Lugo held, and "no contract could further be considered as usurious." The title would not have joined the doctrine so much as replaced it. A century later, Benedict XIV's Vix pervenit (1745) restated the boundary the whole quarrel had been testing — gain from the loan itself remains usury, whatever real titles may stand outside the loan — and chapter 14 has already shown that sentence doing its work.

So: Catholic title, or late-Scholastic pressure valve? On the books, the answer is clean. Carentia never joined the four; it stands in the tradition's lists as an adjacent claim — formulated late, accepted by one great commercial moralist, and rejected on either side of him in time by the two others best equipped to love it. In function, the answer is already in the question. It was a pressure valve: the point where the doctrine's old seal against pricing time met the rising pressure of a commercial world that priced time daily — and hissed. The valve mattered; through it the scholastic system vented enough commercial reality to stay credible in Antwerp. But the tradition's own verdict was the sober one. Hold the valve open and the tank drains: everything the prohibition guarded flows out through "the lack of money," renamed. Within a century and a half of Lugo, the states of Europe had begun licensing openly what his generation still debated in Latin — chapter 30 will tell that story — and carentia pecuniae settled into the role it has played ever since, the ghost grammar underneath the phrase "time value of money." None of this was the tradition failing; it was the tradition working: its own casuists testing a claim against the rule, in public, with reasons, and mostly holding the line at the exact spot where the line was hardest to hold.

sections.title: Duration Without a Price
paragraphs: The halakha did not meet this claim late, and did not meet it as an open question. It met it at the beginning, and named it. The Talmud's shorthand for forbidden interest, chapter 7 taught, is agar natar — payment for waiting; any reward for waiting is forbidden, runs the rule of Bava Metzia 63b. What the seventeenth century debated as a possible exception, the rabbis had installed as the definition of the offense. A lender's compensation for being without his money is not near the line in Jewish law; it is the line.

The tradition even ran the experiment. A Babylonian sage, Rav Chama, rented out coins the way other men rent tools — one peshita, an eighth of a dinar, per dinar per day — and defended the business with a jurist's question: how is this different from renting out a hoe? Chapter 25 told the answer as part of the law of leases. The hoe comes home the same hoe, its wear known and chargeable to its owner; dinars are given to be spent, and what comes home is other dinars — so the daily fee was never rent for a surviving thing but a price for the term of a loan. The report closes with the Talmud's flat epilogue: all of Rav Chama's money was lost. It is as close as any tradition's texts come to a pure carentia charge — no loss shown, no venture named, a posted daily price for the bare absence of money — and the law refused it while it was still one sage's experiment.

Duration itself the halakha handles with structure rather than price, because a loan simply is a duration. An unspecified loan stands for thirty days — chapter 7 carried the default term from Makkot 3b — which is the law building time into the loan's anatomy as part of what the lender gives. What the lender may never do is bill for what he gave. He may not collect the time's worth as damages either — chapter 22 will show that refusal standing firm even where the borrower is at fault — and he may not harvest the waiting in kind: no lodging below the going rate in the borrower's courtyard (the mishnah chapter 25 carried), no favors, no first place in line, not even the flattering words chapter 8 watched the law confiscate as ribbit devarim. The wall runs on both sides of the due date, and it runs through every currency a benefit can be paid in.

Where duration lawfully earns, it earns as something other than duration. In the iska — half loan, half deposit, the instrument chapter 11 anatomized — the deposit half rides the venture as capital genuinely at risk, and when the turnover is slow, the investor's eventual share is larger because the venture ran longer and risked longer, not because a clock accrued against a debtor. Time enters as venture time. The working partner's own months are paid as sechar tircha, a wage for labor, under chapter 12's rule that the man must never work for nothing; and the heter iska (chapter 14; chapter 31 keeps the hard questions) carries the same insistence to industrial scale — the financier recast as investor, the settlement machinery running for exactly as long as the capital is outstanding, so that what looks from outside like interest-for-time is drafted, and must be defended, as profit-share-for-venture. Even the famous asymmetry chapter 24 met — rent may rise for deferred payment, but a sale price may not — draws the same boundary through time itself: a house endures, so its use through time can be honestly sold; coins are consumed, so theirs cannot. That is chapter 25's consumptibility doctrine standing guard at the border of the calendar.

Here, then, is the Jewish answer to the lender's carentia, and it has the economy of a proof. Duration is real, so the law gives it structure: a default term, a venture whose profits may honestly reflect its length, a wage for the months a manager works. Benefit is real, so the law confiscates it wherever it leaks toward the lender. What survives is a rule the seventeenth-century casuists would have recognized as the position Molina defended and Lessius could not hold: duration may deepen a stake; it may not draw a wage.

sections.title: Two Kinds of Lockup
paragraphs: Islam's first answer to the deprivation of liquidity is to canonize it. The qard hasan — the beautiful loan whose anatomy chapter 16 owns — is capital lockup embraced on purpose: the lender cuts a piece from his wealth (the jurists, chapter 16 heard, say the word qard comes from cutting) and hands it away for a term, expecting back the like amount and nothing else. The deprivation is not a cost the instrument regrets; it is the substance of the gift, and the tradition's whole reward apparatus — chapter 16 traced it — consists in relocating the return to a ledger no bank keeps. The law then walls the lockup against every earthly leak: the juristic maxim chapter 6 was careful to grade as a maxim rather than a hadith — every loan that draws a benefit is riba — and the modern standards chapter 16 reported, which bar stipulated excess in any form, at the contract or at its extension. That last clause deserves a slow reading in this chapter, because the extension of a loan is precisely a purchase of further deprivation. The fiqh will let the lender suffer longer. It will not let him sell the suffering.

The saver's version of the question arrives at the other counter of the same bank, and it is carentia pecuniae in modern dress: I am willing to be without my money for a year — what is that worth? A conventional bank answers with a rate stepped up by tenor, which is the Lessius position operating as furniture. The fiqh's standard instruments answer with the mudarabah investment account, and the difference is the whole argument of this Part run through a deposit slip. The depositors' money enters a common pool as investment capital, the bank standing to it as mudarib, working partner, the depositors as rabb al-mal, owners of the capital — chapter 11's contract, wearing a teller's window; chapter 27 met its cousins in the takaful operator's fee. Duration is then recognized not through a promised rate but through weightages: multipliers assigned to each class of account and published in advance, by which a year's money takes a larger share than a week's money of whatever profit the pool actually earns. One much-studied early case, an Islamic bank in Bangladesh, assigned full weight to its thirty-six-month deposits and scaled the rest below them, and stated the rationale in a sentence that repays attention: "The longer the period of deposit, the greater the risk they bear with regard to fluctuation of the rates of profit." A typical published schedule — this one posted by a Pakistani Islamic bank in the summer of 2026, declared before the month began — ran from just under 0.5 for seven-day money to 1.2 for the largest year-long deposits, the pool's net income split half-and-half between bank and depositors and then divided among the depositors by weight.

Read the mechanism against the doctrine and every joint lines up. The long depositor is not paid for waiting; he is paid a thicker slice of what happened, because for twelve months his capital stood in the way of whatever happened — including loss. The no-guarantee rule chapters 10 and 13 established holds the floor: the mudarib may not guarantee the capital, and in a bad year the pool's loss lands on the depositors "in the ratios of investment," as one bank's published mechanism puts it — the weighted account sharing the bad year as faithfully as the good. Lockup buys weight in real outcomes; it does not buy a rate against the calendar. That is the fiqh's carentia ruling, rendered as retail banking. And the tradition polices its own counter: chapter 32 will give the floor to the industry's internal critics, who ask how much of this survives competitive deposit markets — how often the weighted share is smoothed until it tracks a benchmark and the stake behaves like the rate it replaced. The instrument's honesty, as always in this book, is a property of its practice rather than its drafting; chapter 26 watched the same drift overtake certificates that promised their money back at par.

Two kinds of lockup, then, and one refusal. At the mercy layer, deprivation is the gift itself, and pricing it would unmake the instrument. At the investment layer, deprivation buys standing in a venture's real fortunes, loss included. What neither layer will sell — what no layer of this tradition will sell — is the term as such.

sections.title: Weighing Patience
paragraphs: Now the modern files, and first the honest kernel inside the old title, because there is one. Time really does compound something: exposure. Capital that can be lost is likelier to meet its loss in five years than in one; a longer commitment holds the investor's money in harm's way through more seasons, more markets, more chances for the world to turn over. So a longer term can justify more compensation — but derivatively, through the risk title, and only for capital that is genuinely at risk. This is duration-weighted capital at risk: the months multiply the peril, and the peril, not the months, is what earns. Chapter 10's conservation grammar decides the hard cases: guarantee the principal, collateralize it, make it senior and enforceable regardless of outcome, and duration weights nothing, because zero exposure multiplied by any number of months is zero. The Islamic weightage table prices duration exactly this way — the case study said it out loud: the long depositor bears more fluctuation risk — and the iska's slow venture does the same. When Part IX builds the arithmetic, this is chapter 36's file, capital at risk over time; the doctrine it will formalize is already visible here in a Bangladeshi deposit schedule and a Babylonian partnership.

When is liquidity deprivation real, then — real enough to weigh? The tests assemble themselves from the Part's own files, and none of them is new. It is real when it is demonstrated: the lender who had to borrow at cost to cover his own obligation holds a receipt, and chapter 19's discipline pays receipts. Specificity is the second test — a committed use interrupted, under chapter 20's rules of concreteness and causation, not a mood of missed possibility. Structure is the third: capital bound into a venture's fate for the term, where the deprivation rides as exposure and is paid as participation. And whatever passes must be proportionate and counted once — not collected as a liquidity premium, again as a risk premium, and a third time as a fee, the stacking every tradition in this Part condemns. Genuine cases exist and deserve saying plainly. A fund that forgoes recallability so that a workshop can carry inventory through the winter has given the workshop something real, and what it gave will show up honestly — as documented cost if covering it cost anything, as deepened exposure in the risk accounting, as a longer wait for its share of surplus.
