The reply, preserved in the Decretals as the chapter In civitate tua, is one of the most precise instruments in the canonical toolbox, because it answers on two levels at once and declines to confuse them. As to form: a contract of this shape "cannot be reckoned under the name of usury" — non possit censeri nomine usurarum — for there is no mutuum here, only a sale at an agreed price. As to substance: the sellers nonetheless incur sin, nisi dubium sit — unless there be doubt — "whether the goods would be worth more or less at the time of payment." And then the pastoral close, worth hearing for its tone alone: the citizens of Genoa would consult well for their own salvation if they ceased from such contracts, since the thoughts of men cannot be hidden from almighty God.

Read the doubt clause slowly, because the entire Catholic doctrine of sale finance hangs on it. If pepper deliverable against autumn payment may genuinely be worth seven pounds or four by autumn — prices move, ships sink, gluts happen — then six-for-five is not a disguised interest charge; it is today's honest estimate of an uncertain thing, a price with real ignorance inside it, and both parties stand inside the same ignorance. The premium prices the doubt. But where the goods' future value is not really in doubt — where everyone knows the pepper will fetch five in October, and the extra pound is simply the price of October itself — the sale's form is a costume, and underneath it a man is being paid for time, the one estate that chapter 7 heard William of Auxerre rule off the market altogether: the calendar is nobody's inventory. Half a century later, Naviganti's less famous clauses codified the test with the jurists' extra scruple, chapter 10 showed: the seller charging above the going price for deferred payment is excused ratione huius dubii, by reason of this doubt, where the goods' value at the term is genuinely uncertain — and the decretal adds a telling condition, that the seller was not otherwise going to sell, so that the premium compensates a real accommodation rather than harvesting a routine one. Aquinas then stated the negative rule with the bluntness chapter 9 quoted, and it must be requoted here because it is the exact center of this chapter: to charge a buyer more because he will pay later is usury in a sale's clothing — "this waiting for the payment of the price has the character of a loan" (ST II-II, q.78, a.2, ad 7) — and the mirror holds, buying cheap because of prepayment condemned in the same breath, with one homely exception: the seller who freely knocks something off for early money has given a rebate, not priced a financing. The scholastics, in short, refused to let the sale's form settle anything. The just price of chapter 9 supplies the baseline — the cash price, the common estimate — and the deferred premium above it must then point to something real. The only something the credit sale itself contains is genuine, shared uncertainty about value at the term; so doubt became the doctrine's load-bearing wall. A civilization that could not read hearts wrote the rule for the one court that could: the Genoese contract passed the courtroom and failed the confessional, and the tradition held both verdicts at once for five hundred years.

The rabbis drew the same line with a draftsman's economy, in the Mishnah this book has been circling since chapter 3. One may increase the rent, rules Bava Metzia 5:2, but one may not increase the price of a sale — and the Mishnah, as always, teaches by pairing. Rent a man your courtyard and say: pay me now, and it is ten selas for the year; pay month by month, and it is a sela a month, twelve for the year, and it is permitted. Sell a man your field and say: pay me now, and it is yours for a thousand zuz; pay at threshing time, and it is twelve maneh, twelve hundred, and it is forbidden. The two cases are arithmetically identical, a fifth more for the waiting, and halakhically opposite, and the reason is the anatomy this Part exists to teach. Rent falls due as shelter is enjoyed, month by month; the landlord quoting ten-now is discounting his own future claims, not charging for time, because the monthly rate is the true price of a year of use paid as the use arrives — a logic chapter 25 will build a whole instrument on. The field's price, by contrast, is owed whole when the field changes hands; every zuz of the twelve hundred above the cash thousand is a naked charge for the months between delivery and threshing — ribbit in a bill of sale. The category the rabbis assigned it tells its own story: the deferred markup is avak ribbit, the dust of interest — not the biblical fire itself, chapter 3 explained, but its residue, forbidden by the rabbis and left where it settles rather than clawed back by courts. And the Talmud's discussion of tarsha — the credit sale at a single quiet price, never decomposed — shows the sages walking the cliff edge with open eyes. Rav Nachman permitted the merchant who names one deferred price, higher than today's market would pay but never stated as today's-price-plus-waiting: there, he ruled, nothing has been fixed for the waiting as such. Rav Papa, himself a brewer, ran his beer trade on that theory and defended it in the first person — the beer would not have spoiled, he did not need the money, the accommodation ran from him to the buyer. The Talmud preserves the answer of Rav Sheshet, son of Rav Idi, in the same breath, and it turns the ledger around: why follow yourself, he asked, rather than your customers? A man with coins in hand would buy at today's cheap rate; only the man whose hands are empty agrees to the dearer future one. Seen from the empty side of the counter, the quiet premium was pricing the emptiness — chapter 7's finding about the naked loan, surfacing inside the permitted sale. The lane the halakha finally left open is deliberately narrow and deliberately unmarked: a deferred price survives only while it never confesses to being a price for deferral. The moment the two prices stand side by side in one mouth — a thousand now, twelve hundred at threshing — the dust becomes visible, and the law sweeps it. A tradition does not fence a permission that finely unless it knows precisely which animal keeps trying to get through.

sections.title: The Costume Test
paragraphs: Set the three rooms side by side, as this book keeps doing, and the shared design is unmistakable. All three traditions bless the sale and its margin. All three permit the sale to carry deferred payment — commerce could not breathe otherwise, and the Prophet's own armor stood pledge for the principle. All three then post a guard at the same gate: the deferred premium must trace to something other than the calendar — to real doubt, said the canonists; to a price that never itemizes the waiting, said the rabbis; to disclosed costs, real ownership, and a markup earned by genuine dealing, said the jurists of Islam. Which means all three need what chapter 7 called the first question to ask of any instrument, and what this Part will apply five times: a test for when the sale is real.

By now the test has no mystery left in it. Ask of any sale-shaped financing: Did the financier ever own the thing — own it in the world, not in a folder? Did its risk actually sit with him for a real interval, so that the crane, the blight, or the market could have made his problem worse while the goods were his? Is the price a price — fixed once, answering to the thing's worth and the deal's real costs — or does it grow with the calendar, compound with delay, reprice at rollover? And could the transaction be disappointed by anything other than nonpayment? Yes down the line is a sale that finances a purchase, the thing every tradition blessed. No down the line is a loan wearing a sale's clothes — and the traditions' case files on the costume are among the most instructive documents they produced, because each tradition caught its own.

The fiqh's specimen, chapter 3 exhibited: the 'ina double sale, cloth sold dear on credit and bought back cheap for cash in the same sitting, condemned by the majority of the schools precisely because the cloth goes nowhere and the two prices net to money-now against more-money-later. Christendom's twin wore a Spanish name. In the mohatra — usually traced, with some justice, to an Arabic word for hazard — the needy party buys velvet dear on credit and sells it back cheap for cash, often to the same merchant, and walks out with today's money owing tomorrow's premium. The casuists who defended it on the elegant ground that each sale, taken alone, was valid were mocked by name in Pascal's Provincial Letters, and in 1679 the Holy Office under Innocent XI condemned the defense in a proposition whose Latin deserves its place in this book's museum of costumes: Contractus mohatra licitus est — "the contract of mohatra is lawful, though made with the same person, and with a reselling of the same thing, before agreed on, with a design of gain" — condemned, with its sixty-four companions, as "at least scandalous and pernicious in practice." Rome did not bother to dispute that the paperwork was in order. It condemned the arrangement for what it did.

The modern chapter of the file is being written by the tradition with the largest sale-finance industry to police, and its jurists have shown the old reflexes. Take the murabaha's cousin tawarruq, the turning-to-silver: buy a commodity on deferred payment, sell it at once for cash to a third party, and you have financed yourself through two genuine sales — a device the classical schools debated but many tolerated, since unlike the 'ina the goods really move and the parties really differ. Then watch what scale does. In the banked version (organized tawarruq, the industry's own label) the institution sells the customer metal warehoused an ocean away, on deferred payment at a markup, and simultaneously, as the customer's agent, sells the same metal back into the market for spot cash; parcels in London Metal Exchange warehouses are the standard prop, bought and resold within minutes by parties who will never see, store, or want a gram of them, and the same plumbing runs much of the industry's interbank liquidity. In 2009 the Islamic Fiqh Academy — the same body that had blessed the murabaha triangle in 1988 — looked at the assembled machine and refused it: organized and reverse tawarruq are impermissible, resolution 179 rules, because the simultaneous, prearranged legs amount to "a deception... in order to get the additional quick cash" — paper sales netting to riba on the trailing obligation. The resolution reads, across seven centuries and a confessional divide, like the second paragraph of In civitate tua: nobody disputes the forms; the assembly is judged by what it does. The metal in the warehouse is the mohatra's velvet with a commodities code, and the tradition's own supreme juridical body said so — which matters for how this book reports the whole subject. The critique of sale-shaped lending is not an outsider's sneer at Islamic finance, any more than Innocent XI was an outsider to Catholic casuistry or the Gemara's editors to Rav Papa's beer; it is the sound every one of these traditions makes when it catches its own instrument standing too close to the wall.

sections.title: What the Markup Prices
paragraphs: One habit of the modern instrument draws more fire than any other, and it makes the cleanest laboratory for this chapter's last question. Ask what the plus should actually be, and the industry's working answer, for most of its history, was: cost plus roughly what the interest would have been. Institutions financing by murabaha, wrote Taqi Usmani, the Pakistani judge-scholar who did as much as anyone to build and police the industry's standards, "determine their profit or mark-up on the basis of the current interest rate, mostly using LIBOR" — the London interbank rate that served, until its disgrace and abolition, as the world's reference price for money. The practice was criticized from inside on the obvious ground, and Usmani's reply is the classic statement of the instrument's whole defense: if the murabaha fulfills all its conditions — real asset, real ownership, real sale — then "merely using the interest rate as a benchmark for determining the profit of murabahah does not render the transaction as invalid, haram or prohibited, because the deal itself does not contain interest." His illustration has become industry furniture: one brother sells liquor, the other sells lawful soft drinks, and if the second prices his lemonade to match the first's wine, his trade may be imitative, but it does not thereby become the wine trade. Even the defense's author would not leave it there: it remains true, Usmani wrote in the next breath, that "the Islamic banks and financial institutions should get rid of this practice as soon as possible," building benchmarks of their own, because a lawful trade that steers by the meter of an unlawful one has chosen a strange star. The halakha, chapter 14 found, arrived at the same uneasy accommodation from its own side: the standard heter iska forms let the fee-in-lieu be keyed to prevailing interest rates — the partnership document borrowing the loan market's number while refusing its name. And when LIBOR itself finally died (the bank panel ended in June 2023, the synthetic remnant was switched off in September 2024), the world's contracts migrated to the successor rates, and the sale-based industry migrated with them, repapering without missing a payment date. The thermometer changed; the temperature did not.

The honest answer to what that proves comes in halves. A benchmark, the defenders are right, is only a thermometer. Financing has a going price in every economy; a bank that must cover deposits, costs, and losses cannot price its margins off the weather; and the just-price tradition itself, chapter 9 showed, defines fairness by the common estimate — which, for the forbearance of money, is the interest rate, whether or not anyone says so aloud. The critics are right about the rest. An instrument whose margin tracks the loan market's price, repricing with its cycles, booked and stress-tested and securitized alongside its products, has told you what market it actually lives in — and by a much-cited estimate, murabaha in its various dresses carries up to four-fifths of the world's Islamic-finance volume, a figure the tradition's own scholars quote as complaint far more often than as boast. When a benchmark is borrowed long enough it stops being a thermometer and becomes a thermostat: the number no longer reads the price of money but sets it, delivering the loan market's return through a sale's paperwork, at scale. That is the "referendum" chapter 22 watched the late-payment rules run, extended to the whole balance sheet — and it is why the industry's own consciences, from the Fiqh Academy's tawarruq ruling to Usmani's get-rid-of-this-practice, keep insisting that the costume test be applied from inside the house.

So the moral geometry of cost-plus finance, this chapter's closing assignment, can be stated as an audit any reader can now run. Decompose the markup. Part of it prices the goods themselves — the just-price band of chapter 9, policed by candor where the market is thin: the murabaha's named cost, the Rambam's faithful dealer, real expenses honestly loaded. Part of it prices service — procurement, expertise, the accommodation of a buyer who could not pay today: the wages-of-labor title every room recognized, stipendium laboris, sechar tircha, the murabaha's named profit. Another part prices the ownership interval — the hours or weeks the goods were the financier's problem, the crane and the defect and the walked-away promise, al-kharaj bi-l-daman's seat. And some of it may price genuine doubt — In civitate tua's dubium, Naviganti's excuse — value honestly unknown at the term, both parties inside the same fog. Every one of those components is real, auditable, and blessed, and a sale-based financing whose margin decomposes into them completely is what the traditions said it was: trade, permitted and honorable. Whatever remains after they are priced — the residue that answers to nothing but the distance between today and the due date — is the old tenant back in the building, on a bill of sale this time, and no quantity of paperwork changes what it pays for. The instrument is not condemned by this audit; it is constituted by it. The murabaha and the licit credit sale live exactly on the wall, closer to the forbidden thing than any structure the traditions allowed before or since, and they stay honest by the disciplines this chapter has walked — ownership that is real, risk that is borne, costs that confess, doubt that is shared, a price that never grows — enforced by regulators in this world and, where In civitate tua left the remainder, in the next. Chapter 32 will weigh what becomes of those disciplines under an industry's full commercial pressure, and chapter 35 will turn the audit into arithmetic. The next two chapters stay in the workshop, with the instruments the traditions trusted further because their honesty is structural rather than policed: chapter 25, the lease — finance built on things that survive their use, where payment may honestly follow time because use is delivered through time — and chapter 26, the certificate, where ownership itself is divided into paper and sold to many hands. The sale financed the Prophet's own table; the lease and the certificate financed the temples, roads, and fleets of all three civilizations. The question, as always, is less whether the instruments can be honest than whether the people running them at scale can afford to be — and what has to be true, in law and in design, before the honest version is also the profitable one.

chapters.part: Part VII — Instruments: How Contracts and Institutions Try to Escape Usury

chapters.title: Lease-Based Finance: Ijara, Rent, and Usufruct
chapters.label: Chapter 25

paragraphs: Two workshops on the same street burn down on the same night, and in the morning two machinists stand in the ash with two pieces of paper. The first man was renting his lathe: a true lease, the machine's owner across town. His workshop is gone and his trade with it, but his paper died in the fire too — rent stops where use stops, and the lathe that no longer exists is its owner's loss, not his. The second man's paper is called a lease as well. It says so at the top. But read down the page: he insures the machine, he maintains the machine, he bears every risk of the machine's destruction, and his monthly payments — calculated, had he looked closely, as principal plus a return on it — continue in full for the remaining four years, fire or no fire, because a clause the trade calls hell-or-high-water says they do. Same street, same fire, same word at the top of the page, and two opposite fates, because the two papers are opposite contracts. A Roman jurist named Celsus wrote the second man's lesson centuries early. Usufruct is a right in a body, he said — ius in corpore — and when the body is destroyed, the right necessarily dies with it (D. 7.1.2). A right to use survives exactly as long as there is something to use. The insurers, notice, already know which paper is which: on the first machine the owner across town files the claim, because the loss is his; on the second, the "lessee" files it, with the "lessor" named as beneficiary, and the label on the paper has already confessed.

This chapter is about the instrument the fire cannot embarrass — the lease, the second machine in Part VII's workshop, and in every tradition this book reads the most serenely lawful way that capital has ever earned a return through time. The loan of Part III may charge nothing; the sale of chapter 24 lives on the wall, policed clause by clause. The lease stands in open country, so uncontroversial that the usury literature of three faiths mentions it mostly as the contrast case — the thing interest is not. That serenity has exact anatomical reasons, and they are the chapter's first business. Its second business is the modern instrument that borrowed the lease's name and none of its anatomy — the financial lease of the second machinist, in which chapter 3 promised we would watch the floor sanded away — and the tests, ancient and modern, that tell the two apart.

sections.title: The Thing That Survives Its Use
paragraphs: Recall the wall's foundation, because the lease is built on the same stone, right side up. Chapter 7 found the loan's anatomy in the nature of consumables: wine, grain, and coin are used only by being used up, so their use cannot be sold apart from their substance — a lender who charges for the money and again for its use "sells the same thing twice, or sells what does not exist." That argument has a flip side, and Aquinas states it in the same article, as the tradition's own boundary marker: the letting of a house raises no usury question at all, because its use can be granted month by month while the house itself endures and stays the owner's. There, complete, is the lease's license. A durable thing holds two separable goods — the thing itself, and the flow of service it gives off month by month — and law can assign them to different people. Rome, whose lawyers organized everything, gave each assignment its instrument. Under locatio conductio, the broad contract of letting and hiring that chapter 3 met in the taxonomy, an owner lets the use of a thing, or his own services, or a whole work, against the rent the Romans called merces. And where the split needed to survive for a lifetime, Rome carved it as a property right and defined it in a sentence the civil law still recites. Usus fructus est ius alienis rebus utendi fruendi salva rerum substantia: usufruct is the right of using and enjoying things that belong to another — salva rerum substantia, the substance of the things preserved (D. 7.1.1). Read that ablative clause slowly, because the whole morality of rent lives inside it. The usufructuary may take the fruit; he must keep the tree whole for its owner. Use flows to one party, substance stays with the other, and the price paid for the flowing use is as honest as any price in commerce, because something real is delivered every single day the contract runs — this month's shelter, this season's harvest, this year's turning of the lathe. The old taxonomy of chapter 3 even kept a free cousin beside the priced instrument, and the pair teaches the anatomy better than either alone. In the commodatum, the gratuitous loan-for-use, a neighbor borrows the hoe itself and returns that hoe — no rent, a favor between households, ownership never blinking; in the locatio, the same hoe goes out against coin. Both are possible for exactly one reason: the hoe outlives its work. Set the mutuum beside them and the family portrait is complete — the contract for things that die in the using, where nothing can come back but a quantity, and where the traditions therefore let nothing extra come back at all.

Now watch the anatomy exclude money, in the traditions' own courtroom. If use can be sold where use is separable from substance, a clever mind will ask why coins should be different, and the Talmud preserves the mind that asked. Rav Chama, a Babylonian sage, would rent out dinars, the Gemara reports, at a peshita per dinar per day, and his theory was exactly the one this chapter has been building: in what way, he asked, is this different from renting out a hoe? The Gemara's answer is the entire doctrine of Part III in a farmyard image. The hoe comes back to its owner as is — the same hoe, its wear visible and known, its deterioration all the while on the owner's account. The dinars do not come back as is; a borrower does not return the same coins he took, for the coins are given to be spent, and what wears away in the spending can never be weighed. The "rent" on a dinar is therefore not a price for use flowing from the owner's surviving property; it is a charge on a loan, ribbit with a landlord's vocabulary, and the tradition remembers the episode with an ending it plainly regarded as a verdict: all of Rav Chama's money, the same page records, was lost (Bava Metzia 69b). He had tried the oldest maneuver in this book — chapter 7 called it charging one contract's price on another contract's anatomy — and the anatomy will not carry it. A hoe can be rented. A house can be rented. A dinar can only be lent, and the wall of Part III begins where the rentable world ends.

sections.title: The Rent Book of Three Traditions
paragraphs: Around that shared anatomy each tradition kept its own rent book, and the entries are worth reading side by side — partly for the harmony, and partly because each tradition patrols the lease's border with the loan at a different gate.

The halakha's gate is the lender. Rent as such never troubled the rabbis: the courtyard, the field, the animal, the kettle hire out for payment in every tractate without a whisper of anxiety, and chapter 24 met the Mishnah blessing rent that rises for deferred payment — ten selas for the year paid now, a sela a month paid monthly — precisely because each month's rent falls due with each month's shelter, use paid as use arrives. What the same Mishnah forbids, in its opening line, is the landlord-tenant relation flowing toward a creditor: one who lends his fellow money may not live in his courtyard free of charge, nor rent from him below the going rate, because this is ribbit (Bava Metzia 5:2). The house is rentable; the lender is not the one who may harvest it. Free shelter running to the man who holds your note is interest wearing a tenant's face — the disguised benefits of chapter 8, patrolling the lease's side of the street. And the rental relation itself, the rabbis kept honest by the ladder chapter 7 climbed: in the Mishnah's ranking of keepers, the borrower stands at the top, liable even for sheer accident, because all the benefit is his — while the paying renter stands a rung below, not liable for the accident that destroys the thing, because the benefit is split: he has the use, but the owner has the rent, and ownership's risks stay where ownership stays. The kettle of Mar Ukva's household, chapter 10 told, was weighed before each hiring and weighed after, the missing copper charged to the renters' use and the fee licensed by the owners' wearing metal. Use priced, substance guarded, risk seated with title — the halakha's lease is Paul's definition running in Aramaic.

The Latin gate is the conscience, and its rent book is the calmest document in this book's Christian archive. Christendom rented land for a thousand years — glebe and vineyard, mill and meadow, the whole feudal economy a lattice of use granted against render — and its moralists, so quick to smell usury in a deferred sale, hardly stirred. The reason is the one Aquinas gave: the house survives its use and remains the lessor's, so the rent prices a real and continuing conveyance, not a phantom. Usufruct itself lived comfortably inside canon law's world; the usufructuary who took the fruits salva substantia owed nothing to the usury question at all. The scholastics' worries began only where the lease's clean geometry was borrowed by instruments that did not share it — the census, the rent purchased for a lump of cash, where a capital sum went one way and a "rent" flowed back the other, and the schoolmen had to ask whether a man had bought a genuine stream of fruits or merely dressed a loan in an annuity's clothes. Those quarrels, chapter 3 promised, belong to Part VIII, and this chapter needs from them only their premise: nobody in the quarrel doubted the honest lease. The fight was always over who deserved to borrow its reputation.

The fiqh's gate is definition, and its rent book opens, characteristically, with revelation smiling on the whole business. When Musa flees to Midian in the Qur'an's telling, it is a daughter of the household that shelters him who speaks the tradition's charter of hire: "Father, hire him: a strong, trustworthy man is the best to hire" (28:26, in Abdel Haleem's rendering) — and the prophet is duly engaged, for wages, for a term of years. Hiring use and hiring labor sit in the same lawful house, exactly as they did in Rome's locatio. On that floor the jurists built the ijara with their usual precision: chapter 3 gave the definition — a sale of usufruct, manfa'a, a known use for a known price — and the schools' machinery enforced each word. The use must be known and specifiable, or gharar takes the contract; the price must be known, or the same; and — the clause that does this chapter's work — the thing whose use is sold must be the kind of thing that has a use apart from its consumption. Money fails the entrance exam here as everywhere: the fiqh's rental instrument simply cannot be written over dirhams — Rav Chama's hoe question, answered the same way in Arabic. What the three rent books share, beneath the different gates, is the settlement this Part keeps finding: the traditions were never against capital earning through time. They were against capital earning from time alone — and the lease is their standing proof that the distinction is real, an instrument in which every month's payment buys that month's delivered, perishable, unrepeatable use.

One wing of the rent book deserves its own sentence before the chapter turns, because Rome's category and the traditions' care both cover it: the hire of persons. Locatio let a man's services as well as his mule, and the scriptures that police the lease of labor are among the fiercest texts this book has quoted — wages owed before sunset because the laborer is poor and his life depends on them, in Deuteronomy's command from chapter 4; "you shall not keep for yourself the wages of a laborer until morning," in the Leviticus clause chapter 22 carried; the worker paid "before his sweat dries," in the Prophet's word from the same chapter. The logic is this chapter's own, run at human stakes: hire prices delivered labor as rent prices delivered use, day by day as it flows, and holding back the payment after the use is spent converts an honest hire into a forced and secret loan — the laborer financing his employer overnight, at the price of his supper. The traditions guarded the small landlord of one pair of hands more jealously than any owner of courtyards.

sections.title: The Burdens That License the Rent
paragraphs: If the lease's income is honest because ownership stays home, then everything turns on what "ownership" is made to mean — and here the traditions speak with one voice, in the lawyers' oldest maxim about loss. Res perit domino, chapter 3 already carried it: the thing perishes to its owner. Ownership is not a name on a registry; it is the seat where the thing's own fortunes land. The rent is licensed by the roof: whoever owes the repairs may charge for the shelter.

The modern fiqh has written that sentence into regulation with an exactness worth quoting, because the AAOIFI ijara standard reads like the old anatomy annotated by accountants. The lease must be preceded by acquisition — the institution acquires the asset or its usufruct before any lease of it can bite (SS 9, art. 3/1): you cannot sell a flow from a tree you do not yet own, the same gate chapter 24 watched the murabaha standards build. The lessor "must accept responsibility for any defects... which impair the intended use" and "may not exclude his liability" for them (5/1/5) — no contracting out of the ownership seat. He may not shift the major maintenance, the keeping-the-thing-capable-of-service, onto the lessee (5/1/7); the insurance is his to arrange and his to pay (5/1/8). If late payment tempts him toward the meter, the standard bars the door with the discipline chapter 22 walked: no increase in rent may be stipulated for delay (6/3). Even the modern hunger for floating rates got its answer in the lease's own grammar rather than the loan's: rent for later periods may float on a benchmark — the thermometer of chapter 24, admitted here too — but only under "a clear formula which is not subject to dispute," and capped with a ceiling and a floor (5/2/3), so that what varies is still a price being agreed, not a meter running free — the lease may borrow chapter 24's thermometer precisely because the thing being priced is real and the cap keeps the borrowed number a pricing aid rather than an engine. Note too what the maintenance rule does and does not forbid: the wear of use — oil, filters, the scratches of the lessee's own hands — may honestly sit with the user, for it is his use that makes them; what may not move is the owner's kind of upkeep, whatever keeps the thing capable of service at all. The line between a user's wear and an owner's substance is the whole lease drawn in a maintenance schedule. And at the bottom of the standard sits Celsus, translated into paragraph numbering: on the total destruction of the leased asset, the ijara terminates (7/1/3). The body gone, the right gone, the rent gone. No clause in the classical instrument can make a payment outlive the thing it pays for.

Sit with how much moral work that battery of burdens does. The lessor's return arrives through time, month after month, and yet it is not agar natar, not a wage of waiting — because at every moment of the waiting he is long a real asset with real enemies: rot, rust, fire, obsolescence, the defect that surfaces in year three, the roof that owes him a winter's repairs. His income is the fruit of something he still owns, and the owning costs him something every day. Strip those burdens away one by one — make the tenant insure, make the tenant repair, make the tenant carry the destruction risk, promise the owner his stream in every state of the world — and with each clause the owner's seat empties a little more, until what remains is a man collecting a schedule: near to profit, far from loss, the baraita's exact posture, achieved not by guarantee this time but by upholstery. The burdens are not friction in the lease; they are the license for its price, and every one of them is auditable — which is why chapter 10's rule scales here without strain: the income justified by the owner's peril lives exactly as long as the peril does, whether the thing at risk is a widow's kettle or a fleet of aircraft.

sections.title: The Landlord's Coat
paragraphs: Which brings this chapter to the second machinist's paper, and to the promise chapter 3 made when it first showed the honest lease its floor: we would watch what happens when the floor is sanded away — when an instrument "quietly transfers every burden of ownership to the user and keeps only the income, at which point it has become," in that chapter's words, "a secured loan in a landlord's coat."

The financial lease did not need a conspiracy to evolve; it needed only the drift this book has watched in every century. A manufacturer's finance arm, a bank's leasing desk, discovers that owning ten thousand machines is a nuisance but financing ten thousand machines under a landlord's title is a business. So the paper keeps the lease's name and sheds its seat, clause by clause. The lessee maintains — not the wear of use, which even the classical law might apportion, but everything, structure and substance, the whole of the owner's ancient duty. The lessee insures, naming the lessor as beneficiary. The lessee bears destruction: the hell-or-high-water clause of the opening, standard furniture in equipment finance, obliges the payments though the machine burn, sink, or seize. The term runs the asset's whole useful life, so nothing of substance ever really returns to the "owner"; at its end a purchase option for a dollar, or a token sum, tidies the title into the hands that held everything else all along. And the payments themselves are built like the thing they are: cost of the machine, plus a return on that cost for the time outstanding — an amortization schedule wearing rent's name. Run chapter 24's costume test and every answer comes back reversed. Did the financier own the thing in the world, or in a folder? Did its risk ever sit with him for one insurable hour? Is the payment a price for delivered use, or a claim that matures by dates? Could the arrangement be disappointed by anything but nonpayment? The fire already answered. A payment that outlives its machine was never rent.

The lease even acquired its own double sale, completing the costume family chapter 24 catalogued. In the sale-and-leaseback, a company sells its own building or fleet for cash and leases it back in the same set of signatures — two impeccable contracts, and the net of them is money now against a schedule of payments later, secured on an asset that never moved and never changed hands in any sense the eye could catch. Run honestly, with the burdens genuinely migrating to the buyer-lessor, the device can be a legitimate way to put sleeping capital to work; run as drafting, with the "seller" still insuring, maintaining, and bearing the fire, it is the 'ina of chapter 3 with a title deed — and the reader who has come this far can now grade any given specimen without help.

What is striking — and this book keeps finding the pattern — is who said so first and most plainly: the systems with something at stake in the word "lease." The accountants surrendered the label a generation ago. Since the first of January 2019, the main international standard requires the lessee of nearly any substantial lease to book a right-of-use asset and, beside it, a lease liability for the payments owed (IFRS 16) — the drafting profession's own confession that the tenant of such paper is, in substance, a debtor who has financed an acquisition, whatever the document's title page says. Substance over form: Gregory v. Helvering's rule and the Majalla's third article, chapter 3's twin authorities, arriving at the ledger. And the fiqh, with the largest religious lease-finance industry on earth to police, patrols its own version of the drift in its own voice. Usmani's warning to his industry is the chapter's thesis from inside the tradition: leasing "was not originally a mode of financing," and when institutions adopt it as one, "it is not sufficient... to substitute the name of 'interest' by the name of 'rent'" — "there must be a substantial difference between leasing and an interest-bearing loan." The instrument the industry built at the boundary, the ijara muntahia bittamleek — the lease ending in ownership, Islamic finance's lease-to-own — shows the guardrails the tradition insists on when it walks this close to the edge. The rentals may resemble a financing schedule; the customer may fully intend to own the machine at the end. But the standard keeps the anatomy honest at the joints: throughout the term the lessor's ownership burdens stay put — maintenance, insurance, destruction — so the ijara's rent remains licensed rent (the fire in year nine still lands on the lessor, and the rent still dies with the machine, 7/1/3); and the transfer of title at the end may not simply happen inside the lease. It rides on a promise recorded in a document separate from the lease itself (8/1), and when the day comes, "a new contract" must be drawn — a gift or a sale, executed then, at its own moment — "since the ownership to the property is not automatically transferred" (8/3). Two real contracts, in sequence, each with its own anatomy, rather than one financing wearing two masks. Whether the industry's practice honors the seams or merely draws them — the question chapter 24 asked of the benchmark, and chapter 32 will ask of the whole — is a live quarrel among the tradition's own scholars, which is precisely the health this book keeps pointing to. A tradition still arguing about its instruments is a tradition still awake at the gate.

One more figure stands in this section, and the register owes him plainness: the second machinist himself. The financial lease concentrates its comfort upstream and its catastrophe downstream — the small operator who loses shop, machine, and livelihood in one night and still owes four years of payments on the ash has been placed, by drafting, in the seat the traditions spent three thousand years refusing to let the weak occupy: every burden of ownership, no shred of its protection. Whatever else the old rent books were, they were agreed on this: the seat that collects the income keeps the risk, and a document that separates the two has not discovered a new kind of lease but rediscovered a very old kind of loan — secured, this time, more thoroughly than the old law would ever have allowed, for the coat keeps the collateral and the claim together: repossess the machine, sue for the balance, and call the whole arrangement rent.

sections.title: The Lease That Stays Honest
paragraphs: It remains to say what this chapter's instrument looks like when it is doing what the traditions built it to do — because Part VII's assignment is not autopsy but architecture, and the lease, honestly run, is the most naturally non-extractive financing instrument in the whole toolbox. It requires no partnership appetite, no profit audit, no oath at settlement; it only requires that ownership mean what it says.

The specification assembles itself from everything above, and it reads like a checklist because it is one — the ToC's own design bullet, rendered as clauses. The financier owns the asset in the world: acquired before let, registered, insured at his expense, his problem when it fails (3/1; 5/1/5–5/1/8). The rent prices delivered use: it begins when the asset is usable, pauses when the asset is not, scales — where the parties wish — with hours run or output taken, and may float only on a formula with a ceiling and a floor (5/2/3). The term is shorter than the asset's life, or honestly renewed at renewal's real price. Destruction terminates (7/1/3); delay meets triage and, if discipline is needed, the charity-routed pressure of chapter 8, never a meter (6/3; the mercy of 2:280 for the genuinely stuck). Any path to ownership at the end is a real second contract at a real moment — promise, then transfer, seams showing (8/1; 8/3). Nothing in that specification is exotic; every clause is in force somewhere today, in standards this chapter has quoted. The instrument scales institutionally, too, and always has: the great endowments this Part will reach in chapter 29 — waqf, hekdesh, church property, the asset-locked estates of Steward Ownership's ancestors — earned much of their keep across the centuries precisely as standing lessors, patient owners letting real things at honest rents. An economy could finance its workshops, its vehicles, its looms and kilns and tractors this way at any scale it chose — the owner-financier earning a rent licensed by roofs he genuinely must fix, the user paying for use and walking whole out of the fire. Productive assets financed without extraction is not a utopia; it is a rent book, kept the old way.

The lease also hands Part VII its next instrument. An owner with one warehouse can lease it; an owner who needs to raise the warehouse's price from a hundred savers must cut its ownership into paper — certificates that entitle each holder to a slice of the asset and its rents — and the moment ownership becomes paper, every question this chapter settled comes back at scale: whose burdens, whose risk, whose fire? It is no accident that when modern Islamic finance went looking for an instrument to stand where bonds stand, it reached first for the lease — the classic sukuk template is a leased asset cut into certificate form — nor any surprise that the drift this chapter watched in equipment finance reappears there, as chapter 26 will show. The fire test travels; chapter 26 will strike the match under paper. What this chapter adds to the book's argument is a quiet, load-bearing distinction the traditions never let go: time was never the enemy. The lease collects through time, month after month, and every tradition blesses it — because what time delivers under a lease is use, real as bread, from a thing the owner goes on owning, insuring, repairing, and losing. The usurer's sin was never patience; it was selling the calendar while owning nothing that lived inside it.

chapters.part: Part VII — Instruments: How Contracts and Institutions Try to Escape Usury

chapters.title: Asset-Backed Certificates: Sukuk, Bonds, and Participation
chapters.label: Chapter 26

paragraphs: This Part opened in Genoa, with a pope answering an archbishop about merchants' paper, and it is deliberate architecture that the Part's third instrument brings us back — to the same city, two centuries and more on, standing in the counting hall of one of the most remarkable financial institutions of the late medieval world. In 1407, after more than a century of piecemeal expedients, the Republic of Genoa gathered its public debts into a single house, the Casa di San Giorgio. The republic's creditors, great and small, held luoghi: shares of a nominal hundred lire apiece, "without materiality," as the great historian of the Casa puts it, existing as lines in a register. A luogo could be transferred to anyone by simple registration in the official creditors' ledgers; the shares were actively traded, and speculated in, for four centuries. And what the paper held was not a bare promise. Each underlying compera was, in the standard definition, the right to collect, for the holders' benefit and for the entire term, a named tax — already levied or created for the purpose — so that the man who bought a luogo bought a seat at a particular fiscal table: a gabelle already levied or created for the purpose, a duty of the port — revenues with names, yields that rose and fell with the trade of the city. Genoa had invented, or perfected, something this book has not yet examined and the modern world cannot live without: the claim cut into equal pieces and sent traveling — capital raised from a crowd, paper in ten thousand hands.

Paper at scale is Part VII's hinge, because everything the last two chapters established was established between people. The murabaha's candor, the lease's burdens — these are disciplines of a relationship, enforceable because somebody is looking somebody in the eye. A certificate abolishes the eye contact. The holder of piece four hundred and seven has never seen the aircraft, the tax farm, the venture; he may hold his piece for an afternoon; he bought it from a stranger and will sell it to a stranger. The question this chapter asks is the whole moral content of securitization, and it can be put in five words: what does the paper hold? Because two lineages of certificate run through history side by side, alike to the eye and opposite in anatomy. One is paper that owns — a fractional seat in a real thing and its real fortunes. The other is paper that is owed — a fractional loan, the mutuum of chapter 7 cut into coupons and set loose to compound among strangers. Every tradition this book reads blessed the first kind in principle and built versions of it in practice; every tradition's wall stands against the second; and the drift from the first to the second — accomplished quietly, clause by clause, while the name on the paper never changes — is the most consequential costume story in modern religious finance.

sections.title: Paper That Is Owed
paragraphs: Take the bond first, because its anatomy is already in the book. Strip the trading floor away and a conventional bond is chapter 7's contract in formal dress: a sum delivered, ownership of it passing utterly to the issuer; a promise of the sum's return at a date; and between delivery and return, the coupon: increase, calculated on principal and calendar, precisely the agar natar the traditions walled out, now stamped in convenient denominations. Nothing about cutting the loan into a thousand equal pieces changes the analysis; it changes the scale and the sociology. The bond made the creditor's seat fungible: anyone's money could occupy it, briefly, anonymously, and the seat's terms never renegotiate because no one sits in it long enough to be anyone. Chapter 2 watched the Torah's lender bound to a brother whose face he knew, and watched the modern credit market complete what Nelson called the journey to universal otherhood; the bond is that journey's vehicle. A debt owed to everyone in general is a debt owed to no one in particular, and no one in particular has ever forgiven a coupon.

Two honesties must be entered at once, because the traditions enter them. First: the certificate was never the sin. Writing debt down is not merely tolerated but commanded — the written and witnessed debt of chapter 6 — and the halakha's whole civil law runs on instruments; a paper acknowledging that a hundred is owed, transferring for what buyers will pay, offends nothing in any of the three traditions so long as the hundred is all that ever comes back. The trouble is the coupon, not the certificate. Second: the traditions saw early and clearly that paper is a different kind of thing from the things it points at. The Mishnah's ona'ah carve-outs, chapter 9 listed them, exempt documents from the price-fraud rules — because a shtar is not a commodity with a market worth but a claim, worth whatever the promise inside it is worth, and the ordinary machinery of overreaching has no purchase on it. The market learned the same lesson from the trading floor. A bond's price moves with nothing but arithmetic — when the going rate of money rises, yesterday's coupons are worth less, and the paper falls without a single fact about any venture changing anywhere — because there is no venture; the certificate's entire interior is a rate and a date, and its market value is the calendar repricing itself. Ownership paper cannot move that way. Its price carries news — a lean harvest, a grounded fleet, a good year at the port — and the difference between paper that trades on news and paper that trades on arithmetic is chapter 7's whole distinction, quoted daily at market close.

And so the traditions' honest lane for debt paper is narrow and real: the certificate may carry principal across hands and across time, and it may not breed. A written qard, a shtar for a hundred that a hundred discharges, a bill that moves a debt to a new holder for what buyers freely pay — all of this is commerce in claims, blessed and ancient. The line is crossed at the coupon, and crossed again, more quietly, wherever paper is issued at a discount that is simply the coupon folded into the price. What the wall demands of debt's paper is exactly what it demanded of debt: that the claim come home the size it left. Sitting inside that dry procedural rule is the insight this whole chapter runs on: paper has no value of its own; it is a window, and everything depends on what stands on the other side of the glass — a thing, with fortunes; or only a promise, with a date.

sections.title: Paper That Owns
paragraphs: The other lineage is older than the bond and, in every tradition, cleaner. If a venture, a field, a building can have one owner, it can have forty; the law needed only to learn to write fractions. The rabbis wrote them in partnership deeds — the shtar iska of chapters 11 and 13 is already a certificate, paper whose holder owns half the venture's deposit-half and eats its outcome, and nothing in principle stopped such deeds from finding new hands. The instrument's modern institutional career, chapter 14 showed, runs through the heter iska klali — one master partnership document standing behind an entire bank's book, every depositor holding, in form, a sliver of a venture rather than a claim to interest; paper that owns, at national banking scale, with all the questions about whether anyone remembers the ownership that chapter 31 will press. The fiqh wrote fractions with its usual definitional care, and its modern standard-setters have compressed the lineage into a definition this chapter can hang everything on. Investment sukuk, runs the AAOIFI standard's formula, are "certificates of equal value representing undivided shares in ownership of tangible assets, usufruct and services" — undivided shares in ownership: the holder of a sukuk certificate is not owed the aircraft's price; he owns, with ten thousand co-owners, an undivided sliver of the aircraft, the way heirs own a field before partition. The classic structure, as chapter 25 promised, is the lease bound into paper: the holders' undivided aircraft is leased to the airline, the rent flows through to them pro rata, and every doctrine of the last chapter comes with the package — their rent licensed by their ownership burdens, their income dying, in principle, with the asset in the fire. The plumbing is modern — the holders' undivided title is typically parked with a trustee, the certificates evidencing each stranger's fraction — but the doctrine riding in the pipes is chapter 25's, unchanged: distributions are rent, rent is licensed by ownership's burdens, and if the aircraft is lost the certificates hold ash and an insurance claim, not a right to be made whole by anybody's promise. Paper multiplies the owners; it must not be allowed to subtract the ownership. The Fiqh Academy's sukuk resolution states the resulting rule in one clause: the return on all such certificates "should be stemming from income-generating assets" — from the named kitchen, not from the calendar.

And Latin Christendom, though the textbooks rarely put it this way, ran one of history's great experiments in participation paper. The luoghi of San Giorgio were not bonds in the modern sense, whatever later centuries made of the family they founded. A luogo's yield was not a stipulated coupon; it was a provento, a distribution of what the assigned taxes actually brought in, and the holders stood, as a body, in the fiscal weather of Genoa: rich years and plague years, war and the loss of colonies, all of it passing through to the paper. (Whether a luogo's yield was fruit or disguised interest was itself argued, on and off, for as long as the Casa stood — the census quarrel of Part VIII in miniature, and proof that the drift this chapter tracks was visible to consciences long before it had a compliance department.) The scholastics' comfort with such instruments followed the logic this book has traced for three chapters: a man who buys, for a price, the fruits of a named and fruitful thing has bought something real, and bears its fortunes; the quarrels — and they were real quarrels, running for centuries, about when a purchased revenue-stream is a harvest and when it is a disguised loan — belong with the census family and the monti of Part VIII, where the early modern age will fight them at full length. (A disambiguation, before the Part VIII door closes: the papal and civic monti of public finance are not the Monti di Pietà of chapter 17 — the same word, a mountain of money, naming a lending charity in one century and a debt consolidation in another.) What matters here is the design point Genoa proves: participation paper is not a modern invention struggling against ancient categories. It is the ancient category — the societas of chapter 11, given a register and a crowd — and for centuries it financed ports, fleets, and public life on exactly the terms the traditions could bless: many small owners, real assets, named revenues, outcomes shared.

The three traditions' paper, set side by side, agrees on the load-bearing point with an exactness that should no longer surprise any reader of this book. A certificate is honest when it conveys a genuine fraction — of a thing, of a venture, of a named stream of fruits — and its holder eats what the fraction earns and loses what the fraction loses. The Talmud's deed-holder awaits the venture's actual accounting; the luogo-holder's provento shrinks when the port is quiet; the sukuk-holder's distribution is rent from an aircraft he co-owns, and the Fiqh Academy requires him to bear his proportional risk as the price of his proportional gain. Participation, in other words, scales. What does not scale — what the crowd, the register, and the secondary market grind away at from the first day — is the appetite for participation's terms. Ten thousand strangers did not buy the paper to stand in fiscal weather. They bought it to be paid, evenly, quarterly, at par; and the history of the certificate is the history of drafting that tries to give them exactly that while keeping ownership's name on the instrument. Notice, before the drift is walked, what the three old papers all got right about transfer itself: the ledger. Genoa's line in the creditors' register, the sukuk trustee's record, the deed in the partner's strongbox — in each, the paper travels freely while the obligations of ownership attach, entire, to whoever holds it at the moment the roof leaks. Transferability was never the corruption; the corruption is drafting that lets the benefits travel while the burdens stay behind with someone else.

sections.title: The Four Things a Certificate Can Hold
paragraphs: Before the drift can be watched honestly, the reader needs the audit, and it has four layers. Ask of any certificate what its holder can actually reach — a question a careful buyer can put to any prospectus, and the first module of the analyzer chapter 43 will build — and every security ever drafted holds one of four things. It can hold the thing itself, true fractional ownership: the asset's title runs to the holders or their trustee, and if every promise around it burned away tonight, the holders would still, at law, own the aircraft. It can hold a usufruct, not the tree but its fruit for a term: chapter 25's right in a body, alive exactly as long as the body — the sukuk standards themselves list usufructs and services beside tangible assets, so that paper may hold a term of a thing's use, or of a service to be rendered, and the holder's income is the fruit of that term and dies at its end. It can hold a revenue assignment (no title, no usufruct, but a named stream): a named tax, a toll, a schedule of lease payments, flowing to the paper as long as the stream flows — the compera's direct descendants live on in every instrument that finances a bridge from its own tolls, and the moral character of such paper turns entirely on whether the stream's failure is the holder's weather or somebody's guaranteed problem. Or it can hold a promise about all of the above, and here is where the reader must slow down, because the fourth layer devours the other three. A guarantee that the holder will receive his capital back at par, whatever becomes of thing, fruit, or stream — a binding undertaking by the issuer or manager to repurchase the assets at the stated price "regardless of their true or market value at maturity," in Usmani's exact and exasperated description of the market's standard clause — does not add safety to ownership; it replaces it. The holder who cannot lose no longer owns anything; he is owed something, by the very party whose performance was supposed to be the venture's, and the thing, fruit, and stream have quietly become collateral for a loan whose name is still Arabic. A guarantee is how paper resigns from ownership.

The fiqh's standard-setters, to their credit, wrote this analysis before the critics did, and chapter 13's fetched texts carry it verbatim into this one. A sukuk manager — mudarib, partner, or agent — guarantees the capital only "in case of his negligent acts or omissions or his non-compliance"; beyond fault, trust capital may not be guaranteed at all, and instruments may not be "marketed or operated as a guaranteed investment." Combine agency with guarantee and the drafting itself, says the standard, "turns the transaction into an interest-based loan" — tantamount to riba. A genuinely independent third party may volunteer a guarantee of capital, in a different capacity and for no fee — the narrow gate, and note how narrow: the moment the guarantor is anyone inside the venture's economics, the paper has flipped layers. The Fiqh Academy's resolution draws the same two lines with a jurist's economy: no guarantee by the manager except for transgression or negligence, and no redemption at nominal value — the exit price must be the market's or an honestly agreed one, never par-by-promise. Redemption at par is the guarantee wearing its maturity-date clothes; the fixed number of chapter 14, written not into a partnership this time but into ten thousand certificates; and the same verdict follows it: void where the tradition can reach it, riba where it cannot.

sections.title: The Drift Back to Bonds
paragraphs: Now watch the drift run, because the ToC's word is exact — nobody legislated the certificate back into a bond; it drifted, one accommodating clause at a time, under the pressure the section above named: the crowd wants par and coupons, and the industry wants the crowd. And the crowd deserves its steelman before its correction, because the crowd is not a villain. It is the schoolteacher's retirement account, the small trader's reserve, the modern versions of every widow this book has met holding paper because paper is what a person of modest means can hold; such holders cannot audit a venture and know it, and their hunger for a certain number is the hunger for safety of people who have exactly one number to lose. The traditions never mocked that hunger. They answered it with different institutions — the pools and endowments this Part is walking toward — rather than with ownership's name on a creditor's terms. The distributions came first. A true participation pays what the assets earned, which is lumpy; the market's sukuk paid, in Usmani's words, on rates "not linked to the expected profits from the enterprise, but to the costs of financing or to the prevalent rates of interest" — LIBOR's thermometer again, wired now not to a markup but to an ownership instrument. The excess went next: whatever the assets earned above the benchmark was assigned to the manager as an "incentive," which inverts partnership's whole geometry — the crowd holds ownership's name and collects a creditor's stipend, while the insider collects ownership's upside for managing the costume. Shortfalls were smoothed by the manager's advances, until the 2008 resolution barred the manager from undertaking to lend against them, leaving only the honest, disclosed reserve chapter 13 met. Even the accounting rules inside the standards hold the line chapter 14 admired: receivables enter the profit reckoning at their honest collectible value, with "neither time value (interest rate) nor discount" admitted into the computation — the tradition refusing, down in the bookkeeping, the very quantity the drift smuggles in up on the term sheet. And underneath the cash mechanics ran the deepest clause of all, the lawyers' distinction the industry itself coined: asset-backed versus asset-based. In a true asset-backed issue, the assets are actually sold — perfected, bankruptcy-remote, reachable — and the holders' fate genuinely rides on them. In the asset-based issue that came to dominate the market, the "sale" is beneficial only: title never perfects, the holders' recourse at failure runs to the originator's balance sheet like any unsecured lender's, and the assets are scenery. Paper that owns, as drafted; paper that is owed, as enforced.

The tradition's own conscience said all of this first and loudest. Usmani's paper — written from inside the industry's own standards body — concluded that "most of the Sukuk that have been issued are identical to conventional bonds with regard to the distribution of profits," and that the market's favorite mechanisms exist precisely so the instruments "take on the same characteristics as conventional, interest-bearing bonds"; his summary rule for repair is five words of pure Part III: "reward always follows after risk." The AAOIFI board answered with the February 2008 resolution chapter 13 fetched — the guarantee bans, the reserve discipline, the no-par-repurchase rule — and the Fiqh Academy's 2009 Sharjah session, the same sitting that refused organized tawarruq in chapter 24, issued the sukuk resolution quoted above. Three internal verdicts in two years, from the tradition's most senior juridical machinery. Whether the market obeyed — and what it means that the certifying and the structuring are so often paid for by the same issuer — is a question chapter 32 will weigh with the whole industry on the scale.

But one specimen belongs here, because it put the drift's every layer before a court, in public, with dates. In June 2017, Dana Gas — a Sharjah company with some seven hundred million dollars of mudarabah sukuk outstanding since 2013 — announced that its own certificates were "not Shari'a compliant and... therefore unlawful under UAE law," suspended the distributions, and took injunctions in three jurisdictions to hold off its creditors. The market was appalled in both directions at once, and both directions matter for this chapter. The holders discovered what layer their paper really held: when the mudarabah's compliance was impeached, their protection turned out to be the English-law purchase undertaking — the par-repurchase promise — which the English High Court, in November 2017, held "valid and enforceable in accordance with its terms" precisely because it was an ordinary English contract whose obligations did not depend on the Islamic structure at all. The paper was enforced, and what was enforced was not ownership of anything; it was the fourth layer, the promise, standing alone in an English courtroom, severed from the structure it had been drafted to complete. And the issuer's maneuver taught the opposite lesson to the same audience: a compliance doctrine invoked for the first time at the moment it became convenient to stop paying looked, to analysts and to the tradition's scholars alike, less like scruple than like a borrower discovering theology at the due date. The affair ended as such affairs end — a June 2018 restructuring, holders exiting at ninety and a half cents or rolling into new three-year paper — but its testimony stands. When the costume was contested, neither side defended the ownership the certificates proclaimed. They fought about the promise, because the promise was always the instrument.

sections.title: From Backed to Locked
paragraphs: The repair the ToC points to is not better backing. It is a different relationship between the paper and the thing, and the old institutions already modeled it. "Backing" is a snapshot: assets stand behind the paper today, and tomorrow they are swapped, released, re-pledged, or — the asset-based lesson — revealed never to have left the issuer's hands at all. What is merely backed can be quietly unbacked; what is locked has taken vows. Genoa's compere locked: the assigned tax belonged to the holders for the entire term, by the instrument's own definition, not as collateral they might race other creditors to but as the very thing they had bought. The endowments this Part reaches in chapter 29 — waqf, hekdesh, church property, and their modern descendants in Steward Ownership's asset locks — are the lock's full development: property bound to a purpose so that no holder, manager, or successor can strip it. Between the snapshot and the vow runs the whole spectrum of honesty in securitization — the bare representation, the negative pledge that merely promises not to encumber, the perfected security interest, the true sale, and at the far end the purpose-bound corpus that no one may alienate at all — and the traditions' verdicts, assembled across this chapter, sit at the vowed end. Drafting can locate an instrument anywhere on that spectrum; what it cannot do is make the middle of the spectrum feel like the end to the person holding the paper, which is why the disclosure duties of chapter 23 travel with every certificate this chapter has blessed.

So the specification the ToC asks for — what non-extractive securities would require — can be written as the audit run in reverse, and every line of it is already in force somewhere in the instruments this chapter has quoted. The transfer is true: title perfects, the holders or their trustee reach the thing itself at failure, and the originator's insolvency is the paper's weather, not its grave. The return stems from the named fruits — the Academy's income-generating assets, the compera's salt tax — and distributions track what the assets earned, smoothed only by the disclosed reserve, never by advances that are loans in waiting. Losses land on the holders pro rata, as the price of their gains; the manager is paid as a worker or a partner — a fee, a ratio — and never stands as guarantor of the capital his own conduct steers, save for his proven fault. There is no par-by-promise: exits, redemptions, and repurchases happen at market or honestly appraised value, so the certificate can be disappointed, which is the entire moral point. The waterfall is disclosed whole, chapter 23's standard, so the crowd knows which layer it is buying. And where the financed thing serves a purpose beyond its yield — the utility, the housing, the working forest — the asset is locked to that purpose, chapter 29's move, so that the paper's travels through ten thousand anonymous hands can never carry the thing itself out the door. And because certificates travel, the specification must travel with them: every resale re-poses the four-layer question to a new stranger, and honest paper is paper that answers it identically in every hand — the tenth holder reaching the same thing, bearing the same weather, reading the same disclosed waterfall as the first. A security that is participation at issuance and something else by the third trade has merely scheduled its costume change. None of this is exotic; all of it is costly, in exactly the way honesty has been costly in every chapter of this Part: it surrenders the sale-ability of certainty. Paper that owns cannot promise par, and the crowd pays less for weather than for promises. The non-extractive security is, in the end, participation priced as participation — the oldest door in the book, cut into equal pieces without cutting away the doorway — and whether a market can be built that prefers it is not a drafting question but the civilizational one this book's last Parts take up in earnest — chapter 40's return formula, chapter 41's fund design, and the sample waterfalls of Appendix E are, among other things, sketches of what such paper would pay and to whom.

One instrument remains in Part VII's workshop before the endowments close it — the one that answers a different fear. Sale, lease, and certificate finance what people can do; none of them touches what people dread. The pool — insurance, takaful, the mutual aid that chapter 2 called the shield and chapter 28 will render as mathematics — is where the traditions took the logic of participation and pointed it at catastrophe itself, and chapter 27 opens that door. The paper of this chapter will be waiting when the book returns to design: a certificate, honestly cut, is how a community owns a big thing together, and the last Parts of this book are, among other things, an argument that the crowd deserves better instruments than the coupon — paper with weather in it, paper that knows what it holds. Genoa's luoghi held the taxes of a real port, and the paper rose and fell with the ships. That, and not the promise of par, is what it has always meant for capital to be in the world rather than over it.

chapters.part: Part VII — Instruments: How Contracts and Institutions Try to Escape Usury

chapters.title: Insurance, Takaful, Mutual Aid, and Risk Pools
chapters.label: Chapter 27

paragraphs: Modern insurance entered history in a costume, and the costume was a loan. Chapter 10 left Mediterranean commerce holding a problem: the sea loan — capital advanced against a voyage, the debt dying with the ship, a stiff premium if she arrived — stood condemned by name in the Liber Extra of 1234. The lender's premium was payment for carrying the sea's peril, and Naviganti refused to let a hazard clause consecrate a creditor's gain. But the peril did not go away because the premium did. Ships still sank, no merchant could stand alone under a cargo's whole fate, and carrying the sea remained real work with a real price. So the notaries of the Italian ports went to work, and the historian who assembled their paper trail, Florence Edler de Roover, found the solution taking shape under exactly the dress this Part has learned to check for. In the earliest contracts the carrier of the risk appears as a borrower: he acknowledges receipt of a loan, money he had never in fact received, repayable if and only if the ship failed to arrive. If she docked, the fiction dissolved and he kept his true premium; if she was lost, he "repaid" what he had never borrowed, and the merchant was made whole. Other drafts ran the same protection through a fictitious sale. The Church's usury doctrine had as yet no shelf for protection sold plain, so protection traveled under names the law already trusted — and the older scholarship de Roover engaged read Naviganti as the push that sent the merchants hunting. By 1329 the documents of Palermo show the premium contract stepping into daylight; by the 1370s the notarial books of Genoa carry premium insurance as ordinary business; the earliest policies that survive at all come from the Italian ports of the 1340s.

The joke history was telling here runs at this Part's expense, instructively. Three chapters have watched suspect things dress as honest ones — loans as sales, loans as leases, bonds as ownership. Here the traffic ran the other way: an honest thing entered the world wearing the suspect thing's clothes, because it was so new it had no name of its own. And the unbundling underneath the disguise was the very analysis Naviganti had demanded: the sea loan had charged for two services — capital for the venture, and a shoulder for the venture's catastrophe — through one premium riding one debt, and the decretal struck the bundle. The market's eventual answer, once the costumes wore out, was to sell the two services separately: the merchant found his capital where capital was lawfully found, and the insurer carried the sea alone, for a premium that paid for the carrying and for nothing else. That is the story chapter 10 promised this chapter would finish. Insurance did not evolve out of gambling, and it did not evolve out of charity; it evolved out of the usury question — the honest remainder left standing when the Church audited the sea loan and struck the part that was a loan.

The instruments of the last three chapters finance what people intend: the purchase, the workshop, the fleet cut into certificates. This chapter's instrument faces the other way, toward what nobody intends — fire, wreck, death, the failed season — and toward the dread of it that shadows every household this book has visited. Chapter 3's taxonomy gave the instrument its own first-class name, the solidarity pool, and posted at its door the question this chapter exists to answer: whether protection is pooled among members or sold at a margin, and what each arrangement does to the people inside it. But an older accusation must be answered first, for it has been leveled at this instrument in every century of its life, with real evidence behind it. The premium is certain; the payout hangs on chance. Is the whole business a wager?

sections.title: The Wager and the Fog
paragraphs: State the resemblance at full strength before answering it. A man pays a small sum now; a contingency decides whether he collects a large sum later; the counterparty keeps the small sum either way. Drawn as a payoff diagram, the fire policy and the bet on the fire are the same picture, and for a long time the law of the world's busiest insurance market could not tell them apart either. Eighteenth-century London ran the experiment to its limit. A Londoner with nothing aboard a ship could buy a policy on her safe arrival — the trade wrote such contracts "interest or no interest," meaning the buyer need prove no stake beyond the paper itself — and a Londoner could insure a stranger's life and follow the coffee-house odds on his surviving the season. Nothing in the instrument's form distinguished these wagers from a merchant's honest cover: same clauses, same premium, same contingent payout. Parliament eventually drew the line the form could not hold. The Marine Insurance Act of 1745 voided the ships' wagers — policies written interest or no interest were declared null and void — and in 1774 the Life Assurance Act did the same for lives: experience had shown, its preamble runs, that insuring lives and events "wherein the assured shall have no interest hath introduced a mischievous kind of gaming." The remedy became the common law's permanent doctrine: no policy without an insurable interest — a stake the buyer already holds, such that the insured-against day would genuinely wound him — no recovery beyond that stake's value, and the beneficiaries named on the face of the policy. The wager-buyer and the honest policyholder are told apart, in the end, by a single question: which day is each of them waiting for? A man with cargo in the hold dreads the storm his policy covers. A man holding a naked wager on the same ship has been handed a reason to pray for the storm — and, the eighteenth century learned, sometimes to arrange it. Chapter 22 heard the canonists ask the same question of the penalty clause — the lender must not be made to want the default — and the insurable-interest doctrine rebuilds that finding in an underwriter's office: a contract of protection stays honest only while its holder still needs the protected thing to survive.

Islam had run the analysis on gambling itself eleven centuries earlier, and its terms cut to the same joint. The Qur'an's word is maysir, and its original target, the commentators say, was the arrow-game of the jahiliyya — shares in a slaughtered camel riding on marked shafts drawn blind. Its first pass at the subject is surprisingly patient: "There is great sin in both, and some benefit for people," it says of wine and gambling together (2:219, here as throughout in M. A. S. Abdel Haleem's rendering). The patience does not last: gambling stands among the "repugnant acts — Satan's doing — shun them so that you may prosper" (5:90), and the ground given is not probability but fellowship: "With intoxicants and gambling, Satan seeks only to incite enmity and hatred among you" (5:91). Chapter 6 read the doctrine whole: the winner's gain is carved from the loser's substance, with nothing made and nothing traded, and enmity is what the table reliably produces. Against that doctrine the underwriters' statutes read like a Meccan finding in Georgian dress, and the distinction both were groping for can be said plainly. The gambler manufactures his peril; the insured already owns one. The world put the fire in the workshop and the storm across the sea lane; the wagerer's danger exists only because the stakes created it. Insurance and gambling are not neighbors on a spectrum of prudence but opposite answers to chance — one transfers a risk, the other conjures one — and every sound insurance doctrine in the world is a set of fences for keeping the second out of the first's clothing.
