The third is the direction of drift. The classical sequence ran venture first, number second: real iska arrangements, with the settlement sum as their convenience. The institutional sequence runs number first, venture afterward, if ever: the rate is set by the market, the partnership recited to license it, and the instrument's defenders themselves (the striking thing about the responsa) keep requiring the attachable asset, voiding the unverifiable clause, repeating that the document is not magic. A tradition maintains that drumbeat about an instrument for one reason: it knows what the instrument is tempted to become.

The tradition speaks the failure state in examples rather than abstractions; this book's word for it is ribbit-washing, and the term means something precise. The heter iska is not ribbit-washing — it is a partnership instrument with a settlement option, and this chapter has spent its length on the reality of what it transforms. Ribbit-washing is what remains when the working parts are removed one by one — the wage waived into boilerplate, the witnesses named in a far city, the oath drafted to terrify, the venture nowhere — until nothing is left but the label and the rate: a fixed return, collected in all states of the world, from a counterparty whose ruin is contractually nobody's business, under a document that promises an accounting no party could render of a venture no party can locate. The line between the instrument and its failure state does not run between centuries, or between retail form and bank form, or between Poland and Tel Aviv; it runs, case by case, where this tradition always said it runs: through the substance. When the deposit half genuinely stands in a real venture's wind — when a proven loss would truly shrink the obligation, when the accounting is available though rarely invoked, when the manager is a merchant with a warehouse rather than a wage-earner with a wedding to pay for — the heter iska preserves the Torah's substance while sparing its subjects the audit's full cost, and it is what its drafters built: the law's own bridge between the wall and the fair. When those conditions fail, the same clauses in the same order are a costume, and the tradition's own authorities say so in the tradition's own categories — words without a venture, a partnership without a meeting of minds, a settlement sum replacing a truth everyone knows. The instrument does not choose between these fates. The parties do, financing by financing, and the poskim's four-hundred-year vigil over the form is the tradition declining, under every commercial pressure, to stop asking which fate has occurred.

Which leaves the answer chapter 20 was promised. The question held open there was exact: the halakha's reply to the lender's "I could have earned more elsewhere" is the iska recharacterization — compensation sized to a real venture, collectable because the capital genuinely stands in the wind — and the open question was whether the instrument keeps that condition true at banking scale. The honest answer, assembled from the tradition's own record, is: not by itself. The condition is not self-executing. Paper, however brilliant, cannot hold itself to the world. What the instrument does — and no tradition in this book achieved more against the same problem — is keep the condition stated, justiciable, permanently collectable-against. The loss clauses can be invoked, the accounting demanded, the limiting rulings applied; and a banking system that runs on this paper carries, embedded in its own standard terms, the full grammar of the critique its practice must answer. Whether the condition is true in a given financing is a question of fact, not of form, and at national scale the facts are what a sober reader will already have concluded: mostly the settlement sum is paid, the venture is notional, and the wind never reaches the money. The tradition knows. It wrote the candor into its own compendia, and it keeps the form anyway, for the oldest of legal reasons — because the alternative to a form that states the right condition, imperfectly kept, is a market with no condition stated at all. Chapter 30 tells the story of the world that made such bargains feel inevitable — the centuries in which the surrounding civilization stopped asking the substance question altogether; chapter 32 watches the jurists of Islam meet the same pressure on their own instruments, the heter iska's dilemma replayed in another sacred legal language; and the closing Parts of this book ask what the poskim's vigil leaves standing for every tradition at once — whether the substance test can be made not merely statable but computable, so that the wind's actual reach to the money becomes a number somebody must report. Chapter 35 begins that arithmetic. The rabbi of Cracow, who rewrote his own document because two colleagues told him the substance had slipped, would recognize the project at a glance. It is his, at scale.

chapters.part: Part VIII — Modernity, Evasion, and the Return of Form Over Substance

chapters.title: Islamic Finance, Shariah Arbitrage, and the Westernization Problem
chapters.label: Chapter 32

paragraphs: In 1963, in a cotton town on the Nile Delta called Mit Ghamr, a young Egyptian economist named Ahmad El-Naggar opened a savings bank for people who had never trusted a bank. Its model came from the savings and cooperative banks of Germany, rebuilt for a pious countryside: the bank neither paid nor charged interest. A farmer's deposits earned, when they earned, as a share of what the bank's investments in local trade and workshops actually returned, and the money worked in ventures a depositor could walk past on market day. It was small, direct, and by every account beloved; within four years there were nine such banks in Egypt. Then, in 1967, the experiment was wound up — the historians mostly blame the political weather rather than the books — and its story scattered outward into what became an industry. Islamic finance now manages, by its own standard-setters' count, some 3.88 trillion dollars. Nearly every history the industry writes about itself begins in that delta town, rightly, because Mit Ghamr is the promise in miniature: finance without riba, tied to real activity, run for people the existing system had failed to reach.

The idea had books before it had banks. Through the 1960s and 1970s a generation of Muslim economists — Muhammad Nejatullah Siddiqi, whose Banking Without Interest became the movement's manual, Muhammad Umer Chapra, whose Towards a Just Monetary System (1985) gave it its fullest architecture, and their peers across South Asia and the Arab world — worked out on paper what a banking system inside the wall would look like. Siddiqi, looking back across the whole project in 2006, compressed the founding vision into one sentence: "What can be characterized as the 'theory' of Islamic banking was, till the end of the nineteen-seventies, largely a plea for replacing interest in bank lending by profit sharing." The moral center of the plea was the arrangement Part III watched the Qur'an condemn — the financier claiming a predetermined return while the working entrepreneur bears every risk of the business. The blueprint ran the logic of chapter 11 through an entire banking system — the depositor a rabb al-mal to his bank, the bank a mudarib, and the bank in turn a rabb al-mal to the town's enterprises: two tiers of mudarabah, capital earning only as a partner, paid from outcomes and exposed to them, with the naked loan reserved for mercy, where chapter 16 found it. It was the most complete attempt any modern community has made to build what this book's title asks for, and it deserves saying plainly, before any criticism is heard: the attempt was sincere, learned, and aimed at justice.

The banks followed the books. Dubai Islamic Bank opened on the fifteenth of September, 1975, among the first commercial banks anywhere to run under the new banner; the intergovernmental Islamic Development Bank went to work in Jeddah the same year; and through the oil decade the model spread — banks, subsidiaries, the "Islamic windows" of conventional giants, whole national systems — until the industry stretched from Kuala Lumpur to London. With the industry came a quarrel. Chapter 20 left it standing at this chapter's door in the shape of a question — whether the industry's condition is "prudence, contradiction, or an honest transition still under way" — and named the terms of the hearing: this is "the tradition's own quarrel, conducted by its own scholars in its own vocabulary." That framing is the chapter's law. The sharpest critics of Islamic finance are not its enemies; they are its founders, its judges, its board scholars, and its economists, and what they accuse the industry of is not impiety but imitation. Their name for the problem is Westernization, and in their mouths the word has nothing to do with geography — several of the most unsparing critics are Westerners by post or passport. The word names a drift of substance: conventional finance rebuilt inside Islamic wrappers, riba avoided in vocabulary and reproduced in payoff, the promise of Mit Ghamr kept in form and surrendered in content. Whether that charge is fair — and what still stands even if it is — is the hearing this chapter conducts. Part VIII has already visited chapter 30's road, the secularization of interest, and chapter 31's, the heter iska and its art of legal transformation. The fiqh took the third road: it rebuilt the wall at industrial scale, hired guards for it, and then had to ask, in its own committee rooms, what exactly had been built. Nobody in the room is a villain. The depositors are pious savers; the practitioners are bankers asked to do something genuinely hard; the scholars are jurists doing the tradition's oldest work under the newest pressure. The quarrel is about structures, and structures are this book's whole subject.

sections.title: The Landscape the Markup Conquered
paragraphs: The practice began to leave the theory within a few years of the first banks' opening. The instrument was chapter 24's: murabaha, the trust sale with its cost and markup declared, stretched into a financing triangle by the customer's promise to buy. It was honest, familiar to the jurists, and — decisively — it gave a bank margins that looked like margins: fixed, schedulable, fundable. Siddiqi again, looking back: "Within a couple of years of the introduction of murabahah in late nineteen-seventies, it conquered the landscape of Islamic finance, assigning mudarabah or profit-sharing to a corner accounting for less than ten percent of the operations." The conquest never reversed. Half a century on, the industry's own stability report draws the conquered landscape as a pie chart: of the financing on Islamic banks' books in 2024, forty-five percent was commodity murabaha and a further thirty-four percent murabaha proper — seventy-nine percent in the markup family, counting its two forms together — with ijara at nine, and the partnership instruments the theory was written for sharing an "others" slice of eight percent with everything else in the toolbox. The murabaha towers chapter 3 promised this chapter stand exactly where it said they would, visible from any skyline in the Gulf.

Two things must be said about that chart. The first is the practitioners' defense, which Siddiqi reported even while grieving the result. The bankers did try. "Practitioners of Islamic finance report they tried to push through sharing based finance but the results were not encouraging," he wrote; the surrounding legal systems offered a financier none of the protection against false profit-reporting that they offered a lender against default, leaving a bank that chose partnership to be lied to at scale without remedy. Chapter 14 watched the halakha price the same problem with witnesses and oaths sized to a community; a bank auditing ten thousand small ventures has no such machinery, and secular courts would not run the fiqh's evidence rules for it. Some financings, Siddiqi added dryly, simply defy profit-sharing — his example was a municipality laying sewage pipes, an asset with no revenue to share. And the depositors voted, year after year, for what the theory deplored: security of capital, Siddiqi observed, mattered more to the fund owners than the size of its returns. Chapter 26 met the same appetite among certificate holders and declined to mock it; neither will this chapter. Nothing in the conquest of the markup requires a villain — only the pressures this Part keeps finding: information that will not verify, law that will not cooperate, and a crowd that wants principal protected first and enterprise admired second.

The second thing is the critics' point, and it survives every syllable of the defense. A cost-plus credit sale, honestly run, is lawful — chapter 24 spent its length on the disciplines that keep it so: the ownership interval, the confessed cost, the price that never grows, the costume test it gave the whole Part. But lawful is not the same as different, and difference was the promise. An industry that runs four-fifths of its financing through deferred-price sales has built its balance sheet out of obligations that behave, cash flow by cash flow, like the loan book across the street: fixed claims, maturity dates, collateral, and a margin set off the price of money. The tradition's juridical summit has ruled on the family's darkest member: when the Fiqh Academy examined organized tawarruq in 2009 — the warehouse-metal round trip of chapter 24, sale and resale prearranged so that only cash and obligation actually move — it refused the device as "a deception... in order to get the additional quick cash." Sixteen years later, the single largest line in the industry's own chart is commodity murabaha — the instrument family that resolution described, much of it still running in the organized form through the same metal warehouses. That coexistence — verdict upstairs, volume downstairs — is the quarrel of this chapter in a single exhibit, and no outsider had to point it out. The insiders printed both pages.

sections.title: Deposits in a Partnership's Clothes
paragraphs: The promise's other half was the depositor, and here the drift is subtler and, the critics argue, deeper, because it runs through an instrument that still wears the theory's own name. Walk into an Islamic bank today and the savings product on offer is, in law, a mudarabah: an "investment account" whose holder owns the capital and whose bank is the working partner. Every rule of Part IV applies. The holder's return may only be a ratio of actual profit — a guaranteed sum voids the contract, chapter 11's rule; his principal is not owed back, for loss follows capital, the maxim carried there from the caliph Ali; the bank answers for losses only through the fault grammar chapter 13 anatomized — ta'addi, taqsir, breach of terms — and no profit exists to share until the capital stands whole, as chapter 19 found the industry's own standard-setters still printing. On paper, several hundred million people hold venture positions at their neighborhood bank. On paper, the two-tier vision was built.

Then look at the payout history, which is flat as a deposit rate, and ask how a portfolio of ventures produces it. The industry's prudential standard-setter answered in December 2010, in a guidance note whose subject line is its own summary: the practice of smoothing the profits payout to investment account holders. The Islamic Financial Services Board — Kuala Lumpur's prudential counterpart to Bahrain's AAOIFI — wrote down, with admirable candor, what the banks were doing and why. The why is competitive: an account holder whose returns lag the market may "withdraw their funds at short notice and place them with other financial institutions," and retail holders are, in the note's own words, "'defensive' investors seeking low-risk investments with steady but modest returns." The apparatus has three levers. The bank may quietly shrink its own share: entitled by contract to, say, a third of the profits as mudarib, it takes less in a lean year so the depositors' payout holds. It may draw on a profit equalization reserve — money set aside in fat years "before allocating the Mudarib's share," in the standard's definition, "to maintain a certain level of return on investment for investment account holders and to increase owners' equity." And beneath that sits an investment risk reserve, carved from the depositors' own profits "after allocating the Mudarib's share," held "to cushion against future investment losses." Fat years are clipped; lean years are topped up; the venture's weather never reaches the passbook. The industry even has a name for the pressure that drives the whole machine — displaced commercial risk, the risk that the bank must make its own shareholders eat the volatility of the depositors' portfolio because the market will not let it pay a partnership's true and lumpy returns. The critics have sat with that term, because it is the industry's own vocabulary for a strange fact: the bank behaves as if it had guaranteed what its contract scrupulously refuses to guarantee. What the contract dare not promise, the treasury quietly delivers.

The critics' reading follows. The lawyers hold the line perfectly — no guarantee is ever written, and the tradition's standard-setters police stipulated guarantees of mudarabah capital with the severity chapter 13 documented — while the reserves, the forgone shares, and the benchmark-watching treasury produce, year in and year out, the payoff of the thing that may not be written. A partnership whose partner is never allowed to feel the venture is, in substance, a depositor; a profit share managed to track the market's deposit rates is, in substance, that rate; and the "investment" in the account's name is real on paper only — precisely the confrontation chapter 11 promised this chapter, the bond's payoff rebuilt inside a partnership's legal shell. Note what the criticism is not: not that anyone lied — the smoothing is disclosed, standardized, and supervised, the guidance note existing precisely to govern it, cap it, and drag it into the annual report, self-documentation that is the tradition's conscience working in the open — and not that the depositors are wronged in their pockets. They get the steady modest return they demonstrably want, and the widow keeping her remittances at an Islamic bank because her conscience requires it is entitled to safety, not to a lecture on variance; the sober fact under this whole section is that the system's most defensive money belongs to its most faithful savers. The criticism is about what the arrangement does to the claim. The industry's flagship deposit was supposed to be the proof that banking can run on genuine risk-sharing. What the smoothing apparatus proves instead, the critics say, is that the industry itself does not believe its retail liabilities can carry real venture weather — and so the gate of Part IV, celebrated in every prospectus, carries a sliver of the asset side and, on the liability side, a partnership managed until it behaves like the deposit it lawfully cannot be.

sections.title: The Method Gets a Name
paragraphs: The certificate ran the same arc at wholesale scale, and this book has already walked it. Chapter 26 took the sukuk from its honest definition — undivided ownership shares in real assets — through the market's drift: Usmani's finding, delivered from within the industry's own standards body, that "most of the Sukuk that have been issued are identical to conventional bonds with regard to the distribution of profits," their payouts "not linked to the expected profits from the enterprise, but to the costs of financing or to the prevalent rates of interest"; the AAOIFI board's answering resolution of February 2008; the Fiqh Academy's Resolution 178, requiring that returns be "stemming from income-generating assets"; and the Dana Gas affair, in which an issuer impeached its own certificates' compliance and an English court enforced the purchase undertaking — the promise, not the ownership — as "valid and enforceable in accordance with its terms." What belongs to this chapter is the aftermath's shape. The 2008 intervention was the tradition policing itself in public, at real cost to the market that retained its jurists — and it worked as honest policing works: the worst devices retreated. And the market then did what markets do: it repapered, kept its benchmarks, and went on selling certificates whose holders wanted, and mostly got, the payoff of a bond. Usmani's five-word repair standard — "reward always follows after risk" — remains the sentence the industry's product desks must be measured against, and the measuring is a running argument inside the industry itself.

Underneath the certificates, as underneath the markups, runs the number. Chapter 24 gave the benchmark question its instrument-level hearing: the murabaha desks priced their margins off LIBOR for decades, Usmani defended the practice with a jurist's precision — "merely using the interest rate as a benchmark for determining the profit of murabahah does not render the transaction as invalid, haram or prohibited, because the deal itself does not contain interest" — and then, in the same breath, told his own industry it "should get rid of this practice as soon as possible." The habit outlived the advice. When LIBOR itself died — the last bank panel ended in June 2023 — the industry migrated to the successor rates alongside everyone else, repapering, as chapter 24 noted, without missing a payment date. Chapter 20 stated what the habit means at the level of doctrine: the benchmark problem is "lucrum cessans generalized — the market's elsewhere, priced into every contract, unexamined." An industry built to refuse the price of money, steering every product by the price of money, is either navigating by a star it refuses to worship — the defenders' reading, and it is not absurd — or it has told you, in its own pricing screens, which market it actually inhabits.

The man who gave the whole pattern its name is no outsider. Mahmoud El-Gamal holds the chair in Islamic economics and finance at Rice University in Houston, has spent his career inside the industry's conferences and texts, and writes as a believer who wants the law's purposes served. His name for the method is shariah arbitrage, and his definition deserves quoting whole: "Shari'a arbitrage is a particular form of regulatory arbitrage, wherein a captive market of pious Muslims voluntarily chooses not to use certain financial products. Lawyers, in partnership with bankers and jurists, strive to provide them a reengineered version of those products." The engineering method follows: "Conventional financial products are used as building blocks for the reengineered Islamic products approved by jurists" — the interest-bearing loan parked in a special purpose vehicle, the customer's own contract kept clean, the juristic gaze trained on the one document in the stack with an Arabic name. And the spread has a payer: the reengineering costs real money — "otherwise unnecessary transactions," plus "the additional legal and jurist fees required to structure a product and certify it" — and the costs land on the captive market itself. The pious customer pays more than his conventional neighbor for the same economic position, the premium buying not a different payoff but a different description of it. A gap between form and substance is, to a moralist, a scandal; to a market, a spread. El-Gamal's charge is that an entire industry took the spread: that the wall this book has watched three traditions defend became, in the hands of the structurers, a price differential to be monetized — and his proposed cure, it should be said, is not surrender but mutuality, banks and insurers owned by the very savers and policyholders they serve, the pool of chapter 27 offered as the antidote to the arbitrage. As competition thins the spread, he observed, the engineering only coarsens — the industry reaching for tawarruq, its bluntest instrument.

The scholars saw the method's limit case arrive in their own docket. When the swap engineers built the wa'd-based total return swap — a promise structure keyed to the performance of a portfolio the Islamic investor could never lawfully hold, delivering him its returns through a compliant wrapper — it was an American-born shariah scholar, Yusuf Talal DeLorenzo, a veteran of the industry's supervisory boards, who circulated the paper against it: "The Total Returns Swap and the 'Shariah Conversion Technology' Stratagem." His argument, reported here in substance, was that a jurisprudence which certifies the wrapper while ignoring what flows through it has traded the law's purposes for its instruments — that the device must be judged by its consequences, which were, with certainty, the delivery of returns from assets the law forbids. The industry's own conscience, once again, spoke first and sharpest. The pattern by now has a name, a mechanics, and a case file — and each of the three was supplied from inside the house.

sections.title: The Scholars in the Middle
paragraphs: Every product in this chapter passed across a desk where a jurist sat, and the office deserves description before examination: it is the tradition's living machinery, and its holders are heirs of every court this book has admired. A shariah supervisory board is a committee of jurists retained by a financial institution to rule on its products — fatwa by fatwa at design, then in annual review. The office concentrates enormous trust: the industry's entire claim to difference runs through it, and its occupants carry a burden closer to a judge's than a consultant's. The structural problem is that they are paid like consultants. The scholars are selected, retained, and compensated by the very institutions whose products they judge — an arrangement World Bank researchers examined two decades ago and found, in measured language, to compromise the boards' independence. The market for their services is astonishingly narrow at the top: a network study published in 2011 counted roughly four hundred scholars holding some fifteen hundred board seats across the industry, and found the ten busiest men holding four hundred fifty of the eleven hundred forty-one positions at the institutions studied — two of every five seats — with the two most sought-after scholars sitting on eighty-five boards apiece. The study's own worry was generational as much as juridical: "Where is the room for mentoring and apprenticeship systems when the same people of similar seniority tend to occupy the same boards?" The fees are what a market that narrow pays: figures reported in the scholarly literature run to tens of thousands of dollars a year for a single seat and as much as half a million for certifying one large capital-markets transaction. These facts were assembled by the industry's own researchers and are reported here as they report them — plainly, with no imputation against any man's sincerity, for the concentration has an innocent explanation that happens to be true. When the industry exploded, the jurists fluent in both classical fiqh and a derivatives term sheet numbered a few dozen on earth, and every issuer wanted the same trusted names for the reason medieval merchants did: reputation is quality assurance, the name-economy of chapter 11 at work.

But pressure finds a narrow market, and the ugliest quotation in this chapter's file comes from the demand side, not from the scholars. In December 2009 the BBC published a report by John Foster, a former editor of the trade magazine Islamic Business & Finance, quoting an investment banker in Dubai who worked for a major Western financial house: "We create the same type of products that we do for the conventional markets. We then phone up a Sharia scholar for a Fatwa... If he doesn't give it to us, we phone up another scholar, offer him a sum of money for his services and ask him for a Fatwa. We do this until we get Sharia compliance." The quotation is anonymous, one banker, and a description of the buyer's conduct rather than the sellers'; weigh it accordingly — and weigh it against the documented record of the men being dialed, which cuts the other way more often than the anecdote suggests: the 2008 AAOIFI resolution condemned the sukuk market's favorite structures to their holders' faces; the Fiqh Academy refused organized tawarruq against the plain convenience of the industry's entire liquidity apparatus; DeLorenzo's paper was aimed at the most lucrative engineering of its day. Fatwas of refusal exist in quantity, and some of them moved markets. What the anecdote actually documents is the market structure the critics keep pointing at: where certification is privately purchased, dispersed across competing boards, and paid for by the certified, the temptation to shop does not need to corrupt many scholars to corrupt many products — it only needs the phone numbers.

The tradition's answer has been standardization, which is quality control practiced as jurisprudence, and the least-told story in this quarrel. AAOIFI in Bahrain writes the shariah standards this book has been quoting for nine chapters, and governance standards for the boards themselves; the IFSB in Kuala Lumpur writes the prudential rulebook, the smoothing note of the last section among its papers; several jurisdictions have stacked a national or central shariah authority above the institutional boards, so that a product refused at the top cannot be shopped sideways; and the standards bodies publish, examine, and certify, slowly building the apprenticeship the network study found missing. None of this is decoration. Harmonized standards shrink the space in which a stratagem can hunt for its fatwa, much as the Majalla's codifiers shrank the space between Hanafi courtrooms — and the 2008 sukuk resolution demonstrated that a standard-setter can bite the market that feeds it. The quarrel chapter 27 promised this chapter completes the picture, because it is the same question one instrument over: whether a takaful operator may take performance incentives out of the participants' underwriting surplus — the steward paid from the pool's good years — or must be paid wages for stewardship, full stop. The industry's own jurists are divided; the diagnostic, chapter 27's indifference test, is the one this section has been applying to the scholars themselves. A certifier, like a pool operator, is honest in the measure that his compensation is indifferent to the answer he gives. The tradition knows how to write that rule. The open question, stated as the insiders state it, is whether an industry that pays its judges by the product can bring itself to adopt it.

sections.title: The Word, the Payoff, and the Ideal
paragraphs: The whole quarrel comes down, in the end, to a rule this book met in its third chapter, and it is the tradition's own. In contracts, says the Majalla's third article, effect is given to intention and meaning, not to words and phrases — a principle every school of the fiqh states in its own way, and the rule an American court rediscovered in Gregory v. Helvering, disregarding paperwork assembled "as a disguise." Chapter 3 made it the method of this entire book: the names are hypotheses; the payoff is the evidence. Now apply it, as the critics do, to the industry's shelf. The murabaha tower's cash flows are a loan book's. The smoothed investment account's payout series is a deposit's. The standard sukuk's coupon and par redemption are a bond's, and when Dana Gas put the question to a court, what proved enforceable was the promise, exactly as a bondholder's counsel would have drafted it. The swap delivered the forbidden portfolio's return to the pious investor's account. At the level of what each party pays, receives, and can lose in every state of the world, the critics observe, the products are built to be indistinguishable from their conventional templates — that is what a "reengineered version" of a conventional product means. If the payoff is the evidence, the critics conclude, then riba avoided in word and reproduced in payoff is riba still — and the Qur'an's own distinction, "God has allowed trade and forbidden usury" (2:275, in Abdel Haleem's rendering, as throughout this book), was never a distinction between vocabularies.

The defense deserves its full weight, because it is not sophistry. Form is not nothing; it is where law lives. A murabaha's ownership interval is real — the crane can drop the machine on the bank's watch, as chapter 24 insisted — and realness at the margin is what separates a sale from a rate. The contracts differ in enforcement, in bankruptcy, in what happens when the paper is stress-tested — differences that sometimes bite in the customer's favor. A tradition that policed intention alone would dissolve into conscience with no law at all — the Shafi'i caution chapter 3 met in the 'ina dispute, and it is an honest jurisprudence, not a loophole. And the payoff-similarity test proves less than it seems: the lease of chapter 25 and the loan it must not become can also be tuned to resemble each other, yet the tradition keeps both, because anatomy, not resemblance, is the law's subject. So runs the defense, and between it and the critics stands a genuine ikhtilaf — kin, at bottom, to the argument chapter 6 found the tradition conducting over whether the modern bank's interest is the Qur'an's riba at all, alive in its own registers for a century now. This book, which issues no rulings, will not issue one here. But it can report where the argument's weight has been moving, because the movers are the tradition's own senior courts: the Academy that refused organized tawarruq judged an assembly by what it does; the 2008 resolution judged the sukuk market by its payoffs; DeLorenzo's test was consequences; Usmani's was where reward sits relative to risk. When the tradition's own umpires reach repeatedly for the substance test, an industry optimized for the form test should expect to keep losing its hardest cases at home.

So state honestly what the critics get right, because the ledger is the point of the hearing. They are right that the industry has, in bulk, replicated the thing it was founded to replace — Siddiqi's sentence is the finding of this book's whole Part: "While theory aspired to prove Islamic finance was different from the conventional one, practitioners were busy searching for ways to make it similar to it. Convergence rather than divergence was the order of the day." Right, too, that the replication was no accident of villainy but the work of ordinary pressures on an under-defended design — the same pressures at work on chapter 30's road and chapter 31's — which is why the diagnosis of this chapter is the diagnosis of this book: extraction survives renaming, and no tradition's vocabulary is armor against it. Right that the costs of the arbitrage are real and regressive, paid by the pious in fees for the reengineering — in the words of the industry's own economist, "to structure a product and certify it." Right that the certification market's incentives are misbuilt, and that the repairs on offer — standardization with teeth, judges not paid by the judged, El-Gamal's mutuality, Siddiqi's return to the theory — are the tradition's own instruments taken seriously rather than imports. And right, above all, about the stakes, which Siddiqi stated with a founder's bluntness: "Meanwhile the credibility of Islamic finance as the bearer of a new promise is at stake." An industry that marketed itself as the alternative and delivered the replica has spent something no balance sheet records, and the people it was spent by — the depositors who chose it on conscience — are the ones this chapter has kept in view.

And yet the ideal stands where it stood, unembarrassed by the industry's report card, and the happiest part of the hearing remains: what it still has to teach. Strip the prohibition down to its positive content — this book has been doing so for thirty-one chapters — and it teaches three things no conventional textbook teaches. It teaches risk-sharing as justice and as mathematics: capital paid from outcomes, standing where the loss stands, which chapter 28 showed is not sentiment but survival arithmetic — the difference between the ensemble average a portfolio enjoys and the time average a borrowing household actually lives, where a fixed claim compounds ruin and a shared one absorbs it. It teaches asset-linkage: finance made to answer chapter 3's first question, what is this money doing — a thing owned, a use delivered, a venture fed — so the financial economy cannot drift from the real one without its own contracts telling on it. And it teaches the mercy layer: the qard hasan of chapter 16 and the takaful pool of chapter 27, capital deliberately exempted from growth and stationed at the community's worst moments — the layer the industry's own critics insist is infrastructure rather than a boutique, in the ikhtilaf chapter 16 flagged. On each count the ideal is not behind the modern world but ahead of it — ahead of the industry that carries its name and ahead of the conventional system that industry shadows — and the proof is where its arithmetic keeps resurfacing: in the post-crisis literature on equity-like finance, in the mutual and cooperative revivals, in the ESG movement's attempt to make money answer moral questions, which chapter 34 will meet as this chapter's secular sibling, complete with its own boards, its own screens, and its own form-over-substance weather. The blueprint was never the failure; the institution-building was, so far — and that failure is solvable, which is why this book's answer to chapter 20's question is the third alternative: an honest transition, but one that must now be engineered rather than awaited. Parts IX and X take the ideal at its word and do what the founders' generation could not: chapter 35 turns the doctrines into models, chapter 40 into a return formula, chapter 41 into the design of a fund that cannot drift because its payoffs are audited against its names — the non-extractive architecture this whole book exists to specify. The tradition's quarrel with its own industry, heard in full, ends not in a verdict but in a work order.

Hold the last image of Mit Ghamr, because the industry's origin story is also its standing instruction. A small bank in a cotton town, German engineering and Delta piety, no interest paid or charged, savings working in ventures the savers could see, trusted by people no bank had ever bothered to deserve — it existed, it worked, and its memory reads today less like nostalgia than like specification. The critics of Islamic finance, who are its most faithful readers, are not asking the industry to become something foreign; they are asking it to become what it already says it is — and their patience in the asking, resolution after resolution, paper after paper, is itself the most Islamic thing about the whole affair: a tradition that has never once, in fourteen centuries, agreed to stop auditing its own instruments. Whether Christianity's modern teaching still audits its own — or has gone quiet at the very moment its oldest doctrine became newly urgent — is the next room in Part VIII, and chapter 33 opens the door.

chapters.part: Part VIII — Modernity, Evasion, and the Return of Form Over Substance

chapters.title: Catholic Social Teaching and the Uneasy Silence on Usury
chapters.label: Chapter 33

paragraphs: On the fifteenth of May, 1891, Leo XIII — eighty-one years old, elected thirteen years earlier as a caretaker and by now a decade past the brief reign anyone had planned for him — published the letter that founded modern Catholic social teaching. Rerum Novarum, "of new things," took as its subject the condition of the working classes, and near its beginning it compresses the industrial world into a three-sentence diagnosis. Working men, it says, have been "surrendered, isolated and helpless, to the hardheartedness of employers and the greed of unchecked competition" — the sentence chapter 27 met when it watched Leo bless the mutual-aid societies as the guilds' lawful heirs. Then this: "The mischief has been increased by rapacious usury, which, although more than once condemned by the Church, is nevertheless, under a different guise, but with like injustice, still practiced by covetous and grasping men." And then the hiring of labor concentrated in few hands, laying on the poor "a yoke little better than that of slavery itself" (Rerum Novarum 3).

Hold the middle sentence to the light, because this chapter lives inside it. Everything this book has walked is folded in there. "More than once condemned" is a courteous undercount — chapter 30 weighed the pedigree: popes, three ecumenical councils, the unanimous schoolroom. "Under a different guise" is the form-versus-substance rule of chapter 3 in four words, asserted as a present fact about 1891. "With like injustice" refuses in advance the idea that new paperwork changes the moral object. The founding document of the Church's modern economic teaching states, in its opening diagnosis, that usury is alive, disguised, and unrepented — and then it changes the subject. The encyclical turns to wages, property, the state, and association, and the word returns only once, in a list of the employer's sins: the rich must not cut down workmen's earnings "by force, by fraud, or by usurious dealing" (Rerum Novarum 20). Two appearances, both in passing; no definition, no anatomy, no test. The tradition's last full-dress statement of its loan doctrine had come in 1745, in Vix pervenit; its next great economic document is this one; and between the two, the subject itself had been quietly refiled. Chapter 30 told how — the confessors' questions, the not-to-be-disturbed replies, canon 1543 holding doctrine in one clause and releasing practice in the next — and it closed with Rome's wager named: Rome bet on conscience. Part VIII has been auditing the bets. Chapter 31 opened the ledgers of the halakha's contract; chapter 32 sat through the fiqh's hearing on its own institutions; and that hearing ended at this chapter's door, asking whether Christianity's modern teaching still audits its own. So read the social encyclicals — a century and a quarter of them, from Leo's factory gates to a Vatican office writing about credit default swaps — and keep one question running underneath: what does this imposing series say about money, and what did it stop saying about loans?

sections.title: The Condition of Labor
paragraphs: Begin with honesty about the world Leo answered, because the encyclical's choice of subject was not an evasion; it was triage. The nineteenth century's industrial cities held human suffering at a scale and of a kind the old moral manuals had no page for: twelve-hour shifts, child labor, wages set by the hunger of the applicants, tenements, no insurance against the machine that took a hand or the fever that took a father. The guilds that had once organized work — and that had carried, chapter 27 showed, the burial funds and sick-boxes of their members — had been legally dissolved across Europe, and nothing had replaced them. Rerum Novarum says exactly this in its own voice: the old workingmen's associations destroyed, no protective organization raised in their place, and working men handed over, one by one, to a market in labor that priced them like a commodity. A church that had answered that world with a treatise on the loan contract would have deserved to be ignored. Leo answered the wound in front of him.

And the answer, on its own ground, is contract-level analysis of a high order — that is the detail this chapter most needs the reader to see. The encyclical's most consequential teaching concerns the wage bargain, and it proceeds exactly the way chapter 7 proceeded against the loan. Classical opinion held that a wage freely agreed was by definition just: willing worker, willing employer, nothing further to examine. Leo denied the premise. A man who accepts hard terms out of necessity, because the alternative is hunger, has not bargained freely, whatever he signed; beneath every labor contract there runs "a dictate of natural justice more imperious and ancient than any bargain between man and man," and a wage insufficient to support a frugal and well-behaved worker fails it (Rerum Novarum 45). Consent under necessity is not consent; the stronger party's advantage is not a price; there is a floor beneath the bargain that no signature can sign away. Readers of this book have met that argument before — it is the finding at the bottom of chapter 7's anatomy, that the borrower's consent is the consent of a man with no alternatives, transposed from the loan to the wage. The same document defends the worker's right to organize, praises the record of the old guilds — "History attests what excellent results were brought about by the artificers' guilds of olden times," in the sentence chapter 27 carried — and commends the "societies for mutual help" among the age's genuine consolations. Property it affirms against the socialists, but as stewardship, with the patristic lien running beneath it: the universal destination of goods, the doctrine chapter 18 traced from Basil's barns to the Catechism, holds every surplus answerable to need.

So the Church had not forgotten how to audit a contract. It audited the century's new contract — labor — with the old tools: consent examined against necessity, the weaker party's floor established, the stronger party's power named as power. What it did not do, in 1891 or after, was reopen the file on the old contract. The usury of paragraph 3 is a scene-setting villain, not a subject; the encyclical that proves the tradition's analytical machinery still worked chose not to point that machinery at lending. There were reasons. The doctrinal file had been closed within living memory — the replies chapter 30 dated had told confessors, decade after decade, that lenders at the legal rate were not to be disturbed, and an encyclical on the condition of labor was no place to disturb the settlement. The respectable rate was now the savings of the respectable poor as much as the income of the rich; the enemy of the workman in 1891 was the sweatshop and the company store more than the moneylender. But mark what the choice cost, because the rest of this chapter is the invoice. From Rerum Novarum forward, the Church's economic voice would speak of conditions, structures, systems, and duties — the register of social justice — and the register of contract anatomy, which the tradition had owned for six centuries, went into the archive with the doctrine it served. The word usury survived the transfer. The question usury named — what, in this instrument, is the charge actually buying? — did not. Usury survived as an accusation and retired as an analysis.

sections.title: The Reign of Credit
paragraphs: Pius XI chose the anniversary itself for the sequel: Quadragesimo Anno, "in the fortieth year," appeared on the fifteenth of May, 1931, an encyclical on the reconstruction of the social order drafted with the instrumental hand of a German Jesuit economist, Oswald von Nell-Breuning. The date matters: two years into the Depression, with parliamentary economies failing visibly and the totalitarian remedies recruiting, the Church's second charter document faced not the factory but the system. It supplied the vocabulary the tradition still uses for getting scale right — subsidiarity, the rule that the higher body exists to help the lower and never to absorb it — and it renewed the wage and property teaching of 1891. All of that belongs to the social-teaching survey any textbook gives. What belongs to this book is the passage where Pius XI looked directly at finance.

It comes late in the document, in the diagnosis of what forty years of concentration had produced, and it remains the most unflinching thing any pope has written about the money power. Wealth, Pius wrote, was no longer the story; "an immense power and despotic economic dictatorship is consolidated in the hands of a few," and those few are often not even owners but "trustees and managing directors of invested funds," administering other people's capital at their pleasure. Then the sentence that names the seat of the throne: "This dictatorship is being most forcibly exercised by those who, since they hold the money and completely control it, control credit also and rule the lending of money. Hence they regulate the flow, so to speak, of the life-blood whereby the entire economic system lives, and have so firmly in their grasp the soul, as it were, of economic life that no one can breathe against their will" (Quadragesimo Anno 105-106). Three paragraphs on, the autopsy of the age: "Free competition has destroyed itself; economic dictatorship has supplanted the free market," and among the fruits stands "a no less deadly and accursed internationalism of finance or international imperialism whose country is where profit is" (Quadragesimo Anno 109). Nineteen thirty-one, and the description is already complete: ownership separated from control, credit the chokepoint of a whole economy, capital with no homeland but its return.

Now set the passage beside the tradition it descends from, and feel the displacement. The old doctrine asked about the loan: what does this charge price, whose risk is this, what may be taken from a man in need. Quadragesimo Anno asks about the lenders: who holds credit, and what does holding it do to everyone else. Both are real questions, and the second is one the scholastics barely possessed the categories to ask — there is genuine development here, the Church's analysis growing to the size of the thing analyzed. But notice the substitution. The 1931 encyclical that anatomized the credit system does not contain the word usury at all — not once, in a document occasioned by the anniversary of the letter that had called usury rapacious and alive. The lending of money appears as an empire to be broken up, not as a contract to be audited; the analysis runs entirely at the level of power, and the level of the instrument — where the tradition had built its finest machinery — stays dark. A reader in 1931 could learn from Rome that the men who ruled lending strangled the world's breath, and could not learn from Rome what, in any given loan on any given desk, would distinguish an honest charge from a bite. The Church now had a telescope where it once had a microscope, and the two have never since been mounted on the same instrument.

sections.title: Development and the Debt of Nations
paragraphs: The next great enlargement came in 1967, and it moved the question to the scale of nations. Paul VI's Populorum Progressio, "on the development of peoples," is the encyclical of decolonization: written to a world suddenly full of new states born poor, owing money, and selling raw materials into markets they did not set. The line everyone quotes from it stands as a heading in the Vatican text — "Development, the New Name for Peace" — and its moral center is a patristic sentence this book has already carried. To ground the claim that the goods of creation answer to need before they answer to title, Paul reached back to Ambrose, in the quotation chapter 18 carried and weighed: "You are not making a gift of what is yours to the poor man, but you are giving him back what is his. You have been appropriating things that are meant to be for the common use of everyone. The earth belongs to everyone, not to the rich" (Populorum Progressio 23). Restitution, not largesse — the grammar of the fourth-century sermon promoted, sixteen centuries on, to the charter of development economics.

The encyclical also quotes this Part's own villain by name. Surveying the system that had built the colonial economies, Paul condemned the concepts that treat profit as the engine, competition as the supreme law, and ownership as an absolute: "This unbridled liberalism paves the way for a particular type of tyranny, rightly condemned by Our predecessor Pius XI, for it results in the 'international imperialism of money'" (Populorum Progressio 26) — the 1931 phrase requoted in 1967, the tradition citing its own audit and finding it still current. And then, in its program, the document does something this chapter has been waiting for: it talks about loans. Development would need capital; capital would come, in part, as credit; and the encyclical asks for terms that do not devour the borrower. A genuine dialogue between lending and receiving nations, it says, would mean that "developing countries will thus no longer risk being overwhelmed by debts whose repayment swallows up the greater part of their gains," and that "rates of interest and time for repayment of the loan could be so arranged as not to be too great a burden on either party, taking into account free gifts, interest-free or low-interest loans, and the time needed for liquidating the debts" (Populorum Progressio 54). Read those clauses slowly. The concern is ancient and true: repayment that swallows a debtor's gains is the millstone chapter 4 watched the Torah put off-limits as a pledge, scaled to a hemisphere. But the grammar has crossed over. Rates of interest are now a dial to be set considerately — arranged, balanced, moderated between parties — not a category to be examined. Vix pervenit had rejected the adjective as the question: moderation excuses nothing, because the issue is the charge's source, not its size. Two centuries later the Church's own development charter speaks entirely in the adjective's world — fair burden, reasonable rate, patient schedule — the world every decent regulator inhabits, and the world the old doctrine was built to see beneath.

What followed showed both how much that concern could do and how little the dial-grammar could see. The debt crisis the encyclical feared arrived on schedule; by the 1980s the poorest states were exporting capital to their creditors, and John Paul II's Sollicitudo Rei Socialis (1987) named the perversity plainly enough — the instrument created to finance development had turned into a mechanism that drained it, debtor nations shipping out the means of their own subsistence to keep current. In 1991, in Centesimus Annus, the centenary encyclical written with the command economies in rubble, John Paul carried the point to its edge: "The principle that debts must be paid is certainly just. However, it is not right to demand or expect payment when the effect would be the imposition of political choices leading to hunger and despair for entire peoples" (Centesimus Annus 35). That sentence is the release logic of chapter 4 — the sabbatical interruption of debt, the refusal to let obligation compound into ruin — speaking at sovereign scale, and it was kept alive in the debt-cancellation campaigns of the millennium years that marched under the Jubilee's own name. The same encyclical weighed the newly victorious market with a jurist's care: asked whether capitalism had won, John Paul answered that it depends what the word means — an economy of enterprise, markets, property, and free creativity, yes; a system in which freedom in the economic sector escapes every juridical and ethical frame, no — and he preferred to speak of a business or market or free economy, warned that the market can become an idol, and observed flatly that "there are many human needs which find no place on the market" (Centesimus Annus 34). It is a superb ledger of ends: what markets are for, whom debt may not be allowed to crush. And in all of it — the debt passages are where this chapter's question presses hardest — there is no analysis of the debt contract itself. When repayment would starve a people, payment may not be demanded: the tradition's mercy, intact and operative. Why the claim had grown to where it could starve a people — what the original loans priced, whose risk they carried, which of their charges had titles and which were the compound arithmetic of chapter 21's carentia pecuniae generalized — no encyclical asks. The Church, having been the civilization's auditor of loans, had become the world's most credible advocate for debtors; and an advocate, however holy, argues the outcome, not the instrument.

sections.title: Gratuitousness and the Return of a Word
paragraphs: Then the system itself failed an audit nobody ordered, and the tradition's voice changed register. Benedict XVI's Caritas in Veritate appeared in June 2009, nine months after the collapse of the system chapter 30 watched become "normal finance," and it is the encyclical of the crisis: a long argument that an economy cannot run on contract and calculation alone. Its signature teaching sounds, at first hearing, like the gentlest thing in this book, and is in fact one of the most radical: "the principle of gratuitousness and the logic of gift as an expression of fraternity can and must find their place within normal economic activity" (Caritas in Veritate 36) — not beside it, not afterward as philanthropy, but inside the ordinary business of exchange. Part V of this book is the institutional record of exactly that claim — the gemach, the qard hasan, the Monti, the mercy layer of capital that chapter 18 stacked — and Benedict said as much, insisting that the crisis proved the need for finance in which giving and earning interpenetrate. He pressed the point against a temptation this Part knows intimately: it is not enough, he argued, to build "ethical" compartments — funds, labels, certified corners of the market — while the main economy runs unconverted; the whole of finance must be ethical, and by its nature rather than by an external label. Chapter 34, next door, will find the market building precisely the labeled compartments Benedict warned about, and his sentence is the standing test for them.

And in this encyclical, for the first time since 1891 in a document of this rank, the old word walks back on stage. Discussing the financial protection of the weak, Benedict commended the strengthening of micro-finance — rooting it, with a historian's precision, in the civil humanists and the birth of the pawn institutions this book met in chapter 17, the Monti di Pietà — and wrote that in hard times the vulnerable "should be protected from the risk of usury and from despair"; that "the weakest members of society should be helped to defend themselves against usury, just as poor peoples should be helped to derive real benefit from micro-credit" (Caritas in Veritate 65). Usury, named twice, as a live danger to the poor; the Franciscan credit machinery recalled by lineage; despair listed beside it as the thing usury manufactures. Whatever this chapter's title says, that is not silence.

So the record must now be stated with care, because the truth is stranger than the accusation. The word never died. The universal Catechism promulgated in 1992 contains it — one sentence, with teeth: "Those whose usurious and avaricious dealings lead to the hunger and death of their brethren in the human family indirectly commit homicide" (CCC 2269). The Church's own 2004 synthesis of its social doctrine contains it: equitable profit may be sought, but "recourse to usury is to be morally condemned" (Compendium of the Social Doctrine of the Church 341). Benedict, commenting on a psalm at a 2005 audience, deplored in passing "the shame of usury which destroys the lives of the poor." Francis received Italy's anti-usury foundations in February 2018 and gave them sentences of a bluntness the subject had not heard from a pope in a very long time: "Usury humiliates and kills"; "Usury is a serious sin: it kills life, tramples on the dignity of people, is a vehicle for corruption and hampers the common good." And Leo XIV, receiving the same council in October 2025, kept the register: "The phenomenon of usury points to the corruption of the human heart"; "It is a grave sin, at times very grave, because it cannot be reduced to a mere accounting issue." These are not archival curiosities; they are the living pastoral voice of the Church, aimed at a real and unglamorous cruelty — the loan shark, the payday storefront, the debt that eats a family — and the foundations whose three decades of casework those addresses were honoring are doing the Monti's work under a modern name. This register runs sober and deserves to: the families in those offices are chapter 2's person at the door.

Now set beside it what did fall silent, and the shape of the unease comes clear. The Catechism's one usury sentence lives under the fifth commandment — you shall not kill — as a case of indirect homicide. The word does its catechetical work in a homicide paragraph, not in the economics article: the offenses catalogued against the seventh commandment run to retention of goods, fraud, unjust wages, and "forcing up prices by taking advantage of the ignorance or hardship of another" (CCC 2409), and when the Church's own writers want the Catechism on usury, 2269 is the paragraph they cite. The 1983 Code of Canon Law, replacing the 1917 Code, simply has no usury canon: where canon 1543 had stood — the two-clause sentence chapter 30 quoted, doctrine kept and practice released — there is now nothing, and the new Code's one working reference to interest makes it a duty: administrators of church property must "pay at the stated time the interest due on a loan or mortgage" (canon 1284 §2). The wall's last legal trace was replaced by a bookkeeping instruction. No encyclical since Vix pervenit has restated, revised, or even formally revisited the loan doctrine; the settlement of chapter 30 — left undisturbed, pending a future judgment that never came — remains the tradition's last word at the doctrinal level. The Church's own scholars describe the arrangement candidly. The apologists' account, given by writers like Christopher Kaczor and grounded in Noonan's history, is development rather than reversal: the sin was always profit on the naked loan without a just title; the modern economy multiplied real titles until the naked loan became rare; the teaching stands, its matter transformed. It is a serious account, and this book has spent five chapters on the titles that make it serious. But notice what even the friendliest version concedes: if every ordinary loan now carries an implicit title, then somebody, somewhere, should be able to examine a loan and say which title, how sized, and against what shown loss — and no organ of the tradition any longer performs, teaches, or even requests that examination — the condemnation continuing, the anatomy in storage. Usury is once more a sin that everyone condemns and no one computes, which is, as chapter 30 observed of the civil law, exactly how a category retires.

sections.title: Principles Without an Instrument Panel
paragraphs: The two most recent documents complete the arc, and they bring the story to the edge of this book's own project. Francis's Laudato Si' (2015) planted the economy inside creation — integral ecology, a doctrine given a chapter of its own, under which the economy, the earth, and the poor form a single case that must be judged together — and in passing delivered the tradition's tersest verdict on the sector this Part has been auditing: "finance overwhelms the real economy," the encyclical observes, among the lessons of the crisis not yet learned (Laudato Si' 109). Later, in its politics chapter, the knife goes deeper: "Politics must not be subject to the economy, nor should the economy be subject to the dictates of an efficiency-driven paradigm of technocracy," and rescuing banks at public cost without reforming the system "only reaffirms the absolute power of a financial system, a power which has no future and will only give rise to new crises after a slow, costly and only apparent recovery" (Laudato Si' 189). Pius XI would have recognized every clause; the 1931 telescope, pointed again, found the dictatorship still on its throne.

Then, in 2018, Rome did something without precedent in this whole story: it issued a document about financial instruments. Oeconomicae et pecuniariae quaestiones — "Considerations for an Ethical Discernment Regarding Some Aspects of the Present Economic-Financial System," issued jointly by the Congregation for the Doctrine of the Faith and the Dicastery for Promoting Integral Human Development, dated the Epiphany of 2018 — reads, in stretches, like a chapter of this book. It calls finance to its "primary vocation of service to the real economy"; it walks through securitizations and derivatives with their names attached; it finds that credit default swaps bought by parties with no stake create "a unique case in which persons start to nurture interests for the ruin of other economic entities" and condemns "gambling on the failure of others" as ethically unacceptable — Rome discovering, in its own vocabulary, the manufactured short position chapter 27 distinguished from the pool, and putting ruin itself back into the moral accounting, where chapter 28 argued it always belonged. It even reaches the benchmark: the manipulation of interbank reference rates — the LIBOR affair that shadowed chapter 20's doctrine and chapter 32's industry — is named there as a grave ethical violation with consequences reaching everywhere the rates do. Two curial offices, four signatures, and the closest thing to an instrument-level audit the magisterium has produced since Vix pervenit: whoever hoped the Church might again read term sheets found, in 2018, an office willing to start.

Which makes its one meeting with the old word the most precise exhibit this chapter owns. In the paragraph on credit, the document condemns lending that exploits the borrower's position, and defines the wrong like this: "applying excessively high interest rates, really beyond the range of the borrowers of funds, represents a transaction not only ethically illegitimate, but also harmful to the health of the economic system"; such practices, "along with usurious activities, have been recognized by human conscience as iniquitous" (Oeconomicae et pecuniariae quaestiones 16). There it is, in the tradition's own modern hand: usury as excessive interest — the rate too high, the burden beyond the borrower's range. Chapter 30 quoted the historian Ruston's summary of what the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries did to the word: a new generation of moralists redefined usury as excessive interest, and the question passed from public doctrine to private conscience. Four centuries later the redefinition is simply the working grammar of the Church's own finance office — written, it must be said, by men trying to protect borrowers, in a document of real courage. That is what makes the silence uneasy rather than scandalous. Nobody suppressed the old doctrine. It sank, so completely that the office charged with ethical discernment about credit no longer reaches for it even when writing about credit; the anatomy that once distinguished the charge's source from its size is not rejected there, merely absent, the way a tool no living hand has used goes missing from the bench. A verdict without a test is a conscience without jurisdiction.

So state the finding of the audit, in the Part VIII pattern, with the same evenhandedness the other two rooms received. What Catholic Social Teaching has built since 1891 is neither evasion nor decoration: it is as sustained a moral interrogation of economic life as any institution has kept up in the modern era — the wage floor under necessity, subsidiarity and the common good, the universal destination of goods, the debt of nations arraigned, gratuitousness ordered into the middle of commerce, the biosphere added to the ledger, and, latterly, the instruments themselves called by name. On ends, the teaching is complete. What it lacks is the middle layer its own ancestors built: the tests that connect principles to contracts — whose money, whose risk, what does the charge price, which burdens are shown and sized, when is surplus real — the instrument panel chapter 30 inventoried as the price of the settlement. And the lack is strange precisely because the panel is Catholic property in the attic. The mutuum's anatomy, the just price, the titles of Part VI, Lateran V's definition of usury by the absence of work, expense, and risk — chapter 14 carried it — were substantially built in Rome's own workshops. When the American bishops campaign against payday lending, they instinctively quote the Catechism's fraud-and-hardship paragraphs and Benedict's defense of the weak against usury — ends and verdicts — while the tests that would let a diocesan credit union prove, line by line, that its own loans differ in kind sit unclaimed in the tradition's basement. The heter iska's auditors and the shariah boards, whatever chapter 31 and chapter 32 found to criticize, at least exist: institutions whose daily work is holding instruments up against a doctrine. Rome retired the doctrine's institutional eye and kept the doctrine's voice — which is why its modern teaching can grieve extraction magnificently and cannot, any longer, diagnose it in a term sheet.

Renewed contract-level analysis, then, is not a demand that the Church repent of its social teaching; it is the request that the teaching's two halves be reintroduced. The principles are ready — they need no improvement, only instruments — and the old tests were built for exactly the purposes the principles now lack hands for. What would it mean? That an encyclical's heir, or a bishops' conference, or a religious lender could take Oeconomicae's own instrument-courage one floor down: not only that speculation on ruin is iniquitous, but which clauses in this loan price a real title and which price the borrower's need; not only that the vulnerable deserve protection from usury, but a working definition that does not quietly concede Ruston's — one that asks, of every charge, its source before its size. The materials are all on the tradition's own shelves, and some of them — the Monti's cost-recovery rules, the microfinance Benedict blessed — are already half-deployed. The rest of this book is, among other things, an attempt to make that reintroduction in earnest: Part IX takes the principles this chapter has praised and the tests this chapter has missed and builds them into arithmetic — chapter 35 begins with the moral-title ledger, the rule that every euro of return must name its source — and Part X designs the institutions that could run it. Next door, meanwhile, stands the market's own answer to the vacancy. Into the space where religious audit once stood, modern finance has built a conscience of its own manufacture — ESG, impact, sustainability, screens and scores and boards — and chapter 34 asks the question this Part has trained the reader to ask of every such construction: whether the new vocabulary changes what the money does, or only what the money is called. Leo's subordinate clause, it turns out, was truer than its placement. Usury, more than once condemned, is still practiced under a different guise, with like injustice; what the Church of 1891 still owned, and what its heirs have yet to take back down from the attic, is the machinery for telling the guise from the thing.

chapters.part: Part VIII — Modernity, Evasion, and the Return of Form Over Substance

chapters.title: ESG, Impact, and the New Language of Moral Finance
chapters.label: Chapter 34

paragraphs: In January 2004 the secretary-general of the United Nations wrote to the chief executives of fifty-five of the world's largest financial institutions with an unusual request. Kofi Annan's letter, sent under the banner of his Global Compact, invited the banks to help work out how the concerns the world was learning to press upon business — the climate, the laborer at the far end of the supply chain, the honesty of boardrooms — could be carried into the everyday machinery of investing: research, asset management, brokerage. A working group formed, with the Swiss government helping to carry it, and the report that came back bore a title from the golf course, Who Cares Wins, and a roster of endorsers from the commanding heights — Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley, Deutsche Bank and UBS, HSBC and BNP Paribas among them, houses managing more than six trillion dollars. The drafters set aside the era's softer words — sustainability, corporate citizenship — to head off misunderstanding, and wrote instead, with committee precision, of environmental, social and governance issues. Somewhere between the letterhead and the printer the phrase compressed into an acronym, and the acronym escaped the report. ESG now names an industry. In 2006 came the Principles for Responsible Investment, a UN-convened investor network whose signatories promise first of all to carry ESG issues into their analysis and decisions; it counts today more than five thousand signatories representing, on its own tally, above a hundred and twenty trillion dollars. By the census the sustainable-investment industry keeps of itself, some thirty trillion dollars of managed money now works under the label.

Hold that scene against this Part's opening chapter, because the two are mirror images. In 1545 a parliament deleted the moral vocabulary from the price of money; chapter 30 walked the deletion to its terminus and named the result: "Normal finance is finance with no slot for the question this book is about." In 2004 a committee of bankers, convened by a diplomat, began drafting a replacement vocabulary from scratch. Between those two dates lies the whole strange arc this chapter closes. The market did not recover the old grammar — usury appears nowhere in the new lexicon, and neither do the contract-level questions of chapters 3 and 7. But the hunger for a grammar returned from inside: nobody imposed ESG on finance; finance wrote it, at the peak of its confidence, over the signatures of its largest houses. For a generation the market's official conscience had been one sentence long — Milton Friedman's 1970 pronouncement in the New York Times Magazine that the social responsibility of business is to increase its profits — and even that surrendered. In August 2019 the Business Roundtable, one hundred eighty-one chief executives, retired the shareholder-primacy language its own statements had carried since 1997 and committed its members to lead their companies "for the benefit of all stakeholders — customers, employees, suppliers, communities and shareholders." A civilization that had spent four centuries teaching itself that a price cannot be a sin began, within living memory, to insist that a portfolio can be a virtue.

This chapter reads the new vocabulary the way this book has read every vocabulary: from within first, in its builders' own words, and then against the payoff. The builders include some of the most serious people in modern finance, and the sharpest critics below are not the project's enemies but its own executives, founders, standard-setters, and prosecutors — the pattern of this Part, for the third time. And the chapter's claim should be stated now, so the reader can watch it being earned, for it is precise, not cynical. The new moral vocabulary changes what gets disclosed and what gets selected: which companies capital visits, what they must report, what a fund may call itself. Left to itself it does not change who bears loss, what the charge prices, or where ruin lands — in the vocabulary chapter 28 built for this book, it does not by itself alter the payoff geometry. Whether the new conscience can learn the old questions, and what happens where it declines them, is the business of everything that follows.

sections.title: The Acronym and the Anatomy
paragraphs: What the acronym does, in its builders' own terms, is straightforward and genuinely useful. ESG in practice is a family of instruments. Integration folds environmental, social, and governance information into ordinary analysis, on the theory the 2004 report argued: that these factors, ignored, are mispriced risk. Screens exclude what a mandate names — tobacco, thermal coal, cluster munitions. Ratings score issuers on the three letters so that portfolios can be tilted, benchmarked, and marketed. The gains are real, and this book, which has spent thirty-three chapters insisting that moral information belongs inside financial decisions, will not pretend otherwise. Companies now publish, under law in a growing set of jurisdictions, data they once refused their own boards; externalities have names, line items, and auditors; capital is steered — sometimes only rhetorically, sometimes in fact — away from harms the price system alone would never register. And the demand is the most encouraging fact this Part has met: three generations after economics declared the file closed, the owners of capital pay real money for moral information about what their money touches. The hunger whose funeral chapter 30 recorded survived it.

But watch what the instrument sees, because its field of view is the whole argument. An ESG score is a fact about an issuer — a company, rated for its emissions, its labor record, its board. The old panel this book assembled asked its questions of the contract: chapter 3's first question, what is this money doing; chapter 7's anatomy, whose money, whose risk, what exactly does the charge price; Part VI's discipline of titles, every claim made to name its burden; chapter 28's ruin column, the fraction of counterparties a payoff design destroys. Set the two panels side by side and the finding falls out at once: they do not overlap. A bank can stand in the first percentile on governance — independent directors, audited controls, exemplary disclosure — while its consumer book runs on fixed claims against fragile households at charges the old law would have named without hesitating; the score has no cell in which that fact could appear. A green bond can finance a genuinely green turbine while the claim it conveys remains exactly what it was — fixed, senior, payable in every state of the world; the label describes the turbine, not the term sheet. This is why ESG does not solve usury, and the reason deserves saying without any sneer: it was never pointed at the loan. The new conscience audits the company; the old one audited the contract. Usury is a contract-level wrong — one lender, one borrower, one schedule of payments — and an instrument built to rate issuers at portfolio scale cannot see one, any more than a census can see a bruise.

The industry's own people said this early, and the most quoted of them had held its most senior desk. Tariq Fancy ran sustainable investing at BlackRock, the world's largest asset manager, as its first chief investment officer for the subject; he left within two years, and in 2021 published a three-part essay, The Secret Diary of a "Sustainable Investor," recounting how he went from evangelist to critic — "a dangerous placebo," he came to call it, comforting exactly the anxieties that might otherwise force real rules, while the incentives underneath moved not at all. His argument was aimed at the gap between what the label implies and what the instrument does, and the reader of this Part has seen the shape before: it is an insider's substance audit, the same office Usmani and the poskim hold in the two chapters behind us, performed here without a theology.
