Expense arrives with invoices, work with hours, loss with testimony — chapter 19 made even damage swear before collecting — but risk, spoken with enough gravity, is expected to be believed. That is exactly backwards from the tradition's practice and from the craft's: the actuary prices what frightens him; the worshiper is paid for what frightens you. And the residual knows it. Of all the lines on chapter 35's ledger, the risk line is where unexplained euros dress first, because it is the line whose audit modern manners discourage.

So the line goes under discipline — subordinated, in the outline's exact word, to truth. Four oaths, each one already sworn somewhere in this chapter. The danger is real: named scenarios, honest probabilities, honest severities — both factors or no charge — and the price answers the file, never the borrower's desperation, which is chapter 9's screen standing exactly where the Salamancans posted it. The danger is measured where measurement exists: the tables consulted, the mitigants subtracted, the exposure read as a curve through time. The danger is borne by the party charging for it: not rehoused onto a household and billed as if retained; the bearer of the residual danger is the only party with a claim on its price — and the corollary reads strangely until it reads justly: where the household bears the netted danger, the risk wage, if anyone owes one, belongs to the household. A guarantor is an insurer writing cover without premium, and chapter 38 will have things to say about policies of that kind. And the danger is counted once: protections and compensations netted on one page, the way chapter 35's cross-line fence demanded.

One practice enforces all four oaths at once: show the table to the seat that pays for it. A borrower charged five points for danger is owed the scenario arithmetic the five points rest on — Part VI's rule that burdens be shown was never meant to stop at expense receipts, and a risk story that cannot survive being read by its own subject was never a price at all, only a posture with decimals. Nothing disciplines an invocation like an audience that knows the file. Then the two form-rules that follow from the grammar. Where the uncertainty is measurable, the premium is honest — sized to the netted danger, falling as the danger falls, pooled where pooling is the mechanism, as the mutual houses of chapter 27 pooled it. Where it is not measurable, only the share is honest — the claim converts, in whole or in that part, into participation: paid from outcomes, capped like everything in this book, standing in the weather it professes to brave. A design that wants partnership's compensation must carry partnership's exposure; that much has been true since the societas, and no amount of drafting has ever made the middle position — creditor certainty at partner prices — anything but the oldest item in the usury file.

Truth first, in other words; premium and share afterward, each in its province; and nothing at all for invocation. Risk is a fact to be priced, not a god to be paid. The subordination costs honest lenders nothing — their twenty-two hundred euros survive every oath in this section — and it costs the worship everything, which is the point, and which is why chapter 37 matters next: when the front door of the rate closes to unearned risk-money, the money goes around the back, into the order of repayment itself — seniorities, preferences, the quiet geometry of who is paid first and who is paid maybe. "Waterfalls, Preferences, and Synthetic Usury" follows the money there. Chapter 38 will then find the bearers this chapter located — the household, the payroll, the unpaid years — and give their contributions the lines the cap table never drew. The file, meanwhile, goes back in the drawer, lighter by one illusion: its danger has a price now, and the price is not twelve percent of anything but four hundred and fifty euros a year, honestly borne — and the fifty-some thousand that remain above it will need, per the first equation, some other name.

chapters.part: Part IX — Moral Mathematics: Making the Traditions Computable

chapters.title: Waterfalls, Preferences, and Synthetic Usury
chapters.label: Chapter 37

paragraphs: The founder signs the sale documents on a Tuesday afternoon, and everyone in the room congratulates her. The company she started nine years ago is being bought for twelve million euros — a real price, a real buyer, a success by most of the measures a life gets measured with. Her share certificate says thirty percent. On the drive home she does the arithmetic she has been putting off, and the arithmetic does not say three million six hundred thousand. It says six hundred thousand. Somewhere between the certificate and the closing statement, five sixths of her thirty percent went missing, and nothing illegal happened to it. No clause was hidden from her. No rate was charged that any regulator would blink at. The money moved the way the documents always said it would move, in the order the documents always said it would move in, and the order did the work that a forbidden interest rate would once have had to do in daylight.

This chapter is about that order. Chapter 35 built the ledger and found the unexplained euros; chapter 36 put the risk line under oath and closed the front door — a danger, it found, may be paid for once, by the party bearing it, in the amount actually borne — and warned that the refused money would head for the back of the building. The back of the building is the waterfall: the clauses that fix the sequence in which a company's value, in success or in ruin, flows out to the people with claims on it. Repayment order, chapter 35 said, does quietly what interest once did loudly, and it is time to say exactly how — with the arithmetic chapter 9 promised, in the traditions' own terms, as chapter 13 required. The founder's missing three million is not a mystery to be solved; it is a mechanism to be read.

sections.title: The Geometry of the Queue
paragraphs: Begin with what a capital stack is, stripped of its typography. A company's obligations stand in a line. Secured debt stands at the front; unsecured debt behind it; then, in an equity-financed company, the preferred stock, round stacked upon round; then the common shares of founders and employees; and around the line, rather than in it, the losses no filing ranks — the supplier stretched from thirty days to ninety, the payroll that tightens long before any coupon is missed, the town that organized part of its life around the payroll's existence. When value flows in, it fills the line from the front. When loss arrives, it eats the line from the back. That is the entire machine. Everything else — the defined terms, the seventy pages — is the machine's paperwork. And the machine is not a metaphor waiting for a court to disagree: insolvency law enforces the line as law, under a name of engaging frankness — what the American code's lawyers call absolute priority, each rank paid in full before the rank behind it collects a euro. A sale, chapter 23 saw, runs the same waterfall on a happier day. The queue is the one clause that is always, in the end, performed.

Now read the line the way this Part has learned to read everything, by payoff across the states of the borrower's world. A seat at the front of the queue collects the same euros in nearly every future; its payoff is flat; it is, whatever its certificate says, the fixed claim of chapter 35's taxonomy — a mutuum with a seat number. A seat at the back collects only out of realized prosperity and eats every early loss; that is the partnership shape, the societas, the seat the traditions licensed to earn precisely because it could lose. Between the two poles, position in the queue is exposure, measured in meters of drafted distance from the first euro of loss. Chapter 13 drew the map this paragraph is standing on: the liquidation waterfall, it said, is a loss map with the losses at the bottom — and it promised that this chapter would run the map's arithmetic in the traditions' terms. The terms are ready. The halakha graded seats before it graded rates: the investor written near to profit and far from loss, says the baraita chapter 10 verified, is the wicked one — not for profiting, but for the drafted nearness and farness themselves. Rome voided the arrangement outright when it found a partner who could not lose, and chapter 11 told the fable that named it, the lion's partnership; the Digest's one honest exception, chapter 12 showed, was earned asymmetry — the partner whose labor is worth the loss he is spared, who pays for his protection in sweat rather than in drafting. And the queue, notice, is where chapter 36's conservation law comes home to live. Seniority and preference, that chapter found, are subtractions: they remove no danger from the world; they re-seat it. The waterfall is the seating chart. Every meter of safety purchased at the front of the queue is a meter of exposure delivered to the back, and the delivery is signed for by people who mostly never read the map — which is why the geometry stays hidden in plain sight. A rate is a number on a page, comparable across every loan in Europe at a glance. An order is a shape, visible only when you compute what every seat collects in every future, which almost nobody does. The moral information did not disappear from the modern term sheet; it moved from the arithmetic everyone checks into the geometry nobody does. So this chapter's governing questions, companions to the pair chapter 35 posted at the payoff test, are the queue's own: who collects first? And out of whose remainder? Every clause that follows is a drafted answer, and the drafting has a direction.

One more piece of vocabulary, because this Part's own ledger uses the word in the opposite direction and the collision is instructive. Finance calls the common shareholder the residual claimant: she is paid from whatever remains when every prior claim is satisfied, and in the law's eyes that remainder is her whole entitlement. The ledger of chapter 35 hunts a different remainder — the extraction residual, the euros no honest title will claim. The two residuals sit at opposite ends of the same pipe. When a waterfall is honest, the residual claimant collects the venture's true remainder, large or small, because she genuinely stood last. When a waterfall has been engineered, the unexplained euros of the front seats are collected out of the remainder the back seats were promised — the extraction residual is funded, euro for euro, by the residual claimants. The founder's missing three million has just acquired an address.

sections.title: The Machinery of Preference
paragraphs: Now the clauses, one at a time, the way chapter 23 promised they would be walked — each reasonable alone, each defensible in a term-sheet negotiation, and each a component in the assembled shape the last section of this chapter will price.

The liquidation preference is the foundation stone. In its simplest form it provides that when the company is sold or wound up, the preferred investor takes his invested capital back — once — before the common shares receive anything. Stated so, it has an honest face, and even-handedness requires the face be looked at: an investor who pays five times the founder's price per share, for a minority of a company whose books he did not keep, is buying protection against arithmetic he cannot see, and a modest preference is a way of saying the founders may not price their own optimism entirely at his expense. The traditions would recognize the instinct; they spent chapters 19 through 22 licensing genuine protections against genuine burdens. But read the clause by payoff and its second face appears. A preference is a guarantee of capital, written not by a bank but by the other shareholders; it moves first loss from the money onto the founders and employees, exactly as chapter 13 watched the guaranteed iska move it, and the traditions' verdict there was unanimous and structural: guarantee the capital home whole and the partnership has dissolved into a loan in the measure of the guarantee — the deposit half becomes debt, and the mudarabah with a guaranteed principal is void, its profit share riba — the rule the fiqh's standard-setters still print — and the sukuk market of chapter 26 rediscovered it when its par-value repurchase undertakings — capital back "regardless of their true or market value at maturity," in Usmani's fetched phrase — were refused by the tradition's own boards. The preferred certificate says shares; the preference says not yet, not while it matters.

Participation is the second story built on the foundation. A non-participating preference at least makes the investor choose at the exit — take the guarantee back, or convert and share as an owner; protection or participation, the premium's grammar or the share's, chapter 36's two ways of being paid for uncertainty, pick one. The participating preference declines to pick. It takes the invested capital off the top and then shares in the remainder as if fully converted — collecting twice from the same exit, as chapter 23 put it. Run the founder's Tuesday through both drafts and watch the clause earn its keep — the file is staged, like chapter 35's, and kept dice-simple; the clauses are the market's own. Her company carried ten million euros of invested preferred capital, fifty-five percent of the shares, all of it participating. At the twelve-million sale: ten million off the top, then the remaining two million shared across all the shares — fifty-five percent of it, another one million one hundred thousand, to the investors, who leave with eleven million one hundred thousand of the twelve; six hundred thousand to her thirty percent; three hundred thousand to the employees' fifteen. Now redraft with the same preference, non-participating: the investors take their ten million and stop; the two million remainder belongs to the common alone, and her two-thirds of the common is one and a third million. One word — participating — moved more than seven hundred thousand euros from the woman who built the company to the money that was already guaranteed, in a sale where that money had already been made whole. And the certificate's thirty percent, notice, was never a share at all under the participating draft; it was a ceiling she approaches and cannot reach. At a hundred-million triumph she would collect twenty-seven percent; at twelve million, five; at ten million or below, nothing. The number on her certificate is true in one kind of future and the drafting decides which kind arrives first in the queue. Multiples compound the same move without changing its grammar — two times, three times the capital off the top before anyone else's euro — and each multiple is the same guarantee, thickened. Preferences stack, too: each financing round customarily takes its seat senior to the one before, so that a company which has raised four times carries, as chapter 23 counted, a tower of prior claims between the employees' certificates and any euro of proceeds — a tower whose height appears on no cap-table percentage anywhere. Chapter 11, watching the modern limited partnership rediscover preferred returns and guaranteed fees, called the family "the lion's clauses, notarized"; this section has merely been reading the notary's file.

The cumulative dividend is the third story, and the oldest. A preferred dividend that accrues whether or not it is declared — eight percent, say, on the ten million, eight hundred thousand a year, unpaid in lean years but never forgiven — adds itself quietly to the preference; five lean years and the queue in front of the founder has grown by four million euros while nothing was paid to anyone. Read by payoff, an accruing dividend on a protected principal is a coupon: a fixed sum, growing with the calendar, indifferent to the venture's fortunes, payable ahead of the people whose work must generate it. The tradition met this instrument in 1586 and did not hesitate. Sixtus V's bull — chapter 13 quoted its condemnation — aimed at partnership pacts that kept "the very principal, or capital be always safe" or paid a fixed sum "yearly, or monthly" as gain, and declared them "illicit and usurious"; the honest partnership, the same bull said, casts up fruits, costs, and losses together and divides what is actually there. A cumulative dividend on participating preferred stock is the condemned instrument's modern draft, improved in exactly one respect: it no longer calls itself gain on a loan, because it no longer needs to. The queue collects it instead.

sections.title: The Clauses That Change the Weather
paragraphs: The preference machinery fixes who is paid first. A second family of clauses does something stranger: it changes what the instrument is, or when, or at whose choosing — and every change runs in one direction.

Redemption rights let the investor put his shares back to the company after a term — equity with a maturity date. For years the instrument behaves as stock; then, at the holder's election, it presents itself for repayment like a note that had merely been traveling under another name. The Ottoman drafters of the Majalla, chapter 3 noticed, chose exactly this hybrid as the opening illustration of their code's third article — a sale subject to a right of redemption has the force of a pledge; effect is given "to intention and meaning, not to words and phrases" — and the fiqh's modern boards applied the same rule when they forbade the sukuk manager's par-value repurchase promise: fix the exit price in advance, chapter 26 showed, and the certificate's holder no longer stands in the venture at all; he holds a dated claim on a counterparty. A redemption right is rarely exercised, its defenders say, and the defense misses its own point. A put need not be exercised to govern. It hangs over every board meeting in its redemption window; the company that cannot fund the redemption must refinance it, or sell itself, or bend its plans toward whoever can — the option's weather arrives years before its rain.

Anti-dilution provisions, in their full-ratchet form, are the queue's answer to bad news. An investor bought a fifth of the company at ten euros a share. A hard year later, new money will come in only at five. The ratchet reprices his old shares as if he had paid five — his four hundred thousand shares become eight hundred thousand, and the new shares are minted not from the treasury but out of the founders' and employees' percentage, which is the only place shares can come from once the price is fixed. Term-sheet practice keeps a gentler draft on the same shelf — the weighted-average adjustment, which reprices the old shares only in proportion to how much cheap new stock actually arrives — and the distance between the two drafts is a measurement: it shows how much of the clause is insurance against a real wound and how much is appetite wearing insurance's vocabulary. Walk the full ratchet through the states of the world and the shape is familiar to the point of monotony: in the good future the clause sleeps; in the bad future it transfers ownership from the people who lived the bad year, at desks, on reduced salaries, to the capital that was already senior, already preferred, already cumulating — a claim that collects most precisely when the venture does worst. Chapter 2 met this payoff in its oldest form, and the sober rule it filed there applies here without decoration: instruments that harvest the counterparty's worst year are the ones every tradition in this book built its walls against, whatever the harvest is called on the certificate.

Drag-along rights complete the family by adding a clock. A drag-along lets specified holders — in practice, the preferred majority — compel every shareholder to join a sale the dragged shareholders did not choose. Like every clause in this chapter it has an honest use, the prevention of the ten-percent holdout who would tax a transaction everyone else needs; and like every clause in this chapter its payoff must be computed, not assumed, because bundled with a preference it becomes something else entirely: the power to choose, unilaterally, the future in which the preference pays best. A fund approaching the end of its life does not need the company's best decade; it needs the company's next transaction. The drag turns that need into everyone's obligation — the mission sold to meet a preference, as chapter 34 documented, the buyer's purposes nobody in the building would have chosen, the founder signing a Tuesday she cannot refuse. Forced liquidity is where the waterfall stops being a diagram about money and becomes a diagram about time: whose horizon governs, whose patience is structural and whose is revocable, who may convert nine years of a company's life into this quarter's realization event. The traditions' word for uncertainty deliberately sold to the party least able to refuse its terms was gharar, and chapter 23 read these very clauses as a consent problem — the engineered fog. This chapter's addition is only that the fog has a payoff, and the payoff can be computed, and it lands, every time, on the seats the next chapter is about.

Say plainly, before the synthesis, where the weather goes when these clauses change it, because the addresses are chapter 36's and they have not moved. The ratchet's minted shares come out of the employee pool as surely as the founder's stake. The redemption that must be funded in a tight year is funded from the payroll's growth, the maintenance deferred, the reserve never built. The drag delivers the workers to an acquirer as line items in a data room. None of these people appear in the waterfall's defined terms. All of them are in its queue, unnamed, at the back, where the losses eat first.

sections.title: Synthetic Usury
paragraphs: In the late 1860s, the New York financier Russell Sage — Wall Street would come to call him the Money King, and his biographers kept the title — ran into the one instrument his career could not digest: a usury statute. New York capped interest by law, and Sage, the standard account runs, had been convicted under the cap. What followed is the part of the story that belongs to this book. Sage did not petition to change the law, and he did not, in any sense the statute could see, go on lending. He bought stock from men who needed cash, sold each man a call — the right to buy his shares back at a fixed higher price — and bought from him a put, the right to force the shares back on him at that same price. Watch the machine run: the customer has his cash today, exactly as if he had borrowed; whatever the stock does, one option or the other will be exercised, so the shares return to him at the fixed price, exactly as if he had repaid; and the fixed price stands above today's by whatever margin Sage chose — twelve percent, to give it chapter 35's number — a rate of interest distributed among a sale, a premium, and a strike, appearing on no page as interest at all. Financial historians credit Sage as the father of the American options business. The options business should note its paternity honestly: puts and calls entered American finance at scale as a machine for manufacturing loans the usury law could not see.

A century later, in 1969, the economist Hans Stoll proved in the Journal of Finance what Sage had banked on: the put-call parity theorem, the tidiest result in the theory of instruments. Own the share, own the right to sell it at a fixed price, owe away the gains above that price, and you hold — not approximately but identically, state by state — a riskless claim to the fixed sum: a bond; a loan. Payoffs add. Any fixed claim can be assembled out of pieces none of which is a fixed claim, and the assembly is not a defect of financial engineering; it is the theorem financial engineering is built on. Every desk on earth now uses it without a second thought — which is precisely why this book must give it a second thought, because the theorem cuts in a direction its users rarely face. If a bundle of equity and options is identical, payoff for payoff, to a loan at interest, then everything the traditions concluded about the loan attaches to the bundle. Equivalence has no favorite direction. The market's own mathematics closed the gap between form and substance from the substance side, and in doing so proved, with more rigor than any canonist ever commanded, what the canonists had asserted all along: that the payoff is the contract, and the names are stationery — chapter 35's specification, arriving this time from the trading floor. The options desks still call Sage's package a conversion, and the parity is now checked by machines, continuously, across every listed market, enforced by the market's own bailiff: any gap between the loan and its synthetic is free money to whoever closes it first. A rule the traditions enforced with confessors and responsa is enforced today by arbitrage — the market verifies the equivalence to the eighth decimal and declines, at every decimal, to draw its conclusion.

And here is the turn this chapter has been building toward: the traditions had already found the theorem — not its algebra, its arrests. Walk their case files in order. The fiqh's 'ina sale, chapter 3's specimen: two impeccable sales in one afternoon that net, as chapter 3 showed, to money today against more money owed next year — a loan assembled from sales, condemned by the majority of the schools for the net and not the parts; the rabbis, for their part, had fenced the same borderland with a category built for it — avak ribbit, the dust of interest, chapter 3's file for arrangements that are not the forbidden loan itself but carry its afterglow. The mohatra of the Christian casuists, the same machine in velvet; when its defenders argued that each sale, taken alone, was valid, the Holy Office condemned the defense itself, in 1679, in the proposition chapter 24 put on display. The contractus trinus, the perfected instrument: a partnership, plus insurance of the capital, plus the sale of an uncertain future profit for a certain present one — three contracts, each defensible in its own literature, assembling to a guaranteed return on a guaranteed principal. Read it with Stoll's eyes and the trinus is a parity trade, term for term: the partnership is the share; the capital insurance is the put; the certain-for-uncertain exchange writes away the upside like a call; and the assembled position is a loan at interest, which is what Sixtus V's bull called it in 1586, four centuries before the notation existed — the fight over that bull, chapter 13 noted, ran another century, Lessius and his successors defending the assembly until the doctrine itself gave ground. And the modern fiqh completed the set in 2009, when the Academy refused organized tawarruq — warehouse metal bought and sold within minutes to net a cash advance against a deferred debt — because the prearranged legs amount, in the resolution's words chapter 24 carried, to "a deception... in order to get the additional quick cash." Four traditions' files, one finding, and none of it required a formula: parts lawful, assembly forbidden, because the assembly's payoff is the forbidden shape. The scholastics and the jurists were doing put-call parity by hand — slowly, contract by contract, ruling by ruling — and mostly losing, because a hand audit cannot keep pace with a drafting industry. What they lacked was never the principle; it was the computation.

Which returns us, deliberately, to the founder's term sheet, because the modern waterfall is the triple contract at scale, and the mapping is not a metaphor but an inventory. The participating preference insures the principal: the put. The cumulative dividend pays the certain sum, yearly or monthly: the coupon the 1586 bull named. The participation collects the upside; the ratchet re-strikes the position when the price falls; the redemption right adds the maturity; the drag-along adds the enforcement. Assemble them and price the package across the states of the company's world, and the preferred position's payoff lies closer to a secured, coupon-bearing, convertible loan than to anything the societas consensus would have recognized as ownership — participation's compensation riding on protection's chassis, the hybrid chapter 36 refused as a contradiction in the grammar of risk. No single clause is the usury; the stack is the usury — synthetic, in finance's own honest adjective: assembled from parts, equivalent by construction, and deniable clause by clause, which is the assembly's entire commercial appeal. The old confessors could only interrogate the parts. The parity theorem interrogates the whole, and it changes sides the moment it is asked to: the same mathematics that builds the synthetic loan detects it, because equivalence, once proved, convicts in both directions. Sage's trick, run backward, is an audit.

sections.title: Reading the Waterfall
paragraphs: So the audit, plainly stated, because Appendix E will run it on worked examples and the analyzer of chapter 43 will run it wholesale. Take the whole stack — every instrument, every preference, participation, dividend, ratchet, redemption, drag — and compute the package's payoff in each state of the company's world, exactly as chapter 35's payoff test demands of any contract; synthesis, that chapter promised, loses its camouflage here, because a payoff assembled from permitted parts is still a payoff. Then run chapter 35's ledger on what the front seats collect, with chapter 36's netting rule enforced across the queue's whole geometry: a danger removed by preference, participation, ratchet, or drag may not also be priced as if borne. Seniority is protection, and protection is the opposite of the risk title; the seat that engineered its distance from loss holds no claim on loss's wages — the near-and-far grading, run at the speed of a spreadsheet. Whatever return the protected seats collect beyond their shown burdens is the extraction residual, arriving through the order instead of the rate, and the ledger prices what the founder's Tuesday only felt: her missing three million was the residual, and the waterfall was its delivery mechanism. The two-tables practice chapter 36 proposed extends down the queue unchanged. The first table prices the front seats' dangers; the second finds those dangers again, rehoused, in the seats that never negotiated them — and a stack that cannot fill in its second table has already told the auditor which kind of stack it is.

Honesty about the instrument cuts both ways, and the model must carry both edges. Nothing in this chapter condemns order as such. A queue is unavoidable wherever claims outnumber euros; the traditions themselves ordered claims — wages before distributions, the capital whole before profit exists, repair before gain — and a modest, disclosed, honestly priced seniority is among the oldest tools by which cautious money reaches risky ventures at all. The test is the one every clause in this chapter has now taken: protection may be bought, at protection's price, which is surrendered upside and a thinner claim on the venture's success — the front seat that accepts a lender's modest yield is telling the truth twice over. What the test refuses is the assembled instrument that books partnership's compensation from a creditor's bunker, insured against every future and paid as if exposed to all of them. And order, the traditions would add, is a design surface, not merely a hazard: the same geometry that quietly extracts can openly protect. A waterfall can be drafted that fills wages, suppliers, and a resilience reserve before any capital distribution; that caps the capital's total claim; that seats the investor's return behind the enterprise's ability to survive collecting it. Chapter 41 — "Designing a Non-Extractive Fund" — will draft those clauses, Appendix E will publish the worked waterfalls, and chapter 40 will fold this chapter's finding into the non-extractive return formula, where repayment order enters the arithmetic as a first-class term.

What the queue's geometry cannot see, because no cap table records it, is who actually filled the seats at the back. The founder's unpaid seventh year, the engineers' below-market decade, the guarantee signed at somebody's kitchen table — the queue prices these contributions at zero and then charges them the first losses, and the pricing is exactly wrong in both directions at once. Chapter 38 — "Founder Labor, Worker Claims, and Invisible Contribution" — goes to find the missing line items; chapter 39 will then ask what surplus honestly remains once every contribution is on the ledger, and there this Part's constructive arithmetic begins its climb. The file this chapter closes is thinner than the one it opened. The founder's twelve-million Tuesday holds no unexplained forces now, only an order, drafted years earlier, doing what orders do. She was told her share was thirty percent. The waterfall knew better, and now, so does the ledger: a preference is a rate that learned to stand in line.

chapters.part: Part IX — Moral Mathematics: Making the Traditions Computable

chapters.title: Founder Labor, Worker Claims, and Invisible Contribution
chapters.label: Chapter 38

paragraphs: On the day the company was born, a notary read its capital into permanent memory. The deed named the founders, the shares, and the money; the money arrived by wire, time-stamped to the second, and entered the register at one hundred cents on the euro. Every round since has entered the same way — the ten million of chapter 37's file sits in that register now, dated, priced to four decimals, senior in its preferences and exact in its percentages. Ask the register who built this company and it answers without hesitation: money did, on the following dates, in the following amounts.

The register is not lying; it is doing something subtler, which chapter 12 caught the moment this book's partnership law met a modern capitalization table: it is remembering everything that arrived by wire and nothing that arrived any other way. The founder's decade is not in it. The engineers' foregone salaries are not in it. The guarantee a spouse signed at a kitchen table — the policy chapter 36 promised this chapter would have things to say about — is not in it. Chapter 37 followed the repayment queue to its logical end and found the seats at the back priced at zero and charged the first losses; it closed by sending this chapter to find the missing line items. Chapter 35's ledger showed where they belong: a work line the halakha would void a contract over, priced to the dinar by traditions that could not have imagined a term sheet and would have read one in an afternoon. What remains is to do the finding — to walk through what the register forgot, price it the way Part IX prices everything, and then ask what the venture's arithmetic looks like once everyone who filled it appears in it.

sections.title: The Overcounted Input
paragraphs: Begin with a concession the whole chapter depends on: the register's precision about money is a virtue, and the traditions would be the first to say so. A wire has a timestamp because coins can be counted, and counting them protects everyone — the investor against the vanishing deposit, the founder against the phantom commitment, the auditor against the beautiful story. When chapter 12 observed that capital contributions "enter the venture's permanent memory the moment they arrive," it was not describing a conspiracy; it was describing what is easy to verify, being verified. Nobody designed the asymmetry. Labor trickles in nightly, passes through no bank, and leaves no instrument behind; money arrives once, loudly, with paperwork. An accounting system built on evidence will always see the wire first.

But seeing first has quietly become counting fullest, and the overcounting runs four ways at once. First, the money is counted gross of its protections. The register carries chapter 37's investors at ten million euros of contribution, and ten million did leave their accounts; yet the claim that came back was preferred, participating, ratcheted, and drag-equipped — a claim that, as the file's own arithmetic showed, could not lose a euro at any sale price above the round itself. Chapter 36's netting rule applies to contributions exactly as it applies to risk charges: what capital contributes is not the amount wired but the amount genuinely exposed to the venture's weather, and a euro that has arranged its own way out in every scenario but catastrophe has contributed something — but not a euro's worth of exposure. The register books the gross; the venture receives the net; the difference is counted anyway.

Second, the same euro is counted more than once. It appears as contribution when it buys the shares, as protection when the preference attaches to it, as yield-base when the cumulative dividend accrues on it, and as control when the covenants key to it. Chapter 35 posted the fence — a burden may be counted once — and its mirror governs here: a contribution may be counted once. A term sheet that prices the money's arrival, then prices its protection, then prices its patience, then prices its permission, has sold the same ten million to the company four times.

Third, capital's hypothetical alternatives are priced while labor's documented ones are not. Every hurdle rate and discount factor in the file is, at bottom, an opportunity claim — the money could have earned elsewhere, and the venture must clear that imaginary elsewhere before its own results count. Chapter 20 spent a whole file on how carefully the traditions fenced that thought, and chapter 12 noted the irony that has only sharpened since: the founder is the rare claimant who can document her elsewhere to the euro — the salary declined, the offer letter in a drawer — and she is precisely the claimant for whom the modern instruments make no line at all. The strongbox's daydreams are priced into the arithmetic; the person's turned-down job is not. The traditions ran that asymmetry in exactly the opposite direction, paying witnessed months readily and imaginary ones almost never.

And fourth — the deep one — money is counted as the whole of what a venture is made of, when it was never more than half. Chapter 12 put the two-ingredient truth at the center of Part IV: a venture is money and a stretch of human life, and the traditions refused to let the second ingredient be priced at zero. The refusal was not sentimental; it was bookkeeping: a contribution priced at zero does not stop existing — it is simply collected by whoever the arithmetic favors, without appearing in the arithmetic at all. Zero is also a price — the only one no one is ever asked to defend. The rest of this chapter is about the people who are paid it.

sections.title: The Missing Line Items
paragraphs: Take the file's founder, and give her decade the itemization the register never did. The venture ran ten years from deed to sale. Assume — the file is staged, like chapter 35's and 37's, and kept dice-simple — that the role she actually performed would have paid one hundred thousand euros a year in the market she left; she drew fifty, every year but the seventh, when the bridge round was closing and she drew nothing. The difference is not a sacrifice in the devotional sense, whatever it felt like on the seventh year's nights; it is a number: fifty thousand a year for nine years, a hundred in the seventh — five hundred and fifty thousand euros of wages earned by work actually performed, never paid, and left standing in the company. The folk term, chapter 12 noted, has already confessed the substance: sweat equity, equity bought with sweat. The register just never opened an account for the currency. Booked properly, her unpaid half-salary is the most honest capital contribution in the whole file — earned first, in labor the venture consumed, then lent back, month by month, without security, without interest, without a maturity date, and without a single line in the instrument that governs everyone else's money. Chapter 36 found the household holding the netted danger; this chapter finds it also holding an unbooked loan.

Below the salary line sits a stratum of contribution harder to see and just as real. She staked her professional name — the collateral chapter 11 watched the Geniza merchants trade on, the asset that cannot be re-minted — and the venture did not just hold that name as security; it spent it daily. Customers signed because of her, hires moved cities because of her, the bank's facility carried her signature before it carried the company's numbers. A name in daily use as working capital is a contribution by any test this book's lawyers would recognize, and it degrades differently from coins: a failed venture returns the investor's reputation intact and improved ("we back bold things"), while the founder's carries the failure in its file. She spent a decade off the career ladder she would otherwise have climbed, which is why her documented elsewhere grows more expensive every year she stays. And in year two she signed the guarantee. The bank's facility was half a million euros; the signature made her household the claim's insurer of last resort. Chapter 36 priced exactly this shape of promise: take the early years' honest failure rate — call it five in a hundred, per year, for the four years the facility ran — against what the bank would actually have taken from the household after the firm's assets went first, say three hundred thousand euros, and the cover the household wrote was worth some fifteen thousand euros a year in premium. A commercial guarantor writing the same cover would have charged about that — three euros per hundred per year, sixty thousand over the facility's life — and no commercial guarantor on earth would have written it for zero. Her household did. The premium was never paid, never accrued, never booked; chapter 36 located the seat, and the corollary it flagged for this chapter can now be cashed: where the household bears the netted danger, the risk wage belongs to the household. Sixty thousand euros of it, on this file, collected by nobody.

Now the arithmetic that makes the itemization matter. At chapter 37's exit — twelve million, participating preferences operating as drafted — she collected six hundred thousand euros, and the room applauded. Set her decade against the schedule instead. Wages drawn, four hundred and fifty thousand; exit, six hundred; total, one million and fifty thousand euros. The salaried decade she declined would have paid one million, with her evenings free and her house unpledged. The whole premium for ten years of founder work, founder hours, a year at zero, a staked name, and a household underwriting a bank facility comes to fifty thousand euros — five thousand a year — and even that evaporates the moment you price the guarantee alone at its sixty-thousand-euro market rate. Run it as chapter 35 runs everything, contributions in, collections out: five hundred and fifty thousand in unpaid wages plus sixty thousand in unpaid premium is six hundred and ten thousand euros contributed; six hundred thousand came back. In the success case, the sale that made the newspapers, the founder's own capital came home ten thousand euros short. The register recorded none of this, which is why nobody in the room could see that the person being congratulated was the only investor in the company who had just realized a loss on principal.

sections.title: The Quiet Underwriters
paragraphs: The founder at least appears in the register, however junior her stock. Chapter 12 promised this chapter would give an accounting to the stratum below her — the contributors the documents see even less — and chapter 36 named them as the addresses where the file's removed danger actually lives. Keep the telling plain here; these are the seats where the losses land first and the applause never arrives.

Start with the engineers. Ten of them, across the decade, each earning on staged average ten thousand euros a year under their market rate — the discount they accepted against options, against the mission, against the founder's late-night conviction. That is one million euros of salary left in the company: earned, worked for, and converted nightly into the venture's runway. The options were the promised consideration, and the option is worth pausing over, because it is the register's one sincere attempt to see labor — and a lesson in how the seeing fails. An option is a share of the residue, standing behind every preference in chapter 37's queue, vesting on a schedule the employer sets, expiring when the employment does, and worth the most on paper exactly when the venture needs sacrifice least. Set it beside the instrument the fiqh built for the same purpose and the difference is the whole argument: the mudarib's ratio is a first-class claim on real profit, defined at the front of the contract; the option is a junior claim on whatever the front seats leave, defined at the back. The traditions gave the working partner the share's grammar; the modern file gives the working seats the share's vocabulary and the creditor's position to everyone else — chapter 36's hybrid, inverted, with labor holding the honest half. At the twelve-million sale the fifteen percent of common the engineers collectively held paid three hundred thousand euros. Thirty cents on the euro of their documented contribution — in the success case. No covenant protected their million. No ratchet adjusted it when the price fell. No preference stood in front of it. In the law's queue, chapter 37 noted, their earned wages rank as creditor claims, often with priority — but the discount was never booked as wages owed, so there was nothing for the queue to rank. The loss arrived years before any filing could have seen it, in the gap between what their work was worth and what the register was told it cost.

The mission discount deserves its own line, because it is the contribution most cheerfully collected and least often repaid. People accept less to work on something that matters — the fair-trade sourcing, the open code, the care that is not rationed — and the discount is a real transfer from the worker to the purpose. The transfer is tolerable, even honorable, exactly as long as the purpose holds. But the purpose is not theirs to keep. When repayment pressure converts the mission into an asset — chapter 34 documented the sales, and chapter 36 traced the pressure — the discount is retroactively re-priced: what the workers gave to a cause turns out to have been given to a cap table. The mission discount is a loan whose collateral is the mission itself, and nobody holding it has any say in the foreclosure.

Around the payroll stand the contributors with no contract at all. The contractor who carried an invoice ninety days through the tight quarter made a bridge loan and was paid in apologies — an unpriced benefit traveling beside a debt, which chapter 12 would file as the contribution without a charge: chapter 8's crime, chapter 12 said, with the arrow reversed. The spouse whose salary floated the household while the venture consumed the founder's — chapter 12 counted the household among the co-investors, and the guarantee section above shows how right it was. The suppliers who stretched, the users who built their days on the thing and will inherit its failure, the town around the payroll: chapter 36 walked these addresses as bearers of rehoused risk. Walk them again as contributors and the same names come up, because bearing a venture's danger without a premium and supplying its inputs without full payment are the same act in two grammars. Contribution, like danger, is conserved: unbooked is not unmade, merely collected elsewhere — and the elsewhere, as the residual's incidence paragraph in chapter 35 said plainly, is always the seats least able to refuse.

None of this is an argument that every sacrifice is a claim. The sole owner who pays herself nothing is investing in her own property, and owes herself only honesty about it; the volunteer at the gemach of chapter 15 is giving, and the gift — chapter 3 kept the forms distinct for exactly this reason — seeks no return and books no debt. The line the traditions drew, and the line this chapter draws, runs elsewhere: where one party's unpriced input stands behind another party's priced claim, the zero is not modesty but a subsidy, flowing uphill, from the seats without instruments to the seats with them.

sections.title: Three Terms, Revisited
paragraphs: The traditions saw all of this. That is the burden of chapter 12, and the reason its three terms come back now, by name, exactly as its closing paragraph promised — not as history this time, but as the specification for a line the model must be able to fill.

Sechar tircha, first: the wage for trouble. The Mishnah would not let an investor set a man trading on half profits without paying him for the toil spent on the investor's half; the Talmud sized the wage — "as an idle laborer," the price of setting aside one's own trade to watch over another's — and the Shulchan Arukh, at siman 177, let the sum shrink to a single dinar while refusing, to the end, to let it shrink to nothing. Chapter 12 read the dinar correctly: it is declaratory. It forces the contract to say, in its own text, that the working partner's labor is a compensable contribution and not a courtesy, and once the contract has said it, the substance can ride honestly in a tilted split. And before anyone objects that a rabbinic partnership rule has nothing to say to a preferred-and-common capital stack, look at the shape the rule was written for. The iska the halakhists were policing is half loan, half deposit: the financier's money half fenced as a loan the worker must repay regardless, half ventured as a deposit traded at the financier's risk, with the working partner minding all of it. A stack in which the preference cannot lose at any price above the round, while the common seats absorb whatever comes, has re-derived that geometry, a fenced half and a ventured half under one roof, without re-deriving the rule that made it lawful, which was the wage. The codifiers' gloss even marks the boundary from the other side: where both parties truly venture capital, the wage requirement relaxes, because a genuine two-sided partnership is not a creditor-debtor pair in disguise. The halakha, in other words, keyed the wage rule to the money's protection — where the capital is fenced, its keeper's labor must be priced — which is chapter 36's netting rule, discovered from the labor side, several centuries early. Read against the modern file, the dinar rule is a drafting instruction: the term sheet must carry a line, with a number on it, for every working seat's contribution — the founder's foregone salary, the engineers' discount — even where the parties then agree to venture that value rather than draw it. Priced and ventured is partnership. Unpriced and absorbed is the arrangement the rabbis called by its name. The halakha's wage rules came with an enforcement theology the register should envy: wages are a debt, not a distribution — "You shall not keep for yourself the wages of a laborer until morning," chapter 22 quoted from Leviticus, and Deuteronomy's sunset deadline arrives with the reason attached, "because they are poor and their livelihood depends on them." A tradition that would not let a day-laborer's wage sleep overnight in the employer's house was never going to smile on a decade of it sleeping in a cap table.

The mudarib's portion, second. The fiqh built the working partner's compensation into the instrument itself — the ratio is the wage, negotiable, first-class, immune to being fixed away — and then, in the doctrine chapter 12 called the part modern summaries most often miss, made the claim survive the contract's own death. Capital promised and never delivered, a venture void for defective terms: the remedy, echoed in the modern standards, is ujrat al-mithl, the wage of his like — the venture that consumed a man's months owes him a fair wage though every other clause should fail. Now look at the file. The founder's five hundred and fifty thousand is precisely the wreckage case the jurists drafted for: labor actually performed inside an arrangement whose paper never priced it. The fiqh's answer is not that she should have negotiated better. The fiqh's answer is that the claim exists anyway, because the work happened — a wage floor beneath the waterfall, senior to the argument. And the tradition's severity ran in both directions, which is what keeps it honest as a specification: the same jurists who guaranteed the worker's floor forbade him a fixed draw on top of his ratio, because a wage that collects regardless of outcome is a creditor's claim in a partner's seat. Priced, yes; guaranteed against the venture's truth, no. And around the contract doctrine stands the tradition's wage theology, which does not whisper. The Prophet's instruction, carried in chapter 22 with its locus, sets the clock: give the worker his wages before his sweat dries. Sahih al-Bukhari (2270) preserves the stakes as the tradition heard them, in God's own first-person speech: three people will find Me their opponent on the Day of Resurrection — and the third, after the covenant-breaker and the man who sells a free person and eats the price, is the employer who takes a laborer's full work and does not pay his wage. The company the third keeps is the commentary. Withholding earned work, the tradition is saying, belongs to the family of selling people.

Stipendium laboris, third. Aquinas rehabilitated the merchant by reading his margin as a paycheck — gain sought "not as an end, but as the wage of his labor," chapter 12's verified line — and the Gospel had already put the principle in the instruction Jesus gave his own traveling workers: "the laborer deserves to be paid" (Luke 10:7, NRSV). The Monti of chapter 17 ran on the doctrine: clerks paid, buildings kept, cost and labor recovered, profit never taken. What the scholastic term adds to the file is the fence on both sides. One side faces capital: a structure whose returns cannot all be traced to ventured property or expended work is collecting for a phantom — and a cap table that prices the founder's decade at zero while paying its own imagined alternatives has failed the trace in the labor column, whatever its yield. The other side faces labor's own institutional forms, and Part IX needs the discipline as much as any fund it audits: the management fee that swells with assets whether or not anyone worked, the monitoring charge that monitors nothing — the wage title covers work performed, shown, and proportionate, not a percentage that collects like capital while calling itself labor. The stipendium is a title, and titles, this book has now said in every register it owns, are tested by substance — the wage line included. The same honesty governs the schedule's other direction, because a construction built to recover invisible work can be abused to inflate visible legend: the founder's line enters at the market rate for the role she actually performed, not at the valuation her myth would prefer; the schedule prices work, not aura, and a founder who wants more than the role's wage must earn it where everyone else does, in the ventured half. Three traditions, one specification, and it reads almost tautologically once said aloud: work is a contribution; contributions are priced; a price of zero is not a price but a confession.

sections.title: The Contribution Schedule
paragraphs: So the model gains its next construction, and like the ledger it extends, it is doctrine arranged in rows. Call it what chapter 12 called Ulpian's three-word list — pecuniae, operae, cuiuscumque alterius rei, money, labor, or any other thing — a contribution schedule: every input the venture actually consumed, entered by name, dated, and priced at entry. Wages foregone, at the market rate declined. Guarantees written, at the premium a stranger would charge. Reputations staked and careers parked, estimated honestly where estimation is all there is — the schedule prefers a rough number to an exact zero, because the rough number can be argued with, and the zero, as the whole chapter has shown, simply pays whoever the paperwork favors. Chapter 12 compressed the principle into the sentence this section exists to operationalize: "the schedule of contributions is longer than the wire transfers." The register kept only the wires. The schedule keeps the venture.

Like chapter 36's second table, the schedule is deliberately boring to produce, because its inputs are already lying around: the payroll ledger beside the market surveys, the guarantee's face amount in the loan file, the aged invoices, the offer letter the founder declined. Nothing about it requires new law — only a few lines of drafting the traditions would recognize on sight. A shareholders' agreement can carry the dinar's modern descendant: a stated schedule, revisited annually, naming each working seat's contribution at its market price and recording whether it was drawn, deferred, or ventured. A fund that publishes the contribution schedules of its portfolio has told the truth about who builds its returns; a fund that cannot fill the schedule in has learned the same thing chapter 36 said of the second table. And the schedule forces nothing. It does not make employees shareholders by decree, or forbid a founder from working cheap, or outlaw the option; it makes the price of every input visible, so that whatever the parties then agree to operates on truth instead of on the strongest party's silence. The investor with nothing to hide loses nothing here — the share-grammar investor of chapter 36, who funds honest ventures and collects only from real prosperity, gains a document proving exactly that.

Run it on the file, and run the zero line first — capital home before anyone's profit, the ordering every tradition agreed on — but run it for every seat, because sweat capital is capital. The investors contributed ten million; they collected eleven million one hundred thousand; their capital is home, one million one hundred thousand to the good. The founder contributed six hundred and ten thousand in unpaid wages and unwritten premium; she collected six hundred; her capital is short ten thousand. The engineers contributed a million; they collected three hundred thousand; their capital is short seven hundred thousand. Add the shortfalls: seven hundred and ten thousand euros of working-seat principal simply never came home — at a sale everyone toasted. And now subtract honestly, the way chapter 35 taught. Total contributions, wired and sweat together: eleven million six hundred and ten thousand. Sale: twelve million. The venture's entire true surplus — the only money in the story that is gain rather than somebody's input returning — is three hundred and ninety thousand euros, a little over three percent, total, for the decade. The protected seat's excess of one million one hundred thousand decomposes exactly: three hundred and ninety thousand of genuine surplus, and seven hundred and ten thousand that is not surplus at all but transfer — the working seats' unreturned principal, changing hands, renamed on arrival. What the exit calls profit, the schedule may call repayment. The register's version of this story had one number and a hero; the schedule's version has three numbers and a bill.

What would honesty have looked like instead? Not a formula this chapter is entitled to impose — the ratios were always the parties' business, the mudarabah's split negotiable, Ulpian's shares set by honest judgment of what each brought, and the machloket and ikhtilaf over the edges stay as live in the model as they were in the responsa. The order, though, was never negotiable, and the schedule makes it computable: all capital home first, the wired and the sweat alike; then the true surplus — all three hundred and ninety thousand of it — shared by stated fractions over stated contributions. On a plain pro-rata reckoning the money's share would run to something over three hundred thousand, its total finishing a little above ten million three hundred thousand — and the working seats would keep, for the first time, everything else: the founder's principal home with a modest share atop it, the engineers' million home with theirs. Smaller numbers for the front seat, and truer ones; the difference between the two term sheets of chapter 35 was never size but composition, and the difference between these two exits is the same. Nor does the schedule only redistribute; it re-describes. It tells the investors what their one point one million was made of before they spend the story of having earned it. It tells the founder, before the next deed is signed, what the last decade actually paid. And it hands chapter 39 its opening question in computable form, because once every contribution is on the ledger and every principal has its seat in the queue, the number that remains — the money that is not somebody's input on its way back — is the only thing in the file that was ever honestly available to share. Chapter 39, "True Surplus," takes that number apart; chapter 40 will seat contribution beside composition, risk, and order as a first-class term of the non-extractive return formula. The register, meanwhile, can keep its virtues: let it remember the wires to the cent. The schedule remembers the company — and somewhere in its rows, ten years late and sixty thousand euros light, the register finally learns the name of its most senior creditor. She is the same person chapter 36 found seated as the file's most junior investor, and both descriptions are true, which is the finding: most junior by the paper, most senior by the doctrine — the seat every tradition in this book moved to the front of the line, holding wages the arithmetic was never told about.

chapters.part: Part IX — Moral Mathematics: Making the Traditions Computable

chapters.title: True Surplus
chapters.label: Chapter 39

paragraphs: The meeting, for once, is a happy one. The company — say it roasts coffee on a canal in the east of the city and trains its crew out of long-term unemployment, because this file, like chapter 35's and chapter 38's, is staged and kept dice-simple — has finished the best year in its short life. The accountant shares her screen, and at the bottom of a tidy page, above the words available for distribution, stands the number: one hundred and twenty thousand euros. The word does its usual work around the table. Available sounds like a fact about money, the way a full shelf is a fact about bread; it suggests that the only remaining question is how to divide the loaf. This chapter is about that word, and its claim is blunt: available is almost never true, and the distance between what a till holds and what a venture may honestly share is where the oldest sin in this book now does most of its quiet living.

Part IX has been climbing toward this table since it opened. Chapter 35 built the ledger on which every euro of a capital claim must name its title, and assigned this chapter its constructive twin: defining the true surplus that may honestly be shared. Chapter 36 put the risk line under oath; chapter 37 followed the money down the waterfall; chapter 38 put the contribution schedule beside the cap table and reached this chapter's question from the exit side, decomposing a celebrated twelve-million-euro sale into seven hundred and ten thousand euros of transfer booked as profit and three hundred and ninety thousand that was really new — then handed over, in its words, "the money that is not somebody's input on its way back" as the only thing ever honestly available. And the question itself is older than the Part. Chapter 14, closing the partnership arc, watched every tradition refuse the profit written in advance and promised that this chapter would take its question for a title: what, truly counted, is surplus? At a settlement table in a Fustat courtyard the answer was counted out in coins and witnessed oaths. The modern version is asked in January, of a bank balance, by people holding term sheets — and the answer still runs through chapter 14's procession — capital, costs, wages, provisions, reserves — only now the procession stops at the till, and every marcher presents a bill.

sections.title: Available Is Not Surplus
paragraphs: Begin, as chapter 38 began, with a concession: the number on the screen is honest about what it measures. One hundred and twenty thousand euros of cash, cleared and spendable, sits in the account; no one is cooking anything. The register's cash column is the most truthful column it owns, for the reason chapter 12 named: what is easy to verify gets verified. The trouble starts when a custody fact is promoted into a verdict, because surplus was never a fact about the account. Surplus is a conclusion about the year, and chapter 14 already wrote its grammar: profit sits at the end of an audited story, and every attempt to move it forward in time — toward the signing table, toward the January meeting — is the same attempt the traditions spent seven centuries refusing.

Modern accounting, to its credit, half knows this. Its accrual half exists precisely because cash misleads: revenue is not earnings, receipts are not income, and the profession's whole apparatus of provisions, accruals, and depreciation is a machine for correcting the till's first impressions. The fiqh's standards bodies, chapter 14 showed, built the same corrections into partnership law with a jurist's precision — interim profits are retained for the protection of the capital, the working partner's entitlement "is not absolute" until valuation, early distributions ride "on account," provisional, callable back when the real story arrives, and receivables enter the count at honest collectibility with nothing added for the waiting. Every one of those rules is a way of saying that the pile in the till is not yet anyone's increase. Some of it is the venture's own capital, resting there on its way through. Some of it belongs to bills the year has already incurred and not yet seen — the maintenance the machines have earned, the wages the schedule shows below standard, the reserve still hollow from last year's flood. Some of it is next year's story arriving early, or last year's losses not yet admitted. And some of it may not be the venture's story at all: cash borrowed into the account in December looks, on the screen, exactly like cash earned there, and the fiqh's standards closed that door by name, chapter 14 found — the manager smoothing a lean year may draw on a disclosed reserve, never on fresh debt, because a distribution financed by borrowing declares, in that chapter's words, "a surplus no operation ever produced." Cash answers where the money is; surplus answers what happened, and the two questions part company exactly as often as ventures are complicated, which is always. Available says the money can leave; surplus says it may.

The halakha carries the distinction in the most domestic formula it owns, and the formula is worth importing whole. The Mishnah's tractate on the corners of the field opens with a list of deeds "whose fruits a person eats in this world while the principal remains for him in the world to come" — honoring parents, deeds of kindness, making peace — ha-keren kayemet, the principal standing (Mishnah Peah 1:1). The Gemara expanded the list, and the tradition set its version into the daily morning prayers, where it is recited to this day: a community that begins every morning, before breakfast, by distinguishing the fruit, which may be eaten, from the keren, which may not. Chapter 35 met the keren as the zero line of the moral-title ledger — the principal that comes home before anything is gain. The till's version is the same rule run forward: what a venture may consume, distribute, and celebrate is fruit; the keren is not food. Even the modern register remembers a version of the rule when it is being watched — its capital-maintenance doctrines exist to stop distributions from consuming the capital a company's creditors rely on — and then forgets it in the metrics it actually steers by, several of which are engineered to look away from exactly the lines this chapter is about to walk. The most popular of them announces the maneuver in its own name: earnings before, among other things, the cost of keeping the body whole.

So the number on the screen is not a lie; it is a question wearing a statement's clothes. The rest of this chapter is the interrogation — the procession of claims that stand senior to any distribution, taken one seat at a time, each with its tradition and its arithmetic. At the end, whatever no claimant can name will still be standing in the till, and that remainder, at last, will deserve the word.

sections.title: Wages Before Distributions
paragraphs: The first claimants are on the payroll. The roastery employs ten people, and the contribution schedule chapter 38 taught us to draft shows what the register never volunteered: measured against the stated rates for the work actually done, the crew runs thirty thousand euros a year under standard. Chapter 38 named what such a gap is — wages earned, unpaid, and left standing in the company, the most honest capital in the file, lent nightly on no security. What the gap adds up to at an exit, that chapter computed to the cent. What it does at the till is simpler and sharper: it stands first in line, because in every tradition this book reads, a wage is not a distribution. It is a debt, and a debt with a clock on it.

The clocks are scripture. Leviticus, in the clause chapter 22 carried, forbids an employer to keep a laborer's wages "until morning"; Deuteronomy moves the deadline to sunset, "because they are poor and their livelihood depends on them." The Prophet's instruction, carried in the same chapter, sets an earlier clock still: the worker's wages before his sweat dries. Sahih al-Bukhari's warning about the employer who takes full work and withholds the wage, met in chapter 38, files that employer among God's own opponents on the Day of Resurrection. The Epistle of James, addressed to the comfortable in the voice the prophets used, gives withheld wages a physics all their own: "The wages of the laborers who mowed your fields, which you kept back by fraud, cry out, and the cries of the harvesters have reached the ears of the Lord of hosts" (James 5:4, NRSV). The verse's economy is exact — the wage kept back does not rest in the account where the register shows it; it cries out from there, and something hears it. And Leo XIII, whom chapter 33 heard argue the wage bargain like a canonist, set beneath every labor contract "a dictate of natural justice more imperious and ancient than any bargain between man and man" (Rerum Novarum 45) — a floor older than the signatures above it. A tradition that talks this way about a day's mowing was never going to bless a distribution declared across an unpaid payroll.

Run the doctrine into the January meeting and it cuts one way only. A venture that declares one hundred and twenty thousand euros available while its schedule shows the crew thirty thousand under standard is not distributing surplus; it is distributing the wage line — chapter 14's inversion, now with the schedule to prove it. The money moves from the seats that earned it first to the seats that rank ahead of them on paper, and arrives under the one label the surplus line was built to protect. Precision matters here, and chapter 38 supplied it: not every gap is theft. A crew may knowingly price its discount and venture it — priced and ventured is partnership, as that chapter put it — and a cooperative's members may vote to leave their own wages standing in the walls. But the choice must be priced, recorded, and theirs; and even then the gap is their capital, holding a seat in the queue, not a courtesy that evaporates at the first distribution. Unpriced, unrecorded, and outranked, it is — chapter 38 again — the arrangement the traditions already had a name for.

There is one more wage claim, and it is the one this Part has learned to check last because the person holding it checks it never. The founder's line on the roastery's schedule shows ten thousand euros of deferred draw this year — modest, deliberate, and hers. Chapter 38 found her twin at the exit: the founder the paper ranked last and the doctrine ranked first, whose own capital, by that chapter's arithmetic, came home ten thousand euros short at the celebrated exit. The traditions priced her seat long before term sheets did — the mudarib's keep billed to the venture itself, the wage for trouble over which, chapter 12 showed, an iska could be voided, the Monti's clerks paid before the lending was called clean: chapter 12's file, chapter 17's institutions, one rule. Founder sustainability is that rule stated as a going concern rather than a settlement: the venture must carry the cost of the person carrying it. A company whose plan only balances if its founder is consumed is not lean; it is running on an unbooked subsidy with an expiry date, and the year at zero — chapter 38 priced one — is not a business model but a countdown. Sustainability even has a plain test the traditions would recognize: price the role so that a stranger could hold it. If the numbers work only while the seat is filled by someone who will not charge for it, the venture does not have a wage line; it has a benefactor, and the schedule is carrying a fiction. The discipline cuts both directions, as it did in chapter 38: the line pays the role's wage, not the legend's, and a founder who wants more than the work's price must earn it where everyone else does, in the ventured half. But a till that distributes past her deferred line has done to its own center what it did to the crew, one seat quieter.

sections.title: The Three Reserves
paragraphs: The next claimants do not attend meetings. The first is the venture's own body. Machines wear at a rate a maintenance log can state to the month: the roastery's two drum roasters and its delivery van shed about twenty thousand euros of working life this year, invoiced by no one, and the roof over the training floor keeps its own slow ledger. The register, in fairness, sees this one — depreciation is accrual accounting's honest admission that the body is being spent — and the till ignores it anyway, because depreciation is not a payment and January votes on payments. Distribute the cash the accrual already spoke for and nothing happens, for a while. The machine keeps the books now; its ledger is patient, compounds quietly, and presents its bill all at once, in the language of breakdowns, at the moment chosen by the machine. Maintenance deferred is not expense avoided but a loan taken out against the equipment, at terms nobody read. So the till's discipline runs one step past the accountant's: not merely to admit the accrual but to fund it — cash moved on the log's schedule to a line that exists for nothing else, so that the roasters' next overhaul is a withdrawal rather than a crisis. An entry confesses the wear; only a funded line pays for it. The scriptures' oldest treasury story is on the reserve's side here: Joseph reading seven fat years as storage instructions for seven lean ones (Genesis 41), the harvest of the good years standing, unconsumed, precisely because good years are when the storing is possible.

The second reserve guards against the years no log can schedule. Chapter 28 built the arithmetic in a model village and it does not need rebuilding: paths that pool their blows survive; paths that face them alone are absorbed; and the difference between a young pool that fails and one that holds is the solidarity reserve — chapter 10 named it, this book's anti-ruin instrument — standing in the chest before the doubled year arrives, sized in the rule chapter 28 carved: "to the pile-up, not the average year." The roastery's charter states the size plainly: fifty thousand euros, one genuinely bad quarter. Last year's flooded cellar drew the chest down by half, and the apparatus did exactly what it exists to do — the flood cost the members a chest instead of a company. This year's till question is therefore already answered by the charter's own grammar: the chest's twenty-five thousand euros of replenishment stand senior to any distribution, because a reserve refilled only in years nobody needs money is a reserve that will never be refilled. The traditions' living instruments run the same seniority in modern paragraph numbering. The iska's codifiers blessed the disclosed reserve, chapter 13 found, in the same breath that they forbade the guarantee; the fiqh's standards retain interim profits for the protection of the capital before any entitlement hardens; and its banks operate standing reserves — chapter 32 read the prudential guidance — that hold back strong years to cushion weak ones as ordinary machinery. Chapter 28's warning travels with the mathematics: a chest harvested in the calm years has been converted, quietly, into somebody's yield, and the conversion sells the one thing the chest existed to hold. Ruin probability is the honest name for what rises when the replenishment line loses its seniority, and it rises for every seat at once — including, the investors around the table might notice, theirs.

The third reserve holds something no invoice can name. An institution's purpose, chapter 28 observed, walks one path through time exactly as a household does, and it can be ruined the same way — not by one great betrayal but by a run of bad quarters, each survived by shaving the thing itself: the training places cut back, the free seats withdrawn, the patient sourcing traded for whatever keeps protected capital whole. Chapter 34 documented the endgame, missions sold to meet a preference; chapter 14 named the bookkeeping that enables it, purpose counted at zero so that its liquidation books as gain. A mission reserve is the same chest built for the purpose's worst year — capital stationed between the mission and the quarter that would otherwise buy it — and the roastery's charter funds it on a written schedule, ten thousand euros this year, toward a declared ceiling. Grown permanent, locked past the reach of any board's bad quarter, it becomes the endowment, and chapter 29 has already told that story whole: Umar tying up the orchard itself — "keep the corpus intact," as the instruction is carried there — so that only the produce could ever travel. The fruit-and-keren rule, institutionalized against everyone, including its own trustees.

Three reserves, and one discipline that keeps them honest, because this section hands management no blank check. A reserve is a claimant only while it can answer the ledger's questions: a stated size, a stated purpose, a stated schedule, drawn by rules everyone has read and visible to every seat at the table. The roastery's fifty thousand is one bad quarter, written in the charter, auditable by a stranger — not whatever the treasurer fears this year.
