Money parked past its declared size is not prudence; it is a distribution being denied rather than shared, extraction's mirror image, run by the inside against everyone else's lines — and institutions slide there easily, because a swelling cushion feels like virtue to the people whose comfort it cushions. The instrument for the distinction has existed since chapter 13: disclosure. A disclosed reserve at a stated size is the pool's honest machinery. An undisclosed cushion of no particular size is a number with no title — and this Part has a column for those.

sections.title: The Claims Outside the Walls
paragraphs: The till's next claimants never signed anything, which is precisely why the traditions wrote their claims into law. Begin with the ones the enterprise can see from its own windows. Chapter 18 established the grammar with some care: in all three houses, the community's share is owed, not offered — zakat a levy with chartered recipients, tzedakah a debt collectible by the court, the patristic lien on surplus a matter of justice before charity ever enters. The roastery's charter takes the tradition at its word and writes the obligation as a line: ten thousand euros, named, scheduled, and computed before the distribution question is reached, because a debt by the tradition's own grammar cannot rank behind the creditors' celebration. The fence from chapter 18 travels with the line: the transfer must be real and its recipients stated — the zakat's eight chartered classes were that chapter's exhibit in how a tradition writes a distribution list — not a sponsorship budget filed under the tithe's name; and chapter 28's two-questions test reaches charters too, since a community line an enterprise quietly runs as marketing has already answered whose flourishing the pooling serves. Around the stated line stand the quieter neighbors chapter 36 walked as addresses and chapter 38 walked as contributors — the town that carries the payroll's weather, the suppliers who stretched, the users who built their days on the thing. A till that has never once counted them is not wrong about a number; it is wrong about who was in the venture.

Then there are the claimants no window shows. The economists' term for them is external — costs a venture causes and does not carry, landed on seats outside the contract — and the word's own geometry confesses the problem, because the seats are external only to the paperwork. The costs are as real as diesel and as datable as invoices: the wastewater the town treats, the carbon the century will, the neighborhood's air run through the roaster's stack. The conservation law chapter 10 first stated applies without amendment — chapter 36 traced where removed danger goes, chapter 38 where unpriced contribution goes, and unpaid costs travel identically: nothing vanishes; it is collected elsewhere, from the seats chapter 35's residual already taught us to expect, the ones least able to refuse. The traditions' modern documents say it with unusual flatness. "Businesses profit by calculating and paying only a fraction of the costs involved," Francis observes in Laudato Si', in a paragraph noting that nobody prices what the cleared forest actually cost (Laudato Si' 195). The Qur'an's diagnosis is older and wider: "Corruption has flourished on land and sea as a result of people's actions and He will make them taste the consequences of some of their own actions so that they may turn back" (30:41, in Abdel Haleem's rendering). And the covenant's labor law reached the land itself long before either document — the shmita of chapter 4, the seventh year in which the field's own rest is written into the same code that will not hold a laborer's wage past sunset. A tradition that would not price the mower at zero did not price the meadow at zero either. Stewardship in the fiqh runs on the same appointment — chapter 18 carried the Prophet's word that the world is sweet and green and its people are installed in it as God's vicegerents, to see how they act — and the church's universal destination of goods, chapter 18 again, holds every surplus answerable to a wider table than the one that votes on it.

What can a till do with a claim whose collector never comes? Exactly what chapter 38 taught it to do with the founder's unpriced decade: prefer the rough number to the exact zero. The roastery's charter states an internal price on its own footprint — ten thousand euros this year, retired against the wastewater contract and the offsets the members chose after an afternoon's argument — and the number is imperfect, disputable, and infinitely more honest than its absence, because zero is not a measurement but a shrug, and it is the one estimate guaranteed to be wrong. The rough line does what pricing always does in this book: it makes the cost visible while it is still negotiable, it disciplines the operation that must now budget against it, and it converts a moral embarrassment into a negotiation the parties can actually have. A "surplus" computed by leaving the town and the river off the schedule is chapter 14's inversion at the widest radius the book has yet drawn — extraction from claimants who cannot even attend the meeting, booked as prosperity by the people who can.

sections.title: What May Be Shared
paragraphs: Now the procession can be counted, and the counting is short, because everything hard happened on the way here. Capital's own line stands where the traditions put it and nothing in this chapter has moved it: the zero line, every principal, wired and sweat alike, home or provided for before anything on earth is surplus — settled doctrine since chapter 13 seated the losses and chapter 14 the remainder, with chapter 38 widening only the roll of who counts as having principal. But between the zero line and the distribution stands everything this chapter has walked: wages to standard, the founder's named line, the body's maintenance, the chest refilled to its charter size, the mission's reserve on its written schedule, the community's owed share, the rough-numbered line for the seats outside the walls. Call the sum what the traditions would have called it: the life-preserving claims — the venture's food and tools. The halakha's collection law, chapter 22 showed, hands exactly those back to a debtor before even an unquestioned creditor collects: the court may take everything and must return the thirty days of food, the bed, the craftsman's two awls and two planes, because — as that chapter put it — "Collection may empty the estate, but it may not unmake the person." The Qur'an commands the creditor holding a genuine claim on a debtor in difficulty to wait for ease, and better, to remit. Neither tradition doubted the debt; both subordinated its collection to the debtor's remaining alive. The venture's till deserves the same two-queue clarity. On the ledger of claims, capital is senior, and the doctrine keeps it so. In the queue of actual cash leaving a living enterprise, the claims that keep the enterprise alive collect first — and far from robbing capital, the ordering is what keeps capital's own zero line worth holding, since a distribution taken out of the payroll, the roof, and the chest is a distribution collateralized by the venture's next collapse. The honest investor of chapter 36 loses nothing at this table and knows it; a seat that objects to funding the reserve that protects its own principal has told the room which of chapter 28's two pools it thought it was running. The design consequence belongs to Part X, but it fits in a clause: capital that wants distributions has an interest in wanting the senior lines funded, which is why the fund chapter 41 will draw caps its return and recycles its surplus — an instrument shaped so that its appetite and the venture's survival point the same way.

So run the roastery's January, line by stated line. Wages to standard, thirty thousand. The founder's deferred draw, ten. Maintenance as logged, twenty. The chest's replenishment, twenty-five. The mission reserve's schedule, ten. The community's owed line, ten. The priced footprint, ten. One hundred and fifteen thousand euros of the one hundred and twenty on the screen were never anyone's to distribute — ninety-six cents of every available euro already had a name on it, which the label on the page simply declined to read. What remains is five thousand euros, and the remainder is the chapter's whole finding: small, true, and clean. It answers every question the ledger knows how to ask. It is increase a living venture can part with and remain whole, sharable by the stated fractions over the stated contributions, chapter 38's schedule doing at the till what it did at the exit. The board that distributes it has extracted nothing from anyone — which no board distributing the larger number could say, because the till's version of chapter 38's decomposition is that the other one hundred and fifteen thousand would reach the shareholders as a transfer, collected from the crew, the machines, the chest, the purpose, the town, and the river, and handed over under profit's name. What the account calls available, the procession has already spoken for.

And with the remainder named, the Part's affirmative theology can finally be said out loud, because this book has never been against gain. Aristotle's old shudder at coin breeding coin, chapter 1's inheritance, was answered across three traditions not by forbidding increase but by insisting it be real — chapter 14 compressed the answer into three words, surplus is fruitfulness, and chapter 35 gave the words a ledger's grammar: "Surplus is the only line that grows with the venture's success, because it is the only line that shrinks with the venture's failure." What this chapter adds is the test that makes the word operational, and the book has been holding the test since its lease chapter: the usufruct of chapter 25 lets its holder take the fruit while the substance stays whole — salva rerum substantia — and a distribution is nothing but the owners' usufruct on their own venture, bound by the same ablative clause. Fruit is what the tree can spare; everything else is the tree. The rabbis' morning formula knew it — eat the fruits, the keren stands. Umar's orchard knew it — the produce travels, the corpus never. Hosea's farmer, whom chapter 15 heard through the Talmud, knew which harvests a person actually eats. Nor is the honest till's remainder doomed to stay small: the senior claims weigh heaviest exactly where ventures are young — wages catching up to standard, reserves filling toward their charter sizes, maintenance steadying — so true surplus widens as a venture matures, which is the shape fruitfulness has always had; orchards bear little in their planting years. Extraction runs the arc backward, largest at the start and brief, and the roastery that toasts the full one hundred and twenty thousand spends its next years paying the distribution back — with interest, in breakdowns, departures, and an empty chest when the bad quarter comes — the false distribution being what chapter 14 said such numbers always are: a claim paid out of the venture's substance rather than its increase.

One line of Part IX's machine remains to be built. Chapter 35 gave return a ledger; chapter 36 priced its danger honestly; chapter 37 exposed the order of its collection; chapter 38 completed the roll of its contributors; and this chapter has defined the only pool it may honestly be paid from. Chapter 40 assembles the pieces into the non-extractive return formula — return of capital, real costs, real losses, real work, and a bounded share of exactly this chapter's remainder, with the reserves standing and the residual at zero. The formula's last input is the till's last number: whatever survives the procession. In the meeting on the canal, the accountant changes one word on the page, and the board votes the five thousand with something unfamiliar in the room — the knowledge, line by stated line, of what the money it is not distributing is doing instead. It is the smallest distribution in the company's history, and the first one nobody else paid for.

chapters.part: Part IX — Moral Mathematics: Making the Traditions Computable

chapters.title: The Non-Extractive Return Formula
chapters.label: Chapter 40

paragraphs: Go back to the desk in Amsterdam. Two term sheets, one young company, the same half million euros, the same cap of two euros and ninety cents for every euro advanced — chapter 35 opened this Part with them and found that no instrument in the modern reporting stack could tell them apart. Five chapters later, everything can. The moral-title ledger of chapter 35 asks each of their euros for its title. The oath of chapter 36 makes their risk charges show the danger, netted of every protection, borne where it is billed. The geometry of chapter 37 reads their repayment order as the rate it quietly is. The schedule of chapter 38 counts their founders' and engineers' unpaid years as the capital those years always were. The procession of chapter 39 stands between their claims and the till and lets through only what a living venture can actually spare. Each chapter built its instrument, used it, and set it down. What none of them did — what this chapter exists to do — is pick all five up at once and turn them around, from reading contracts to writing one.

That reversal is the whole announcement. Part IX has so far been an audit; from here to the end of the book it is a workshop. The pieces assemble into a single design rule — the non-extractive return formula — and the rule can be displayed the way chapter 35 displayed the first equation, in words, because the words are the mathematics. This is that equation's constructive twin, the same line solved for the only unknown the traditions ever cared about:

Permitted return = capital returned, wired and sweat alike + costs shown + losses proven + work and service priced + liquidity deprivation that passes its tests + opportunity bounded to a particular elsewhere + a capped share of true surplus — with the reserves standing senior, and the residual held at zero.

Every term arrives from a chapter that already built its fences, which is why this chapter can be short on derivation and honest about what it is doing: assembly. The formula adds no new doctrine and settles no live dispute; where the houses disagree about a line's size, the disagreement rides inside the line, exactly as it rode inside the responsa and the manuals. What the formula changes is the direction of travel. A test that could only convict contracts after signing can now draft them before it, and the drafting, walked line by line, turns out to be the most compact summary the traditions of this book have ever been given.

sections.title: Principal and Repair
paragraphs: The first term is the zero line, and it needs the least argument, because chapter 35 built it from all three legal languages at once — the Talmud's horn, the scholastics' sors, the fiqh's head of the wealth, one homely agreement that what you advanced comes back to you, the same and whole, and that its coming back is not gain. The Qur'an's settlement of the riba war, carried verbatim in chapters 6 and 19, ends on exactly that line. The formula takes the zero line with both of the disciplines this Part attached to it. From chapters 13 and 14, the ordering: the capital is made whole before anyone's profit exists to share, the first rule both partnership traditions wrote into their settlement tables. From chapter 38, the widening: every principal comes home before anything on earth is surplus — the wired principal the register remembers to the cent, and the sweat principal it never opened an account for, the founder's unpaid decade and the engineers' discount standing in the schedule at the market rates declined. A formula that returned only the money's capital would repeat the modern instrument's first error in the traditions' own vocabulary. Return of capital, in this book's arithmetic, is a roll call, not a wire confirmation. And the line polices its own imitations, because chapter 26 met capital "returned" by promise rather than by fact: the par-value repurchase that guarantees an exit price to a claim dressed as ownership is not the zero line honored but the zero line counterfeited — return of capital names what the venture actually gives back, not what a counterparty undertook to pay regardless.

Above the zero line sit the two repair lines, and chapter 19 wrote their specification in advance — its promise, kept here, was that this formula would carry "actual cost recovery and actual loss recovery as named, separate, bounded lines." Cost is the planned burden of running money: origination, administration, accounts, audit, the clerk and the premises. The tradition's most rigorous institutions stood on this line and nowhere else — the Monti before their council, the qard funds under the resolution chapter 16 carried, permitting the service charge that recovers actual cost and forbidding the one that recovers more — and the line's grammar has not moved since: shown, allocated to this financing, recovered once, at zero margin. Each of those words is a fence with a history. Shown is the invoice and the timesheet, the modern descendants of the witnesses the iska posted around its claims. Allocated divides the burdens this financing caused from the institution's own keep — a fund's fundraising, its investors' reporting, the overhead of its existence belong to the fund's side of the desk unless a stated policy honestly assigns them, because a borrower billed for whatever happened to be nearby is carrying the institution, not the loan. Once is chapter 35's oldest fence run through the accounts. And zero margin is what keeps the line repair instead of revenue: honest counting is not free — chapter 14 priced the sworn accountings and valuations that make partnership possible — but the moment a cost line clears more than it spends, whatever it clears belongs to some other line's discipline or to no line at all.

Loss is the unplanned burden — the wound an event actually caused — and it enters the formula with chapter 19's whole method attached: name the event, trace the cause, produce the papers, measure the repair, count it once, and watch the direction of the lender's hope. The two lines stay separate because their temptations differ. Cost inflates by habit, percentages quietly outgrowing the work; loss inflates by imagination, injuries asserted where none can testify. Both are bounded at the same edge — the burden proven, the repair ending where the wound ends — and neither may carry a target. A fund that needs its damages to hit a budget has already told the auditor what the damages are for; repair priced to a return is not repair, and the formula refuses it the way Rava's netting rule and the standards' provisions refused it, centuries apart, in the same spirit. Nothing in these two lines makes capital richer, which is their point, and the reason the traditions trusted them first.

sections.title: The Wage and the Wait
paragraphs: The fourth term prices work and service, and Part IX has already argued it twice — once as doctrine, once as arithmetic. The doctrine is the oldest three-way agreement in this book: the halakha voiding an iska over an unpaid dinar of the trouble-wage, the fiqh giving the working mudarib his ratio and, in the wreckage cases, ujrat al-mithl, the wage of his like, the schoolmen reading the honest merchant's gain as stipendium laboris, the wage of his labor. The arithmetic is chapter 38's, and the formula inherits it whole — contribution seated, as that chapter promised, "beside composition, risk, and order as a first-class term." The contribution schedule is how the work line gets its numbers: every working seat's input named, dated, and priced at entry, the founder's role at the role's market wage, the stewardship of a fund priced as the work it actually performs — sourcing, diligence, accounts, governance, the sitting-with-the-founder in the bad month. Service earns the same way work does, by happening: a stewardship fee answers for what was done, for whom, and to what use, and support the enterprise neither asked for nor felt is not service but a subscription the stronger party wrote for the weaker one to pay. So the line comes with chapter 38's two fences built in. Facing capital: a return that cannot trace to expended work or ventured property has no business here. Facing labor's own institutional forms: a fee that swells with assets whether or not anyone worked is a percentage collecting like capital while calling itself labor, and the line prices work, not aura — the founder's legend and the manager's letterhead both pay for themselves. Between the fences, the line is generous on principle. Moral finance runs on real hours, and a structure that will not pay for them is not purer than one that will; it is planning to consume its own people, an extraction with the direction reversed, and chapter 39 already named where that plan ends — in a benefactor where a wage line should be, and a countdown where an institution should be.

The fifth term is the one the formula could most easily have left out, and the reason it stays in is the reason it rarely pays: honesty about the tradition's own long argument. Being without one's money — carentia pecuniae, chapter 21's file — can be a real burden, and the seventeenth century's best minds disagreed honestly about whether that burden could ever be sold. The halakha had answered early and structurally: waiting itself takes no wage — the agar natar of chapter 7's file, payment for waiting, is the thing forbidden, not a title needing fences. The formula carries the entry chapter 21 nonetheless promised it would carry, "an entry called liquidity deprivation," and carries it under that chapter's full discipline: the line must be capable of reading zero, and it reads zero wherever no test puts a number in it. The tests are the file's — the deprivation particular, dated, and shown, a burden this lender actually carried for this financing, not the season's inconvenience every lender can recite. Patience, where it is real, is better paid in weight than in rate — the longer-committed capital taking the deeper share of realized surplus, chapter 21's grammar — and a fund that fears what waiting could do to it builds the chest of this chapter's eighth term rather than billing its nerves to the borrower. On the mercy layer of the stack, the gemach and qard hasan floors of chapters 15 and 16, the line reads zero by design, because there, in chapter 21's words, "the deprivation is the gift"; price it and the instrument is unmade. A line that usually reads zero may look ornamental; it is the opposite. Writing it down is what keeps its residue honest — whatever cannot pass the line's tests may not ride the contract under some vaguer word for time.

sections.title: The Elsewhere and the Share
paragraphs: The sixth term is the most dangerous line the formula carries, because it prices a world that did not happen, and the formula's answer is to keep chapter 20's whole cage around it. Opportunity enters bounded to a particular elsewhere: a named alternative, in the claimant's real practice, already in train, causally severed by this financing — mourned afterward, on proof, at hope's price and never harvest's, in chapter 20's rule; discounted for every contingency the real venture would have faced; capped at the loss it claims to repair; counted once against the files of chapters 19 and 21, which name different wounds or name nothing. The elsewhere must also be lawful, and chapter 20's cage said what that refuses in five words — "a forgone extraction is not a compensable injury" — which reaches further than it looks: a mission fund measuring itself against yields its own charter forbids is mourning a world it had already renounced. A clause that appears in every contract fails the whole cage at once, having stopped compensating anyone for anything in particular. The professional lender still walks Hostiensis's refused circle — money whose only elsewhere was another loan has forgone nothing any of the three traditions would price — and the modern fund inherits the circle's logic upstream: its own promises to its own investors, the hurdle it must clear, the cost of its capital are decisions about whether to invest, not debts the borrower contracted. A fund that has promised extraction to its funders has not acquired a title; it has only chosen, in advance, who will be asked to perform the extraction. The formula's answer to that arrangement is the same at every scale: the promise upstream must bend to the lines downstream, or the mission language is a letterhead. And the line's size stays where the houses left it, which is to say disputed. Aquinas set it at zero; the later schoolmen opened it under conditions; the halakha, rather than pricing the forgone world, redrafted the financing so the lender stood inside the earning — the heter iska of chapters 20 and 31, after which nothing is forgone; the fiqh keeps the line flat at nothing, having refused time a rental price altogether. The formula does not vote. A house that zeroes the line runs the formula with the line at zero, and the formula is still the formula — which is precisely how a design rule respects a machloket it has no standing to settle.

The seventh term is the one the whole architecture exists to protect, and the only one that can grow: real surplus participation. Its pedigree is Part IV entire — the societas, the iska, the mudarabah, capital earning as from property of its own because it stood to lose as an owner loses. Its base is not revenue, not cash, not the January number that says available; it is chapter 39's remainder — "the till's last number: whatever survives the procession" — after wages to standard, the founder's line, the maintenance funded, the chests refilled, the community's owed share, the priced footprint. Its form is chapter 14's distinction, on which the whole partnership arc turned — "A ratio asks the world what happened; a rate tells the calendar what is owed" — and the formula has no line where a calendar can collect. Its timing is late by construction: profit is a remainder, found by counting and never promised, so the share is discovered at the settling, exactly as the Fustat quays and the standards' valuations always insisted. Its license to grow is bought with its exposure to shrink — the symmetry chapter 35 wrote into the ledger's seventh line — and the fraction itself stays where every tradition left it, with the parties: the mudarabah's split was always negotiable, Ulpian's shares were set by honest judgment of what each partner brought, and the formula constrains the base, the timing, and the cap while leaving the ratio to the people whose venture it is. And its relation to danger is the settlement chapter 36 negotiated. Where a danger is measurable, netted of every protection, and genuinely borne, its honest small premium survives — the twenty-two hundred and fifty euros of that chapter's file, not the twenty-five thousand the pricing memo wanted. Past the edge of measurement, where young ventures actually live, only participation pays honestly, because a share is the one instrument that cannot claim the venture's weather without standing in it. The share is capped. On this the traditions' modern boards and this book's model agree without strain: a bounded multiple, stated at signing, after which capital's claim is complete and further surplus belongs to the venture, its people, and its purposes — the design chapter 41 will draft and Appendix E will work in numbers. A cap does not make a share honest by itself, as chapter 37's stacked certificates proved; but a share that refuses any cap has told the room it wants partnership's upside with perpetuity's appetite, and the formula, which asks every euro its errand, has no line for appetite.

sections.title: The Reserves That Stand
paragraphs: The eighth term is not a way capital gets paid; it is the condition under which anyone gets paid, and writing it into the return formula — not beside it, in it — is half of what makes the formula non-extractive rather than merely tidy. Before the surplus line opens, the reserves stand: the maintenance the machines have already earned, funded rather than merely admitted; the solidarity reserve refilled to its charter size — the anti-ruin reserve chapter 10 named for the whole book and chapter 28 sized, "to the pile-up, not the average year" — so that ruin probability falls for every seat at once and the bad quarter costs the venture a chest instead of a life; the mission reserve on its written schedule, standing between the purpose and the quarter that would otherwise buy it. Chapter 39 established their seniority at the till, and the formula makes the seniority a term of the instrument itself: a distribution that reaches capital across an unfunded reserve is not a return under this formula at all; it is the residual, collected early, out of the venture's next collapse.

The same term runs at the portfolio layer, where it does the work chapter 36's map assigned to the pool. A fund holds many paths; each of its companies holds one. Dangers that are measurable across the many — the failure rates, the bad quarters, the ordinary mortality of ventures — belong in a chest at the fund, funded from the fund's own arithmetic, so that no single company is asked to promise its survival to smooth the ensemble's year. The traditions' living instruments already run the seniority in modern paragraph numbering — the disclosed reserve the iska's codifiers blessed in the same breath that they forbade the guarantee, chapter 13's finding; the interim profits the fiqh's standards retain for the protection of the capital before any entitlement hardens, chapter 14's; the standing reserves its banks operate as ordinary machinery, chapter 32's — and the formula asks of a fund only what those instruments ask of a venture. Chapter 28's two-questions test travels up the layers with it: a chest is judged by whose ruin it prevents, and a fund reserve that exists to steady the fund's reported year while its companies each face their own weather alone has answered the test in the wrong direction — the pooling must reach the paths that can actually be ruined, or it is the ensemble comforting itself. The term carries its own fences: a stated size, a stated purpose, a stated schedule, drawn by rules everyone has read, per chapter 39; money parked past its declared size is a distribution being denied rather than shared. And chapter 28's warning travels with it — a chest milked in the calm years has been converted into somebody's yield, and a solidarity reserve that never moves the ruin column was, in that chapter's verdict, a marketing line. Capital, notice, is not the term's victim but its beneficiary of record. The reserves are what keep the zero line worth holding — a fact the honest investor of chapter 36 grasps without help, and the extractive one discovers in the only year it matters.

sections.title: From Theology to Term Sheet
paragraphs: Now the ninth term, which is less a line than a verdict standing at the end of every line. Run chapter 35's first equation on any claim: whatever is left, after the zero line and the honest titles have taken everything they can carry, is the extraction residual. The formula is that equation with the last term held at zero — by construction at the drafting table, by audit ever after. Held at zero at signing, it is a design rule: no term in the instrument may collect what no line can explain. Measured at zero in operation, it is a verification: the promise kept, year by year, in arithmetic a stranger can re-run. And behind both uses stands the fact chapter 35 refused to let the subtraction launder — a residual is never abstract: it is paid by the borrower's worst year, the household whose guarantee is called, the crew whose gap was never booked, the purposes chapter 34 watched sold to meet a preference — the seats, in chapter 35's words, least able to refuse it. Holding the term at zero is not bookkeeping fastidiousness; it is the whole of the book's case, stated as a constraint. Between the two uses, the formula stays honest about the one thing it cannot do, which is end the old arguments; a strict house and a mild house will size the liquidity and opportunity lines differently, and the formula, like chapter 35's ledger, reports both runs side by side rather than crowning either. What no house will bless is the unexplained remainder, and the worked file shows how much of one an ordinary instrument carries. As written — chapter 35's hundred thousand for five years at twelve percent, doubly secured — the file claimed sixty thousand euros above principal and could explain about six: four thousand of shown expense, twenty-two hundred and fifty of honestly netted danger, nothing on any other line. The formula would have signed the six and struck the rest. The same contract, redrafted in the formula's plainest mode — cost-recovery credit, the Monti's mode of chapter 17, the serviced qard of chapter 16 — carries a claim about a tenth the size and a residual of exactly nothing. Redrafted as participation, it converts the refused fifty-four thousand into a capped share of remainders that may pay more than that or nothing, depending on what the venture actually does — which is the entire moral difference between a return and a rent. One name is deliberately absent from the walk. The agreed penalty of chapter 22 holds no line here, exactly as it held no standing line on chapter 35's ledger: a genuine penalty is priced to collect nothing, booked only in the delay states, against culprits, and a penalty budgeted as revenue has already failed both chapters' tests at once. The formula leaves it where the doctrine left it — at the door, useful, and watched.

The tenth term is the translation itself — theology into LP distributions, with no softening of either word. The vocabulary waiting on the other side is settled market furniture: limited partners who fund, a general partner who manages, the management fee run at a habitual two percent of committed capital, the carried interest at a habitual twenty percent of the gains, the preferred return near a habitual eight that the fund must clear before its carry begins, and the distribution waterfall that sequences it all — whole-fund in the drafting the market calls European, deal by deal in the American. None of this furniture is wicked, and none of it is a title; they are customs waiting to be asked the formula's questions, and the asking re-derives every clause. The management fee is a work line, so it answers work's tests: priced to the stewardship actually performed and shown, capped against the drift chapter 38 named, in which a percentage collects like capital under labor's name — two percent of committed capital is an answer to what the work costs only by coincidence. Fund expenses are a cost line: shown, allocated by stated policy, recovered once, at zero margin, and never collected from both sides of the fund at once — investors funding an operating capacity the portfolio is then billed for again. The preferred return is this Part's oldest acquaintance under its newest name: a number written in advance, accruing with the calendar, indifferent to any venture's actual year — the certain sum the 1586 bull condemned in partnership dress, chapter 13's file, chapter 37's cumulative coupon, here promoted to the fund's own constitution. The formula's redraft does not abolish the investors' protection; it relocates it into truth: the fund's investors hold the zero line — their capital home, wired and sweat alike, before any carry exists — and above it a stated share of true surplus, in place of a clock that ticks against companies that had different years. The carry itself, so redrafted, becomes the most defensible euro in the building: a remainder share, collected after every principal is home and every reserve stands, capped like everything else — the general partner as working partner, paid in the share's grammar for work and judgment, which is what the twenty percent always half-remembered it was. And the waterfall is where chapter 37's finding folds in, as that chapter promised: "repayment order enters the arithmetic as a first-class term." Ask the two market draftings the queue's own question — may carry collect while any seat still holds unreturned principal? The deal-by-deal order says yes, paying the manager on the winners while the losers' capital is still in the ground; the whole-fund order says not yet; and the formula's order says it in full, writing itself down the page in one motion — operating claims and wages, the reserves to charter, every principal, wired and sweat, then shared remainders to the cap, then nothing: surplus past the cap stays with the ventures or recycles to the next fund's floor, per the design of chapter 41. One coherence rule governs the whole translation, and it runs upstream. A fund can be no more patient with its companies than its own capital is with it, unless it absorbs the difference in its own design — which is what the reserves, the caps, and the recycling are for. The gift and mercy layers chapter 41 will draw exist precisely so that the stack's patience is funded somewhere real rather than promised everywhere and held nowhere; a fund that signs the formula downstream while owing the old arithmetic upstream has not translated the theology, only relocated the extraction to its own investor meetings. And the translation is a reporting practice before it is a boast. A fund that runs this formula publishes the runs: the fee against the work performed, the expenses against the policy, every reserve against its charter size, every distribution against the remainder it came from — the investor's letter carrying the formula's lines the way chapter 36's honest fund carried its two tables and chapter 38's carried its schedules, so that the claim of non-extraction is, every year, a set of subtractions a stranger can check rather than an adjective the marketing renews. A creed that cannot reach the distribution clause is a preamble. This one reaches it, term by term, and the terms hold in both directions — the same lines that draft a new fund's waterfall will read an old fund's, which is the analyzer's whole business when chapter 43 arrives.

So the desk in Amsterdam can be cleared. The first term sheet — the one that could answer — was never a mystery; it was this formula, met before the book had taught the reader to recognize it: costs invoiced, a penalty that expects to collect nothing, danger charged only where the money actually loses, the rest a stated, capped share of profits that exist on the day they are shared. What chapter 35 could only tell apart by interrogation, this chapter can write on demand, and Part X will spend five chapters building the institutions that write it — the fund of chapter 41, drafted layer by layer; the contract library of chapter 42; the analyzer of chapter 43, which runs this formula wholesale on term sheets that never heard of it; the accounting of chapter 44, which keeps the answers honest after signing; and the temptations of chapter 45. The formula's finding fits in a sentence, and it is the book's oldest conviction made computable: a non-extractive return is not a smaller number; it is a number made entirely of answers. Seven titles above a zero line, the reserves standing, the remainder at zero — and every euro beyond the principal arriving, for the first time in the instrument's long history, with its errand written on it.

chapters.part: Part IX — Moral Mathematics: Making the Traditions Computable

chapters.title: Designing a Non-Extractive Fund
chapters.label: Chapter 41

paragraphs: An architect who wants to know whether a building will stand does not linger over the facade. She draws the section: the cutaway that shows the foundations, the bearing walls, what rests on what, and what happens to the whole if any one floor fails. Finance has such a drawing too. The market calls it the capital stack — every source of a venture's money, drawn in order of who gets paid first and who absorbs loss first, from the senior debt at the top of the queue down to the common equity holding the bottom. Chapter 37 spent a chapter reading such drawings and delivered its verdict in one line: "a preference is a rate that learned to stand in line." The order is never decoration; a stack can extract through its seating what no clause would dare charge as interest. But that chapter ended on the instrument's other face. The same geometry that quietly extracts can openly protect, and order is a design surface. This chapter takes up the pencil.

The commission is the one Part IX prepared. Chapter 35 established that instruments can be "designed to a moral geometry, not merely audited against one" — its own words, and the fact on which this chapter now builds a fund. Chapter 40 assembled the non-extractive return formula, the building code every drawing in Part X must satisfy: capital home before gain exists, costs and losses recovered at their proven size, work priced as work, patience weighed only where it carried a real burden, surplus shared by ratio under a cap, the reserves standing senior, the residual held at zero. What remains is the architecture — the actual floors, in the actual order, with the actual money. So take a fund invented for the purpose, ten million euros of committed capital serving a community of young ventures, and draw its section. The proportions that follow are the designer's to argue about; the order is not, because the order is where the theology lives.
The stack, bottom to top — bottom meaning first to absorb loss and last to claim return, the ground the rest stands on:

1. The gift layer (€500,000) — granted outright; expects nothing back; absorbs first losses; funds the floors above.
  2. The gemach / qard hasan layer (€700,000) — revolving zero-return loans; principal back, nothing more, ever.
  3. The cost-recovery credit layer (€2,300,000) — bridge and working-capital loans repaid with documented costs and not a euro beyond.
  4. The takaful / mutual-aid / solidarity-pool layer (€800,000) — the community's shared chest for defined perils, owned by its members.
  5. The risk-sharing layer (€4,200,000) — mudarabah, iska, societas: capped participations that earn only from realized surplus and lose when the venture loses.
  6. The mission-locked equity layer (€1,000,000) — patient ownership stakes in steward-owned companies, exit only by mission-preserving buyback.
  7. The community reserve layer (€500,000) — the fund's own standing chest: never deployed, never distributed, sized to the bad stretch.

Seven layers, and not one of them invented for this book. Every floor is an instrument from an earlier chapter, built centuries ago, tested in use, and waiting, which is why the drawing can be walked layer by layer with credits instead of blueprints. Chapter 36 mapped the territories where the traditions put honest money to work — "tables where tables are honest, chests where perils can be gathered, partnerships where nothing can be known in advance" — and promised that the fund this Part was building would use the same map in the same order. Here it is, drawn to scale. Notice, before the walk begins, how the drawing quarrels with the market's own section. In the conventional stack, the bottom absorbs loss in exchange for unlimited upside: equity eats the first wound because equity owns the last euro of any triumph, and every seat above it buys protection by surrendering appetite. In this stack the logic of the bottom is inverted. The floors that absorb the most expect the least, and what they are compensated in is not upside but purpose — the gift layer and the mercy floor exist so the community survives its worst months, and their return is that the survival happens. What the stack adds to the old instruments is the architecture they were always implying: each layer renounces something exactly so that the layer above it can exist without pretending. Every layer earns its seat by what it refuses to collect.

And the layers are not a menu; they are a path. Follow one venture through the drawing. A two-woman workshop takes a bridge loan from the credit floor in its first winter, repays it with the documented forty euros it actually cost to make, and joins the pool that spring against the perils every workshop shares. In its third year it wants a second lathe and a hire, and the risk-sharing floor buys in: a participation, capped, collected only from settled remainders. In its seventh year, grown into the town's anchor employer, it converts to steward hands with the mission-locked floor financing the buyback, and somewhere in that decade there was a January when the founder's child was in the hospital and the mercy floor carried the payroll for six weeks at zero, because that is what the floor is for. Five instruments, one company, no seam at which anyone's emergency became anyone's yield. A conventional fund meets that workshop once, prices it once, and needs its exit; the stack meets it at every altitude of its actual life, which is what the traditions' whole inventory was assembled to do.

sections.title: Where the Stack Begins
paragraphs: The bottom of the stack is a gift, and the placement is the whole doctrine. All three traditions rank giving as the economy's true ground floor — the tzedakah that is owed rather than felt, the zakat that is calculated rather than moved, the almsgiving chapter 18 weighed as commanded infrastructure rather than optional warmth — and all three, chapter 15 showed, rank the loan above the gift precisely because rescue that expects repayment leaves the rescued standing. A fund built on their ledger begins the same way. The gift layer is capital that has already said goodbye: donated in, spent as granted, or held as the stack's first-loss ground. Because it demands nothing, it can do the two jobs no priced layer can — catch the falls no structure can price, and stand under the mercy floor so that the mercy floor never has to earn. The market has been rediscovering this seat under its own vocabulary: catalytic first-loss capital, the blended-finance drafting in which a foundation or a public funder takes the junior position so that warier money can stand above it. The label is honest as far as it goes, and the traditions would add two fences to it. The first is chapter 34's warning: a gift that exists to sweeten someone else's extraction has been enlisted, not given — a first-loss layer that lets the layers above collect the old arithmetic in safety is subsidizing the very thing this stack was drawn to refuse, so the gift stands under mercy floors and capped claims or it stands under nothing. The second is that the gift layer is governed like every other floor, not scattered from it: grants move on published criteria, are recorded like disbursements, and answer to the same reporting as every priced layer, because generosity without bookkeeping decays into patronage, and patronage is a claim in disguise. Chapter 40 wrote the deeper rule as upstream coherence — patience must be funded somewhere real rather than promised everywhere and held nowhere. This is the somewhere.

One floor up sits the mercy loan, and here the fund is not innovating; it is franchising. The gemach of chapter 15 and the qard hasan of chapter 16 are the same machine in two liturgies: a pool of given and deposited capital, lent at absolute zero, guarded by guarantors and community knowledge, repaid at rates that embarrass the professionals, and revolving — out, back, out again, a founding gift still rescuing strangers a century later. The machinery travels into the stack intact. Depositors, where the layer takes deposits, may reclaim their principal and not a cent more; the layer's administration is waged and priced at documented cost, chapter 16's receipts-never-percentages specification; underwriting, guarantors, and collection stay as rigorous as any bank's, because the home chapters proved that rigor and mercy are not trade-offs — what mercy forbids is only that the rigor become a revenue line. Its job in the stack is the one chapter 16 specified when it told the builder to seat the layer deliberately, sized to the shocks that actually arrive, "upstream of the growth layers and unembarrassed beside them." The shocks in a venture community are not exotic: the founder's two bad months, the bridge between an invoice and its payment, the repair that cannot wait for a board cycle. Each is exactly the emergency the beautiful loan was built for — principal for a season, nothing riding back — and each, left to the layers above, would be priced into a permanent claim. Dignity is engineered in rather than hoped for, standard terms and confidential rolls, because clientage is a design failure, not a price of charity. On this floor the return formula's liquidity entry reads zero by design, chapter 21's rule, since here being without the money is the very thing being given; a fund that cannot bear that zero has no business drawing this floor, and a fund that can has bought something the priced floors cannot make — a community whose worst months do not compound. And it was this floor, before any other, that taught funds to revolve. What the market calls a revolving loan fund, and what Part X will keep meeting as the evergreen structure, is — as chapter 15 promised this chapter would say explicitly — "the gemach's shape scaled up": capital designed to circulate serially instead of extracting and exiting, the wheel as a fund's whole body plan.

sections.title: Credit at Cost, Perils in Common
paragraphs: The third layer is where the fund starts running priced instruments, and the price is the strictest one the traditions ever blessed: everything shown, nothing beyond. Cost-recovery credit is the Monti's mode from chapter 17 and the serviced qard of chapter 16's resolution — the loan whose service charge recovers actual, documented expense and forbids itself anything more — and chapter 40 has already fenced its grammar into the formula: shown, allocated by stated policy, recovered once, at zero margin. In the stack this layer is the workhorse: the working-capital line, the inventory bridge, the equipment loan — credit for ventures that need a lender, not a partner. That distinction is a dignity as much as a mechanic. A bakery that needs six months of flour financing should not have to sell a share of itself to buy a season of liquidity, and a stack with an honest credit floor never forces participation on a venture that only needed a bridge. What the layer refuses is as load-bearing as what it provides. It refuses margin, so its receipts can be audited against invoices rather than appetites; it refuses percentages that scale with size and term while the work does not, chapter 16's oldest specification; and it refuses to let the fund's own overhead migrate downward onto borrowers as a "cost of capital," because the fund's keep belongs to the fund's side of the desk. The layer also carries the Part's insolvency posture, because a credit business is defined at its worst tables: distress is met first as discernment rather than enforcement; the penalty clause keeps chapter 22's grammar — expecting to collect nothing, armed only by true delay, aimed only at culprits; and a late borrower meets a redrawn schedule before a compounding claim. Priced and policed this way, the floor does something quietly radical to the whole drawing: it proves the stack can run a credit business — underwriting, collections, defaults and all — with the extraction residual at a standing zero, which is the demonstration the Monti made before their council and the reason this book keeps returning to them.

Beside it stands the pool, because some of what a venture community fears is not a financing need at all but a peril: the fire, the lawsuit, the founder's illness, the client that vanishes owing a quarter's revenue. Chapter 36's settlement sorts the stack here, and it is worth quoting as the sorting rule: "What can be measured can be pooled; what cannot be measured can only be shared." Perils that are nameable, pre-existing, and measurable across many members belong in this layer, gathered, in chapter 27's grammar, as the members' own — the books the chevra, the confraternity, the friendly society, and the takaful fund all kept, that chapter's census showed; the unmeasurable — whether the venture itself will find its market — belongs two floors up, where only participation pays honestly. The design rules arrive from chapter 27 intact, a specification rather than a sentiment: contributions enter as the members' own money, tabarru' or dues, never as a seller's revenue; the fund belongs to those it shelters; its administrator is paid a disclosed wakala wage for work, indifferent to whether claims run light or heavy, and fenced off the surplus; the light year's remainder thickens the reserve or goes home to the members; exclusions police conduct, never misfortune; pools pool upward, retakaful and mutual reinsurance, so that no single chest's weather is final; and outside capital may serve the pool — a backstop, an operator's interest-free advance in the industry's standard rescue — but never own it. One honesty the design owes its own doctrine, plainly: a pool defends members, so the gate is where its mercy stops, and chapter 28 warned that a community which pools brilliantly inside and prices or excludes at the door has moved the extraction to the gate. A fund's pool is judged there — at the smallest member, at the venture whose dues are hardest to pay — before it is judged on its actuarial tables. Carried honestly, the layer takes the sharpest modern perils off every other floor's price. The risk-sharing layer above need not smuggle insurance into its participation ratios; the credit layer need not pad its costs against catastrophe; each instrument can charge for exactly what it is, because the dangers that can be counted are standing in the one room built for counting them.

sections.title: The Partnership Floors
paragraphs: Now the floors the whole Part IV arc was for. The risk-sharing layer is the stack's largest commitment and its plainest doctrine: capital enters ventures as the societas, the iska, the mudarabah always insisted — as a partner, earning from realized surplus by ratio and standing in losses as an owner stands — under the full discipline the book has already built. Profit is a remainder, found by counting, never promised, chapter 14's law, with the interim retentions and sober valuations its modern standards require. No guarantee dressed as partnership: the stack may hold disclosed reserves against bad seasons, chapter 13's licit pool, but the moment any instrument promises the capital's safety plus a return, it has reassembled the stacked contract the 1586 bull in chapter 13's file met with the word detestable, and it belongs to a different book. Patience is paid in weight, not rate, chapter 21's grammar: the longer-committed participation takes the deeper share of what actually happened, never a percentage of the calendar. The fund's own stewardship of these positions — sourcing, diligence, the accounting that makes ratios collectible, the sitting-with-the-founder in the bad month — is priced on the work line at the work's wage, chapter 38's fence, not skimmed from the participations as a percentage collecting like capital. And every participation is capped: a bounded multiple, stated at signing, after which the claim is complete. Run the arithmetic on the file this book already owns — chapter 35's half-million-euro participation, capped at two euros and ninety cents per euro advanced — and the ceiling is one million four hundred fifty thousand euros, ever. If the venture flourishes, the fund collects its capped share from true surplus, chapter 39's remainder, and is done; everything after that belongs to the venture, its people, and its purposes, or turns the wheel below. If the venture fails, the fund's capital fails with it, netted only by whatever protections were honestly priced in the one layer built for pricing them. That symmetry is not a marketing stance; it is the license — the thing that lets the return exist at all in three legal languages at once.

The mission-locked equity layer is smaller, slower, and structurally the most interesting floor in the drawing, because it holds the instruments chapter 29 built the case for and this chapter, as that chapter promised, now reaches for by name. The layer takes ownership stakes only where the charter has retired the exit: the asset lock, binding the company's value to its purpose so that mission-built worth cannot be converted into a seller's prize; Steward Ownership's two commitments, control held by people bound to the mission — never marketable, never heritable — and profits serving purpose rather than owners; the golden share, the one-percent guardian holding, in chapter 29's image, "one key that opens nothing and locks everything"; the Employee Ownership trust, holding the company for those who work in it. Where a company arrives at the fund's door not yet locked, the lock is the deal: conversion to steward hands is written into the investment itself, priced and scheduled, so that the fund's money finances the dedication rather than waiting politely for it. Equity in such a company cannot be venture capital's equity, because the payoff that model needs — the appreciating exit — has been deliberately welded shut. What remains is exactly what the traditions said ownership honestly was: a share of fruit, for as long as the tree is held, with departure by redemption — the mission-preserving buyback, at a formula written the day the money went in, returning the shares to steward hands on a schedule the company can survive. This is the endowment's logic from chapter 29 — waqf, hekdesh, church patrimony, the whole family of deeds that retired capital from the market — running at business speed: what cannot be sold cannot be sold out, in that chapter's words, and a fund that wants its portfolio's missions to outlive its own involvement buys into locks, not in spite of them. The layer will never post the stack's largest number. It exists because some of what a community needs held — its clinic, its grid cooperative, the workshop that anchors a town — should be held by capital that has agreed, in writing, to be the last money that could ever hollow it.

sections.title: The Chest the Fund Keeps
paragraphs: The seventh layer never leaves the building, and the drawing is incomplete — worse, dishonest — without it. The community reserve is the fund's own standing chest — the anti-ruin reserve chapter 10 named and chapter 28 sized, stationed now at fund level: capital held against the pile-up, drawn by written rules, and counted a working layer even though it earns nothing, because what it manufactures is every other layer's ability to keep its promises. Chapter 28 proved the mechanism at village scale and named the design consequence this chapter was built to receive: portfolio resilience is nothing but "the village model wearing a term sheet," and the industry is now held to it. A fund holds many paths; each venture holds one. So the fund layer, which genuinely lives across the ensemble, is where the smoothing honestly belongs — the steady cadence, the reserve, the shock absorption — precisely so that no single venture's worst year is mortgaged to a calendar. Schedule the chest, never the household: promises of regularity are made at the pool, and patience is granted at the path, which is the exact inversion of the instrument chapter 37 audited, where the schedule sat on the company and the flexibility belonged to capital.

The chest's rules travel up from the home chapters unchanged. It carries a stated size, set against the worst plausible stretch rather than the typical year, chapter 28's sizing discipline; a stated purpose; and a stated schedule for filling and drawing, because an undocumented reserve is a discretion, and discretions drift. It fills the way chapter 39 ordered the till — senior to every distribution, replenished before any surplus exists to share — and it can begin the way the old pools began, chapter 28's founding-cohort device: an entry contribution at the door, so the chest opens with a bad year already banked instead of promising to grow brave later. It obeys the two-pools test: a reserve is judged by whose ruin it prevents, and a chest that exists to steady the fund's reported year while its ventures each face their weather alone has answered in the wrong direction. It must actually move the ruin column — chapter 28's verdict on the reserve that never does is that it was a marketing line — and, the same chapter's warning, it may never be milked in the calm years, since a chest converted to yield has quietly sold the one thing it existed to hold. Held to those rules, the layer pays for itself in a currency the drawing has already spent twice. It is what makes the fund's own patience survivable, chapter 21's condition, so that waiting never has to be billed to anyone; and it is what lets the mercy floors run at zero without fragility, because the institution above them is never one bad quarter from becoming a creditor with regrets. Capital, here as in chapter 40, is the chest's beneficiary of record — the honest investor's principal is safest in exactly the year the chest was sized for — and the crowning irony of the whole section drawing is that its least productive floor is the one holding the roof up.

sections.title: The Cap, the Wheel, and the Guardian
paragraphs: Now the top of the stack, where the investors stand, and the two clauses that make the whole drawing a single instrument. The first is the cap. The fund's funders hold the zero line first — every principal home, wired and sweat alike, before any carry or distribution exists — and above it a stated share of true surplus to a bounded multiple, stated at signing, after which the fund's obligation to capital is, in the oldest sense, finished. Nothing about the seat is grudging: the investor's terms are written in the same grammar as every floor below — capital whole, work priced, a capped ratio of what actually happened — which is what makes the stack one instrument rather than a mission wrapped around an ordinary fund. The honest investor of chapter 36 recognizes the trade at once, because it is the one the traditions always offered: less than the market's promise in exchange for claims that are all answers — and the investors such terms select are the ones whose own charters can hold them, the foundation, the endowment, the family office with a purpose clause, the public funder whose mandate is the region's ventures surviving. The waterfall beneath the promise is the one chapter 37 commissioned: operating claims and wages filled, the reserves funded to charter, every principal returned, then shared remainders to the cap — the investor's return seated, in that chapter's words, "behind the enterprise's ability to survive collecting it." Chapter 39 named the alignment this ordering buys: an instrument shaped so that "its appetite and the venture's survival point the same way." An investor in this stack has no seat from which to profit by the portfolio's squeezing; the only route to the capped share runs through funded reserves and living ventures, so the appetite itself has been conscripted into the architecture. Appendix E will run these waterfalls in worked numbers, and Appendix D holds the metrics the runs are graded by.

The second clause answers the question every cap creates: where does the rest go? Surplus past the cap either stays with the ventures that made it or flows to the stack's own floor — replenishing the reserve, refilling the mercy layers, funding the next wheel's turn — and this is the point at which the fund stops being a portfolio with better manners and becomes a different body plan. The market's own label for funds without a terminal date is evergreen: no fixed end, proceeds turned back into new deployments rather than paid out toward a closing. The traditions have been running the reference implementation for centuries — the gemach that never closes, the waqf whose corpus outlives its founder by half a millennium, the Monte still lending five hundred years on. A terminal fund must, by its charter, convert everything to cash and leave; its final act is liquidation by design, however gentle the decade before it. An evergreen stack built on this chapter's floors points the other way: capital that finishes its capped errand is either retired or turned back into the ground floors, the wheel of chapters 15 and 16 running at institutional scale, so that success compounds into thicker chests, fuller mercy floors, and further ventures rather than into a farewell distribution. Nothing about the shape is soft. The wheel still underwrites, still prices its credit at shown cost, still caps and collects; it has simply been pointed at continuation instead of exit, and a fund pointed at continuation can make promises — to founders, to workers, to a town — that no self-liquidating vehicle can honestly sign.

Which leaves the last obligation on the drawing, and the oldest lesson in this Part: none of it administers itself. Chapter 29 taught that drift is a design load — the waqf captured by its mutawallis, the steward-firm captured by its stewards — and chapter 45 will spend a chapter on the temptations peculiar to religious finance. The stack's answer is architectural, not exhortatory. Give the deed a guardian: an independent, asset-locked holder of standing, the golden share's logic raised to fund level, whose consent is required for precisely the acts that would undo the drawing — unlocking a layer, raising the cap, milking the chest, redrafting the waterfall. Give the floors a voice: the borrowers, stewards, and members the layers exist for sit where they can be heard, in the pool's assembly and the fund's council, because the people at the thin end of a structure feel its drift before any auditor books it. Publish the runs, chapter 40's reporting practice: every fee against its work, every reserve against its charter size, every distribution against the remainder it came from, so that non-extraction stays a set of subtractions a stranger can check. Watch the side doors: the related-party fee, the affiliated management company, the service contract that collects like capital while calling itself administration — chapter 38's fence, patrolled on a schedule. And re-ask the layers the formula's questions annually, because a claim that was honest at signing can rot in place: the fee that outgrew the work, the reserve parked past its stated size, the participation that collected its cap and kept collecting. The interfaith contract library of chapter 42 supplies the clauses for all of it; the analyzer of chapter 43 will read this same stack back, term sheet by term sheet, and grade the drawing against the code it was built from.

Step back from the section, then, and read the building whole. At the bottom, money that expects nothing, so that the floors above never have to pretend. Rising through it, money that expects less than the market at every station — principal only; costs only; the pooled peril only; the capped share of what actually happened — each layer refusing exactly the claim the floor above would otherwise have been forced to invent. At the top, investors whose road to a return runs through funded reserves, living ventures, and a written cap. And standing beside the whole drawing, a guardian whose single share exists to say no. What the traditions ran from closets, courtyards, and chests, a fund can now run from a waterfall — provided the waterfall was drawn by someone who knew what the closets knew. Nothing in the section is new money; it is old mercy, given a modern org chart and told to hold the line. The gemach's counter, the Monte's chest, the takaful pool, the partnership's honest ratio, the waqf's unsellable deed: one building, seven floors, every euro in it arriving — as chapter 40 taught this book to demand — with its errand written on it. A capital stack, it turns out, is a creed read from the ground up. The next chapter opens the drawer of contracts that make each floor signable.

chapters.part: Part X — Institutions for the Future

chapters.title: The Interfaith Contract Library
chapters.label: Chapter 42

paragraphs: Every financing in the world, whatever its theology, ends at the same piece of furniture: a table with pages on it. The pages carry small plastic flags where the signatures go. Nothing the parties believe is in the room unless it is in the pages — not the sermon, not the pitch deck, not the handshake warmth, not one of the forty-one chapters behind this one. A conviction that has not become a clause stops at the door of the closing room, and the door is soundproof. The last chapter drew a fund as a section drawing, seven floors of layered mercy and discipline, and ended by promising to open "the drawer of contracts that make each floor signable." This chapter is the drawer. It holds ten documents, and the claim made for them is deliberately narrow: nothing in them is new. Every clause descends from an instrument some tradition built, tested, policed, and wrote down centuries ago. What is new is only the assembly — the old fences, in modern enforceable language, on pages with flags where the signatures go.

The traditions themselves would recognize the project before they recognized the paper, because all three of them, sooner or later, stopped trusting doctrine to travel on its own and wrote it into forms. Doctrine was written twice: once to be believed, once to be signed. The rabbis of Poland, chapter 31 told, standardized the heter iska into a printed instrument precisely so that a merchant who could not follow the Talmudic argument could still transact inside it — the wall democratized, compliance at the price of a signature. The notaries of Genoa, chapter 11 showed, kept formularies whose compressed boilerplate carried the commenda's whole risk grammar from one shipowner to the next without either of them reopening the theology. The Monti of chapter 17 lent under chartered capitoli that fixed what the counter could charge before the first pledge crossed it. And the modern fiqh, chapters 13 and 14 reported, maintains a standards body whose model provisions tell an Islamic bank's drafting department, article by article, what a mudarabah may and may not say. A standard form, in every one of these houses, is how the tradition made its discipline affordable to people who would never afford a scholar. The library exists so that the fund of chapter 41, and any smaller venture with none of its apparatus, can do the right thing at the marginal cost of doing anything at all.

Chapter 40 made the promise this chapter keeps. Its formula, it said, could now be written on demand, and Part X would build the institutions that do the writing: the fund first, then this library. So here are the ten instruments, the drawer's full inventory, each named for the work it does:

1. The interest-free loan agreement — the mercy floor's paper: principal out, principal home, nothing else, ever.
  2. The cost-recovery loan agreement — credit at documented cost: everything shown, nothing beyond.
  3. The solidarity-pool participation agreement — membership in the shared chest, not a policy purchased from it.
  4. The mudarabah-inspired profit-sharing agreement — capital and effort, joined by ratio.
  5. The iska-inspired investment agreement — the two-halves instrument, with its wage and its witnesses.
  6. The societas-inspired partnership agreement — consent, contribution, and a common fate.
  7. The mission-preserving buyback agreement — the exit that returns a company to its purpose.
  8. The asset-lock covenant — the deed that takes value off the market.
  9. The stewardship governance charter — the offices, vetoes, and voices that keep the drawing drawn.
  10. The anti-extraction disclosure schedule — the exhibit on which every other document confesses.

Ten documents, three parent traditions, one skeleton. (Appendix C holds the wider field, a classified map of the traditions' whole contractual inventory; the drawer is the signable subset, drawn to one fund's needs.) Before walking the shelves, it is worth stating what every instrument in the library answers in its own terms, because the recurring anatomy is the point. Each names its parties and the path the money takes. Each states what may be collected, and, the harder discipline, out of what: invoiced cost, proven loss, waged work, a ratio of realized surplus, never the bare calendar. Each says where losses land, in writing, before there are any. Each carries a bad-month protocol, because a contract that has never imagined its counterparty's worst quarter has been drafted for a different world. And each ends with a short list of clauses the parties alone cannot amend — the locked terms, answerable to a guardian — because the library learned from chapter 29 that drift is a design load. The word interfaith in the chapter's title is meant exactly, not decoratively. These are not Jewish documents, Christian documents, or Islamic documents; they are secular, enforceable instruments drafted so that a signatory from any of the three houses finds the fences of home already inside. On the deepest rules the houses simply agree, and the drafting is easy: all three insist that capital's gain ride a realized outcome, so the ratio clauses below would read as native law in any of them. Where the houses genuinely differ, the library does not referee. It drafts to the strictest common floor and leaves each tradition's further permissions where they belong, with each tradition; that is a drafting posture, the designer's own, offered for argument rather than announced as doctrine. A merchant of the Cairo Geniza, chapter 11 found, "could tell you, precisely, which tradition's rules his money was traveling under." A signatory in this library enjoys a stranger comfort: the honest answer is all three at once.

sections.title: The Mercy Papers
paragraphs: The first drawer holds the two lending instruments, and the shorter document is the stricter one. The interest-free loan agreement is the gemach and qard hasan machinery of chapters 15 and 16 reduced to operative clauses. Parties: the fund's mercy floor, or any free-loan pool, and a borrower with a bridge to cross. Principal: stated, dated, and scheduled. Mercy names its dates — the halakha's default term for an unspecified loan, thirty days, is the tradition's oldest reminder that even kindness runs on a calendar. Consideration flowing back: the principal — all of it, and only it; no fee, no charge, no gift-in-expectation, no benefit smuggled through softer channels. The perimeter clauses do what chapter 15's design grammar demanded: the borrower's file stays confidential; terms are standard across borrowers, so that no one's rescue is bespoke charity; and the document is deliberately mute about gratitude, because the tradition that coined ribbit devarim — increase by words — knew that a thank-you exacted is interest paid in a devalued currency. Where the floor takes deposits, the deposit clause is one line: depositors take back exactly what they placed and nothing riding on top, the deposit earning nothing because it risks nothing. And the pool writes its own continuation into the paper: repayments return to the fund and go out again, the revolving clause, so that the instrument's afterlife is the next borrower — the wheel of chapter 15, here a term rather than a metaphor.

What gives the paper its spine is the security package, and here the library copies the free-loan societies at their least sentimental: guarantors, named and signed; documentation a bank would recognize; the pool's rolls kept like a lender's, not a donor's. Chapter 15's finding travels intact — rigor is not extraction's property, and the discipline that collects a mercy loan back is what lets it be lent again. What the instrument refuses is the meter. There is no late-fee clause, because agar natar, reward for waiting, is the exact thing this paper exists to refuse; the remedies for the slow borrower are a redrawn schedule, then the guarantor, then the community's long memory — in that order. A mercy loan that starts charging for delay is no longer a mercy loan, whatever its heading still says.

The cost-recovery loan agreement is the same paper with one additional permission, fenced on every side. The lender here may run a service charge, and the charge lives inside chapter 40's four fence-words, received through the last chapter as the credit floor's grammar: shown, allocated, once, and at zero margin. The schedule of recoverable costs is an exhibit, not a discretion: origination, administration, collection, audit, each at documented actual expense, allocated to the loan by a stated policy — and the policy itself is attached, so that a borrower can see not only what was billed but why it was billed here, the exhibit standing guard against costs that wander toward whichever account complains least. Two further refusals complete the fence. The charge may never be a percentage: a charge set as a share of principal has already confessed, chapter 16 showed, since "real service costs do not double when the loan does," and a percentage charge on a mercy instrument is interest that has changed its name and kept its appetite. And the lender's own general keep may not migrate downward: the fund's housekeeping is the fund's expense, chapter 41's rule, not a solemn-sounding cost of capital on the borrower's statement. This is the Monti's counter from chapter 17 rendered in modern clauses — its verdict, quoted, that "a charge pinned to costs inherits a ceiling" — and it is chapter 16's serviced qard, priced by receipts and never by rates.

Then the two clauses this instrument is proudest of, because they govern the bad month. First, hardship. The paper distinguishes the borrower who cannot from the borrower who will not, and for the first it writes chapter 22's rule into operative text: the insolvent is "entitled to time, not merely eligible for it." The clause descends from the verse that chapter carried, in Abdel Haleem's rendering: "If the debtor is in difficulty, then delay things until matters become easier for him; still, if you were to write it off as an act of charity, that would be better for you, if only you knew." Deferral is the debtor's right under the document, triggered by demonstrated inability; write-off is named in the drafting as the act the parties agree is better. Beneath both stands the collection floor, the schedule of what may never be seized — the tools of the borrower's trade, the bed, the month's food, the mercies chapter 22 carried out of the old codes — written as an unwaivable clause. Second, the penalty.
