A century after the founder's death. By the texts' own count, the monks of Vesali set out a collecting bowl for coins on observance days, and the quarrel over that bowl becomes the young order's first great money crisis (Interlude II).

Around the second century before our era. A railing medallion at the Bharhut stupa carves the laity's side of the bargain, Anathapindika's purchase of the Jeta Grove, the ground drawn as a tiling of coins; around the year 120 of our era, the donor Ushavadata records at Nasik the developed instrument: imperishable principal lodged with the town guilds, its interest clothing and feeding the monks (Interlude II).

End of the fifth century. A man named Chen Pin pawns a bolt of hemp cloth at a Chinese monastery treasury — the earliest pawnshop transaction the historians can point to — and until the Tang the pledge-loan trade is effectively a monastic monopoly (Interlude II).

Sixth century. Xinxing's Sanjie movement builds the Inexhaustible Treasury at the Huadu monastery in Chang'an, boundless giving channeled through one institution, until the emperor Xuanzong liquidates it in 713 (Interlude II).

1255. Japan's records first name the mujin; the temple rings run for centuries as mutual aid without interest, then commercialize by degrees; a business statute reaches them in 1915, and in 1951 a mutual-bank law converts the survivors (Interlude II).
Medieval Jewish commercial law. The halakha of credit equipped for a commercial civilization.

Maimonides' codification. A millennium after the Mishnah's sages, the Mishneh Torah catalogs the interest laws with a codifier's completeness and states the iska's two halves at their starkest: the loan half on the manager come what may, the deposit half on the investor (chapters 7, 8, and 13).

1437. Florence charters its Jewish lenders under the condotta (the word Italian cities also used when they engaged a mercenary captain), with the licensed rate capped at twenty percent; within a generation almost every central and northern Italian city but Venice and Genoa holds such a charter (chapter 17).

The Shulchan Arukh at siman 177. The code files the iska machinery at the address where every later drafter finds it, the working partner's wage shrinkable to a single dinar but never to zero (chapters 12, 13, and 31).

By the sixteenth century. The Jewish communities of the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth sit at the center of a working credit economy (leaseholders, merchants, traders), not at its margins (chapter 31).
Scholastic extrinsic titles. The mutuum stays barren by definition while compensation grows around it, title by argued title.

Twelfth century. Gratian's compilation carries the blunt arithmetic, that whatever exceeds the principal is usury; and in the mid-1180s Urban III's Consuluit, answering a confessor's query, rules that the lender's hope alone can be the usurious price (chapters 1 and 8).

Thirteenth century. William of Auxerre gives the debate its most beautiful sentence: the usurer sells time, the common possession of all creatures. On 5 September 1234 Gregory IX promulgates the Liber Extra, compiled by Raymond of Peñafort, and its decretal Naviganti rules that even the lender who takes the voyage's peril on himself may not charge past the principal. Around 1260 Moerbeke's Latin Politics reaches the schools, and within a generation Aquinas joins Aristotle's sterile coin to the theologians' case (chapters 1, 7, 10, and 11).

Mid-1290s. Peter John Olivi (1247–1298), writing the Tractatus de contractibus at Narbonne, defines the merchants' word capitale: money aimed by its owner's settled purpose at probable profit already does capital's work, and deserves capital's name (chapter 20).

Fifteenth century into the sixteenth. The pastoral theologians of the banking cities — Antonino in Florence, Bernardino of Siena (1380–1444) — concede compensation for a trade genuinely torn away while writing chiefly against the abuses; Conrad Summenhart's seven-part anatomy of contracts is printed at Hagenau in 1500 (chapter 20).

25 October 1586. Detestabilis avaritia condemns the contractus trinus — partnership, capital insurance, and an uncertain profit swapped for a certain one, stacked into a guaranteed return — and rules the assembly usurious (chapters 13 and 37).

1605–1642. Lessius, who cross-examined the merchants on the Antwerp exchange, formulates and accepts the deprivation title that Molina (1535–1600) had refused; Juan de Lugo's synthesis of 1642 reads foregone gain and endangered principal as one family of compensable detriment (chapters 19, 20, and 21).
1679. The Holy Office under Innocent XI condemns the casuists' defense of the mohatra, the buy-dear-on-credit, sell-back-cheap-for-cash pairing that nets a loan at interest (chapters 24 and 37).

1 November 1745. Vix pervenit: usury arises in the loan contract as such (moderate gain, rich borrowers, and fruitful use excuse nothing), while genuine titles outside the loan stand. The Holy Office applies the letter to the whole Church in 1836; from 1830 to the 1870s the replies converge on the not-to-be-disturbed formula; and canon 1543 of the 1917 Code restates the doctrine while releasing the practice, both in one sentence (chapters 7, 14, and 30).
Islamic contract elaboration. The fiqh builds out its lawful instruments and patrols their edges.

The classical grammar. The lawbooks develop what the rulings founded: mudarabah profit divided by ratio and only from profit, the musharakah loss rule the jurists trace to the caliph Ali, sale and lease and advance sale each hedged with its conditions of possession and risk (chapters 11, 23, 24, and 25).
Around 1100. Al-Ghazali's Ihya supplies the money theory: coin exists to measure and move other goods, and riba is the perversion that turns the measure into the merchandise (chapter 1).

Sixteenth century. Ottoman founders begin endowing money itself: the cash waqf, its corpus lent out to fund the teacher and the lamps. Civizade attacks the practice on classical grounds before his dismissal in 1541; Birgivi answers in 1572 with a treatise titled as a drawn sword; practice settles in the funds' favor, and the courts' registers of the early seventeenth century record whole towns among their debtors (chapter 29).

The Majalla. The Ottoman codification writes the classical sale law into modern articles (ma'lum, known, at every joint) and shows how codification narrows the room a stratagem needs, a lesson the modern standard-setters relearn (chapters 23 and 32).
Confraternities, guilds, and mutual-aid institutions. The pool keeps the books of every era in between.

9 June 136. At Lanuvium the worshipers of Diana and Antinous cut their by-laws into a temple porch: entry at a hundred sesterces and an amphora of good wine, dues of five asses a month, three hundred sesterces from the chest at a member's death — the burial club dating itself by the consuls (chapters 3, 27, and 28).
The aqila. Islamic law keeps the older custom under which a man's kinsmen share the blood-money he owes: liability pooled long before anyone priced a premium (chapter 27).

Confraternity and guild chests. Medieval parish brotherhoods and trade fraternities collect dues against sickness, against a daughter's dowry, against burial, and escort their dead to the grave as the Lanuvium club once did — the same equipment, rededicated (chapter 27).

1564. Eliezer Ashkenazi organizes the first of the modern chevra kadisha societies, patterned deliberately on the guilds around it; Judah Loew, the great rabbi of Prague, codifies its rules (chapter 27).
1891. Rerum novarum reads the guilds' abolition as the workman's abandonment and commends the mutual-help societies by name as their lawful successors (chapters 27 and 33).
Monti di Pietà. The charitable pawn bank, and the era's mercy and cruelty bound into one story.

1361. A London fund endowed to make pledge loans without charge pays its costs out of its own capital and closes as the arithmetic dictates, the failure mode the Monte's small charge is designed against (chapter 17).

13 April 1462. Perugia's council adopts its Lenten preacher's proposal and votes three thousand florins for the first Monte; Orvieto follows within a year, Monterubbiano in 1465 — a Franciscan and a Dominican founding it together — Viterbo in 1469, Siena in 1472, Genoa in 1480, Milan in 1483 (chapter 17).

1484–1494. Bernardino of Feltre (1439–1494) plants Monti from Mantua onward and becomes the institution's engine. The record stays whole here, as chapter 17 keeps it: his Lent of 1475 in Trent is followed by the death of a child named Simon, and the town's Jews are tried on the ritual-murder libel and executed; expulsions follow at his urging: Perugia 1485, Gubbio 1486, Ravenna 1491, Brescia 1494, the year he dies at Pavia, venerated at once. The cult built on the libel is not suppressed until 28 October 1965 (chapter 17).

1494–1498. The opposition goes to print: Bariani's De Monte Impietatis at Faenza, then Cajetan's treatise, the most thorough of the attacks; the objectors' strongest card is equity, the rescue billed to the rescued (chapter 17).
4 May 1515. The Fifth Lateran Council's Inter multiplices closes the question: the Monte may charge its borrowers its running costs, and nothing for gain (chapters 14 and 17).

1534 onward. Ypres from 1534, Rome in 1539, Avignon for France in 1577, Madrid in 1702, Mexico City in 1775 on a silver fortune, Paris re-founded in 1777 and still lending at the same address; Italy counts five hundred fifty-six working Monti in 1896; and Siena's Monte of 1472, re-founded in 1624 on the pledged Maremma pastures, trades today as Banca Monte dei Paschi di Siena (chapter 17).
Heter iska expansion. Hillel's kind of move, made standard form.
1591. Cracow calls Rabbi Isaiah Menahem ben Isaac, Mendel Avigdors to Polish Jewry, who sets about repairing the venture deed his own fame had spread (chapter 31).
1607. The Council of Four Lands enacts his model rules on credit: communal legislation drafted in the shadow of the Torah's oldest prohibition (chapter 31).
1667. The Nachalat Shivah, the notaries' handbook printed at Amsterdam, seats the heter iska in the standard repertoire beside the marriage deeds (chapter 31).

The heter iska klali. Drafted for modern volume, the general permission of venture rides standard terms into Israel's banking system and the New York courts; Rabbi Moshe Feinstein's responsa set the twentieth-century debate's frame (chapter 31).
Friendly societies and modern mutual aid. The pool professionalizes without giving up its members.

1793. Parliament passes the first friendly-societies act; the registry that grows from it counts nearly fourteen million members by 1905, and in 1945 the societies still cover some eight and a half million Britons (chapters 27 and 28).
1810. The Oddfellows organize and put a surgeon in every lodge; the Rechabites pool the temperate; Tredegar's miners build the society that doctors the whole town (chapter 27).

1892. Eleven immigrants pool ninety-five dollars in a Henry Street synagogue; their free-loan society has since revolved hundreds of millions of dollars, interest-free, with repayment running near ninety-nine percent (chapters 15 and 28).
1983 and 1986. Iran writes the qard hasan into its banking statute, and the Fiqh Academy at Amman confines loan fees to actual service expenses, nothing beyond (chapter 16).

December 1985. The Islamic Fiqh Academy at Jeddah refuses the commercial insurance contract for its gharar and names cooperative insurance the lawful form; takaful and retakaful answer, and the Academy's criteria follow at Oran in 2012 and Riyadh in 2013: a non-profit fund, a manager who is only an agent (chapter 27).

2001. In Lahore, a widow's request that no interest-bearing loan could honestly meet sets Dr. Muhammad Amjad Saqib and his friends lending at zero from their own pockets; Akhuwat, named for brotherhood, grows from that seed to millions of interest-free loans, repaid at better than ninety-nine percent by 2020 (chapter 16).
Modern Islamic banking. The wall rebuilt at industrial scale — and the tradition auditing its own instruments in public.

1963. Ahmad El-Naggar opens the Mit Ghamr savings house in the Nile Delta, paying and charging no interest and placing deposits in local ventures; the experiment is closed down by 1967, by which time Egypt has nine such houses (chapters 30 and 32).

1975. The Islamic Development Bank starts work in Jeddah, and Dubai Islamic Bank opens on 15 September, by most counts the first full commercial bank of the type; in February 1976 the Makkah conference of scholars and economists declares bank interest riba in every form (chapters 30 and 32).

1988. Meeting in Kuwait, the Fiqh Academy licenses the murabaha triangle on the classical conditions — the institution must genuinely possess the goods and carry their risk until delivery (chapter 24).

February 2008. AAOIFI's sukuk resolution turns Usmani's audit (most issued sukuk pay like conventional bonds) into standards: no capital guarantees, no repurchase at par; in 2009 the Academy at Sharjah refuses organized tawarruq, and in December 2010 the prudential standard-setter takes on payout smoothing by name (chapters 13, 26, and 32).

2017–2018. The Dana Gas affair: an issuer disowns its own certificates' compliance, an English court enforces the par repurchase as an ordinary contract, and the holders learn which layer of their paper was real (chapter 26).

June 2023–September 2024. LIBOR is switched off and the markup industry repapers to the successor benchmarks on schedule; the 2024 stability report counts seventy-nine percent of the industry's financing in the markup family, with the partnership instruments sharing the eight-percent remainder with everything else in the toolbox (chapters 24 and 32).
Catholic Social Teaching. The tradition resumes its interrogation of economic life at modern scale.

15 May 1891. Leo XIII issues Rerum novarum, the founding document of modern Catholic social teaching, which names usury in its opening argument: condemned repeatedly, practiced still in altered dress (chapter 33).

15 May 1931. Quadragesimo anno, drafted with the economist Nell-Breuning's hand, dissects the credit dictatorship, the few who govern the lifeblood of the economy, without once using the word usury (chapter 33).
1967–1987. Populorum progressio carries the question up to the scale of nations; Sollicitudo rei socialis then names the inversion: development finance become a drain on the developing (chapter 33).

1991–1992. Centesimus annus presses the debt principle to its limit in the centenary year; the new Catechism keeps one sentence with teeth, counting the usurious starving of a brother as indirect homicide, and the 2004 Compendium repeats the condemnation (chapter 33).

June 2009. Caritas in veritate, published nine months after the crash, argues that markets need trust and gift and not calculation only, and returns the old word to a document of the highest rank for the first time since 1891 (chapter 33).

2015–2018. Laudato si' sets the economy inside creation and passes its terse verdict on finance outgrowing the real; in 2018 two curial offices jointly issue Oeconomicae et pecuniariae quaestiones, the magisterium's first document since Vix pervenit to read financial instruments one by one, and Francis tells Italy's anti-usury foundations in February that usury humiliates and kills (chapter 33).
October 2025. Leo XIV holds the register: usury a grave sin, and never a mere accounting issue (chapter 33).
Ergodicity economics and modern risk-pooling theory. The mathematics that vindicates the pool.
1745 and 1774. Parliament voids the wager policies, marine and then life, requiring an insurable interest in the thing insured — the law walling the pool off from the bet (chapter 27).
1762. The Society for Equitable Assurances is founded in London on an idea still novel: that the right price of a life policy can be worked out in advance (chapter 27).
1921. Frank Knight splits the word risk in two: the countable kind that tables and pools can carry, and the kind with no population of cases behind it (chapter 36).

2019. Ole Peters's Nature Physics paper puts the ergodicity problem before economics: what a gamble averages across many players is not what it does to one player over time: the arithmetic of ruin the traditions had guarded by rule (chapters 10 and 28).

2023. Graham Boyd and Jack Reardon's The Ergodic Investor and Entrepreneur carries the time-average case to practitioners: wealth compounds in sequence, so the order of gains and losses matters, and strategy should treat unpredictability as a partner rather than an enemy (chapter 28).
Contemporary non-extractive finance. Old instruments under new charters.

1876 and 1889. Jacobsen deeds the Carlsberg brewery to a foundation; Abbe vests the Zeiss works in the Carl-Zeiss-Stiftung, whose 1896 statute a reader of chapter 29 will recognize as a waqf deed in German legal dress (chapter 29).
2004. The United Kingdom legislates the community interest company, its asset lock compulsory and irremovable (chapter 29).
2007–2009. The Bellagio meetings convene finance to ask whether investment can be organized for good on purpose, and the Global Impact Investing Network follows (chapter 34).

2010. A microfinance flotation oversubscribed more than thirteen times in August and, in October, an Andhra Pradesh emergency ordinance against usurious rates and coercive recovery, drafted after officials counted fifty-four borrower deaths, put the extraction question into a modern statute book (chapter 34).

2022. Patagonia's owners place all voting shares in a purpose trust holding them to the mission and the economic shares in a nonprofit, performing the endowment move at market scale in the open (chapters 29 and 34).

Steward Ownership and the mission-locked forms. Employee Ownership trusts, golden shares, perpetual purpose trusts, the braided capital stack: Parts IX and X assemble these into working instruments, and there the timeline hands the reader back to the book (chapters 29 and 41 through 44).

chapters.part: Appendices

chapters.title: Contract Typology
chapters.label: Appendix C

paragraphs: Appendix A holds the book's words; this appendix holds its forms. Fifteen entries classify the contractual inventory the chapters have walked: every arrangement by which the three traditions let capital move, and the assemblies by which people have tried to move it dishonestly. Each entry states the form's anatomy (what changes hands, what comes back, where loss sits), names its instruments across the traditions, gives the test that separates the honest specimen from its counterfeit, and routes the reader to the chapters holding the sources and the quarrels. The order is the table of contents' own: the exchange forms first, then the venture forms and their paper, the protection form, the grace forms, the counterfeit, and finally the five instruments of the book's own constructive turn, the financing floors of chapter 41's stack, classified here rather than deployed. The signable subset, ten documents fitted to one fund, is chapter 42's library; this appendix is the field those documents were chosen from. One rule governs every row, laid down in chapter 3 and applied ever since: "The names are hypotheses; the payoff is the evidence."

Loan. The transfer of money, or of anything consumed in its use, against the return of its equivalent — chapter 3's one object held in the vocabulary of three legal traditions: mutuum, milveh, qard. Ownership crosses with the handover; what returns is the tantundem, the same in quantity and kind; the claim is personal, following the borrower whatever his venture does, and its payoff stands written before the venture has an outcome to report. That fixity is the form's signature among its siblings, and the source of its law: because the lender has parted with the thing entirely and retains nothing that could earn, all three traditions bar any stipulated increase, from the first coin, and post fences well past the coin, as far as benefits in kind and interest paid in words (chapter 8). The traditions' honest deployments of the bare loan are the mercy instruments classified below; nearly everything else in financial history that calls itself lending at profit is examined in this book under some other row of this table. Anatomy and boundaries: chapters 3 and 7; persons and communities: chapters 2 and 4.

Sale. A thing for a price, both transferred at once, no claim surviving the exchange. The traditions bless the merchant's margin ("buying cheap and selling dear is how merchants eat," as chapter 3 put it) and police the exchange for equivalence instead: the rabbis' ona'ah band with its one-sixth trigger, the Latin doctrine of the just price, the fiqh's gharar rule that the thing sold must exist, be known, and be deliverable, so that a price is never set against a mystery (chapters 9 and 23). The sale is the benchmark against which every financing in this table is measured, because its gain is the cleanest kind: realized in one completed exchange of real things. Its counterfeits arrive when time or prearrangement creep in — the deferred premium (the next row) and the boomerang sale (the hybrid row). Full doctrine: chapters 3, 9, 23, and 24.

Deferred sale. A sale whose price waits (goods now, payment at term), and the seam where the sale form meets the loan's temptation, since a padded term price collects for the waiting under a sale's name. All three traditions permit the form; all three guard the same gate, each with its own instrument. The canonists allowed a term price above the cash price only while the goods' worth at the payment date remained genuinely uncertain, so that the premium prices shared ignorance, never the calendar (chapter 24). The rabbis ruled that rent may rise for time but a sale price may not, and filed the padded deferred price under avak ribbit, the dust of interest (chapters 3 and 24). The fiqh's murabaha, the disclosed cost-plus sale, demands that the financier really own the goods for a real interval (his title, his risk), with cost and markup confessed, and a price fixed once, never to grow with delay; in the form called murabaha to the purchase orderer it now carries most of the industry that bears Islam's name (chapters 24 and 32). Test: whether anything but the calendar explains the premium.

Lease. The sale of a thing's use, in slices of time, possible only for things that survive their use — a field, a house, an ox, never bread or coin. The lessor keeps ownership and ownership's burdens: maintenance, structural failure, the thing's perishing are his — the rent is honest because it is income from an asset the lessor still owns and still risks. The rabbis accordingly rent courtyards without ribbit anxiety and refuse the "rental" of money, whose use cannot be separated from its spending; the fiqh's ijara is defined as a sale of usufruct, valid only if the lessor first acquires the asset and answers for its defects; Christendom's rent and usufruct doctrine runs on the same floor (chapters 3 and 25). The failure mode is the lease that walks every burden of ownership across to the user while retaining nothing but the payment schedule — at which point the traditions, like the accountants, reclassify the instrument as the secured loan it is (chapter 25).

Partnership. Capital committed to a shared venture rather than transferred against a fixed claim: ownership retained, exposure retained, and a share of surplus earned by that exposure. Loss follows an iron map — money-loss to the money's owner, labor-loss to the laborer — and no clause may walk an investor's loss onto his partner while his gain stays behind: the lion's partnership is void in Roman law, the guaranteed iska half collapses into loan, and the mudarabah whose capital is indemnified is void, its stipulated share condemned as riba (chapters 11 and 13). The instruments are the traditions' proudest: the societas of consent and common fate; the musharakah, capital from both sides, profit by agreement, loss strictly by capital shares; the iska, half loan and half deposit by the Nehardean formula; the mudarabah and the commenda (the next row). Partnership is, as chapter 3 introduced it, "the door all three traditions deliberately left open in their wall against usury" — and the most imitated silhouette in this table: the costumes of the hybrid row are cut to its pattern. Chapters 11 through 14.

Profit-sharing investment. The partnership family run as finance: one party brings money, the other work, and the financier is paid a ratio of realized profit fixed at signing — never a stipulated sum, which voids the contract. In the mudarabah, the investor's capital alone bears money-loss while the working mudarib stands as an amin, a trustee liable for transgression, negligence, or breach of mandate, never for the venture's ordinary fate; the commenda gave the same architecture to the Mediterranean, the traveling tractator trading on the seated investor's capital; the iska engineered the mix with rabbinic caution, its working partner owed a real wage — the sechar tircha that stands beside Aquinas's stipendium laboris as pay for genuine work (chapters 11 and 12). Profit here is discovered at the reckoning, never promised before it, and chapter 14's law governs the count: profit must come from profit, with interim payouts held back or sobered until the reckoning is real. The modern deployment, with its retentions, valuations, and caps, is chapter 41's risk-sharing floor.

Asset-backed certificate. Fractional ownership written on transferable paper. Chapter 26 states the row's whole test: "A certificate is honest when it conveys a genuine fraction — of a thing, of a venture, of a named stream of fruits — and its holder eats what the fraction earns and loses what the fraction loses." The form is old in every tradition: the shtar iska is already a certificate, its holder awaiting the venture's actual accounting; Genoa's Casa di San Giorgio cut a city's tax revenues into the luoghi, participation paper with a market price; the fiqh's sukuk are the standard-setters' modern version: certificates of ownership in assets or ventures, built to pay from what the assets yield. The counterfeit is the certificate engineered back into the bond it was meant to replace (par value protected, coupon-like distributions smoothed, recourse running to the issuer rather than the asset), the drift the industry itself names in its distinction between asset-backed paper and merely asset-based paper (chapters 26 and 32). Test: whether the holder owns something or is merely owed something.

Insurance / mutual guarantee. Protection against a defined peril, funded by many premiums and paid to the stricken: a form with two possible owners, and the ownership decides its moral character (chapter 27). The fiqh's jurists condemned the commercial contract sold at a fixed premium as an exchange built on excessive gharar — a known payment against an unknowable return — and engineered the objection away rather than the protection: in takaful, the members' payments enter as donations to a fund the members own together, an operator runs it for a fee or a profit share, and the pools reinsure one another through retakaful (the terms of art are in Appendix A). The mutual genus is older and broader: guild boxes and confraternities, the friendly societies of the industrial age, the communities' own burial and sickness funds — members carrying one another rather than buying a stranger's promise. The common law adds its own fence, insurable interest: protection may answer a peril the insured really bears, never manufacture a wager on a stranger's ship (chapter 27). Where the peril is shared and the chest is owned in common, the form crosses into the pool proper, the mutual-aid row below. Chapters 27 and 28.

Gift / endowment. The forms that refuse to create a claim. The gift transfers without counter-obligation: tzedakah, built on the root for justice — owed to the poor, not volunteered; zakat, the obligatory levy whose name carries purification, with voluntary sadaqah above it; the Gospel's instruction to lend expecting nothing, which keeps the loan's shape and removes its claim (chapters 4, 5, 6, and 18). Maimonides' ladder belongs to this row's law: the highest giving (gift, loan, partnership, or employment) is whichever restores a person to standing (chapters 3 and 18). The border needs patrol in both directions, since gifts that arrive just before or just after a loan can be interest in kindness's clothing (chapter 8). Stretched past its giver's lifetime the gift becomes the endowment: the waqf with its three bars (no sale, no gift, no inheritance) and its audited substitution; the hekdesh of Temple, community, and poorhouse; the church's locked patrimony under conciliar law since Chalcedon. The endowment exists precisely so that its capital is never again anyone's to extract (chapter 29).

Hybrid and synthetic forms. Not a form but a method: assembling individually licit contracts until, together, they pay what a forbidden one would have paid. The specimens run the width of the tradition. The 'ina double sale — sold for one hundred twenty deferred, bought back for one hundred cash — condemned by most schools as riba in costume, defended in one line of analysis that weighs only the visible contracts, an honest and permanent ikhtilaf (chapter 3). The rabbis' avak ribbit category exists because the dust of interest settles where the biblical definition cannot reach (chapters 3 and 24). Latin Christendom's perfected specimen was the contractus trinus (partnership, plus insurance of the principal, plus the sale of an uncertain profit for a certain one, three defensible agreements stacking into a guaranteed return), condemned by Sixtus V in 1586 and quarreled over for a century more (chapter 13). The heter iska, by contrast, earns a wary respect: a genuine repartnering of credit, whose uses and whose perils the tradition's own critics weigh in chapter 31. The modern stack (participating preferences, cumulative dividends, redemption rights) rebuilds the triple contract at scale (chapter 37, whose verdict this table applies row by row: "No single clause is the usury; the stack is the usury."). Diagnosis: chapters 30 through 32 and 37; the method of reading: chapter 3.

Cost-recovery credit. Lending whose charge prices the work of lending, never the loan itself: the borrower repays principal plus the documented cost of running the fund, and no one earns a margin on his need. The charter case is Christian: the Monti di Pietà, the pawn banks the Franciscans preached into being, lending the poor small amounts against pledged objects at a charge sized to bare operating cost. The Fifth Lateran Council ended a generation of dispute in 1515, ruling that expenses may be recovered and profit may not (chapter 17). The fiqh reached the same line in modern form: a service fee on benevolent lending is permissible within actual expenses, and anything beyond is riba (chapter 16). Chapter 40 wrote the row's modern specification as the cost line of its formula — shown, allocated, once, and at zero margin — and chapters 41 and 42 deploy it as the fund's credit floor and its loan paper. The row's characteristic corruption is the percentage that outgrows the work it claims to price; the remedy is the invoice. Chapters 16, 17, and 40 through 42.

Interest-free solidarity loan. The bare loan run as mercy and engineered to revolve: principal out, principal home, nothing else, ever. The Jewish form is the gemach, the free-loan fund of gemilut chasadim — donated capital revolving at zero, its security guarantors and good records rather than any charge, from the medieval communities to the free-loan societies of the immigrant cities (chapter 15). The Islamic form is the qard hasan, the beautiful loan the Qur'an casts as lent to God: a true debt, due in full, its lender entitled to nothing past the principal (gratitude the borrower adds freely is virtue; the same increase, expected by the lender, is riba), institutionalized from household circles to Akhuwat's national scale (chapter 16). The row's discipline surprises first-time visitors: rigor is what keeps mercy solvent, and the funds keep books like lenders precisely so they can keep lending like givers. Both systems treat repayment as part of the mercy: it restores the borrower's standing and refills the fund for the next borrower. Chapters 15 and 16; the signable version is chapter 42's first instrument.

Mutual-aid / solidarity-pool agreement. Membership in a shared chest against defined perils: the contract-form the traditions built specifically against ruin, which chapter 3 refused to file as a footnote to the others. Members pay small scheduled contributions into a fund that is their own common property; when the named blow lands on one of them, the chest answers by rule. The pool carries its members' downside and no venture's upside: nobody collects a dividend from a light year, which is what separates membership in a chest from the purchase of a policy (the insurance row above). The ancient instances are complete specimens — the Roman burial club at Lanuvium with its dues, its funeral benefit, and its effigy rite for a withheld body; the Talmud's donkey-driver and sailor compacts, replacing a lost animal or boat while excluding the negligent; the confraternities and friendly societies that carried the pattern into the industrial age (chapters 3 and 27). Its mathematics is the book's deepest argument: pooling moves none of the group's averages while sharply lowering each member's chance of ruin (chapter 28). Chapters 3, 27, and 28.

Mission-locked equity. Ownership stakes in companies whose charters have retired the exit: an asset lock ties the company's worth to its purpose, so that no sale can turn mission-built value into a private windfall; control sits in steward hands, unmarketable and unheritable; and the investor's stake leaves only by the mission-preserving buyback, its price fixed by formula when the money enters, its pace set so the company outlives its own redemption (chapters 29, 41, and 42). The form is the endowment's logic translated into corporate instruments — the waqf's bars, the hekdesh's covenant, the patrimony's inalienability, reappearing as the statutory lock of the community interest company, the golden share's veto over the acts that would undo the dedication, the purpose trust, and Steward Ownership's binding commitments (chapter 29). Capital in this row is patient by construction: it earns from real results while it stays, and its leaving is priced to protect the purpose rather than to capture it. Design and deployment: chapters 41 and 42; ancestry: chapter 29.

Non-extractive revenue participation. The table's last row is the book's own synthesis: capital paid a stated share of a named, realized result — participation by ratio, capped at a bounded multiple fixed at signing, collected only out of the result actually counted, and therefore honestly zero in the year the venture has nothing to give. The share's honest base is chapter 39's true surplus — the remainder after wages to standard, the founder's line, maintenance, and the reserves — rather than gross revenue: chapter 40 bases the share there, not on takings, so that no participation collects ahead of wages, upkeep, or the chests. Participation in a merely named stream is as old as Genoa's tax paper (the certificate row); the discipline lies in naming the right stream. The full specification is chapter 40's formula, in which every unit of return above principal carries a title (cost shown, loss proven, work waged, surplus shared by ratio under the cap), and the whole stack is published so a stranger can check it (chapter 42's disclosure schedule). Worked numbers: Appendix E; the metrics: Appendix D; the fund that runs it: chapter 41.

chapters.part: Appendices

chapters.title: Moral Geometry Metrics
chapters.label: Appendix D

paragraphs: Appendix A holds the book's words, Appendix B its dates, Appendix C its forms; this appendix holds its measures. Seventeen entries catalog the gauges the chapters built one at a time and chapter 43's analyzer computes wholesale: for each, what it measures, how it is computed, how to read it, and where its doctrine lives. The suite has a spine, laid down when chapter 35 first turned the doctrine into arithmetic, in two questions that govern nearly everything a contract can be asked. "How closely does the claim's collection track the venture's actual fortunes?" — that chapter's question of form — and "how much of the claim answers no burden anyone can show?" — its question of size. Every gauge below is one of those two questions pointed at a particular part of the machinery: the ledger, the queue, the reserves, the locks, the pools, the paths. Two rules govern the registry. First, these are computations, not accusations — each metric is built so that any two readers, however opposed, land on one number, and what the number means remains an argument the home chapters equip the reader to have. Second, the seventeen are never added up: the book's machine returns memos, not grades, because a moral geometry compressed to one digit stops being geometry, and chapter 43 rests its whole tenth module on that refusal. A reader wanting the constructions in motion should run the worked scenarios of Appendix E beside these pages; the metrics grade what those waterfalls stage.

Moral-title coverage ratio. The ledger's own gauge: of everything a capital claim will collect above return of principal, the fraction that sits on a proven titled line. The construction is chapter 35's moral-title ledger run to completion: every euro the instrument will claim across its life, seated on the zero line or on one of the seven standing lines (expense, work, loss, risk, liquidity, opportunity, surplus), a seat granted only where the title is "genuine in fact, not merely in name": the invoice for the expense line, the wage record for work, the netted shortfall for loss, the shown danger for risk, the documented deprivation for liquidity, the named and evidenced elsewhere for opportunity, the realized result for surplus. One fence crosses the whole computation before the ratio is struck — "a burden may be counted once," so a danger priced into the rate, retired by the collateral, handed to a guarantor, and billed once more at default enters the numerator one time, not four. Coverage of one means every claimed euro has named its work. Anything less is measured by the next entry, because the two gauges are one fact read from opposite ends. Construction and lines: chapter 35; the fences line by line: Part VI; the audit that keeps coverage honest after signing: chapter 44.

Extraction residual. The book's verdict quantity, and the only metric the whole suite exists to drive toward zero: the share of a claim that, in chapter 35's definition, "answers no shown burden, no work, no borne risk, no realized share." It is found by subtraction: run the ledger, let the zero line and every honest title absorb what they can evidence, and weigh the remainder. That is what makes it a measurement rather than a charge — the construction accuses no one, names no motive, and lands on the same number from either side of the table. Two committed disciplines give the reading its teeth. The residual is funded, "euro for euro, by the residual claimants," chapter 37 showed, so a nonzero residual always has addressees, not just a size; and the non-extractive formula of chapter 40 holds the term at zero "by construction at the drafting table, by audit ever after," so for any instrument claiming that formula's name, the residual is not a score to optimize but a promise to keep. Naming and construction: chapter 35; who pays it: chapter 37; the zero: chapters 39 and 40; the yearly bottom row: chapter 44.

Capital-at-risk index. How much capital is actually out in the venture's weather, netted, over time. Chapter 36 supplied both corrections that make the gauge honest. "Capital at risk is a curve, not a number": exposure is read period by period, the whole principal exposed to the last day on an interest-only claim, a melting stake on an amortizing one, so that a risk charge priced on day-one exposure overcharges every year after the stake begins to melt. And exposure is read after netting: take off the collateral, the guarantors, the seniority, the covenants (every shelter the same paper erected) and let the risk line price only what is still exposed once its own protections have done their work. The index is that netted curve, and it is computed twice, once per side, because chapter 36's column check found a contract the lender's column showed as nearly safe holding "a three-in-a-hundred chance of the house" across the table. Read it against the fence that has policed the risk line since the sea loan: danger earns payment where it is borne, not where it is merely priced. Construction: chapter 36; the title it disciplines: chapters 10 and 35; the module that runs it: chapter 43.

Founder-labor visibility score. How completely the venture's consumed inputs made it onto the record at entry prices. The register never forgets the wired money; chapter 38's contribution schedule exists for everything else — "every input the venture actually consumed, entered by name, dated, and priced at entry" — and this score is the schedule's completeness. Wages foregone are checked against the going standard rate for the work in fact performed; the founder's declined salary is priced at the rate she turned down, because "Zero is also a price," and it is the only one the cap table never has to defend; the house guarantee, the equipment, the years of evenings enter at entry value, reality being the entrance requirement chapter 14's doctrine of proportion sets for any contribution. Low visibility predicts chapter 38's exit arithmetic: distributions recorded as profit that the completed schedule shows to be repayment, senior seats collecting applause the unrecorded lines paid for. Full visibility means nothing was priced at zero by silence. The schedule: chapter 38; the two-ingredient doctrine behind it: chapter 12; wages under standard: chapter 39; the pre-filled disclosure form: chapter 42.

Mission-reserve sufficiency score. Whether the purpose has a funded chest standing between it and the quarter that could buy it. Chapter 39 built the reserve, the purpose's own chest, funded on a written schedule toward a declared ceiling — because a purpose, like a household, gets exactly one path, and enough lean quarters can shave it to nothing without one dramatic decision. Chapter 41 wrote the rules the score checks: a stated size set against the worst plausible stretch rather than the typical year, a stated purpose, a stated schedule for filling and drawing, since "an undocumented reserve is a discretion, and discretions drift." Sufficiency is the balance and the schedule measured against that charter, with seniority verified (the reserve fills before any surplus exists to share, per chapter 39's procession) and with chapter 41's ownership test applied: "a reserve is judged by whose ruin it prevents," so a chest that smooths the fund's numbers while the mission weathers alone points the wrong way, whatever its balance. A reserve tapped in good years to sweeten a distribution scores as what it has become: yield wearing a rescue's name. The reserve: chapter 39; the rules: chapter 41; the sizing discipline: chapter 28; the endgame it exists to prevent: chapter 34.

Surplus authenticity score. Whether what the till calls surplus has earned the word — whether it is chapter 39's true surplus or merely a January balance. Chapter 39's procession is the construction: before any distribution, the claims that stand senior — wages to standard, the founder's line, maintenance as logged, the chests replenished to charter, the community's owed line, every principal wired and sweat — each paid or provisioned, in order, out of a January number that only ever says available. The score is the fraction of actual distributions that left through that procession rather than around it, graded by the sentence that carries the test: "Available says the money can leave; surplus says it may." Authentic surplus traces to a realized result — profit from profit, chapter 14's rule, never from revenue, never from the borrower's principal returning in a costume, never from a drained reserve. Distributions that fail the trace are reclassified by the audit of chapter 44 and land, like every unexplained euro, on the residual. The procession: chapter 39; the base of the surplus term: chapter 40; the accrual honesty behind the January number: chapters 14 and 39; the yearly re-run: chapter 44.

Fixed-claim severity score. How fixed the claim really is, and how hard the fixity bites. The construction is chapter 35's payoff reading run across chapter 43's state grid: compute what the claim collects in each state of the venture's world, and score the flatness — a claim collecting alike in distress and in prosperity carries the loan's signature whatever the certificates say, while a claim paid only from prosperity that actually arrived has partnership's shape though nobody wrote the word. Severity weighs the flatness where it matters — chapter 28 proved that a constant subtraction swells against a shrinking base — so the claim is read at its weight in the bad states, not the average ones. Two committed verdicts calibrate the reading. A flat payoff at the front of an equity queue is chapter 37's "mutuum with a seat number"; and a flat claim carrying a risk charge is pricing insurance it never issues, chapter 35's rendering of the book's oldest test. The payoff reading: chapters 35 and 37; why fixity kills: chapters 10 and 28; the loan's anatomy underneath: chapter 7.

Risk-shift index. Where the danger actually went. Every protection is a transfer: collateral moves loss to the pledger, a guarantee to the household that signed it, seniority to whoever stands behind, a penalty to the stumbling. This index re-runs the losses through chapter 36's netting map to say which clauses moved them, and onto whom. It is the counted-once fence read as a flow: the four collections chapter 35 forbids on one danger are four arrows on this map, and the index totals the arrows that point away from the party charging for risk. The calibrating doctrine is Part IV's — loss belongs where capital stands — so a stack in which capital collects the risk line while the losses land on guarantors, workers, and the founder's unpaid years reads as shifted precisely to that degree. Chapter 13 supplies the test's oldest form — the loss clause is where a contract tells the truth — and chapter 37 its modern one: follow the waterfall to the seats that absorb the bad states, and compare them with the seats that were paid to. Loss allocation: chapter 13; netting and the two-sided count: chapter 36; the queue's geometry: chapter 37.

Governance-asymmetry index. The gap between who bears the venture's fate and who can steer it. The construction is chapter 43's steering map made a measure. Inventory the consequential acts (amending the waterfall, unlocking a layer, raising the cap, drawing the reserve outside its charter, forcing the sale) and record, for each, whose consent is required and whose is not; the index is the distance between the consent map and the exposure map, weighted toward every path that lets a party revise next year the very title it collects under. The committed checkpoints do the grading. Chapter 29's maintenance cargo: two keys wherever money moves, trustee and beneficiary never the same person, pay fixed to the office and blind to the flows through it. Chapter 41's guardian: an independent, itself asset-locked consent standing in front of "the acts that would undo the drawing". Chapter 38's side doors: the affiliate and management channels that turn control into claim without ever standing in the queue. And the drag read as chapter 43 reads it, "the power to sell other people's company," with the index pricing how far that power can travel before anything with standing can stop it. Low asymmetry means the steering sits with those in the weather. The map: chapter 43; the cargo: chapter 29; the guardian and the acts: chapter 41; the side doors: chapter 38.

Form-substance divergence score. The distance between what the paper says it is and what it does. The reading rule has been fixed since chapter 3 — effect is given to intention and meaning, not to words and phrases, the Majalla's third article and Gregory v. Helvering converging on one sentence — and the score arithmetizes it: classify every instrument by its payoff, classify it again by its label, and measure the disagreement, because "The names are hypotheses; the payoff is the evidence." Assembled packages are tested whole under chapter 37's parity discipline — clauses whose combined payoff comes out flat in every state add up to a fixed claim, no matter how many instruments share the work — and single instruments against their own conditions: the heter iska run without its witnesses and oaths, chapter 31's own authorities warn, is a loan in partnership dress; the murabaha that never truly touches the goods is, in chapter 32's internal critique, the conventional product wearing the tradition's clothes. Zero divergence is the honest specimen: the label survives its payoff. Divergence is the counterfeit's one universal signature: every fraud in this book, ancient or synthetic, is a gap between name and geometry. The rule: chapter 3; the legal transformations and their tests: chapters 31 and 32; synthesis detection: chapters 37 and 43.

Cost-recovery discipline score. Whether a service charge is actually recovering costs. The standard is the strictest one under which a lending institution can still exist — the Monti di Pietà's, vindicated at the Fifth Lateran Council in 1515 — and the fence-words the credit floor carries from chapter 40 through chapter 42 are the score's four checks: shown (each cost line evidenced), allocated (attributed to the lending it serves), once (no cost recovered twice across fees), and at zero margin (the charge budgeted to break even, falling when costs fall). Chapter 17 supplies the diagnostic the score operationalizes: the honest charge pays for the apparatus surrounding the loan, appraisal desk to auction room, and would vanish if a benefactor covered the desk some other way; the loan itself remains gratuitous. A fee that grows with the appetite of the book rather than the cost of the desk has become a rate and is scored as one, whatever line it was booked to; the excess lands on the residual. The institution and its trial: chapter 17; the fence-words: chapters 40 and 42; the expense title underneath: chapter 19.

Mercy-capital purity score. Whether the mercy instruments are running clean. The floors this gauge patrols are the ones the traditions built to run at zero — the gemach, the qard hasan, the alms-fed pools of chapter 18 — and purity is scored against their own rulebooks, which are stricter than any regulator's. Nothing collected past principal, in money, in kind, or in words; the fences of chapter 8 run to benefits and flattery, not just coins. Queue and eligibility by need, never by donor advantage: chapter 15's separation of the giving hand from the deciding hand. The loan a real debt, mercy lending in expectation of repayment (the instrument whose repayment is optional is alms under a different name, chapter 16's boundary), but with deferral standing as a right wherever inability is shown, per chapter 22, and with the patience funded — a hardship promise that no reserve stands behind scores as the fragility it is, chapter 21's condition, answered at fund level by the anti-ruin reserve chapter 41 stations behind the mercy floors. Purity of one means the beautiful loan is still beautiful on audit: capital that circulates, collects its principal, and takes nothing for the service of being merciful. The instruments: chapters 15 and 16; the fences: chapter 8; the gift floor beneath: chapter 18; funded patience: chapters 21 and 41.

Asset-lock integrity score. Whether the lock actually locks. The doctrine is chapter 29's — the corpus detained while the fruit alone travels, held by the waqf's three bars against sale, gift, and inheritance, by the hekdesh's trustees under outside authority, by Chalcedon's ban with an oeconomus to answer for it — and the score tests a modern lock's drafting against that standard. Walk every amendment path — the ordinary resolution, the merger, the redomiciliation, the supermajority the collecting party controls — and record which of them opens it. A lock any such path can open is what chapter 43 called "a wall with a gate in it," and scores as a gate. Substitution is checked the way the jurists checked istibdal: permitted for the corpus's own preservation, under an authority distinct from the trustee, never as disguised sale. And the guardian is counted: a consent with no stake in the undoing — independent, and locked itself — seated in front of chapter 41's undoing acts, with the standing to refuse and keep its seat. Integrity of one means the corpus outlives its own trustees' worst quarter — locked, in chapter 39's words on the endowment, "past the reach of any board's bad quarter." The three bars and their keepers: chapter 29; the mission-locked layer and the guardian: chapter 41; the steering audit: chapter 43.

Ruin-probability reduction score. What the arrangement does to the chance of reaching the floor. Ruin, throughout this book's mathematics, is an absorbing state, a place a path enters and never leaves; this score is the book's central claim about solidarity made falsifiable. Run the same ventures through the same weather twice, once solo and once under the arrangement being graded (the chest, the entry reserve, the contingent claim), and read the movement in the ruin column. Nothing else counts as the answer. Collections may stand nearly unmoved, the ensemble may not notice, and the arrangement may still have changed what one life can survive — that is chapter 28's demonstration, calibrated on its village, where provision comfortably above the average blow still lost, household by household, to the worst blow, and stopped losing only when the common chest stood. The score prices ruin beyond offset, chapter 28's specification: no one's collapse is netted away against a neighbor's good year; and its threshold is that chapter's blunt one: the reserve that leaves the ruin column where it stood was never architecture, whatever the brochure says. The floor and the reserve against it: chapter 10; the proof and the sizing: chapter 28; the pools it grades: chapters 27 and 41; the module that runs it: chapter 43.

Time-average resilience score. What the claim does to the path a venture actually lives. The book's survival mathematics runs on the distinction Appendix A carries and chapters 10 and 28 built: the ensemble average, taken across many parallel cases at a stroke, and the time average, accumulated along one compounding sequence, the only average anybody lives. This gauge works on the time axis by construction: take the venture's path year by year under the claim being graded, let each year compound on the last, and read the growth the single path keeps — graded at the worst year, not the mean one, because the mean is the property of whoever holds the whole cohort, and a venture holds one path. The finding this score exists to catch is chapter 10's: a fixed claim can look flawless in the ensemble's books and still be consuming the trajectory it collects from. A resilient claim caps its own drag: it takes from good years, waits through bad ones, and leaves the path's compounding intact. Read this score beside the previous one — ruin is the floor, resilience the slope, and an honest instrument answers for both. The two averages: chapter 10 and Appendix A; the proof: chapter 28; the pricing consequences: chapter 36; the grading module: chapter 43.

Solidarity-pool sufficiency score. Whether the pool can carry what it exists to carry. Two audits, and the pool must pass both. First the membership grammar of chapter 27, because a pool owned wrong is not a pool: contributions enter as the members' own (as dues, as donations, as tabarru'), never as a seller's revenue; the administrator's wage is fixed and indifferent to refusals; exclusions police conduct, never misfortune; outside capital serves, never owns. Then the arithmetic of chapter 28, because a pool sized wrong is a promise scheduled to break: the solidarity reserve sized against the worst stretch it can plausibly be asked to meet; opened funded, by way of the entry contribution the old pools took at the door, rather than hoping to grow brave on schedule; and never drawn down in good years to flatter a distribution, a chest turned yield source having stopped being a chest. Sufficiency is provision read against the blows the pool must absorb, calibrated by the village's discipline: a jar even slightly short of the worst blow loses every time it arrives. The grammar: chapter 27; the sizing and the proof: chapter 28; the fifth form's anatomy: chapter 3; the fund-level chest: chapter 41.

Institutional-drift risk score. The standing pressure on an institution to become what it grades. Drift, chapter 29 ruled, is a design load, to be planned for the way an engineer plans for weather, and chapter 45 catalogs the temptations that are its names. This score counts the channels the drafting leaves open and weights each by who profits through it: compensation keyed to flows rather than fixed to office; reserves drawable in calm years; fees that grow with appetite; locks openable by those collecting behind them; classifications amendable without a vote, because "Classifications are commitments," and chapter 44 showed that an institution rebooking penalties as yield has amended its theology "in the middle pages of a report nobody reads". The committed antidotes are the checklist the score runs: counting done in public where the money comes in; removal power lodged with an authority that is neither trustee nor beneficiary; the disclosure schedule renewed annually and drafted for a stranger; the analyzer turned on the institution's own paper on a calendar, not on a suspicion. Low drift risk is not innocence; it is an architecture that assumes the third generation will be ordinary and locks accordingly — the oldest lesson of the endowments, from Interlude II's cave-wall benefactions to the monastic estates of chapter 29. The design load and its instruments: chapter 29; the bookkeeping where drift shows first: chapter 44; the temptations by name: chapter 45; the published self-examination: chapters 42 and 43.

chapters.part: Appendices

chapters.title: Sample Non-Extractive Waterfalls
chapters.label: Appendix E

paragraphs: Appendix A holds the book's words, Appendix B its dates, Appendix C its forms, Appendix D its measures; this appendix holds its runs. Seventeen scenarios follow, each a waterfall worked in numbers: which seats collect, in what sequence, out of which euros, and what the sequence does to everyone in the line. They are the worked examples chapter 37's audit commissioned, the sketches chapter 26 ordered of what non-extractive paper "would pay and to whom," the waterfalls chapter 41 drafted and chapter 42 papered. Every file obeys the discipline chapter 28 set for its village: every rate chosen for transparency, every result checkable with a pencil, none of it a claim about any historical venture. Files the chapters already computed return here under their own committed numbers, credited as they arrive — the founder's Tuesday of chapters 37 and 38, the roastery's January of chapter 39, the village of chapter 28, the half-million-euro participation of chapters 35, 40, and 41. One file is new: call it the workshop, the young company of chapter 35's two term sheets, taken at the honest sheet's word. Its paper: €500,000 advanced as a capped participation; a total ceiling of two euros and ninety cents per euro advanced, which is €1,450,000, ever, by chapter 41's arithmetic; a stated thirty percent share of true surplus (a staged fraction); a reserve charter of €60,000, one genuinely bad quarter, sized by the roastery's rule; a crew of eight. Scenarios one through six run the workshop across six futures. Seven and eight run the cautionary stacks the honest paper exists to refuse. Nine through seventeen walk the instruments of chapter 41's ten-million-euro stack, layer by layer, each in its own liturgy. Every run obeys the commission chapter 37 wrote and chapter 41 drafted: "operating claims and wages filled, the reserves funded to charter, every principal returned" — wired and sweat alike — "then shared remainders to the cap," the investor's return seated "behind the enterprise's ability to survive collecting it." The metrics of Appendix D grade what these waterfalls stage; the analyzer of chapter 43 runs the same audit wholesale; and no run is ever compressed to a single digit, for chapter 43's standing reason.

Failure scenario. The workshop dies in year three; the market it served moved, and no clause could have moved it. Wind-down realizes €150,000. The waterfall runs the committed order: wages owed to the crew, €35,000, paid first; suppliers, €45,000; the costs of an orderly closing, €10,000. The remaining €60,000 goes to the participation, and the participation's loss, €440,000 of the €500,000 advanced, lands where the paper priced it. The shortness is the doctrine: the seat that contracts for a share of surplus is the seat that eats the loss, up to the capital and no further — the boundary chapter 13 found the fiqh stating as cleanly as anyone. The founders lose their years; the contribution schedule of chapter 38 prices what they lost (€60,000 of logged under-standard wages) rather than pretending the years were free. Appendix D's gauges, run on the wreck, return the one comfort the geometry allows: the extraction residual is zero. Money died here, and none of it moved to a seat that had drafted itself away from dying.

Partial recovery scenario. Year five: after a hard stretch that drew the chest down to €40,000, the workshop is sold to a competitor for €400,000. Proceeds plus remaining chest: €440,000. Wages and suppliers are already current — keeping them current is what the chest was drawn down for — and the closing costs €20,000. The participation takes home €420,000 of its €500,000. No surplus ever existed, so the thirty percent share collects thirty percent of nothing; chapter 37's ordering, "the capital whole before profit exists," makes the rest of the arithmetic unnecessary. The loss of €80,000 is capital's own. For contrast, at this file's scale: a cumulative dividend of the kind chapter 37 priced, eight percent accruing, would have stood €200,000 of coupon (five lean years at €40,000) in front of these same proceeds, collecting hardest in exactly the future least able to pay it. Appendix D's fixed-claim severity score exists to see that coming.

Sustainable survival scenario. The workshop lives, and is never spectacular. Year six, the pattern year: €90,000 sits in the account in January. The procession of chapter 39 marches first — wages brought to standard, €25,000; maintenance as logged, €15,000; the chest refilled to charter, €20,000; the mission reserve's scheduled €10,000 — leaving €20,000 of distributable cash, split by the stated policy: €10,000 reinvested, €10,000 redeemed against the participation's principal. Seven years at that tempo return €70,000 by year ten, a seventh of the way home, and the ceiling of €1,450,000 is a figure on a document nobody rereads. The paper anticipated this future. Chapter 42's clause is the mechanism: installments run "from free cash after wages, suppliers, and the reserves at their charter sizes" and stretch, "without penalty, when the till says wait"; the remedies for a slow stretch are "a redrawn schedule, then the guarantor, then the community's long memory," in that order, with no late-fee clause to compound the waiting. Zero in a lean year is a price, not a default. The participation may never reach its cap, and that possibility was inside the price of calling it a participation.

Mission-preserving buyback scenario. Year seven, the future chapter 41 narrated: "grown into the town's anchor employer," the workshop converts to steward hands. The participation has collected €450,000 by then. The buyback formula, written the day the money went in per chapter 41, completes the claim at the ceiling's arithmetic: €1,450,000 less €450,000 leaves €1,000,000, paid in five annual installments of €200,000, each subordinated to the procession as a condition precedent, each stretching without penalty when a year says wait. On the last payment the shares return to steward hands, the economic rights end, and, in chapter 40's sentence, "further surplus belongs to the venture, its people, and its purposes." Total collections: €1,450,000 on €500,000 over roughly twelve years, complete. The mission never met a buyer; the exit was what chapter 42's destination clause drafted it to be, "a homecoming rather than an auction," priced at signing and survivable by construction.

Moderate surplus scenario. The middle future. From year four the procession leaves modest distributable cash: enough that principal comes home by year nine, while the thirty percent share of true surplus adds €180,000 across years four through twelve. Total collected, €680,000 on €500,000 over twelve years; the €1,450,000 ceiling never binds. Two readings. First, every distribution in the run passed the same gate — no arrears standing, the chest at charter, the reserve schedule current — so the payments could keep a rhythm the members could plan around without any single year choking the company to keep a date. Second, in the moderate future the cap cost the investor nothing: an uncapped honest partnership would have paid nearly the same euros. The cap is not a price paid in every future; it is a promise about the good one, which the next scenario reaches.

Large surplus scenario. The workshop compounds. True surplus crosses €300,000 a year by year five, still climbing; principal is home in year six; the thirty percent share collects €80,000, €120,000, €150,000, €180,000, €200,000, €220,000 across years five through ten — €950,000 above principal, which is the ceiling, reached. The claim is complete: two euros and ninety cents for every euro advanced, in ten years. From year eleven the venture's entire surplus, the share included, stays with the venture, its people, and its purposes, and an uncapped thirty percent would have collected €200,000 and more, every year, indefinitely. This is the future in which the design pays most of its price, and it pays on purpose: each layer, chapter 41 said, "renounces something exactly so that the layer above it can exist without pretending." The traditions had long since stated the shape. "A debt under damdupat can be heavy; it cannot be bottomless," the first interlude reported from the Indian codes. The capped participation reads the same sentence to capital: a return can be handsome; it cannot be endless.

Forced-sale cautionary scenario. Now the stacks the honest paper refuses, run so the refusal has numbers. A funded company carries €2,000,000 of participating preferred at one times, fifty-five percent as converted, with a drag-along; the fund holding it is at the end of its life. An offer stands at €4,000,000 today; the plan the room believes in reaches €9,000,000 in two years. Run both futures. Today: the preferred takes €2,000,000 off the top plus fifty-five percent of the €2,000,000 remainder, €3,100,000 in all; the common splits €900,000. In two years: €2,000,000 plus fifty-five percent of €7,000,000 is €5,850,000 preferred, €3,150,000 common. Both seats collect more by waiting. The sale happens today anyway because, as chapter 37 put it, a fund at the end of its life "does not need the company's best decade; it needs the company's next transaction," and "the drag turns that need into everyone's obligation" — the mission "sold to meet a preference," toward "the buyer's purposes nobody in the building would have chosen," the workers riding into the data room as line items. The numbers cannot even call the choice greedy; they show the clock, not the arithmetic, choosing the future. Whose horizon governs is a term of the contract, and it should be read as one.

Preferred-equity extraction scenario. The founder's Tuesday, rerun under chapter 37's committed numbers. Sale: €12,000,000. The preferred: €10,000,000 invested, participating, holding fifty-five percent as converted; the founder thirty percent; the employees fifteen. As drafted, the preferred takes its €10,000,000 off the top, then fifty-five percent of the €2,000,000 remainder: €11,100,000 of the twelve. The founder's thirty percent pays €600,000; the employees' fifteen, €300,000. Redraft one word — the same preference, non-participating — and the preferred takes €10,000,000 and stops; the €2,000,000 remainder belongs to the common alone, one and a third million of it to her. One word moved more than seven hundred thousand euros. Chapter 38's schedule then decomposes the protected seat's €1,100,000 excess exactly: €390,000 of genuine surplus, and €710,000 "that is not surplus at all but transfer — the working seats' unreturned principal, changing hands, renamed on arrival." Chapter 37 gave the residual its address: it is funded, "euro for euro, by the residual claimants." A preference, that chapter concluded, "is a rate that learned to stand in line" — and this is the line, with the amounts filled in.

Non-extractive partnership scenario. The same Tuesday, redrafted as the paper chapter 26 sketched. The €10,000,000 enters as partnership capital: no preference, no participation stacked on top, no accruing coupon. At the €12,000,000 sale, chapter 38's order runs — all capital home first, wired and sweat alike: the €10,000,000, and the €710,000 of sweat principal the contribution schedule priced at entry (the under-standard years, the deferred draws, the founder's own ten thousand); then the true surplus, all €390,000 of it, shared by stated fractions over stated contributions — at a staged sixty–forty between capital and work, €234,000 and €156,000. The investors leave with €10,234,000, which is €866,000 less than the participating draft paid them, and every euro of the difference sits on a titled line in somebody else's column: the crew's principal home, the founder's decade repaid, a surplus that had earned the word. Both drafts were legal. Only this one can fill in chapter 36's second table; and the test Sixtus V set for the honest partnership, as chapter 37 rendered the bull — it "casts up fruits, costs, and losses together and divides what is actually there" — closes over it without remainder.

Gemach-style emergency support scenario. Chapter 15's file, under its own numbers. A gemach of $10,000 lends $500 bridges, repaid over ten months: roughly twenty households a year carried across their bad week, two hundred rescues in a decade, and the ten thousand dollars all still there for the third decade and the fourth. The instrument's grammar does the work: no interest, ever; a guarantor and community knowledge in place of collateral; a repayment plan in place of a late fee. The waterfall is a circle, out, back, out again, and the arithmetic of revolving mercy is the entry's whole point: capital given once rescues indefinitely — the founders' ninety-five dollars of 1892 still out working thirteen decades later. In chapter 41's stack the same machine holds the €700,000 second layer: at the file's scale, fourteen hundred five-hundred-euro bridges per revolution, the floor that catches what no participation should be asked to price.

Qard-hasan-style bridge support scenario. Chapter 16's anatomy at bridge scale. A member's business is stranded by a late receivable; the fund advances €3,000. Owed back: €3,000, carrying "no stipulated benefit of any kind," in cash, kind, or favor. Ten months, redrawn to twelve when repayment needs the room. If the borrower, made whole, freely adds something at settlement, the classical rule permits it — the tradition's exemplar repaid a borrowed camel with a better one, as chapter 16 told it — provided nothing was stipulated, promised, or prearranged; the excess is gratitude, not price. The same instrument works at industrial scale as the shock absorber chapter 27 found inside regulated takaful: when a pool runs dry, the operator advances the deficit as qard hasan, repaid from future surpluses. The waterfall line is one line long, principal out, principal home, and its emptiness is the design; a charge for the crossing would be the first step toward pricing the flood.

Takaful-style mutual-aid shock scenario. A staged pool. Forty members contribute €250 each; the year's chest is €10,000; every contribution enters under tabarru', "a donation rather than a price" in chapter 27's phrase, so no one has sold anyone certainty. The operator stands outside the fund as hired administration at a disclosed fee, €1,200, priced as work. The shock: one member's shop floods; the assessors certify €6,000; the chest pays, that being what the chest is for. The year-end ledger keeps chapter 27's three books — "the cost of running the thing, the reserve that keeps it standing, and the surplus of the light years." This year: costs €1,200, claims €6,000, the reserve line €1,000, surplus €1,800 — which, in the committed sentence of the industry's own criteria, "can be retained in the fund or distributed, totally or partially, among policyholders." It stays home or goes home; the operator is excluded from it by seat, not by virtue. Forty people bought each other's worst week, and the price of the purchase is published.

Mudarabah-style profit-sharing scenario. €100,000 from the rabb al-mal; the mudarib brings the venture, the skill, and the months. The stated split of realized profit: sixty to capital, forty to work — a ratio, chapter 11's rule insists, that "must bite on actual profit," never a guaranteed sum. Year one, profit €30,000: €18,000 and €12,000. Year two, loss €20,000: it falls on the capital, up to the capital, and the mudarib is owed nothing and owes nothing. "The mudarib loses his months, his labor, and his hoped-for share, which the jurists regarded as loss enough," as chapter 11 put it. Year three, the venture is wound up at €95,000: less than the capital that entered, so across the whole life no profit ever existed to split; the investor's loss is €5,000, the manager's wage for three years is zero, and both outcomes were in the price of the words they signed. Now the test that guards the instrument: add one clause guaranteeing the €100,000 home whole, and the verdict chapters 13 and 37 carried is structural, not stylistic — the partnership "has dissolved into a loan in the measure of the guarantee," and the profit share it promises is riba. The scenario's arithmetic is easy; the discipline is refusing the clause that would make it easier.

Heter-iska substance-test scenario. €200,000 placed under a standard heter iska: half loan, at the manager's risk; half deposit, at the investor's; and a named settlement sum, the sechum ha-hitpashrut, of €12,000 a year, payable in lieu of opening the books. Run the instrument twice. Live run: a bad year comes, and the manager does what the form contemplates — brings the witnesses, proves the loss; the deposit half's share of the loss falls on the investor, as the codified rule chapter 13 carried has it (the entrusted half "stolen or lost, the administrator is not liable to pay"), and she collects less than the settlement sum, in a hard enough year less than principal. The evidentiary machinery — witnesses findable, the shevu'ah swearable, loss provable — is, chapter 31 showed, the instrument's true signature; kept live, the named figure is a settlement between partners, not a rate. Dead-letter run: the acceptable witnesses are named only in a far city; the oath is drafted never to be sworn; and the €12,000 arrives on schedule every year, profit or loss, for a decade. The poskim struck the far-city device down themselves, on the ground chapter 31 quoted: "verification that cannot occur is not verification." Appendix D's form-substance divergence score is the same ruling as arithmetic, and the substance test fits in one sentence: a settlement figure that has never once been declined, varied, or verified against a real year is chapter 11's guaranteed sum in new paperwork — a loan's payoff "wearing a partnership's clothes."

Cost-recovery Monti-style credit scenario. A revolving credit fund at cost. Capital €200,000, lending small bridges against pledges and invoices; the year's audited operating costs — the two clerks' wages, the rent, the audit itself — come to €9,000, recovered pro rata across the year's lending as a disclosed charge and recalculated annually from the books. No profit line exists for costs to wander toward: the charge answers the Fifth Lateran definition quoted in chapter 17, "a moderate sum for their expenses and by way of compensation," intended "exclusively to defray the expenses" of staff and upkeep, "provided that no profit is made therefrom"; and the schedule of recoverable costs is "an exhibit, not a discretion," per chapter 42. The arithmetic that makes cost recovery a mercy rather than a fee is the counterexample chapter 17 preserved: the London fund of 1361 paid its expenses out of the capital itself, and plain arithmetic ate it, every year's costs carved from the corpus until there was no corpus. A fund that recovers its documented costs, and nothing above them, is not charging for money; it is arranging to still exist next year, at scale, for strangers.

Mission-reserve-first distribution scenario. The roastery's January, under chapter 39's committed numbers, run here as paper rather than as virtue. The screen says €120,000 available. The procession marches as a condition precedent written into the distribution clause itself, the drafting move chapter 42's buyback schedule demonstrated: "Wages to standard, thirty thousand. The founder's deferred draw, ten. Maintenance as logged, twenty. The chest's replenishment, twenty-five. The mission reserve's schedule, ten. The community's owed line, ten. The priced footprint, ten." One hundred and fifteen thousand of the one hundred and twenty were never anyone's to distribute; the true surplus is €5,000. "The board that distributes it has extracted nothing from anyone." "Available says the money can leave; surplus says it may." The scenario's addition to chapter 39 is only the enforcement: because the reserve is filled before any distributable amount legally exists, a lean year cannot be voted against the mission, and a reserve tapped in a good year to sweeten a distribution is reclassified by chapter 44's audit as what it became — in Appendix D's phrase, "yield wearing a rescue's name."

Ergodic solidarity-pooling scenario. The village of chapter 28, closing the appendix under its own numbers, because every waterfall above assumes what this one proves. Twenty households; six units saved per year against a hundred-unit blow.
