Jars: a household needs seventeen years of uninterrupted saving before one blow is survivable, and across twenty years more than eleven of the twenty are ruined on average, about fifty-seven in a hundred, in a village that as a whole was never poor. One chest, the same six units each: the first year's blow of a hundred lands on a chest of a hundred and twenty and is carried, that year and every year; ruin falls to about nine in a hundred. Bank one blow in advance and it falls below six; bank two, toward three; give a town of a hundred its one-blow reserve and ruin runs about one in a hundred. The sizing rule travels with the arithmetic: a solidarity reserve, chapter 28 ruled, is "sized to the pile-up, not the average year." And that chapter already drew the conclusion these pages have been staging: "portfolios are villages." The community reserve layer of chapter 41's stack, the €500,000 held "never deployed, never distributed, sized to the bad stretch," is the village chest at institutional scale, standing between every path in the portfolio and the floor. It appears in no waterfall as a payee, which is the point. It is the reason the other sixteen scenarios could afford their gentleness: the seat held empty so that everyone else's seat holds.

chapters.part: Appendices

chapters.title: Reading Guide
chapters.label: Appendix F

paragraphs: Appendix A holds the book's words, Appendix B its dates, Appendix C its forms, Appendix D its measures, Appendix E its runs; this appendix holds its books. One rule governs the shelf: every source named here did verified work in a chapter of this book — its wording checked, its dates pinned, its claims read at the granularity the chapter reports — and nothing is listed on hearsay, because a guide that recommends what it has not examined would fail the audit this book runs on everyone else. The thirteen clusters follow the table of contents. Each names the texts first, then the way in for a reader starting cold, then the chapters where the book put the source to work, since the chapters carry the disputes, the case files, and the full circumstances that a shelf list cannot. Where a tradition's texts are quoted in these pages, they are quoted from named renderings — the 1989 New Revised Standard Version for the Bible, M. A. S. Abdel Haleem for the Qur'an, Eliyahu Touger for the Mishneh Torah, the book's own close renderings with exact loci for the Talmud, the Digest, and Aquinas — and a reader who wants to meet the sources in the same form should start with those.

Primary Jewish sources. Begin where the law does: the three Torah passages of chapter 2 (Exodus 22:25, Leviticus 25:35–37, Deuteronomy 23:19–20), and then the Mishnah's interest chapter in Bava Metzia with the Gemara that grew around it, the folios this book kept returning to: 61b on the two kinds of forbidden increase, 63b where any reward for waiting is named, 68b's wage seminar, 70a–71a on orphans' money and precedence, 75b where the lenders' own joke is filed, 104b where the iska is born, 42a on burying money properly. The Davidson edition of the Koren Steinsaltz English, freely readable on Sefaria, is the way in; this book's renderings are its own, made against that text with exact loci. From the Talmud, go to the codes: Maimonides' Mishneh Torah in Touger's translation (the partnership laws of Sheluchin veShutafin 6:1–3 that chapter 13 reads, the laws of sale that chapters 23 and 24 read, and Gifts to the Poor 10:7, the ladder's top rung, met in chapters 3 and 18), then the Shulchan Arukh's laws of interest, met in chapter 12 at siman 177, with the Tur behind it. Doctrine lives in chapters 2, 4, 7, and 8; instruments in chapters 12, 13, 15, and 18; the modern practice in chapter 31.

Primary Christian sources. The scriptural spine is chapters 4 and 5; read them beside the 1989 NRSV, the version this book quotes. The doctrine then runs through documents a reader can hold: canon 17 of Nicaea (chapter 1); Aquinas at Summa Theologiae II-II, questions 77 and 78, the anatomy chapters 7, 9, and 12 walk clause by clause; the Liber Extra that Raymond of Penyafort assembled for Gregory IX in 1234, where Naviganti sits at X 5.19.19 (chapter 10); Consuluit, Urban III's answer, where the lender's hope alone makes the usurer (chapter 8). The councils are best met in the standard conciliar English of the Tanner edition, carried in full at papalencyclicals.net: above all Session 10 of the Fifth Lateran, the bull Inter multiplices of May 1515, the council's formal definition of usury and its verdict on the Monti (chapters 14 and 17). Benedict XIV's Vix pervenit of 1745 closes the doctrinal file (chapters 7 and 30); Sixtus V's Detestabilis avaritia reaches English in Jeremiah O'Callaghan's Usury, Funds and Banks (chapter 13); the older collections travel under Denzinger's numbering (chapter 14). The standard modern road into all of it remains John T. Noonan's Scholastic Analysis of Usury (1957), the study behind chapters 10, 21, and 30.

Primary Islamic sources. The Qur'an in M. A. S. Abdel Haleem's translation, the rendering this book quotes throughout: start with the riba verses, 2:275 through 2:280, and the charity verses around them (chapters 2 and 6). The hadith collections (Bukhari, Muslim, Abu Dawud, Ibn Majah) are readable with collection and number at sunnah.com, the carrier against which every hadith quoted in this book was checked; chapters 6, 10, 16, and 24 hold the load-bearing reports, from the curse on the whole cast of a riba loan to the Prophet's own credit purchases. For the law worked out, three modern bodies of text: the Majalla, the Ottoman civil code, in Tyser's English, whose articles on sale, deceit, and intention this book cites by number (chapters 3, 10, and 23); the AAOIFI Shari'ah Standards, on mudarabah and partnership, sukuk, gharar, insurance, and waqf, with the February 2008 sukuk resolution that disciplined a market (chapters 13, 24 through 27, 29, and 32); and the resolutions of the International Islamic Fiqh Academy, from the 1985 insurance ruling to the 2013 Riyadh criteria for the cooperative pool (chapters 16, 24, 26, 27, and 32).

Hindu Dharmaśāstra and Arthaśāstra sources. Interlude I's texts are all readable in the old translations online. The Manusmriti in Bühler's translation (Sacred Books of the East volume 25, from 1886, at sacred-texts.com), whose vulgate numbering the Interlude follows, since later critical editions renumber, carries the eighteen titles of law, the caste-graded tariff of 8.142, and the doubling ceiling of 8.151; Jha's edition with Medhatithi's commentary, at wisdomlib.org, lets a reader watch the great early commentator at work. Yajnavalkya's code with the Mitakshara, the commentary scholars place around 1100, long the working law of Anglo-Indian courtrooms, sits in the same library, beside the dharmasutras of Gautama, Vasishtha, and Baudhayana. Kautilya's Arthaśāstra, in Shamasastry's translation, prices the whole system in one chapter, 3.11 on the recovery of debts. Behind every secondary account stands Kane's History of Dharmaśāstra, the standard authority historians of the literature lean on. The Interlude walks all of it, including damdupat, the doubling ceiling still enforced in the courts of the Bombay tradition.

Buddhist Vinaya and temple-finance history. Start with the rules themselves: Nissaggiya Pacittiya 18, 19, and 20 (the monk's renunciation of money, buying and selling, and barter) with rule 10's steward mechanics, and the Jetavana purchase at Cullavagga VI.4; the Book of the Discipline carries the rules in English. Thanissaro Bhikkhu's Buddhist Monastic Code is the modern commentary a beginner wants, and his sutta translations at Access to Insight and dhammatalks.org, with Narada Thera's rendering of the layman's discourse at Digha Nikaya 31, carry the lay-facing texts Interlude II quotes. The scholarship then tells the astonishing institutional story: Gregory Schopen's "Doing Business for the Lord" (Journal of the American Oriental Society, 1994; reprinted in Buddhist Monks and Business Matters, 2004), where a Vinaya orders the endowment lent at interest; Yang Lien-sheng's "Buddhist Monasteries and Four Money-raising Institutions in Chinese History" (Harvard Journal of Asiatic Studies, 1950); and Jacques Gernet's Buddhism in Chinese Society: An Economic History from the Fifth to the Tenth Centuries, written in French in 1956 and Englished by Verellen in 1995, still the standard economic history — with the Dunhuang loan documents behind it. Interlude II holds the file, from the silent steward to the Inexhaustible Treasury.

Medieval commercial history. The sea is the way in. Goitein's A Mediterranean Society reconstructs the Geniza merchants whose paperwork chapter 11 reads, down to the India traders' archive of his final years; Udovitch's "At the Origins of the Western Commenda: Islam, Israel, Byzantium?" (Speculum, 1962) puts the parentage question this book leaves unsettled because the scholarship does; the cartulary of the Genoese notary Giovanni Scriba shows the commenda splitting profits before a notary of the 1150s. Florence Edler de Roover's "Early Examples of Marine Insurance" (Journal of Economic History, 1945) documents the earliest insurers writing protection as loans they had never received, the costume story chapter 27 tells; Koyama's "Evading the 'Taint of Usury'" reads the same evasions as an economist; Felloni's work on the Casa di San Giorgio anchors chapter 26's oldest financial machine. For the late-scholastic exchange floor, Wim Decock's "Lessius and the Breakdown of the Scholastic Paradigm" (Journal of the History of Economic Thought, 2009), Toon Van Houdt's study "Lack of money," and Monsalve's 2014 companion article in the same journal carry chapter 21's story at Antwerp. And because this history has a wound in it: Hsia's Trent 1475 (Yale, 1992) is the trial-record study behind chapter 17's plain account of what the preaching campaign against the Jews of Trent cost them.

Modern Islamic finance criticism. The quarrel is the tradition's own, and the reading list is its critics in their own words. M. N. Siddiqi's "Islamic Banking and Finance in Theory and Practice: A Survey of State of the Art" (Islamic Economic Studies, 2006) is the theorist's audit; the murabaha that "conquered the landscape" is his phrase and his complaint. M. Umer Chapra's Towards a Just Monetary System (1985) states the profit-sharing vision the industry was supposed to build. Mahmoud El-Gamal's "Limits and Dangers of Shari'a Arbitrage," in the Harvard Islamic Finance Project's Islamic Finance: Current Legal and Regulatory Issues (2005), names the reengineering method cold, and his companion essay on mutuality as the antidote points where chapter 27's pools already stand. Taqi Usmani speaks for the jurists twice: An Introduction to Islamic Finance, with its benchmark defense and its plea to be rid of the practice, and the AAOIFI paper "Sukuk and their Contemporary Applications," whose finding that most issued sukuk mirror conventional bonds set off the 2008 correction. John Foster's BBC report "How Sharia-compliant is Islamic banking?" (December 2009) preserves the fatwa-shopping banker chapter 32 weighs against the scholars' refusal record. Chapters 20, 24, 26, and 32 hold the full proceeding.

Modern halakhic finance. The documents come first: the shtar heter iska of Mendel Avigdors of Cracow, the late-sixteenth-century tikkun Maharam that standardized the instrument; Joshua Falk's Kuntres al Diney Ribbit with the Council of Four Lands' credit rules of 1607; the Nachalat Shivah, whose author came to the formula's defense; and the Chachmat Adam's later version, the line that runs to the wall signs in Israeli banks (chapters 14 and 31). The modern responsa then test the machine: Moshe Feinstein's Igrot Moshe at Yoreh De'ah II:62, the scope ruling with its attachable-asset repair, and II:63 on the corporate borrower, a ruling R. Shlomo Zalman Auerbach opposed, a machloket chapter 31 reports without adjudicating. Bleich's survey "Heter Iska in American and Israeli Courts" follows the document into secular litigation, where judges must decide whether the partnership is real. Read chapter 12 first for sechar tircha and siman 177, then chapter 31 for the whole architecture (witnesses, oaths, settlement sum) and for what the poskim themselves say ribbit-washing looks like.

Catholic Social Teaching and modern finance. The encyclicals are all at vatican.va in official English, and the sequence chapter 33 audits reads quickly: Rerum Novarum (Leo XIII, 1891), where the tradition's economic voice returns with usury in its third paragraph; Quadragesimo Anno (Pius XI, 1931), drafted by Nell-Breuning, on credit's reign; Populorum Progressio (Paul VI, 1967) on development and debt; Sollicitudo Rei Socialis and Centesimus Annus (John Paul II) on the debt of nations and the market's two answers; Caritas in Veritate (Benedict XVI, 2009), where gratuitousness enters the balance sheet; Laudato Si' (Francis, 2015) for the ecology of the whole; and Oeconomicae et pecuniariae quaestiones (2018), the joint instrument-level document that reads term sheets, credit default swaps included, in Rome's own hand. Around them: the Catechism at 2269 and 2409, the Compendium at 341, and the two codes' quiet swap of canon 1543 (1917) for canon 1284 (1983), the exhibit chapters 30 and 33 explain. Chapter 34 carries the teaching into ESG's world; the addresses of Francis in 2018 and Leo XIV in 2025 show the old word alive in Rome's mouth.

Mutual aid, friendly societies, guilds, confraternities, and takaful. The oldest document on this shelf is a by-law: the burial society of Lanuvium, CIL XIV 2112, dated by its consuls to June of AD 136, readable in English in Harland's collection of Greco-Roman associations — dues, benefits, arrears rules, all of it (chapter 3). The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica's article "Friendly Societies," on Wikisource, surveys the movement Rose's Act of 1793 first encouraged, with the counts (nearly fourteen million members) that chapter 28 reads as anti-ruin infrastructure; the Marine Insurance Act 1745 and the Life Assurance Act 1774 (the latter still on the statute book at legislation.gov.uk) mark the state drawing the line between pooling and wagering (chapter 27); the mathematician Dodson's work for the Equitable begins actuarial fairness in earnest. For the living instruments: chapter 15's free-loan societies, from the Hebrew Free Loan Society founded in 1892 on ninety-five dollars; Akhuwat's lending through mosques and churches, with Munir's study "Akhuwat: Making Microfinance Work" (2012) as the outside look (chapter 16); and the takaful texts already shelved in the third cluster — the Academy's 1985 and 2013 resolutions, AAOIFI's insurance standard — which chapter 27 reads beside the chevra kadisha and the lodge.

Mathematical finance, actuarial fairness, and ergodicity economics. The prehistory is short and startling: Ulpian's annuity table at Digest 35.2.68, Rome pricing lifetimes in three bands, which chapter 10 reads with the modern actuarial scholarship, and Dodson's mathematics for the Equitable, where fairness first became a calculation (chapter 27). The modern shelf is two items and a method. Ole Peters's "The ergodicity problem in economics" (Nature Physics, 2019) states the divergence this book's Part IX runs on (the ensemble average nobody lives versus the time average everyone does) in the coin-toss gamble chapter 28 stages at a kitchen table. Graham Boyd and Jack Reardon's The Ergodic Investor and Entrepreneur (2023) carries the finding into venture finance and the design of companies. The method is this book's own from there: chapter 28's village, run twice, with every number checkable by pencil; chapter 10's two averages planted in Talmudic soil; the ruin arithmetic that Appendix D gauges and Appendix E stages. A reader who wants the mathematics without the theology can start at Peters; a reader who suspects the theology got there first can start at Bava Metzia 70a.

Steward ownership and non-extractive capital. The movement's own texts are the entry: the Purpose Foundation's steward-ownership principles (self-determination and purpose-orientation, control held by stewards rather than sold or bequeathed) and its practical companion, "Steward-ownership: a short guide-book to legal frameworks," which chapter 29 reads beside the fiqh of the waqf. The living exhibits publish their own constitutions: the Carl-Zeiss-Stiftung, founded by Ernst Abbe in 1889 and governed by his 1896 statute; Robert Bosch GmbH, whose ownership pages state the trust arithmetic plainly; Carlsberg; and Patagonia's announcement of September 2022, under the title "Earth is now our only shareholder." Employee Ownership trusts, met in chapter 34, put the same locks in workers' hands. Chapter 29 maps these onto the mutawalli and the asset lock; chapters 41 and 42 then draft the instruments a Steward Ownership conversion signs: the stack, the waterfall, the ten documents. This book's Parts IX and X are, in effect, this cluster's missing manual: what the locked company owes its capital, and what its capital may honestly collect.

Contract analysis and moral-economy accounting. The shelf for the book's last discipline is mostly the book. The ledger that seats every euro on a named title is chapter 35's; the analyzer that runs the audit wholesale, in ten modules and no composite score, is chapter 43's; the audit year, with its reclassifications and its found euros, is chapter 44's; the ten signable documents are chapter 42's library; and the three appendices before this one hold the forms, the measures, and the runs. Two legal texts stand behind the whole method and reward reading in the original: article 3 of the Majalla, in Tyser's English, and the United States Supreme Court's Gregory v. Helvering, 293 U.S. 465 (1935) — the Ottoman jurists and the American justices converging on the rule chapter 3 laid down for every instrument in this book, that intention and meaning outrank words and phrases. AAOIFI's Standard 31, on gharar, shows a living tradition grading contractual uncertainty with the same seriousness (chapter 23). The reader who has reached this page needs no further list; the method is portable, the paper is everywhere, and the last instruction is chapter 3's first one — read the payoff, not the name.
